title: Geometry-Derived Capacitance Dyadics with Floquet Sideband Correction for Anisotropic Periodic Patch Metasurfaces
abstract: Homogenised sheet models describe periodic metallic patch layers using a scalar sheet capacitance, which is only valid when the effective response is isotropic. An isotropic response exists for unit cells with patch geometries that have rotational symmetry of order three or higher. Lower-symmetry unit cells with irregular or random geometries generically require a full 2 x 2 surface-capacitance dyadic. We present a framework that computes this dyadic directly from the arbitrary gap-connected patch geometry on a unit cell of a hexagonal lattice. The two-dimensional Bravais periodicity fixes the two independent macroscopic loading directions, the connectivity of the gap ensures a full-rank response for the geometries considered here, and the point-group symmetry of the patch constrains the form of the dyadic. A quasi-static boundary value problem on a single periodic cell then determines its independent entries. We use the surface-capacitance dyadic in the anisotropic surface- wave dispersion relation, which includes the leading spatially-dispersive first shell Floquet-sideband correction. For each new patch geometry, the dyadic and the first-shell correction are obtained from a single quasi-static cell problem and from the reconstructed boundary. So anisotropic surface- wave dispersion follows without a per-geometry full-wave eigenmode band sweep or sheet-tensor retrieval. We validate this geometry-to-dispersion chain against full-wave eigenmode simulations across six representative symmetry classes, showing that the correction captures band flattening near the Brillouin-zone boundary and improves agreement relative to the local dyadic model.
one_liner: A geometry-derived capacitance dyadic predicts anisotropic patch-metasurface dispersion with a Floquet sideband correction.
why_it_matters: The method avoids repeated full-wave band sweeps while retaining anisotropy and Brillouin-zone-edge band flattening.
detailed_summary: The framework extracts a full 2 × 2 surface-capacitance dyadic from a quasi-static problem on one hexagonal-lattice unit cell with arbitrary gap-connected patch geometry. It adds a first-shell Floquet-sideband correction to the anisotropic surface-wave dispersion relation. Tests across six symmetry classes show improved agreement with full-wave eigenmode simulations, particularly near the Brillouin-zone boundary.
main_result: A single-cell calculation predicts anisotropic surface-wave bands and captures boundary-region band flattening without per-geometry tensor retrieval.
application_angle: The approach can accelerate the design and optimization of anisotropic metasurfaces, surface-wave components, and patterned electromagnetic interfaces.

title: Generalized Rotating-Wave Approximations Hierarchy for the Interacting Two-Qubit Rabi Model
abstract: We investigate the two-qubit quantum Rabi model for identical qubits symmetrically coupled to a single bosonic mode and interacting with each other through transverse and longitudinal couplings. We extend the adiabatic, generalized rotating-wave (GRWA), and squeezed generalized rotating-wave (SGRWA) approximations to include the qubit-qubit interactions, including self-consistent and variational choices of the bosonic parameters. The resulting analytical hierarchy allows us to distinguish the interplay between both kinds of qubit-qubit interactions and the effects of displacement, neighboring-manifold mixing, and squeezing on the low-energy properties. We find that the transverse interaction mainly changes the collective-spin structure of the states, while the longitudinal interaction also modifies the displacement-dependent oscillator overlaps and introduces an additional two-boson coupling. We compare the analytical results with numerically exact diagonalization for the low-energy spectrum, ground-state energy, mean photon number, two-qubit concurrence, and spin correlations. The results provide a compact analytical description of how direct qubit-qubit interactions modify both the spectrum and the eigenstate structure beyond the rotating-wave approximation for few-qubit light-matter systems.
one_liner: An analytical approximation hierarchy captures interacting two-qubit Rabi physics beyond the rotating-wave approximation.
why_it_matters: It offers compact models for spectra, photons, entanglement, and spin correlations in strongly coupled few-qubit light–matter hardware.
detailed_summary: The work extends adiabatic, generalized rotating-wave, and squeezed generalized rotating-wave approximations to two identical interacting qubits coupled to one bosonic mode. Transverse coupling chiefly changes collective-spin structure, whereas longitudinal coupling also modifies oscillator overlaps and creates an additional two-boson term. Comparison with exact diagonalization covers low-energy spectra, photon number, concurrence, and spin correlations.
platform_or_system: Two interacting qubits coupled to one bosonic mode
main_result: The generalized hierarchy reproduces low-energy observables while resolving how transverse and longitudinal qubit interactions alter dressed states.
application_angle: These approximations support rapid analysis and parameter design for ultrastrong-coupling cavity and circuit-QED devices.

title: Ternary-Valued FDTD Method for Nonlinear Optics: Third-Harmonic Generation on a Multiplier-Free Solver
abstract: I show that a finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) solver with field variables restricted to the ternary alphabet $\{-1,0,+1\}$ can reproduce nonlinear optical physics quantitatively on both CPUs and field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). Building on the general ternary-valued FDTD algorithm, in which each Yee cell stores an integer state that accumulates the discrete curl of neighbouring symbols without being drained, I extend the scheme to inhomogeneous and Kerr media and to Mur absorbing boundaries, without performing any multiplication operations. Dielectric contrast is implemented as a multiplexer, since the difference between ternary symbols takes only a few values, the instantaneous Kerr nonlinearity as a coefficient look-up table and the Mur boundary coefficients as canonical signed-digit shift--add chains. The scheme reproduces the third-harmonic conversion efficiency of a floating-point reference to within $1.4\%$. A symmetry of the governing physics, expressed through the even harmonics forbidden by centrosymmetric $χ^{(3)}$, provides a reference-free self-check for both ternary and floating-point models. The complete solver fits on a small, low-cost FPGA and contains no multiplier anywhere in its datapath, placing nonlinear optical modelling within reach of embedded and autonomous platforms rather than of high-performance computers.
one_liner: A multiplier-free ternary FDTD solver reproduces third-harmonic generation on CPUs and a low-cost FPGA.
why_it_matters: Quantitative nonlinear-optics simulation becomes feasible on compact embedded hardware without floating-point multipliers or HPC resources.
detailed_summary: The solver restricts fields to {-1, 0, +1} and extends ternary FDTD to inhomogeneous Kerr media and Mur absorbing boundaries. Multiplexers, lookup tables, and signed-digit shift–add chains replace multiplication throughout the datapath. Its third-harmonic conversion efficiency agrees with a floating-point reference within 1.4%, while forbidden even harmonics provide a reference-free consistency check.
main_result: The compact solver models third-harmonic generation within 1.4% of a floating-point reference and fits on a small FPGA.
application_angle: It enables embedded, autonomous, and potentially real-time modeling of nonlinear photonic structures at low cost and power.

title: Formally verified harness for Shor's order finding algorithm with $O(n^{2+ε})$ gate cost
abstract: It is commonly understood that factoring a general $n$-bit biprime via Shor's order finding algorithm requires $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ gates by leveraging schoolbook integer arithmetics for addition and multiplication. Recent developments in quantum arithmetic circuits leveraging recursive Toom-Cook schemes have improved the cost scaling to $O(n^{2+ε})$. Here $ε>0$ depends on algorithm implementation details of the recursive multiplication steps, which allow for a vast number of design choices. The challenge in navigating such design space also presents an opportunity for demonstrating innovative practices in quantum software engineering in the era of open agentic science. We present a formally verified harness that ingests a design specification (namely a "policy" that describes a recursive circuit design scheme) from an external source, which may be an AI agent, and produces a set of formalized proofs covering mathematical correctness of the algorithm implementation, asymptotic scaling of the end-to-end gate cost, as well as the correctness of translating the verified algorithm to a detailed circuit implementation with an intermediate representation. The harness is published as an open challenge where human researchers and AI agents can search for more efficient factoring circuits while retaining machine-checked guarantees of correctness and end-to-end asymptotic complexity.
one_liner: A formally verified harness checks Shor order-finding designs with near-quadratic asymptotic gate cost.
why_it_matters: Machine-checked correctness and resource scaling can make AI-assisted searches for efficient fault-tolerant factoring circuits more trustworthy.
detailed_summary: The harness accepts an external policy describing a recursive arithmetic-circuit design based on Toom–Cook multiplication. It produces formal proofs of mathematical correctness, end-to-end O(n^{2+ε}) gate scaling, and correct lowering into a detailed circuit intermediate representation. The open challenge allows human or AI designers to explore implementation choices while retaining machine-checked guarantees.
main_result: The harness certifies algorithm correctness, asymptotic gate cost, and circuit translation for externally proposed Shor order-finding designs.
application_angle: It can accelerate reliable co-design of lower-cost factoring circuits and their eventual mapping to fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Phase-conjugate Gaussian encoding for continuous-variable quantum key distribution with a single phase-sensitive amplifier
abstract: Phase-conjugate encoding is naturally compatible with shared phase-sensitive amplification and joint detection, offering a compact optical receiver architecture for continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD). Here, we develop a unified encoding and security framework for two-mode Gaussian CVQKD with tunable phase-conjugate intermode correlations matched to a joint receiver comprising a single phase-sensitive amplifier (PSA) and one balanced photodetector. We present both coherent-state and squeezed-state prepare-and-measure protocols that use the same transmitted ensemble. The two preparations can be implemented through classically precoded Gaussian displacements of coherent sidebands or a directly generated two-mode squeezed vacuum, respectively, without an actual optical mode converter. The encoding and detection scheme separates low-variance joint quadratures for key generation from high-variance joint quadratures carrying private random modulation. This complementary modulation can reduce Eve's Holevo information without changing the Alice--Bob mutual information. Numerical results show that optimized correlated coherent-state encoding achieves higher asymptotic key rates at long distances and extends the positive-key range compared with optimized single-mode coherent-state modulation. The optimal intermode correlation increases with transmission distance, and the range advantage persists under the symmetric correlated two-mode Gaussian attacks considered here. These results provide a theoretical basis for the design and implementation of PSA-enhanced two-mode CVQKD with phase-conjugate encoding.
one_liner: Phase-conjugate two-mode Gaussian encoding improves long-distance CVQKD using one phase-sensitive amplifier and one detector.
why_it_matters: The scheme combines a compact receiver with higher modeled key rates and a longer positive-key range than optimized single-mode modulation.
detailed_summary: The protocols use tunable phase-conjugate correlations with a joint receiver containing one phase-sensitive amplifier and one balanced photodetector. Coherent-state and squeezed-state preparations share the same transmitted ensemble, while complementary modulation separates key quadratures from private random modulation. Under the modeled symmetric correlated two-mode Gaussian attacks, optimized coherent-state encoding improves long-distance asymptotic key rates and extends the positive-key range.
platform_or_system: Two-mode Gaussian CVQKD link with PSA receiver
main_result: Optimized correlated coherent-state encoding outperforms optimized single-mode modulation in asymptotic long-distance key rate and range.
application_angle: The architecture offers a practical route to compact, PSA-enhanced CVQKD receivers with reduced detector complexity.

title: Rate-1/2 Quantum LDPC Codes for Multi-tier Superconducting Hardware
abstract: Quantum error correction is essential for scalable quantum computing, while its resource overhead is governed in large part by the encoding rate, namely the number of logical qubits encoded per physical data qubit. Recent quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) constructions have entered the ultra-high-rate regime with encoding rates above 1/2, but their syndrome-extraction circuits generally rely on reconfigurable connectivity or long-range qubit transport, making them difficult to implement on fixed-connectivity superconducting hardware. Here we introduce Armillary codes, a family of ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes whose algebraic structure is generated by native iSWAP routing under hardware constraints. The construction jointly enforces stabilizer commutation and correct parallel syndrome extraction, while admitting radial and circumferential couplings in crossing-free routing layers. We construct explicit codes with rates above 1/2, stabilizer weight 12, Tanner-graph girth 6, and distances from 12 to 16, with layouts on 5 or 6 hardware tiers. Compared with the Gross and Mitten codes at the same distances, the Armillary codes achieve encoding rates about 6 and 2.5 times those of the Gross and Mitten codes, respectively, while maintaining lower hardware-complexity scores. In circuit-level simulations, the \([\![8688,4348,16]\!]\) code approaches the teraquop regime, achieving a logical error rate of \(1.62\times10^{-12}\) per logical qubit per round at a physical error rate of 0.1\%. These results show that the rate-\(1/2\) regime of qLDPC codes can be extended from reconfigurable platforms to superconducting hardware, providing a route toward low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum processors.
one_liner: Armillary qLDPC codes achieve rates above one-half with crossing-free routing tailored to multi-tier superconducting processors.
why_it_matters: The construction pairs high encoding density with fixed-connectivity layouts and simulated teraquop-scale logical reliability.
detailed_summary: Armillary codes derive their algebraic structure from native iSWAP routing and enforce both stabilizer commutation and parallel syndrome extraction. Explicit five- or six-tier layouts have rates above 1/2, stabilizer weight 12, girth 6, and distances from 12 to 16. Circuit-level simulation of the [[8688,4348,16]] code gives 1.62 × 10^-12 logical errors per logical qubit per round at a 0.1% physical error rate.
main_result: A rate-above-1/2 qLDPC family attains distance 16 and near-teraquop simulated performance on hardware-constrained layouts.
application_angle: The codes offer a route to lower-overhead fault-tolerant superconducting processors without reconfigurable connectivity or long-range transport.

title: Quantum geometric spectroscopy with Schrödinger cat states
abstract: We propose a spectroscopic approach that reads out the quantum geometry of matter from the quantum decoherence of Schrödinger-cat light, in the same way that optical absorption reads out the energy structure of matter. For a cat-state probe comprising a superposition of two coherent states, the interbranch coherence of the outgoing light encodes the overlap between the matter states driven by the two branches. We show that, when the electromagnetic fields of the two branches differ only slightly, cat-branch decoherence is quantified by dynamical quantum geometry, which characterizes infinitesimal displacements on the matter-state manifold. For frequency-selective kitten probes of equilibrium matter, we further establish a partition law for the quantum geometric tensor between light and matter, enabling optical readout of matter quantum metric and Berry curvature through, for example, the brightening of a stellar zero in the outgoing Husimi function. For nonequilibrium matter in a pure state, short-pulse cat probes also provide a time-resolved witness of multipartite entanglement through the transient quantum metric, which can be extracted from homodyne measurements of the outgoing light. By turning cat-state decoherence, conventionally regarded as a loss of quantum information, into a carrier of information about matter, this approach establishes a spectroscopic principle that directly probes quantum-state geometry and fluctuations alongside conventional response-based spectroscopy.
one_liner: Schrödinger-cat light turns probe decoherence into an optical readout of quantum metric, Berry curvature, and transient multipartite entanglement.
why_it_matters: It proposes a spectroscopy beyond conventional response measurements, using quantum-light coherence to access matter-state geometry and fluctuations.
detailed_summary: A cat-state probe drives matter along two nearby trajectories, and the outgoing interbranch coherence measures the overlap of the corresponding matter states. In the small-displacement limit, decoherence encodes the dynamical quantum geometric tensor, including quantum metric and Berry curvature. Frequency-selective kitten probes and short pulses enable equilibrium geometric spectroscopy and time-resolved entanglement witnessing, respectively.
main_result: The work establishes protocols for extracting matter quantum geometry and transient multipartite entanglement from cat-state decoherence and optical measurements.
application_angle: The method could enable nonclassical optical characterization of correlated and nonequilibrium quantum materials using Husimi-function or homodyne readout.

title: Quantum Sensing of Defects
abstract: Metrology of defects (or impurities) is a major challenge in quantum sensing, with implications for material science, nano-scale metrology, and the development of high-precision quantum devices. In this work, we employ single and multi excitation sensors for the metrology of defects, with the system Hamiltonian encoding the structure of the sensor and the defect treated as a perturbation potential. We evaluate the quantum Fisher information of the ground state of the system to quantify the metrological performance of the sensors in locating a defect and in estimating its coupling strength. In doing so, we identify two distinct sensing regimes, determined by the ratio between the defect screening parameter and the inter-sensor site spacing, and establish the scaling behavior for the resulting estimation precision. Furthermore, we analyze the joint estimation of defect position and strength as well as the performance of two-excitation sensors, demonstrating how the number of excitations and their interactions influence sensitivity. Our results provide tools for optimizing defect detection with quantum sensors, with potential applications in solid-state quantum technologies.
one_liner: Ground-state quantum Fisher information reveals distinct scaling regimes for estimating a defect's position and coupling with few-excitation sensors.
why_it_matters: The results provide design rules for optimizing impurity and defect metrology in solid-state quantum sensing platforms.
detailed_summary: The defect is modeled as a perturbing potential acting on structured single- and multi-excitation sensor systems. Ground-state quantum Fisher information quantifies precision for defect position, coupling strength, and their joint estimation. Two regimes emerge according to the ratio of defect screening length to sensor-site spacing, while excitation number and interactions modify sensitivity.
main_result: The analysis derives sensing-precision scaling laws and identifies two screening-dependent regimes for defect localization and strength estimation.
application_angle: These scaling rules can guide sensor geometry and excitation design for nanoscale impurity characterization and solid-state device diagnostics.

title: Lieb-Robinson Bounds for Electric Quantum Walks
abstract: We derive Lieb-Robinson type bounds with optimal propagation velocity for shift-coin and split-step quantum walks in rational electric fields. The velocity decays exponentially fast in the period of the field, showing long intervals of suppressed spreading. The proof rests on bounds for the imaginary part of the analytically continued dispersion relation of the electric walk. We show that the infimal Lieb-Robinson velocity coincides with the asymptotic velocity for these walks, while a nonhomogeneous example demonstrates that the two types of velocity need not agree in general. We also obtain an exponential tail estimate on the probability of a walk to lie outside the effective light cone.
one_liner: Optimal Lieb-Robinson bounds show exponentially suppressed propagation in rational-field electric quantum walks and quantify leakage beyond the light cone.
why_it_matters: The results give rigorous control of transport speed and localization-like intervals in quantum-walk platforms used for simulation and photonics.
detailed_summary: The authors derive Lieb-Robinson-type bounds for shift-coin and split-step quantum walks under rational electric fields. The optimal propagation velocity decreases exponentially with the field period and equals the asymptotic velocity for the studied homogeneous walks. They also establish an exponential probability tail outside the effective light cone and show that the velocity equivalence can fail in nonhomogeneous systems.
main_result: The work obtains optimal propagation velocities and exponential out-of-light-cone bounds, proving exponentially slow spreading as the rational-field period grows.
application_angle: The bounds can inform controlled transport, localization, and finite-time error estimates in photonic or other discrete-time quantum-walk simulators.

title: Quantum Sensor of Mechanical Vibrations
abstract: We report the use of a single trapped-ion motional mode as a probe of mechanical vibrations of the Paul trap structure. By exciting vibrations of the trap using an ultrasonic transducer mounted outside the vacuum chamber and probing the ion motion through motional sideband interactions, we observe a clear resonance response of the axial mode. We further demonstrate detection of trap vibrations with amplitudes as low as 0.6 picometers. These measurements show direct coupling between macroscopic mechanical motion and trapped-ion dynamics, providing a route toward vibration sensing using quantum control of motional states.
one_liner: A single trapped-ion motional mode detects mechanically driven Paul-trap vibrations with amplitudes down to 0.6 pm.
why_it_matters: It directly connects macroscopic structural motion to quantum-controlled ion dynamics, enabling ultralow-amplitude vibration diagnostics inside ion traps.
detailed_summary: An external ultrasonic transducer excites the Paul-trap structure while a single ion's axial motional mode probes the resulting motion. Motional-sideband interactions reveal a clear mechanical resonance response. The experiment resolves vibration amplitudes as small as 0.6 pm, demonstrating direct coupling between the macroscopic trap assembly and ion motion.
platform_or_system: Single ion in a Paul trap
main_result: The experiment demonstrates trapped-ion detection of trap-structure vibrations down to a reported amplitude of 0.6 pm.
application_angle: The technique could support in situ vibration characterization, noise mitigation, and mechanical health monitoring for precision trapped-ion processors and sensors.

title: Noise-Aware Testing of NISQ Quantum Programs: Self-Baseline Oracle with a Controlled False-Positive Rate
abstract: Testing quantum programs on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices faces a test-oracle problem: hardware noise and finite-shot sampling make the runs of a correct program vary as much as those of a faulty one, so oracles with a fixed acceptance threshold produce false positives that depend on the program and the backend. We present a noise-aware testing framework built on self-baseline calibration: each run of the program under test is compared with repeated executions of a trusted reference program on the same backend, and the acceptance threshold is the $(1-α)$ quantile of the finite-shot null distribution of the Jensen-Shannon divergence, so the oracle's false-positive rate is a level set in advance. A noncentral chi-square model predicts detection power, a homogeneity test and a two-run sentinel detect drift, a mutation engine labels every mutant exactly within a three-class noise-aware taxonomy, and zero-noise extrapolation attributes rejections to faults or noise. In simulation on nine core benchmarks, 32 QASMBench programs, ten real bugs, seven noise regimes and three device snapshots, the oracle's false-positive rate is 0.0011 at $α= 10^{-3}$ over 9,000 correct runs, against 36-74% for fixed thresholds, 8.9% for a QOIN-style filter and 10.8% for a globally calibrated threshold, while attaining the highest F1 on non-equivalent faults (0.941). On an IBM Heron device, using about 14 minutes of QPU time, it rejected none of 82 correct runs and detected 120 of 121 faults and semantic mutants, and a two-run sentinel reduced drift-induced false positives from 27.4% to 1.8%.
one_liner: A self-baselined NISQ test oracle controls false positives under hardware noise while detecting 120 of 121 faults on IBM Heron.
why_it_matters: Reliable, backend-aware testing is essential for validating quantum programs when device drift and finite-shot noise can mimic software faults.
detailed_summary: The framework compares each program run with repeated trusted-reference executions on the same backend and selects a Jensen-Shannon-divergence threshold from the finite-shot null distribution. Simulation produced a 0.0011 false-positive rate at a target level of 0.001 and an F1 score of 0.941 for non-equivalent faults. On IBM Heron, it rejected none of 82 correct runs, detected 120 of 121 faults or semantic mutants, and reduced drift-induced false positives from 27.4% to 1.8% with a sentinel.
main_result: Self-baseline calibration delivered controlled false-positive behavior and near-complete fault detection in both simulation and a roughly 14-minute hardware experiment.
application_angle: The approach offers a practical regression-testing and drift-monitoring workflow for quantum software deployed across noisy, time-varying processors.

title: Telecom-band optical parametric oscillation in a passive silicon microring resonator at cryogenic temperatures
abstract: At telecommunications wavelengths, free carriers generated by two-photon absorption limit optical parametric oscillation (OPO) in silicon. Here, we demonstrate telecom-band OPO in a passive silicon microring resonator without electrical carrier sweep-out, driven by a single continuous-wave (CW) pump at 4.5 K. We achieve an on-chip OPO onset power of 2.25 mW and a total conversion efficiency of 1.9% into all parametric sidebands at a pump power of 4.8 mW. Despite CW pumping, the parametric output emerges as a train of pulses synchronized with microsecond-scale self-pulsing. At higher pump powers, OPO emission is absent during intervals of sustained sub-GHz oscillations in the pump transmission, narrowing the temporal window for OPO. Furthermore, by adjusting the pump detuning, we observe OPO at temperatures up to 55 K. These results demonstrate that nonlinear cavity dynamics govern the temporal structure and operating conditions of cryogenic silicon OPOs, providing new insights into controlling the oscillation regimes and temporal characteristics of on-chip nonlinear light sources compatible with cryogenic quantum photonic circuits.
one_liner: A passive silicon microring produces telecom-band optical parametric oscillation at 4.5 K without electrical carrier sweep-out.
why_it_matters: The result advances compact nonlinear light sources that can operate alongside cryogenic quantum-photonic and detector hardware.
detailed_summary: A continuous-wave pump drives telecom-band optical parametric oscillation in a passive silicon microring cooled to 4.5 K. The on-chip threshold is 2.25 mW, and total sideband conversion reaches 1.9% at 4.8 mW. The output forms microsecond-synchronized pulse trains, and detuning control sustains OPO operation at temperatures up to 55 K.
main_result: The device achieves passive telecom-band OPO from 4.5 K to 55 K, with a 2.25 mW onset power and 1.9% total sideband conversion.
application_angle: Such cryogenic, chip-scale telecom sources could support wavelength generation and nonlinear processing in integrated quantum-photonic and communication systems.

title: Near-synchronous multiphoton quantum interference
abstract: Nonclassical multiphoton interference is an important resource for optical quantum information processing, and its output statistics depend on the distinguishability of the input photons. In this paper, using time delay as a tunable parameter, we theoretically analyze the interference behavior of independent pure-state single photons with identical Gaussian spectral envelopes under near-synchronous conditions. Using the immanant representation of the single-photon internal-state overlap matrix to express the weights of the exchange-symmetry components, we determine the leading asymptotic behavior and approximation error of each weight, and characterize the weight suppression laws when different groups of photons become synchronized on different scales. Given the local identity classes of the delay functions and the vanishing orders of pairwise delay differences, the vanishing orders of the weights of the exchange-symmetry components can be computed in polynomial time by integer minimum-cost flow. On this basis, we provide a network-independent total-variation error bound for the complete output photon-number distribution, establish a quantitative relationship among the photon spectral width, synchronization precision, and interference statistics deviation, and provide a quantitative basis for the analysis and approximation of near-synchronous multiphoton interference.
one_liner: A theory of nearly synchronized Gaussian single photons quantifies how timing mismatches alter multiphoton interference statistics.
why_it_matters: It provides network-independent error bounds linking photon bandwidth and synchronization precision to deviations in photonic quantum-processing outputs.
detailed_summary: The authors analyze independent pure-state photons with identical Gaussian spectra and tunable relative delays. Immanants of the internal-state overlap matrix resolve exchange-symmetry weights and their suppression as photon groups synchronize on different scales. A polynomial-time minimum-cost-flow procedure determines vanishing orders, while a network-independent total-variation bound controls the error in the full output distribution.
platform_or_system: Gaussian single photons in linear-optical networks
main_result: The work derives asymptotic symmetry-weight laws and a total-variation bound connecting spectral width, timing precision, and output-statistics error.
application_angle: The bounds can guide synchronization tolerances and controlled approximations in multiphoton interferometers and photonic quantum processors.

title: Cavity Control of Emission Dynamics from Spin Defects in Hexagonal Boron Nitride
abstract: Optically addressable negatively charged boron vacancy ($\mathrm{V_B^-}$) defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are promising for quantum sensing at room temperature. The two-dimensional structure of hBN allows direct access to the local environment, enabling proximal sensing of target materials. However, its broadband emission and low quantum yield hinder efficient light-matter interaction, and the coupling of $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ optical dipoles to confined cavity fields remains poorly understood. In this study, we integrate $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defects with a tunable plano-concave microcavity, achieving three-dimensional optical confinement. This approach yields photoluminescence (PL) enhancement and cavity-modified optical decay dynamics, providing insights into the orientation of the $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defect dipole. Time-resolved PL measurements identify a distinct fast decay component, suggesting a complex dipole geometry for the defects. Therefore, a tilted optical dipole model is considered to attribute the fast and slow decay components to in-plane and out-of-plane dipole contributions, respectively. Additionally, optically detected magnetic resonance and excitation-polarisation-dependent PL measurements provide further insights into local symmetry breaking and potential optical dipole configurations. These results highlight the role of optical dipole orientation in $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defect-cavity coupling.
one_liner: A tunable microcavity enhances hBN boron-vacancy emission and reveals orientation-dependent fast and slow optical decay channels.
why_it_matters: Understanding and controlling defect–cavity coupling could improve photon collection and readout from atomically thin, room-temperature quantum sensors.
detailed_summary: Negatively charged boron vacancies in hBN are integrated with a tunable plano-concave microcavity providing three-dimensional optical confinement. Enhanced photoluminescence and modified decay dynamics include a distinct fast component, interpreted using tilted dipoles with in-plane and out-of-plane contributions. ODMR and polarization-dependent measurements further probe local symmetry breaking and possible dipole configurations.
platform_or_system: V_B^- defects in hBN coupled to a plano-concave microcavity
main_result: The experiment demonstrates cavity-enhanced emission and cavity-modified decay that exposes the complex optical-dipole orientation of V_B^- defects.
application_angle: Better dipole alignment and cavity engineering could increase optical readout efficiency for proximal room-temperature quantum sensing.

title: A simple solvable $Z_N$ Hamiltonian in any dimension
abstract: We construct local $Z_N$ clock Hamiltonians from Baxter-Fendley chains coupled according to an arbitrary finite oriented simple transverse graph. Bounded edge lengths and vertex degrees give finite-range multispin interactions, with $2d$-site bulk terms on a $d$-dimensional rectangular lattice. For open longitudinal boundaries, an explicit nonlocal unitary transformation decouples the chains and gives a free parafermion spectrum. On rectangular lattices this holds for any combination of open and periodic transverse boundaries. For periodic longitudinal boundaries, neighbouring chain charges fix the closing-bond twists. In each joint charge sector, the energies are sums of the corresponding twisted periodic-chain energies. As an example, we construct a three-dimensional array of chains perpendicular to a Penrose rhombus tiling.
one_liner: A family of local multidimensional Z_N clock Hamiltonians is exactly reducible to decoupled chains with free-parafermion spectra.
why_it_matters: The construction supplies analytically tractable benchmarks for studying parafermionic phases, disorder, and many-body dynamics across complex lattices.
detailed_summary: Baxter–Fendley chains are coupled through an arbitrary finite oriented transverse graph to produce finite-range local Z_N clock Hamiltonians. For open longitudinal boundaries, an explicit nonlocal unitary decouples the chains and yields a free-parafermion spectrum. Periodic longitudinal boundaries are handled sector by sector through charge-dependent closing-bond twists, including a three-dimensional construction based on a Penrose tiling.
platform_or_system: Multidimensional Z_N clock and parafermion lattice models
main_result: The authors construct exactly solvable local Z_N Hamiltonians in arbitrary dimension and determine their spectra for broad open and periodic boundary conditions.
application_angle: These solvable models can serve as benchmark targets for analog or digital quantum simulators exploring parafermionic many-body physics.

title: Recovery of accidental bound states in the continuum in vertically asymmetric photonic lattices through radiation-source parity restoration
abstract: Vertical asymmetry generally precludes accidental bound states in the continuum (BICs) in planar photonic lattices, yet the underlying physical mechanism remains unclear. In this study, we show that accidental-BIC formation is governed by the definite parity of the transverse radiation-source profile rather than by geometric vertical mirror symmetry. A semianalytical coupled-mode analysis shows that an accidental BIC occurs when the radiation overlap integral of a leaky Bloch mode vanishes. We decompose the overlap into contributions from the even- and odd-parity components of the transverse radiation-source profile. Complete radiation suppression requires both contributions to vanish simultaneously. In vertically symmetric lattices, the source profile has definite even or odd parity, causing one contribution to vanish identically. Thickness tuning can null the remaining contribution and produce an accidental BIC. In vertically asymmetric lattices, by contrast, both parity components are generally present. The waveguide dispersion forbids their simultaneous vanishing, thereby precluding an accidental BIC. Introducing a parity-restoring layer into a vertically asymmetric lattice restores definite parity to the transverse radiation-source profile, thereby enabling the formation of an accidental BIC. Finite-element simulations confirm the analytically predicted recovery of accidental BICs for both TE$_0$ and TE$_1$ Bloch modes.
one_liner: A parity-restoring layer recovers accidental photonic bound states in the continuum despite vertical geometric asymmetry.
why_it_matters: The result offers a practical route to ultrahigh-Q resonances in asymmetric photonic stacks that are easier to integrate with functional materials.
detailed_summary: A semianalytical coupled-mode treatment identifies the transverse radiation-source profile, rather than geometric mirror symmetry itself, as the relevant parity object. Accidental BIC formation requires both even- and odd-parity radiation-overlap contributions to vanish; ordinary asymmetric lattices generally cannot satisfy both conditions. Adding a parity-restoring layer reinstates definite source parity, and finite-element simulations confirm BIC recovery for TE0 and TE1 Bloch modes.
main_result: The study predicts and numerically verifies recovered accidental BICs in asymmetric lattices by restoring radiation-source parity with an added layer.
application_angle: The mechanism supports high-Q asymmetric resonators for integrated lasers, filters, nonlinear optics, and refractive-index sensing.

title: Variational Corrections to Strong-Disorder Renormalization in the Two-Dimensional Random Transverse Field Ising Model on Quantum Hardware
abstract: Strong-disorder renormalization-group (SDRG) methods provide an effective description of disordered quantum many-body systems by identifying the dominant couplings for the low energy physics. However, the resulting renormalization-group flow is approximate and neglects correlations beyond the RG description. Here, we investigate whether variational quantum optimization can be used to correct these approximations. Building on the emergent-coupling-based ansatz (ECBA) developed for the one-dimensional random Heisenberg model, we introduce a formulation adapted to the two-dimensional random transverse field Ising model. The SDRG flow determines the structure of the circuit, while variational optimization allows the state to deviate from the RG approximation. We study the resulting ansatz numerically and experimentally on an IQM superconducting quantum processor. For a 16-qubit system, we perform full variational optimization on the quantum processor, while a 49-qubit system is investigated using pre-optimized parameters, achieving a relative energy accuracy of 89% and 97%, respectively. Our results demonstrate that RG information can be translated into shallow, hardware-compatible quantum circuits while variational optimization enables corrections beyond the underlying RG approximation also for two-dimensional systems.
one_liner: SDRG-informed shallow circuits receive variational corrections on an IQM processor for 16- and 49-qubit disordered Ising systems.
why_it_matters: It shows how physics-informed circuit structure can reduce variational complexity while correcting approximate many-body states on current quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The strong-disorder renormalization-group flow is converted into an emergent-coupling-based circuit ansatz for the two-dimensional random transverse-field Ising model. Variational parameters allow the prepared state to move beyond the approximate RG description while preserving a shallow, hardware-compatible structure. Experiments on an IQM superconducting processor use full on-device optimization for 16 qubits and pre-optimized parameters for 49 qubits, reporting relative energy accuracies of 89% and 97%, respectively.
main_result: The hardware experiments achieve 89% relative energy accuracy at 16 qubits and 97% at 49 qubits using SDRG-structured variational circuits.
application_angle: The approach could enable scalable ground-state approximation for strongly disordered two-dimensional models with limited circuit depth.

title: Global bound-state spectrum and spin- and angular-momentum-dependent confinement in an inverse-$3/2$ magnetic quantum dot
abstract: We investigate the bound-state spectrum and confinement thresholds of a two-dimensional electron governed by the Schrödinger--Pauli equation in an inverse-$3/2$ radial magnetic-field profile. The radial problem reduces to the biconfluent Heun equation, but instead of restricting the solution to the quasi-exact polynomial sector, we impose the bound-state condition globally through a spectral Wronskian between the endpoint-selected Frobenius solution and the subdominant asymptotic solution. The resulting spectrum contains continuous nonpolynomial bound-state branches on which the known quasi-exact solutions appear as isolated exact points. In this global description, the polynomial index $N$ remains a termination index within the quasi-exact sector but does not uniquely label the spectral branches. An independent exact analysis of the continuum edge yields spin- and angular-momentum-dependent critical couplings that can lie below the quasi-exact restriction $U_0a>4$, where $U_0$ is the Coulomb-strength parameter and $a$ is the magnetic-profile length scale. These results establish quasi-exact solvability as a set of special analytic points embedded in a broader biconfluent-Heun spectrum with spin- and angular-momentum-dependent confinement thresholds.
one_liner: A global spectral treatment reveals nonpolynomial bound states and spin-dependent confinement thresholds in a magnetic quantum dot.
why_it_matters: The analysis expands the design space for spin-selective magnetic confinement beyond isolated quasi-exact solutions and conventional coupling limits.
detailed_summary: The radial Schrödinger–Pauli problem for a two-dimensional electron in an inverse-3/2 magnetic field is solved globally using a spectral Wronskian between endpoint-selected and asymptotically subdominant solutions. This exposes continuous nonpolynomial bound-state branches containing the known quasi-exact polynomial solutions only as isolated points. Exact continuum-edge analysis yields confinement thresholds dependent on spin and angular momentum, including critical couplings below the usual quasi-exact restriction.
platform_or_system: Two-dimensional electron in an inverse-3/2 magnetic quantum dot
main_result: The work establishes a broader bound-state spectrum with spin- and angular-momentum-dependent confinement thresholds beyond the quasi-exact polynomial sector.
application_angle: The predicted thresholds may inform magnetic nanostructures designed for spin-selective electron trapping and quantum-dot state engineering.

title: Laser Processing for Energy Applications
abstract: Laser processing has emerged as a transformative technology in the energy sector, enabling precise, efficient, and scalable solutions for energy generation, storage, and sustainability. This chapter explores the diverse applications of laser technology in energy applications. It begins with an overview of laser-driven inertial confinement fusion for energy production, highlighting key experimental facilities and crucial laser parameters. The role of lasers in solar energy harvesting is examined, including photovoltaic cell optimization, concentrated solar power, and laser-assisted recycling of solar modules. The chapter further reviews recent developments into laser-based techniques for enhancing electrochemical performance through surface texturing at various scales. Advancements in lithium-ion battery technology are also discussed, focusing on next-generation materials, battery manufacturing processes, and the impact of laser techniques on performance, safety, and scalability. The chapter concludes with insights into future prospects for laser applications in sustainable energy solutions.
one_liner: Review of laser processing across fusion, photovoltaics, electrochemical surfaces, and lithium-ion battery manufacturing.
why_it_matters: Connects laser parameters and scalable processing methods to energy generation, storage performance, safety, recycling, and sustainability.
detailed_summary: This review surveys laser-driven inertial-confinement fusion, photovoltaic optimization, concentrated solar power, and laser-assisted module recycling. It also covers multiscale surface texturing, next-generation battery materials, and laser-enabled lithium-ion battery manufacturing. The chapter emphasizes performance, safety, scalability, and sustainable-energy prospects rather than presenting a single new experiment.
main_result: The review synthesizes how laser-based processing can improve energy generation, electrochemical performance, manufacturing, and recycling.
application_angle: It provides a technology map for deploying precision laser processes in scalable clean-energy production and storage workflows.

title: Relaxing the i.i.d. state preparation assumption with the block QKD protocol
abstract: In this work, we propose a novel approach to handling the independent and identically distributed assumption for the state preparation in prepare-and measure QKD protocols. Contrary to previous approaches, we do not prove the security using sub-protocols, and instead opt to guarantee security in the presence of correlations by dividing the communication into finite blocks of consecutive pulses, and adding an additional assumption of no dependence between each block. In turn we obtain a protocol which uses only a relaxed i.i.d. assumption and is easier to implement than subprotocol-style approaches since it does not require separate statistics for each sub-protocol, whose number grows with the correlation length of the underlying dependency.
one_liner: A block-based prepare-and-measure QKD protocol accommodates correlated state preparation under a relaxed i.i.d. assumption.
why_it_matters: The method avoids correlation-length-dependent subprotocol statistics, potentially simplifying secure QKD implementations with imperfect transmitters.
detailed_summary: The protocol partitions consecutive optical pulses into finite blocks and permits correlations within each block while assuming independence between blocks. Security is established directly for the block protocol rather than through multiple subprotocols. This removes the need to collect separate statistics for a number of subprotocols that grows with the source correlation length.
main_result: The proposed block protocol provides QKD security with correlated state preparation under independence only between finite pulse blocks.
application_angle: It offers a simpler route to secure practical QKD transmitters whose emitted states retain short-range temporal correlations.

title: Subwavelength confinement of optical and acoustic waves for enhancing Brillouin gain in a planar waveguide structure
abstract: We propose a planar waveguide structure consisting of two layers separated by a gap that provides subwavelength confinement of optical and acoustic modes and a large overlap integral between them. This, in turn, leads to an increase in Brillouin gain. Using the structure of two Si$_3$N$_4$ layers with a subwavelength gap from SiO$_2$ as an example, we demonstrate that a hybridized transverse-magnetic (TM) optical mode exhibits strong field confinement in the SiO$_2$ gap. Simultaneously, a high-frequency acoustic mode can be confined in the same gap, providing a high spatial overlap between the optical and acoustic fields. This provides a high opto-acoustic interaction with a Brillouin gain up to $5$ W$^{-1}$m$^{-1}$. The proposed structure is compatible with planar photonic integration and offers a promising platform for compact, low-threshold Brillouin lasers and coherent phonon generation.
one_liner: A dual-layer planar waveguide co-confines optical and acoustic modes in a nanoscale gap, yielding predicted Brillouin gain up to 5 W⁻¹m⁻¹.
why_it_matters: Strong co-localization in a planar-compatible geometry could enable compact, low-threshold Brillouin lasers and integrated coherent-phonon sources.
detailed_summary: The proposed waveguide uses two Si3N4 layers separated by a subwavelength SiO2 gap. A hybridized TM optical mode and a high-frequency acoustic mode are simultaneously concentrated in that gap, increasing their spatial overlap. Modeling predicts an opto-acoustic Brillouin gain as high as 5 W⁻¹m⁻¹ in a geometry compatible with planar photonic integration.
main_result: Co-confinement of optical and acoustic fields produces a predicted Brillouin gain of up to 5 W⁻¹m⁻¹.
application_angle: The design supports integrated low-threshold Brillouin lasers, microwave-photonic functions, and coherent phonon generation.

title: Compact Dielectric Barrier Discharge Source for a Pulsed Supersonic Beam of Metastable Triplet H$_2$
abstract: We present a compact dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) source for producing pulsed supersonic beams of metastable molecules, designed to mount directly onto existing gas valves without modification. Unlike plate or corona discharge sources, the DBD produces no static electric field in the expansion zone and relies on capacitively coupled microdischarges that are inherently self-limiting. Charge accumulation on the dielectric terminates each event within nanoseconds and locally suppresses re-ignition, so that successive microdischarges are distributed across the nozzle. Arc formation and the associated hot spots are thereby prevented, and the gas is excited uniformly over the duration of the pulse. The source requires only a single custom ceramic nozzle and a compact printed circuit board (PCB) carrying the drive electronics, mounted directly in front of the valve. The high-voltage pulses are generated in-vacuum on the PCB from a DC supply voltage. Complete design files, circuit schematics, fabrication details, and validated simulation files are provided to allow straightforward reproduction. The DBD is applied to produce H$_2$ in the metastable c$^3Π_u^-$ state. This state can be used as an intermediate step for state-selective preparation of H$_2^+$ molecular ions by pulsed field ionization of optically prepared molecular Rydberg states, without requiring vacuum-ultraviolet radiation. We characterize the source by time-of-flight and Resonance-Enhanced Multiphoton Ionization (REMPI) spectroscopy, obtaining an excitation fraction on the order of $10^{-8}$ into the metastable state. The dependence of the yield on stagnation pressure and discharge voltage is consistent with collisional quenching as the dominant pressure-dependent loss.
one_liner: A valve-mounted dielectric-barrier discharge generates pulsed supersonic beams of metastable triplet H2 without static fields or arc hot spots.
why_it_matters: The compact, reproducible source enables metastable-molecule preparation for state-selective H2+ production without vacuum-ultraviolet radiation.
detailed_summary: The source combines a custom ceramic nozzle with an in-vacuum PCB that generates high-voltage pulses from a DC supply and mounts directly on an existing gas valve. Self-limiting, capacitively coupled microdischarges distribute excitation across the nozzle while suppressing arcs and static fields in the expansion region. Time-of-flight and REMPI measurements show an excitation fraction of order 10⁻⁸ into the H2 c3Πu− state, with pressure behavior consistent with collisional quenching.
main_result: The compact source produces a characterized pulsed beam of metastable triplet H2 with an excitation fraction near 10⁻⁸.
application_angle: It provides reproducible hardware for state-selective H2+ ion preparation and molecular quantum-control experiments without VUV sources.

title: Deterministic nonlinear domain engineering algorithm with variable sub-coherence-length domains
abstract: We present a new and improved deterministic algorithm that calculates the poling domains for the implementation of arbitrary phase-matching functions (PMF) in quasi-phase-matched nonlinear crystals for parametric down-conversion photon sources. In contrast to previous work, the algorithm presented here makes full use of the limits of the fabrication process, such as the minimum feature size and resolution of the lithographic process underpinning the poling procedure. This minimizes the tracking error to the target electric field and improves the accuracy in reaching the desired PMF. We give a tutorial on how to calculate the target function for arbitrary PMFs and run the algorithm. We also demonstrate the procedure on a relevant application in quantum sensing, where we use a quadratic phase on the PMF to implement a broadband photon spectrum while maintaining high nonlinearity across the crystal. The designed crystal is experimentally tested, and the result matches expectations.
one_liner: A deterministic poling algorithm uses variable sub-coherence-length domains to synthesize arbitrary phase-matching functions with fabrication-aware accuracy.
why_it_matters: Better control of nonlinear-crystal spectra can improve engineered photon-pair sources for broadband quantum sensing and photonic experiments.
detailed_summary: The algorithm calculates quasi-phase-matching domains while explicitly incorporating lithographic minimum feature size and resolution. Variable sub-coherence-length domains reduce electric-field tracking error and improve reproduction of arbitrary target phase-matching functions. The authors design and experimentally test a crystal with a quadratic phase profile that supports a broadband photon spectrum while retaining high nonlinearity across the crystal.
main_result: A fabrication-aware domain design experimentally realizes the expected broadband, quadratically phased response with high effective nonlinearity.
application_angle: The method enables customized SPDC photon spectra for broadband quantum sensing, spectroscopy, and tailored entangled-photon sources.

title: Observation of Crossover from Repulsive to Attractive Interactions between Two $nS$-Rydberg Atoms in Dual-Species Atom Arrays
abstract: Dual-species Rydberg atom arrays provide a flexible platform for engineering long-range interactions beyond the conventional isotropic blockade regime. We spectroscopically study interactions between different $s$-state Rydberg levels in a $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$--$^{85}\mathrm{Rb}$ optical-tweezer array. By varying the principal-quantum-number difference $Δn$ around $61S_{1/2}$, we observe a crossover from repulsive to attractive interactions. We identify a distinct regime at $Δn=2$ in which Förster-enhanced electronic spin exchange dominates over orbital exchange and produces a strongly bond-orientation-dependent pair spectrum. Time-domain collective-excitation measurements reveal this geometry-dependent spin exchange through a pronounced anisotropy of the double-excitation probability. For $Δn=1$, by contrast, orbital exchange dominates and the interaction is nearly isotropic. These results establish the principal-quantum-number difference and bond orientation as complementary control parameters for tailoring Rydberg interaction spectra and collective excitation dynamics, opening new opportunities for engineering spin-dependent Hamiltonians in programmable atom arrays.
one_liner: Dual-isotope Rydberg arrays show tunable repulsive-to-attractive interactions and orientation-dependent spin exchange controlled by level spacing.
why_it_matters: Principal-quantum-number offset and bond orientation provide new controls for programming spin-dependent interactions in neutral-atom quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The experiment probes interactions between different nS Rydberg levels in a dual-isotope 87Rb–85Rb optical-tweezer array near 61S1/2. Changing the principal-quantum-number difference drives a crossover from repulsive to attractive interactions. At Δn=2, Förster-enhanced electronic spin exchange produces a strongly orientation-dependent spectrum and anisotropic double excitation, whereas Δn=1 is dominated by nearly isotropic orbital exchange.
main_result: The experiment observes interaction-sign reversal and geometry-dependent spin exchange tunable through the Rydberg-level offset.
application_angle: These controls expand the Hamiltonians available for neutral-atom simulation, programmable spin models, and collective quantum dynamics.

title: The Kitaev model on finite hyperbolic PBC clusters
abstract: We construct and solve the three-colored Kitaev model on finite hyperbolic lattices with periodic boundary conditions. We describe a self-contained procedure which uses finite quotients of orientation- preserving triangle groups to generate regular maps on compact genus-g surfaces. From these, one can extract their lattice connectivity, plaquette structure, homology cycles and Wilson sectors while implementing consistent boundary conditions. On the example of {8, 3} and {12, 3} lattices, we enumerate a selection of quotients with up to 72 vertices, which constitute the discrete steps in a finite-size scaling analysis. For the isotropic point, corresponding to the spin-liquid phase in the thermodynamic limit, we identify the ground state superselection sectors, quantify their deviation from the homogeneous π flux sector and show how the selected flux background depends on the quotient geometry. We then discuss how the resulting ground state sector degeneracies are entirely generated by physical lattice symmetries acting on both the plaquette fluxes and non-contractible Wilson loops. Finally, we study the behaviour of the finite-size two-vison gap and matter fermion correlations. We find that the gap does not decrease monotonically with increasing system size, while one still recovers the expected algebraic decay of the correlations at the isotropic point, even for the considered modest system sizes.
one_liner: Finite hyperbolic Kitaev clusters reveal geometry-dependent flux sectors, symmetry-generated degeneracies, and algebraic matter-fermion correlations.
why_it_matters: The construction supplies controlled finite benchmarks for studying topological spin liquids and testing future hyperbolic-lattice quantum simulators.
detailed_summary: The authors generate periodic finite {8,3} and {12,3} hyperbolic lattices as compact genus-g surfaces using quotients of triangle groups, with clusters of up to 72 vertices. Exact solutions identify geometry-dependent ground-state flux and Wilson-loop sectors, whose degeneracies arise from physical lattice symmetries. The two-vison gap is nonmonotonic with size, while matter-fermion correlations recover the expected algebraic decay at the isotropic point.
main_result: A systematic finite-cluster construction reproduces spin-liquid correlations while exposing quotient-dependent flux sectors and symmetry-generated ground-state degeneracies.
application_angle: The resulting cluster library can benchmark programmable quantum simulators and finite-size diagnostics of curved-lattice topological matter.

title: Specifying & Verifying Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
abstract: Building quantum computers is challenging due to the noise that affects qubits. Quantum error correction tackles noise by encoding information in quantum error-correcting (QEC) codes. These codes are often complex, increasingly found by computational search, presented in diverse formalisms with informal arguments, and hard to reason about algorithmically. Given that the rest of the quantum computing stack relies on a QEC code's properties for correct computation, we propose a formally verified foundation for QEC codes. We present QECLean, a Lean-based framework for formally specifying and verifying QEC codes. QECLean backs every claimed QEC-code property with a machine-checked proof, unifies the diverse presentations of codes in the literature through common abstractions, and makes new codes easy to specify. We present a new compositional technique, code combinators, for proving code distance analytically. Code combinators allow us to prove the distance of large codes that are out of reach for algorithmic techniques; for example, we show that IBM's $[[360, 12, \leq 24]]$ code has distance 24, which was previously only known as an upper bound. Furthermore, we show how our approach allows us to formalize and prove entire code families, such as the surface code. Our work lays the foundation required for reasoning about circuit-level implementations of codes on given architectures and for building end-to-end verified compilers for quantum computers. QECLean is available at https://github.com/Stavan-Jain/QECLean
one_liner: QECLean provides machine-checked specifications and proofs for quantum codes, including an exact distance-24 proof for IBM's [[360,12,≤24]] code.
why_it_matters: Formal proofs can prevent incorrect code assumptions from propagating into fault-tolerant hardware designs, circuit implementations, and compilers.
detailed_summary: QECLean is a Lean-based framework that expresses diverse quantum error-correcting codes through common abstractions and attaches machine-checked proofs to claimed properties. Its code-combinator method proves distance compositionally, including distance 24 for IBM's [[360,12,≤24]] code, whose 24 value was previously only an upper bound. The framework also formalizes complete families such as surface codes and is designed to support later circuit- and architecture-level verification.
main_result: QECLean formally proves code properties and establishes that IBM's [[360,12,≤24]] code has distance exactly 24.
application_angle: It provides a verified foundation for selecting hardware codes and building trustworthy fault-tolerant compilers and architecture mappings.

title: SCOPE: A Physical Execution Latency-Guided Quantum Circuit Compilation Framework
abstract: Quantum computing requires compilers to translate algorithms represented in the quantum circuit model into unitary operations supported by physical devices. Limited coherence time makes physical execution latency an important compilation objective. Gate fusion can shorten pulses, but gate count and depth do not capture fused targets' control demands. Evaluating every candidate with quantum optimal control (QOC) would embed pulse optimization in structural search. We present Schmidt-guided Compilation for Optimized Pulse Execution (SCOPE), driven by an operator Schmidt time surrogate. The target's angular distance from product operators measures the required nonlocal change; dividing it by a coupling-limited evolution-rate bound gives a lower bound on exact implementation time. Trace-angle and waveform constraints complete block scores for critical-path evaluation during genetic search. Local QOC determines final pulse durations. Under a numerical nearest-neighbor control model, all 104 results across 13 instances from four application families have shorter QOC critical-path durations than an adapted efficient pulse generation framework with advanced synthesis for quantum circuits (EPOC). Using eight-run instance means, the equally weighted reduction is 42.50\%, with a geometric mean speedup of 2.00. In a shared six-qubit quantum Fourier transform (QFT) ablation, time-surrogate guidance reduces mean QOC duration by 22.21\% relative to gate-count guidance and 21.01\% relative to depth guidance, validating the surrogate's joint use in fitness evaluation and mutation-region selection.
one_liner: SCOPE uses a physics-based execution-time surrogate to compile circuits with substantially shorter optimized pulse critical paths.
why_it_matters: Reducing physical pulse duration directly preserves coherence and can improve algorithm fidelity beyond what gate-count or circuit-depth objectives predict.
detailed_summary: SCOPE scores fused circuit blocks using an operator-Schmidt lower bound on nonlocal evolution time, augmented by trace-angle and waveform constraints. A genetic search optimizes the critical path before local quantum optimal control determines final pulse durations. In a numerical nearest-neighbor model, all 104 results across 13 instances beat an adapted EPOC baseline, with a 42.50% equally weighted mean reduction and 2.00 geometric-mean speedup.
main_result: SCOPE shortened QOC critical-path duration in all 104 tested cases and achieved a geometric-mean speedup of 2.00 over the adapted baseline.
application_angle: The method targets lower-latency physical execution on coherence-limited processors without embedding costly pulse optimization throughout structural search.

title: TCBP-JOBS: GPU-Accelerated Quantum Error Correction Decoding and Noise Learning with Near-Optimal Accuracy
abstract: Achieving near-optimal quantum error correction (QEC) decoding accuracy often requires computationally expensive searches that limit both large-scale simulation and real-time operation. We introduce trajectory-calibrated belief propagation (TCBP), which learns calibrated fault probabilities from BP trajectories, and jittered OSD beam search (JOBS), which uses these probabilities to guide parallel GPU searches. Across surface, color and bivariate-bicycle code memory and surgery circuits, TCBP-JOBS achieves logical error rates comparable to those of the Tesseract most-likely-error decoder at physical error rates of 0.1% to 0.4%, and up to 4.5$\times$ lower on the largest codes. Serial speedups over Tesseract's sparsified presets range from 10$\times$ to 7,400$\times$, and against unsparsified long-beam Tesseract they reach 13,000$\times$ on the bivariate-bicycle codes, at logical error rate ratios of 0.97 to 1.57. At lower physical error rates ($10^{-4}$ to $5\times10^{-4}$), rare-event splitting on the gross code shows that Tesseract is more accurate. Batched execution accelerates offline simulation for rapid, efficient exploration of large-scale QEC design spaces. For QPUs with longer logical clock cycles, our serial memory and logical-surgery experiments demonstrate accuracy comparable to Tesseract while meeting the millisecond-scale latency requirements of online feed-forward operation. Beyond memory and logic decoding, we demonstrate using TCBP-JOBS for confidence scores for postselection in memory and magic-state cultivation, enabling end-to-end color code cultivation. Together, these methods provide a GPU framework for accelerating QEC research via accurate decoding, noise estimation, and confidence assessment.
one_liner: TCBP-JOBS combines learned fault calibration with GPU beam search for fast, near-optimal QEC decoding and confidence estimation.
why_it_matters: The framework brings high-accuracy decoding closer to real-time feed-forward while greatly accelerating large-code simulation and decoder studies.
detailed_summary: TCBP learns calibrated fault probabilities from belief-propagation trajectories, and JOBS uses them to guide parallel jittered OSD searches on GPUs. Across surface, color, and bivariate-bicycle memory and surgery circuits, the decoder is generally comparable to Tesseract at 0.1–0.4% physical error and reaches serial speedups from 10× to 13,000×, although Tesseract is more accurate in tested lower-error regimes. The same framework produces confidence scores for postselection and supports end-to-end color-code magic-state cultivation.
main_result: TCBP-JOBS delivers near-Tesseract logical accuracy with large speedups and millisecond-scale decoding in demonstrated memory and surgery workloads.
application_angle: It supports real-time logical feed-forward, rapid QEC design-space simulation, noise estimation, and confidence-based magic-state postselection.

title: Quantum adiabatic and diabatic optimization: A Hilbert space engineering strategy with Rydberg arrays
abstract: Neutral-atom arrays provide a versatile platform for encoding combinatorial optimization problems with arbitrary graph connectivity [Nguyen et al., PRX Quantum 4, 010316 (2023)]. Although the dynamics of individual encoding gadgets has been studied [Bombieri et al., PRX Quantum 6, 020306 (2025)], understanding annealing bottlenecks in larger networks remains challenging. We investigate how engineering the Hilbert-space geometry controls quantum annealing in a family of blockaded-chain models motivated by these encodings. While boundary terms encode the target maximum independent set problem, the bulk geometry induces an auxiliary optimization problem associated with independent sets of cliques. Spectrally, the energetics of the quantum system can be approximated by physically derived clique weights. When the target problem and the auxiliary problems are consistent, the low-energy modes lie predominantly within the target subspace. This spectral structure motivates a diabatic annealing strategy that exploits target-compatible excited states, as tested on the diamond-chain graph family. These results provide a framework for predicting annealing bottlenecks, and demonstrate Hilbert-space engineering as a strategy for improving neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols.
one_liner: Rydberg-chain geometry is engineered to create target-compatible excited states that enable improved diabatic quantum optimization.
why_it_matters: The work links physical array geometry to annealing bottlenecks, offering a design rule for more effective neutral-atom optimization hardware.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes blockaded Rydberg-chain models in which boundary terms encode a maximum-independent-set target while bulk geometry induces an auxiliary clique problem. Physically derived clique weights approximate the spectrum and predict whether low-energy modes remain concentrated in the target subspace. For diamond-chain graphs, this structure motivates a diabatic protocol that traverses target-compatible excited states to mitigate annealing bottlenecks.
main_result: Hilbert-space geometry predicts annealing bottlenecks and enables a diabatic strategy based on target-compatible excited states in diamond-chain instances.
application_angle: The framework can guide atom-array layout and annealing schedules for practical combinatorial optimization with programmable neutral-atom processors.

title: Quantitative measurement of microwave power at millikelvin temperatures: Comparison between dispersively and directly coupled superconducting qubits
abstract: The Rabi frequency of a two-level system is directly proportional to the electric field amplitude being incident on this system. Taking advantage of this relationship, it is possible to use two-level systems as quantitative sensors of electric fields. Here, we apply this concept to superconducting qubits and use them for quantitative measurement of microwave power at millikelvin temperatures. Our superconducting circuit design includes three transmon qubits directly coupled to the central microwave feedline and three transmon qubits coupled dispersively via readout resonators to the feedline. We compare both coupling schemes to assess their reliability for microwave power sensing. Further, we describe the modeling behind each power-sensing method, including an uncertainty estimation based upon repeated measurements. By combining dispersively coupled and directly coupled qubits on the same device, we are able to explore different power ranges: from $-155\;$dBm to $-130\;$dBm for the directly coupled qubits and from $-95\;$dBm to $-55\;$dBm for the dispersively coupled qubits. When determining the microwave-line attenuation for a frequency of $6.0\;$GHz from room temperature to the millikelvin stage of the cryostat, we obtain best estimates and uncertainties for the directly coupled transmons of $(74.7\pm 0.2) \;$dB and for the dispersively coupled transmons of $(75.4\pm 6.8) \;$dB. The larger uncertainty of the dispersively coupled qubit measurements indicates that these qubits are less reliable for power sensing than the directly coupled qubits, most likely, due to the additional coupling resonator, whose transfer function is difficult to estimate accurately. Our results constitute the first step towards validation of qubit power sensing in dilution fridges, leading towards traceability for cryogenic microwave measurements.
one_liner: On-chip transmon sensors quantify cryogenic microwave power and compare direct with resonator-mediated coupling across complementary power ranges.
why_it_matters: Reliable in-fridge power calibration is essential for reproducible qubit control, microwave-chain validation, and traceable cryogenic measurements.
detailed_summary: A six-transmon chip compares three qubits directly coupled to a feedline with three coupled dispersively through readout resonators. Rabi-based models measure powers from −155 to −130 dBm for direct coupling and −95 to −55 dBm for dispersive coupling. At 6.0 GHz, inferred room-to-millikelvin attenuation is 74.7±0.2 dB directly and 75.4±6.8 dB dispersively, showing markedly better reliability for direct coupling.
main_result: Directly coupled transmons measured 6.0-GHz line attenuation as 74.7±0.2 dB and outperformed dispersively coupled sensors in uncertainty.
application_angle: The approach could provide in situ calibration and eventual measurement traceability for microwave delivery chains in dilution-refrigerator quantum systems.

title: Reinforcement Learning designs Quantum Repeater Protocols on Networks beyond the Chain Scenario
abstract: Small-scale quantum repeater protocols have been shown to distribute entanglement over existing telecommunication infrastructure by means of short range quantum communications and long range classical messages. For larger networks, there are a number of theoretical proposals about how to operate the network to achieve a good performance under varying metrics. Moreover, since the dimension of the space of possible protocols grows exponentially with network size, plenty of those proposals are based on heuristics that reduce the search space. One of these is entanglement routing, which simplifies the problem on non-linear networks by allocating a series of disjoint paths and running chain protocols simultaneously on them. However, in this work we claim routing leads to suboptimal protocols. In fact, inspired by works on linear chains, we apply reinforcement learning to non-linear networks and optimize over the larger non-routing protocol space. Then, we find protocols that outperform a routed extension of the swap-ASAP protocol, even in the parameter regimes where the latter is widely recognized as the state of the art. These results indicate that routing must be discarded in favor of non-routing methods, while they pave the way towards the design of a sensible Quantum Internet architecture.
one_liner: Reinforcement learning discovers non-routing repeater protocols that outperform path-based swap-ASAP strategies on nonlinear quantum networks.
why_it_matters: The result challenges routing as a default quantum-network design principle and opens a larger protocol space for improving entanglement distribution.
detailed_summary: The authors apply reinforcement learning to optimize repeater operations on nonlinear network topologies without restricting entanglement distribution to disjoint routes. The learned protocols outperform a routed extension of swap-ASAP, including regimes where that heuristic is considered state of the art. This indicates that joint, network-wide scheduling can exploit resources unavailable to path-based approaches.
main_result: Learned non-routing protocols outperform routed swap-ASAP protocols on nonlinear quantum-network topologies.
application_angle: The approach could improve entanglement-distribution control and resource scheduling in future heterogeneous quantum-internet deployments.

title: Rethinking Entropic Uncertainty: How measuring without a trace leads to longer keys
abstract: In recent years, the entropic uncertainty relation (EUR) has been one of the most prominent tools to obtain tight key rates secure against general coherent attacks for a broad class of quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols. Despite its success, the fundamental question of how to incorporate the statistics of more than two mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) directly into the EUR is yet to be answered. Here, we introduce a simple yet powerful shift of perspective: Instead of the usual tripartition into the systems of Alice, Bob and Eve, we treat Alice and Bob as one joint system and introduce an additional register as the third system. This register contains the results of appropriately chosen virtual measurements that leave no trace in the real branch of the protocol, but act as a conditioning on the counterfactual phase error measurements. We show that this allows us to obtain tight key rates for QKD protocols using an arbitrary number of MUBs directly and natively from the EUR. Moreover, we demonstrate that this approach has a much broader relevance beyond the inclusion of multiple MUBs, allowing for improvements in many existing security proofs and the treatment of previously unexplored aspects for a wide range of protocols.
one_liner: Virtual trace-free measurements extend entropic-uncertainty security proofs to QKD protocols using any number of mutually unbiased bases.
