why_it_matters: The framework can produce longer secure keys and simplify coherent-attack analyses for multi-basis and previously difficult QKD protocols.
detailed_summary: The work reformulates entropic-uncertainty analysis by treating Alice and Bob jointly and adding a register containing outcomes of carefully chosen virtual measurements. These measurements do not alter the real protocol branch but condition counterfactual phase-error statistics. The construction yields native key-rate bounds for arbitrary numbers of mutually unbiased bases and may tighten other QKD security proofs.
main_result: The proposed uncertainty-relation framework derives tight coherent-attack key rates for QKD using an arbitrary number of mutually unbiased bases.
application_angle: Tighter security bounds can increase usable secret-key lengths and broaden the range of QKD protocols amenable to rigorous finite-resource analysis.

title: Geometry of squeezed states. The phase-space metric, relative vacua and cosmology
abstract: Geometry enters quantum theory in two places. The space of quantum states carries a symplectic form, which generates unitary evolution, and a metric, which governs uncertainties and transition probabilities. The classical phase space acquires a metric of its own when a vacuum is chosen: quantizing a linear system amounts to choosing a compatible complex structure, equivalently a compatible metric $g$. We take this second metric as the primary object and show that it plays, on phase space, the role that the quantum metric plays on the space of states: fluctuations of linear observables are $g$-norms of Hamiltonian vector fields, and along coherent states $g/2\hbar$ \emph{is} the quantum metric. Squeezed states then have a simple description. A squeezed vacuum is the vacuum of another metric, and squeezing is a property of a pair of metrics, a relative vacuum, whose invariants are the eigenvalues $e^{\pm2r_i}$ of $L=g_0^{-1}g$. We work out the harmonic oscillator in detail, including why a rotated squeezed state no longer minimizes the product of the displayed uncertainties. Quadratic evolution deforms the metric, and only the part of the generator that is self-adjoint with respect to the reference changes the $r_i$, at a rate we give exactly. For fields, a vacuum is unitarily implementable relative to a reference exactly when it lies at finite distance from it in the space of vacua. For a massless field in de Sitter space we revisit the two canonical charts compared by Grain and Vennin: relative to the reference of the standard squeezing formalism the Bunch--Davies state has $\sinh r_k=1/(2|kη|)$, and relative to the vacuum that a radiation era beginning at time $η$ would select it has $\sinh r_k=1/(2k^2η^2)$. The second comparison squeezes twice as fast and is unitarily implementable; the first is not.
one_liner: A phase-space metric formulation recasts squeezed vacua as relative geometries and gives exact squeezing rates under quadratic evolution.
why_it_matters: The framework unifies observable fluctuations, state geometry and vacuum comparisons, clarifying squeezing across oscillators, fields and cosmological settings.
detailed_summary: The paper treats the compatible phase-space metric selected by a vacuum as the central geometric object governing linear-observable fluctuations. Squeezing between two vacua is characterized by eigenvalues of the relative metric, and exact changes in squeezing parameters under quadratic evolution are derived. Applied to a de Sitter massless field, the framework distinguishes two vacuum comparisons with different squeezing rates and unitary implementability.
main_result: Squeezed vacua are characterized by relative phase-space metrics, with exact invariants and evolution rates derived for quadratic systems.
application_angle: The geometric formulation can support analysis and control of multimode squeezing in bosonic quantum platforms, although the paper is primarily theoretical.

title: Experimental simulation of a Hilbert-space inner-product change
abstract: We simulate an effective change in a single qubit's inner product (IP) by implementing the channel $\mathcal{F}^η$ on a superconducting quantum processor. Whereas previous experiments simulated parity-time (PT)-symmetric dynamics with a fixed IP, this experiment implements the IP-change channel itself for metrics associated with PT-symmetric systems. Building on an earlier adversarial verification approach, we derive a process-fidelity threshold that rules out mixtures of qubit unitary operations with random discarding of runs. We test the channel for 40 metrics using a single qutrit and a two-qubit Stinespring dilation. The measured fidelities exceed the threshold in 24 of 40 qutrit instances after readout error mitigation, compared with 16 of 40 unmitigated two-qubit instances. Without mitigation, 14 of 40 qutrit instances pass. These results demonstrate a direct simulation of an effective Hilbert-space IP change and its verification against a specified adversarial class, while showing the importance of readout treatment in comparing the encodings.
one_liner: A superconducting processor directly simulates an effective qubit inner-product change and verifies it against an adversarial channel class.
why_it_matters: The experiment turns a formal metric change into a testable quantum channel and quantifies how encoding and readout mitigation affect verification.
detailed_summary: The experiment implements an inner-product-change channel for metrics associated with parity-time-symmetric systems on a superconducting processor. Forty metrics are tested using both a single-qutrit encoding and a two-qubit Stinespring dilation. After readout-error mitigation, 24 of 40 qutrit instances exceed a fidelity threshold excluding mixtures of unitaries with random run discarding; 16 of 40 unmitigated two-qubit instances pass.
main_result: The processor simulates and adversarially verifies an effective Hilbert-space inner-product change across 40 target metrics.
application_angle: The protocol provides a hardware-level route for studying generalized quantum dynamics while benchmarking encoding choices and mitigation methods.

title: Windowed Singularity Subtraction for the Spectral Integral Method
abstract: In 2004, the spectral integral method (SIM) was proposed to solve TM$_z$ scattering by homogeneous two-dimensional dielectric objects and perfect electrical conductors with smooth boundaries. Its error decreases exponentially as the number of boundary points increases linearly. Plasmonic resonances, however, require TE$_z$ polarization and permittivities with a negative real part. The extension of SIM to this case shows that the original global singularity subtraction suffers catastrophic cancellation, with a round-off floor that grows exponentially with the attenuation accumulated across the object. To resolve this issue, this work introduces a windowed singularity subtraction that limits this cancellation amplification to an exponential factor that the user can set independently of the object size, provided the window is adequately resolved. Numerical results verify the accuracy of the proposed method.
one_liner: Windowed singularity subtraction prevents catastrophic cancellation in spectral-integral simulations of plasmonic TE scattering.
why_it_matters: The method preserves high numerical accuracy for large or strongly attenuating plasmonic objects, where the original subtraction develops a severe round-off floor.
detailed_summary: Extending the spectral integral method to TE-polarized plasmonic scattering exposes catastrophic cancellation in its original global singularity subtraction. The proposed window confines cancellation amplification to a user-selected exponential factor independent of object size, provided the window is sufficiently resolved. Numerical tests verify the resulting accuracy.
main_result: Windowed singularity subtraction removes the object-size-dependent round-off barrier in spectral-integral TE scattering calculations.
application_angle: The technique enables more reliable simulation of plasmonic resonances for designing metallic and negative-permittivity photonic structures.

title: Quantum Networks with Realistic Photonic Memories
abstract: Ensemble based photonic memories paired with photon pair sources are the essential ingredient for many quantum networking protocols. Most protocols and theoretical analyses focus on networks of identical nodes, however, realistic networks consist of nodes that may vary from device to device. We investigate a network of non-identical memories and develop mitigation strategies for the variation in performance. We find that by strategically distributing the memories among the nodes and individually adapting the emission probabilities based on the memory efficiency the effect of the variance on fidelity and duration can to a large extend be mitigated. Generally, our analysis shows the importance of accounting and compensating for device variations to avoid deteriorating the performance. Lastly, we also link our results to memories where efficiency decays as a function of storage duration. Here, we show that our approach provides a visible improvement for networks with non-identical and decaying memories.
one_liner: Memory placement and source-probability adaptation mitigate fidelity and latency losses in quantum networks with nonidentical photonic memories.
why_it_matters: The study replaces idealized identical-node assumptions with device-aware controls that can improve realistic repeater-network performance.
detailed_summary: The authors model quantum networks whose ensemble-based photonic memories vary in efficiency from node to node. Strategic assignment of memories and per-source adjustment of photon-pair emission probabilities substantially reduce degradation in fidelity and distribution duration. The same controls also improve networks containing nonidentical memories whose efficiencies decay during storage.
main_result: Device-aware memory placement and emission-probability tuning mitigate performance losses from efficiency variation and storage-time decay.
application_angle: The strategies offer practical calibration and deployment rules for repeater networks assembled from imperfect, heterogeneous memory hardware.

title: Entanglement distillation, nonlocal magic, and state sharing in an isospectral non-Hermitian bipartite model
abstract: An invertible nonunitary similarity deformation leaves a two-qubit Hamiltonian's spectrum unchanged while varying a selected normalized right eigenstate in the fixed physical inner product. We embed this state in a two-parameter maximally correlated family that includes local dephasing and noisy circuit preparation. Hashing and a matching diagonal relative-entropy bound give the exact distillable entanglement and the PPT comparison distances at every finite tensor power. Correlated PPT catalysts cannot improve the Bell-pair distillation rate. The optimized CHSH value is \(2\sqrt{1+t^2}\): every state with nonzero coherence violates CHSH, while complete dephasing is separable. A calibrated finite-sample bound and two equal-fidelity preparations clarify which noise parameters determine the rate. For pure inputs, the binomial Schmidt spectrum gives logarithmic collectively optimized nonlocal magic with vanishing density, despite a positive entanglement density and extensive pairwise-frame magic. Fixed Clifford decoding gives six- and eight-copy CCZ concentration probabilities \(P_6=\frac12(1-2^{-\mathcal M_γ})\) and \(P_8=1-2^{-\mathcal M_γ}\). The same family permits explicit swapping recursions, symmetry-resolved entanglement, and a comparison of qubit stabilizer and fermionic Gaussian resources. These calculations keep the relevant operation classes separate when comparing many-copy limits.
one_liner: An exactly solvable two-qubit family links non-Hermitian deformation to entanglement distillation, CHSH violation, magic concentration, and state sharing.
why_it_matters: The model supplies analytic benchmarks for separating entanglement, nonlocality, and magic resources under dephasing and noisy state preparation.
detailed_summary: An isospectral nonunitary deformation tunes a normalized two-qubit right eigenstate without changing the Hamiltonian spectrum. For its noisy maximally correlated extension, hashing matches a diagonal relative-entropy bound, yielding the exact distillable entanglement at every finite tensor power; correlated PPT catalysts do not improve the rate. The work also derives the optimized CHSH value, many-copy magic scaling, fixed-Clifford CCZ concentration probabilities, and explicit entanglement-swapping recursions.
main_result: The study obtains exact finite-copy entanglement rates and analytic nonlocality, magic-concentration, and swapping results for a dephased two-qubit family.
application_angle: These closed-form results can benchmark noisy entanglement preparation, purification, resource conversion, and network-state-sharing protocols.

title: Exponential Quantum Memory Advantage for Late-Graph Smoothness and Spectral Estimation
abstract: Graph signal processing tests how smoothly the decisions of next-generation massive sensor networks with $N$ nodes vary over their neighbour graph. Memory becomes the bottleneck when the neighbour graph arrives only after data erasure, a late-graph setting motivated by dispersed sensor networks and telemetry. We analyse three collection scenarios, reliable rounds, continuous broadcast and ordered capture, and test the Dirichlet energy $\mathcal E_G=\mathbf z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf L\mathbf z/N$ of the fused decision map $\mathbf z\in\{\pm1\}^N$, with late-graph Laplacian $\mathbf L$, against two thresholds. Hidden Matching uses $O(\log N)$ qubits on fused bits, but in reliable rounds and continuous broadcast, where nodes report $b$ sub-bits separately, a classical record buffer before it uses $O(N b)$ bits; classical methods need $Ω(\sqrt N)$ bits in the worst case. The recently introduced Quantum Oracle Sketching builds quantum oracles from random data streams without storing them. We combine coherent loading of separately reported sub-bits, exact in reliable rounds and by Quantum Oracle Sketching in continuous broadcast, with nonlinear fusion and Hidden Matching readout. The register count $R$ does not grow with $N$, and the memory is $O(\log N)$ logical qubits and classical bits, at fixed $b$, graph bounds, thresholds and error targets: an exponential memory advantage over every classical receiver and over Hidden Matching with that buffer. We prove unbiasedness in reliable rounds, preparation bounds in continuous broadcast, classical lower bounds and, for a planner-supplied multi-hop coefficient stream, spectral error bounds. Broadcast simulations match analytic averages at $N=1024$, without resolved bias growth up to $N=2^{20}$. Fault-tolerant hardware, gate rates and, in continuous broadcast, report counts remain open.
one_liner: Quantum stream loading and Hidden Matching estimate late-arriving graph smoothness using O(log N) memory where classical receivers need polynomial memory.
why_it_matters: It proposes an exponential receiver-memory advantage for sensor-network telemetry when measurements vanish before the graph needed to interpret them becomes known.
detailed_summary: The protocol estimates the Dirichlet energy of a fused binary sensor map when the neighbor graph arrives only after the original reports are erased. Coherent sub-bit loading, nonlinear fusion, and Hidden Matching require O(log N) logical qubits and classical bits at fixed task parameters, while classical methods require Ω(sqrt(N)) bits in the worst case and straightforward buffering costs O(Nb). The authors prove preparation and error bounds across collection models and report simulations through N=2^20, while leaving fault-tolerant resources and gate-rate feasibility open.
platform_or_system: quantum receiver for streamed sensor telemetry
main_result: The proposed receiver achieves O(log N) memory for late-graph smoothness and spectral estimation, establishing an exponential asymptotic advantage over classical receivers.
application_angle: The approach targets memory-constrained fusion of dispersed sensor, broadcast, and telemetry streams whose network topology is supplied only later.

title: Spectral integral method for reflection and transmission by one-dimensional periodic arrays of penetrable cylinders
abstract: The spectral integral method (SIM) is extended from a single cylinder to an infinite one-dimensional (1-D) periodic array (a grating) of identical, homogeneous, arbitrarily shaped smooth cylinders. The cylinders may be dielectric or metallic with complex electrical permittivity. Interactions among all members of the array are carried exactly by the 1-D quasi-periodic Green's function, Gp, in the exterior boundary integral equation, so only the boundary of one reference cylinder is discretized. Gp is written as the free-space Green's function plus a regular part that is infinitely differentiable on the reference cylinder whenever the cylinders do not touch. The regular part and its gradient are evaluated with Ewald's method. Floquet reflection and transmission amplitudes, as well as reflectance, transmittance, and absorptance, are obtained from the boundary data. For the analytic boundaries and numerical examples considered here, the SIM exhibits root-exponential convergence in N for glass and gold gratings, where N is the number of samples on the boundary, for both polarizations, at oblique incidence and with several diffraction orders. Several numerical examples are provided.
one_liner: A spectral integral solver computes diffraction by infinite 1D arrays of penetrable dielectric or metallic cylinders with root-exponential convergence.
why_it_matters: Accurate unit-cell modeling of arbitrary smooth scatterers can accelerate the design of gratings and periodic photonic structures with loss and multiple diffraction orders.
detailed_summary: The spectral integral method is extended to infinite one-dimensional periodic arrays of homogeneous, arbitrarily shaped smooth cylinders. A quasi-periodic Green function captures all inter-cylinder interactions while only one reference boundary is discretized; its regular component and gradient are evaluated by Ewald summation. Tests on glass and gold gratings show root-exponential convergence for both polarizations, oblique incidence, complex permittivity, and several propagating diffraction orders.
main_result: The method accurately recovers Floquet reflection, transmission, and absorption with root-exponential convergence in the boundary sample count.
application_angle: The solver supports efficient electromagnetic design of lossy gratings, filters, couplers, and periodic components used in classical or quantum photonic links.

title: The speed limit of gravitational entanglement and the cost of noise
abstract: Is gravity quantum? A proposed test lets two small masses, each in a superposition of two places, become entangled through their mutual gravity. Gravity is weak, so the masses must stay coherent for seconds while random forces disturb them. Here we ask how fast gravity can entangle two masses, and what noise costs. Without noise we find the maximum rate exactly: it falls as the inverse cube of the separation, and two positions per mass achieve it. Above a noise level set by the masses and their separation, gravity's leading pull can be imitated by classical signals, and every strategy is limited to a rate falling at least as the inverse fourth power. Exact, continuous error correction shields the masses from noise but hides them from each other: the best rate falls as the inverse seventh power, and six positions on a hexagon come within 10% of it at large separation.
one_liner: Exact bounds show how separation, classicalizable noise, and continuous error correction sharply limit gravity-mediated entanglement rates.
why_it_matters: The bounds quantify the coherence and geometry demands confronting experiments that seek evidence of gravity-generated entanglement between mesoscopic masses.
detailed_summary: For two masses placed in spatial superpositions, the authors derive the exact noiseless gravitational entanglement-rate limit, which scales as inverse separation cubed and is achieved with two positions per mass. Above a mass- and distance-dependent noise threshold, the leading gravitational interaction can be reproduced by classical signaling, forcing all strategies to scale no better than inverse fourth power. Exact continuous error correction suppresses noise but also weakens the useful interaction, producing inverse-seventh-power scaling; a six-position hexagonal geometry approaches the asymptotic optimum within 10%.
main_result: The work establishes exact or asymptotically tight entanglement-rate bounds scaling as r^-3 without noise, at best r^-4 above the classicalization threshold, and r^-7 under exact continuous correction.
application_angle: These limits guide mass spacing, superposition geometry, coherence, and noise targets for laboratory tests of gravity-mediated quantum entanglement.

title: Optimal Quantum Sensing Algorithms for Discrete-Frequency Spectroscopy
abstract: Spectroscopy is a versatile tool that drives scientific discovery and underpins modern technologies. Quantum sensing offers promising opportunities to advance spectroscopy through enhanced sensitivity and spectral and spatial resolution. However, existing approaches largely focus on improving general measurement capabilities, often overlooking the structure of specific sensing tasks and leaving potential performance gains untapped. Here, we develop an algorithmic approach to quantum sensing tailored to various spectroscopic tasks, providing new avenues for improvement. Specifically, we consider general time-varying signals supported on a known set of $N$ candidate frequencies, a setting we call discrete-frequency spectroscopy. We formulate three types of practically motivated sensing tasks---Detection, Search, and Learning---that require progressively more spectral information. For all tasks, we design optimal quantum sensing algorithms achieving a $\sqrt{N}$ speedup over conventional frequency-scanning approaches. Optimal Detection and Search need only a single-qubit sensor under $π$-pulse control, whereas optimal Learning provably requires coherent processing with a quantum computer. End-to-end numerical simulations incorporating various experimental imperfections predict up to two-orders-of-magnitude speedup in Detection. As an example, we analyze the feasibility of our Detection and Search algorithms for real-world molecular screening based on state-of-the-art nitrogen-vacancy centers. We also show how quantum-computing-enhanced Learning enables wireless communication in a weak-signal regime where conventional methods fail. Our results establish a practical route toward realizing quantum advantages via designing task-specific sensing algorithms.
one_liner: Task-specific quantum algorithms deliver an optimal sqrt(N) speedup for detecting, locating, or learning signals on N candidate frequencies.
why_it_matters: The protocols translate quantum algorithmic advantage into experimentally relevant spectroscopy, including NV-center molecular screening and weak-signal communications.
detailed_summary: The paper formulates Detection, Search, and Learning for signals supported on a known set of N discrete candidate frequencies. Optimal Detection and Search use a single-qubit sensor with pi-pulse control, whereas optimal Learning provably requires coherent quantum-computer processing; all achieve a sqrt(N) speedup over frequency scanning. End-to-end simulations with experimental imperfections predict up to a two-order-of-magnitude Detection speedup, and feasibility is analyzed for state-of-the-art NV-center molecular screening.
platform_or_system: pi-pulse-controlled qubit sensor and quantum processor
main_result: Optimal algorithms achieve a sqrt(N) speedup across discrete-frequency Detection, Search, and Learning, with substantial simulated gains under realistic imperfections.
application_angle: The methods could accelerate molecular screening, spectrum discovery, and weak-signal wireless reception using NV sensors or other coherently controlled qubits.

title: Resolving and Suppressing Temporally Correlated Noise in Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) requires suppressing errors in both space and time, yet standard logical memory experiments primarily probe spatial faults. Here, we use a 105-qubit Willow superconducting quantum processor to realize and scale the surface code stability experiment, which is alternatively sensitive to temporal error chains. Scaling from patch sizes of $3 \times 3$ to $7 \times 7$, we realize a timelike block suppression factor of $μ_T = 1.47 \pm 0.25$, demonstrating the ability to maintain temporal error suppression as the number of qubits increases. By extending the stability experiment for many cycles, we uncover a sum-of-exponentials behavior in error suppression caused by a temporally correlated error: data-qubit heating to the third excited state $|3\rangle$. We fully capture this effect with a parameter-free, device-level leakage model incorporating higher-state transport during syndrome extraction cycles. To suppress this error, we develop and realize a walking stability circuit, reaching a logical error probability floor of $\le 3.20\times 10^{-8}$ at 60 cycles---two orders of magnitude below the standard construction---and limited by ionizing radiation error bursts. Finally, by adaptively terminating syndrome extraction based on decoder confidence in an offline analysis, we reduce spacetime logical error by 38% and time overhead by 34% compared to the optimal fixed-cycle strategy.
one_liner: A 105-qubit superconducting processor exposes time-correlated leakage in surface-code operation and suppresses it with a walking stability circuit.
why_it_matters: The experiment identifies a concrete temporal fault mechanism and lowers the 60-cycle logical-error floor by two orders of magnitude on scaled hardware.
detailed_summary: Surface-code stability experiments on a 105-qubit Willow processor scale from 3x3 to 7x7 patches and achieve a timelike block suppression factor of 1.47 ± 0.25. Long runs reveal sum-of-exponentials suppression caused by data-qubit heating into the third excited state, reproduced by a parameter-free device-level leakage model. A walking stability circuit reduces the logical-error floor to at most 3.20e-8 at 60 cycles, while confidence-based adaptive termination cuts spacetime logical error by 38% and time overhead by 34% in offline analysis.
main_result: The walking circuit suppresses leakage-driven temporal errors to a logical-error floor of at most 3.20e-8 after 60 cycles, two orders below the standard circuit.
application_angle: The techniques provide practical circuit, modeling, and decoder strategies for controlling correlated temporal faults in scalable fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Double quantum dots as dynamical impurities in one-dimensional transport
abstract: We study single-electron scattering in a tight-binding chain capacitively coupled to double quantum dots, which act as dynamical two-level-system impurities with electrically tunable level splittings. For a single impurity, we solve the scattering problem exactly and show Feshbach-like perfect elastic reflection, whose resonant condition distinguishes the initial two-level state. For several impurities in a strongly reflecting chain, transmission peaks at an intermediate mean level splitting. At small splittings, energy exchange with the impurities can weaken constructive interference between backscattered paths, consistent with the initial rise in transmission. As excitation channels close, virtual transitions can enhance reflection and drive transmission below its purely elastic value $T_0$. At larger splittings, these virtual processes weaken and transmission approaches $T_0$. We discuss how gate-controlled transmission measurements in quantum-dot arrays could test these predictions.
one_liner: Gate-tunable double quantum dots act as dynamical impurities that produce state-dependent resonant reflection in a one-dimensional electron channel.
why_it_matters: The predicted transport signatures offer an electrical route to probe two-level-state dynamics and energy exchange in quantum-dot arrays.
detailed_summary: The authors exactly solve single-electron scattering through a tight-binding chain capacitively coupled to a double-dot two-level system. A Feshbach-like resonance gives perfect elastic reflection at a condition that depends on the impurity's initial state. With multiple impurities, real and virtual transitions generate nonmonotonic transmission as the mean level splitting is tuned.
main_result: The model predicts state-selective perfect reflection for one impurity and nonmonotonic transmission for multiple dynamical impurities.
application_angle: Gate-controlled conductance measurements could characterize two-level dynamics and interaction-mediated scattering in quantum-dot hardware.

title: The SymTFT and Quantum Phases of Matter
abstract: The symmetry topological field theory (SymTFT) provides a unified framework for ordinary and generalized symmetries of quantum many-body systems. By encoding symmetry in a topological theory in one higher dimension, it separates symmetry data from the details of a specific quantum system. In this review, we give a pedagogical introduction to this framework and survey its applications to phases of quantum matter. For fusion category symmetries in ${(1+1)}$d, we explain how the SymTFT characterizes anomalies, classifies gapped phases, and organizes the symmetry structure of gapless phases. We also give a broad overview of further developments of this framework, including extensions to symmetries in higher dimensions, continuous symmetries, fermionic systems, mixed states, and spacetime symmetries.
one_liner: A pedagogical review explains how symmetry topological field theory organizes anomalies and quantum phases across diverse many-body systems.
why_it_matters: It consolidates a general theoretical language for classifying gapped and gapless phases, but reports no new sensing experiment or device.
detailed_summary: This review formulates symmetry data as a topological field theory in one higher dimension, separating universal symmetry structure from microscopic details. It emphasizes fusion-category symmetries in one-dimensional quantum systems, including anomaly detection and classification of gapped phases. Extensions to higher dimensions, fermions, mixed states, continuous groups, and spacetime symmetries are surveyed.
main_result: The review unifies established SymTFT methods for describing anomalies and organizing gapped and gapless quantum phases.
application_angle: The framework can guide theoretical identification of symmetry-protected phases, although the paper has no direct experimental sensing demonstration.

title: Parametric and Universal Thouless Invariants in Matrix Product States
abstract: We investigate the classification of continuous families of translation-invariant injective matrix product states on an infinite chain, parametrized by a paracompact Hausdorff space $X$ and subject to a compact Hausdorff symmetry $G$. We construct an invariant for phases of such families, valued in $\check{H}^1(X;\widehat{G})$, that generalizes the known $\widehat{G}$ phase invariant for $G$-symmetric Thouless pumps. The phase invariant is constructed as the pullback to $X$ of a single universal Čech cohomology class on a classifying space of $G$-symmetric translation-invariant injective matrix product states. Several examples are given over various parameter spaces where this invariant is nontrivial.
one_liner: A universal cohomological invariant classifies symmetry-preserving continuous families of injective matrix product states.
why_it_matters: The construction supplies rigorous tools for identifying topological pumping phases in parametrically controlled one-dimensional quantum systems.
detailed_summary: The authors classify continuous, symmetry-constrained families of translation-invariant injective matrix product states over a parameter space. They construct an invariant in the first Čech cohomology group with coefficients in the character group of the symmetry. The invariant is obtained by pulling back a universal class and is shown to be nontrivial in several examples.
main_result: A universal Čech-cohomology invariant generalizing the symmetric Thouless-pump phase label is constructed and evaluated in nontrivial examples.
application_angle: The invariant may support the design and diagnosis of quantized many-body pumps, including implementations in programmable photonic or atomic lattices.

title: Robust Passive Quantum Memory in Three Dimensions, Part I: Thermal and Zero-Temperature Perturbative Stability
abstract: Whether a three-dimensional quantum many-body system with geometrically local, bounded-degree interactions can passively protect encoded quantum information has remained a central open question since Kitaev introduced topological quantum computation. Passive protection requires stability against both thermal noise at nonzero temperature and generic static Hamiltonian perturbations Balasubramanian, Davydova, and Lin (BDL) recently established unperturbed three-dimensional thermal self-correction using a recursively defined family of stabilizer Hamiltonians. However, they left open whether their construction remains stable against quantum perturbations, even at zero temperature. In this paper, we show that a slight variant of the BDL code family achieves stability along both boundary axes of the perturbation-temperature phase diagram as the system size grows. Following BDL, in the absence of perturbation it is thermally stable below a critical temperature, achieving a stretched-exponentially long memory lifetime when coupled to any local Markovian thermal bath generated by single-site system-bath interactions satisfying detailed balance with bounded coupling rates. At zero temperature under arbitrary weak, superpolynomially decaying quantum perturbations, the family maintains a uniform bulk spectral gap, superpolynomially small ground-space splitting, and a superpolynomially long closed-system unitary memory lifetime for quasi-locally dressed logical observables. To prove this zero-temperature stability, we establish local topological quantum order across the multiscale hierarchy using a linearly dilated relaxation of the usual Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis criteria. In the companion paper, we combine the tools developed here with finite-temperature worldline cluster expansions to establish passive self-correction throughout the phase diagram's positive-temperature perturbed interior.
one_liner: A three-dimensional stabilizer-code family is proved stable against thermal noise and weak quantum perturbations on two limiting axes.
why_it_matters: The results advance passive quantum-memory hardware by establishing both long thermal lifetimes and perturbative zero-temperature stability.
detailed_summary: A modified BDL three-dimensional stabilizer family retains stretched-exponentially long memory below a critical temperature without perturbations. At zero temperature, arbitrary weak superpolynomially decaying perturbations preserve a uniform bulk gap, superpolynomially small ground-space splitting, and long dressed-logical lifetimes. The proof establishes multiscale local topological quantum order using relaxed stability criteria.
main_result: The code family achieves thermal self-correction when unperturbed and superpolynomial perturbative stability at zero temperature as system size grows.
application_angle: These guarantees strengthen the theoretical foundation for self-correcting memories that store quantum information with reduced active error correction.

title: Distrustful entanglement-based Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is the one of the most explored application of quantum information theory. While practical QKD systems are being deployed around the world, a major issue of these setups are that one has to trust the measurement devices of both parties. On the other hand, the most secure among such schemes are called device-independent (DI) QKD protocols, where no component of the setup is assumed to be trusted. However, due to their high technological demand, their loophole-free version currently remain out of practical reach. Inspired by the real world, we consider the traditional QKD in a distrustful measurement setting, that is, the measurement devices can only be trusted upto some level of confidence, which might still be large but not completely trusted. We then derive a general lower bound on the asymptotic key rate in this scenario. Then considering perfect detectors and source, and the entanglement-based BB84 (BBM) protocol, we show that to obtain secure keys one needs to trust their devices more than 92 %. However, we observe that such a protocol can not be realised with any level of distrust using the realistic detectors and sources at the current technology. Finally, we also consider the BBM protocol with arbitrary dimensional systems and observe that they are more robust to distrust than qubit systems. Consequently, with the same level of distrust, along with same detector and source efficiences, one can get better key rates with high-dimensional systems.
one_liner: A QKD security analysis quantifies how partial distrust of measurement devices reduces secret-key rates in entanglement-based BB84.
why_it_matters: It exposes a sharp gap between partially trusted security models and present hardware while identifying high-dimensional encoding as more robust.
detailed_summary: The paper derives a general asymptotic key-rate lower bound when measurement devices are trusted only to a specified confidence. For ideal sources and detectors in entanglement-based BB84, secure key generation requires more than 92% device trust. Under the studied realistic efficiencies, no distrust level is tolerable, whereas higher-dimensional systems improve robustness and key rate.
main_result: The analysis finds a greater-than-92% trust threshold for ideal qubit BBM and improved distrust tolerance from higher-dimensional systems.
application_angle: The bounds can inform security certification and motivate high-dimensional QKD hardware when fully device-independent operation is impractical.

title: AI Scientist Discovered Robust Quantum Control
abstract: Protecting quantum coherence is a central theme of modern quantum technologies. Carefully designed control pulses can extend coherence by suppressing disorder and unwanted interactions. However, designing robust pulse sequences remains challenging in interacting multi-level systems, where multiple independent error channels must be controlled in the presence of experimental imperfections. Here we introduce QORA, a multi-agent artificial intelligence framework that integrates theoretical reasoning, automated experimental calibration and control for closed-loop discovery of quantum control sequences. Applied to a dense ensemble of spin-1 nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, QORA discovers AID-ROD, a series of AI-discovered sequences that nearly double the measured spin coherence time relative to the state-of-the-art human-designed sequence DROID-C3PO. Subsequence analysis by human researchers reveals a hierarchy of error suppression: 18-pulse blocks suppress linear and quadratic onsite disorder and common-mode drive-amplitude errors, while their arrangement over a longer cycle reduces dipolar interactions, providing a physical explanation for the observed improvement and robustness in AID-ROD. These results demonstrate AI-guided experimental discovery of robust quantum control and identify a design strategy for protecting coherence in interacting multi-level systems beyond qubits.
one_liner: A multi-agent AI closed loop discovers pulse sequences that nearly double coherence in a dense ensemble of spin-1 NV centers.
why_it_matters: The experiment demonstrates automated discovery of interpretable, robust controls for interacting multilevel quantum sensors and processors.
detailed_summary: QORA combines theoretical reasoning, automated calibration, and experimental feedback to search for robust control sequences in a dense spin-1 NV ensemble. Its AID-ROD sequences nearly double measured coherence relative to the human-designed DROID-C3PO benchmark. Analysis attributes robustness to nested suppression of onsite disorder, drive-amplitude errors, and dipolar interactions.
main_result: AI-discovered AID-ROD control sequences nearly double the experimentally measured spin coherence time over a leading human-designed sequence.
application_angle: Longer robust coherence can improve NV-based sensing and the performance of interacting multilevel quantum hardware under realistic control errors.

title: Microwave-optical quantum transduction with quantum-well exciton polaritons
abstract: Linking superconducting quantum processors over optical fiber requires microwave-optical quantum transducers that are efficient, high-bandwidth, and low-noise. This combination has been out of reach because of the weak nonlinearities of conventional electro-optic (EO) materials. We propose a transducer with an engineered, strong EO nonlinearity using the quantum-confined Stark effect (QCSE) of quantum-well excitons. The QCSE transducer leverages the strong light-matter interactions and extreme polarizability of quantum well excitons. Strong coupling to an optical cavity forms exciton-polaritons whose vacuum EO coupling is up to five orders of magnitude larger than in a typical thin-film lithium niobate device. We describe a GaAs/AlGaAs stepped-quantum-well transducer design with predicted transduction efficiencies above 60% and fewer than 0.01 added noise quanta over a $\sim$60 MHz bandwidth, using pump powers below 10 $μ$W and loaded optical and microwave quality factors of only $3\times10^4$ and $10^3$. We further show that the cavity protection of the polariton provides robustness against inhomogeneous broadening of the quantum well excitons.
one_liner: Exciton-polariton electro-optics could enable efficient, low-noise microwave-to-optical conversion at microwatt pump powers.
why_it_matters: The design targets a central bottleneck in optically networking superconducting quantum processors without demanding extreme cavity quality factors.
detailed_summary: The proposal uses the quantum-confined Stark effect in stepped GaAs/AlGaAs quantum wells strongly coupled to an optical cavity. The resulting exciton polaritons are predicted to provide vacuum electro-optic coupling up to five orders of magnitude above typical thin-film lithium niobate devices. Modeling indicates over 60% conversion efficiency, below 0.01 added noise quanta, and roughly 60 MHz bandwidth with pump power under 10 μW.
main_result: The proposed device achieves predicted efficiency above 60% with fewer than 0.01 added noise quanta across about 60 MHz.
application_angle: It offers a potential low-power optical interface for connecting superconducting quantum computers over fiber networks.

title: Probing scalar-mediated Lorentz violation with hydrogen masers and spin-precession of molecules
abstract: We propose using hydrogen maser spectroscopy and molecular spin-precession experiments, traditionally employed in precision frequency measurements and searches for the electron electric dipole moment, as complementary probes of light scalar-mediated, spin-dependent fifth forces. We investigate their sensitivity to Lorentz-violating interactions mediated by scalars with masses ranging from $\mathcal{O}(10^{-4}~μ\mathrm{eV})$ to $\mathcal{O}(10~\mathrm{keV})$. While hydrogen maser spectroscopy and molecular spin-precession measurements probe different combinations of Lorentz-violating couplings, we find that the strongest projected sensitivities can be achieved using spin-precession of ultracold molecules, benefiting from their extended coherence times. These experimental approaches provide access to previously unexplored regions of parameter space, probing interaction ranges extending from centimeter to sub-angstrom scales. Our proposals highlight the potential of precision atomic and molecular experiments to search for new spin-dependent scalar-mediated interactions and violations of fundamental spacetime symmetries.
one_liner: Hydrogen masers and ultracold molecular spin precession are proposed as probes of scalar-mediated Lorentz violation.
why_it_matters: Established precision-measurement platforms could test unexplored spin-dependent interactions over ranges from centimeters to sub-angstrom scales.
detailed_summary: The study derives sensitivities of hydrogen-maser spectroscopy and molecular spin-precession experiments to light scalar-mediated, spin-dependent fifth forces. The two platforms probe complementary combinations of Lorentz-violating couplings over scalar masses from about 10^-4 μeV to 10 keV. Ultracold molecules provide the strongest projected reach because of their long spin-coherence times.
platform_or_system: Hydrogen masers and ultracold molecular spins
main_result: Projected measurements access previously unexplored Lorentz-violating parameter space across interaction ranges from centimeters to below an angstrom.
application_angle: The proposal repurposes mature frequency and molecular-coherence techniques for sensitive tests of new physics and spacetime symmetries.

title: Shortest-path percolation and structural robustness of quantum internet networks
abstract: We study shortest-path percolation on spatial networks that model the quantum internet based on optical fibers. In this process, the removal of paths describes the consumption of the entangled links used for communication. We compare finite and unrestricted path-length bounds for networks whose average degree either increases with system size or remains approximately constant. We show that networks become more robust as the average degree increases, whereas networks with approximately constant average degree exhibit a data collapse for the fixed finite bounds considered. Using Monte Carlo sampling of the shortest-path-length distribution, we estimate an equivalent path cost, a finite bound that approximately reproduces the degradation of the network in the unrestricted case. For networks with fixed average degree, this cost grows approximately as the square root of the number of nodes. Increasing the bound beyond this value requires additional computation time without appreciably changing the percolation dynamics. As a complementary result, for Erdős-Rényi random networks, we find an empirical relation between the initial average degree and the approximately common crossing point of the percolation curves for different path-length bounds.
one_liner: Shortest-path percolation quantifies how consuming entangled routes progressively degrades fiber-based quantum internet networks.
why_it_matters: The results identify useful path-length limits for realistic robustness simulations and clarify how connectivity controls network resilience.
detailed_summary: The work models entangled-link consumption by removing shortest communication paths from spatial fiber networks. Networks become more robust with increasing average degree, while fixed-degree networks show collapsed percolation behavior for finite path bounds. Monte Carlo sampling yields an equivalent finite path cost that scales approximately as the square root of node count for fixed-degree networks.
main_result: A finite path bound scaling roughly as √N reproduces unrestricted degradation in fixed-degree networks without unnecessary computational cost.
application_angle: The framework can guide topology design, routing policies, and efficient resilience testing for deployed quantum communication networks.

title: A Geometric Framework for Local-to-Global Symmetry: Global Constraints on Local Dynamics
abstract: Aggregate molecular systems are routinely understood by decomposing them into local structural units, such as monomers in J/H-aggregates, chemical moieties, motifs, and functional groups. Implicit in such decompositions is the assumption that these local structures remain meaningful within the aggregate. Here, we ask how the symmetries of constituent structures relate to aggregate symmetry, and how this relation determines the constraints that global symmetry imposes on transitions between local symmetry sectors. We construct a covariant local-to-global representation from framed local symmetry data and show that its reconstruction map intertwines with a global quantum representation. By identifying which global symmetry sectors overlap each local symmetry sector, we resolve symmetry-enforced dynamical exclusions into site-resolved pathways. Through Frobenius reciprocity, these exclusions can be determined from standard character tables of the local and global symmetry groups, with the character values in the inner product paired according to the relative positions and orientations of local structures within the aggregate. Although motivated by molecular aggregates, the construction is formulated for arbitrary geometries modeled by a homogeneous space of an ambient transformation group.
one_liner: A representation-theoretic framework maps global aggregate symmetry constraints onto site-resolved local transition pathways.
why_it_matters: It provides a systematic way to predict symmetry-forbidden dynamics in molecular aggregates using standard character tables and geometry.
detailed_summary: The authors construct a covariant local-to-global representation from framed local symmetry data and prove that its reconstruction map intertwines with a global quantum representation. Overlaps between global and local symmetry sectors resolve aggregate-level selection rules into site-specific allowed and excluded pathways. Frobenius reciprocity reduces the calculation to character tables augmented by the relative positions and orientations of local units.
main_result: The framework converts global symmetry restrictions into geometry-aware, site-resolved constraints on transitions between local symmetry sectors.
application_angle: It can support the design and interpretation of excitation transport and optical transitions in structured molecular and excitonic materials.

title: Probing the real-time decoding accuracy bounds in trapped ion architectures
abstract: Fault tolerant quantum computers will rely on real-time decoders that process syndromes faster than the QEC cycle duration. The millisecond cycle times offered by trapped ion platforms relax low-latency decoding demands, but simulations and experiments have not yet exploited this time budget to reach maximum logical error suppression. We show how a hybrid sliding window decoding scheme composed of a lower-accuracy and a higher-accuracy decoder can yield substantially improved logical error rates, while preserving low latency. All windows are handled by the lower-accuracy decoder, with some windows being infrequently switched to the higher-accuracy decoder. We extract soft-output information from the lower-accuracy decoder efficiently for any QLDPC code, which allows us to identify decoding windows of low confidence. We simulate memory experiments of bivariate bicycle (BB) codes, using trapped-ion informed noise models. Depending on the physical error rate and BB code, we find up to 3-4 orders of magnitude logical error rate reduction compared to the $\texttt{BP-LSD}$ decoder, and up to 2-3 orders of magnitude lower logical error rate compared to the $\texttt{Beamsearch}$ decoder. By leveraging available classical processing time, our decoding protocol significantly boosts decoding accuracy, ultimately reducing the demands on increasing code size.
one_liner: Confidence-triggered hybrid decoding sharply improves logical error rates while retaining real-time operation in trapped-ion QEC.
why_it_matters: Using the millisecond trapped-ion cycle budget for selective high-accuracy decoding could reduce code-size and hardware overheads.
detailed_summary: The protocol applies a fast decoder to every sliding window and selectively invokes a more accurate decoder when efficiently extracted soft outputs indicate low confidence. Simulations use bivariate bicycle codes and trapped-ion-informed noise models. Depending on code and physical error rate, the method lowers logical error rates by up to 3–4 orders versus BP-LSD and 2–3 orders versus Beamsearch.
main_result: Hybrid sliding-window decoding delivers up to four orders of magnitude lower logical error rates without exceeding the available real-time budget.
application_angle: The approach trades available classical processing time for stronger fault tolerance, potentially reducing the number of physical qubits required.

title: Bandwidth-tunable thermal emitter via dynamic resonator coupling and loss
abstract: We demonstrate a dynamically tunable omnidirectional thermal emitter that can be switched from a narrowband emission state to a broadband state. The structure is a metal-backed multilayer with subwavelength thickness across the mid-infrared, which forms an angle-insensitive (up to 60°) optical cavity with one input port. We used an ultrathin VO2 layer to dynamically switch the coupling and loss coefficients of this optical cavity, resulting in narrowband emission from the vibrational mode of a polar dielectric layer that is part of the multilayer stack when the VO2 is in its insulating phase, and broadband emission from a nearly impedance-matched cavity when the VO2 is switched to its lossy metallic phase. We fabricated the structure around a free-standing silicon membrane and integrated it onto a printed circuit board (PCB), which enabled electrical switching of the emitter at the ten-to-hundred millisecond scale, and can be used for free-space identification, tagging, or communication.
one_liner: An electrically switched VO2 cavity toggles omnidirectional mid-infrared emission between narrowband and broadband states.
why_it_matters: The fabricated, PCB-integrated emitter combines directional robustness, spectral reconfiguration, and practical electrical switching.
detailed_summary: The subwavelength metal-backed multilayer forms a one-port optical cavity that remains angle-insensitive to 60°. Switching an ultrathin VO2 layer between insulating and metallic phases changes both cavity coupling and loss, selecting narrowband polar-dielectric emission or broadband near-impedance-matched emission. A free-standing silicon-membrane device integrated on a PCB switches electrically on a 10–100 ms timescale.
main_result: The fabricated emitter electrically switches between narrowband and broadband thermal emission while maintaining operation over angles up to 60°.
application_angle: Its reconfigurable infrared signature is suitable for free-space identification, dynamic tagging, and low-rate optical communication.

title: Fundamental physics with quantum sensors in space
abstract: Quantum sensors such as atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers can be used as sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model. Space offers microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, access to varying gravitational potentials, and unique opportunities involving the Sun, Moon, planets, and asteroids. These proceedings of the Aspen Center for Physics workshop on "Fundamental physics in space with quantum sensors," held February 22-27, 2026, summarize the scientific case, current capabilities, and space mission concepts for investigating dark matter, testing general relativity, and detecting gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from the ground.
one_liner: A workshop report maps how space-based quantum sensors could probe dark matter, gravity, and otherwise inaccessible gravitational-wave bands.
why_it_matters: It consolidates the scientific case, enabling technologies, and mission concepts for moving precision quantum sensing beyond terrestrial limits.
detailed_summary: These proceedings survey atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers proposed for fundamental-physics measurements in space. They connect microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, and varying gravitational potentials to searches for dark matter, tests of general relativity, and gravitational-wave detection. The report also summarizes current capabilities and candidate mission concepts discussed at the 2026 Aspen workshop.
main_result: The report defines the scientific opportunities, enabling capabilities, and mission concepts for spaceborne quantum tests of fundamental physics.
application_angle: It provides a roadmap for designing space missions that extend precision sensing into regimes unavailable to ground-based instruments.

title: Transient Synchronization and Entanglement through Shared Dissipation in Circuit QED
abstract: We propose a superconducting circuit in which two resonators couple through DC-biased SQUIDs to a common lossy auxiliary mode. Adiabatic elimination yields collective damping and correlated noise with an overlap $ξ$ whose magnitude is tuned by the flux biases and whose sign follows the relative sign of the couplings. The full three-mode dynamics confirm this reduced description. For detuned resonators, we derive the exceptional-point condition, above which the mean amplitudes lock to a common frequency. For resonant modes, unequal collective decay produces transient synchronization, antiphase or in phase depending on the relative sign of the couplings, with an analytical synchronization time set by the collective decay splitting and the initial mean amplitudes. For initially separable squeezed states, the same relaxation converts local squeezing into transient entanglement, quantified by logarithmic negativity. We obtain closed-form expressions for the squeezing threshold above which entanglement appears and for the time at which it disappears. Thermal noise suppresses entanglement without changing the mean-amplitude synchronization time at fixed parameters. For realistic circuit parameters, these effects occur within a few hundred nanoseconds and are accessible through output-field measurements. A single tunable shared channel thus produces an exceptional point, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement, and provides a controllable source of correlated noise for superconducting circuits.
one_liner: A tunable shared dissipative channel synchronizes two circuit-QED resonators and converts local squeezing into transient entanglement.
why_it_matters: The scheme turns engineered loss into a controllable resource for correlated noise, exceptional-point physics, synchronization, and entanglement.
detailed_summary: Two resonators couple through DC-biased SQUIDs to a common lossy auxiliary mode, producing tunable collective damping and correlated noise after adiabatic elimination. Detuned modes cross an exceptional-point threshold and frequency-lock, while resonant modes show transient in-phase or antiphase synchronization. For separable squeezed inputs, the same relaxation generates transient logarithmic negativity, with analytic thresholds and lifetimes; realistic dynamics occur within hundreds of nanoseconds.
main_result: A single tunable dissipative channel produces exceptional-point behavior, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement on experimentally accessible timescales.
application_angle: The architecture offers an output-field-accessible method for reservoir engineering and correlated-noise control in superconducting quantum processors.

title: Magic state cultivation with lattice-surgery escape on superconducting hardware
abstract: Magic state cultivation (MSC) is a low-overhead protocol for fault-tolerantly preparing logical magic states. In this work, we implement two MSC variants to prepare a magic state in a distance-5 code on a publicly available IBM Nighthawk processor. The first is a lattice-surgery escape, recently proposed by Hirano et al. and experimentally studied here for the first time. The second is a grafting escape, previously demonstrated by Rosenfeld et al., and extended here by incorporating a switch into a matchable code. Both protocols begin with fault-tolerant cultivation of a T state on a color code, followed by an escape into a larger code. We decode the results using minimum-weight perfect matching or Tesseract on circuit-level error models calibrated to the hardware noise. Compared with the previous experiment, our cultivated T state achieves a logical error probability of 2e-5 at the T-state injection angle, nearly 10x lower with about 3x the retainment. Moreover, our execution of the grafting escape has a 2x lower logical error rate per stabilizer round at a higher retainment. When comparing the two protocols under identical execution conditions and complementary gap postselection based on decoder confidence, lattice-surgery escape into the surface code preserves a T-state fidelity above 0.99 ten rounds after escape at about 5% retainment. By contrast, matchable-switched grafting drops below 0.95 fidelity at comparable retainment. Furthermore, the lattice-surgery escape reaches a logical error rate per stabilizer round of about 0.14% with around 11% average shot retainment. These results establish lattice-surgery escape as a practical MSC protocol that benefits from a direct transition into a surface code, and demonstrate the lowest MSC error and the highest surface-code magic-state fidelity reported to date, advancing the experimental realization of fault-tolerant non-Clifford gadgets.
one_liner: Distance-5 magic-state cultivation with lattice-surgery escape achieves record-low logical error and over 0.99 surface-code fidelity on IBM hardware.
why_it_matters: It experimentally advances a lower-overhead route to the high-fidelity logical magic states required for fault-tolerant non-Clifford operations.
detailed_summary: The authors implement lattice-surgery and matchable-switched grafting escapes for a cultivated distance-5 logical T state on an IBM Nighthawk processor. Cultivation reaches a logical error probability of 2e-5 at the injection angle, nearly tenfold below the prior experiment with about threefold higher retainment. Lattice-surgery escape preserves fidelity above 0.99 after ten surface-code rounds at roughly 5% retainment and reaches about 0.14% logical error per stabilizer round at approximately 11% average retainment.
main_result: Lattice-surgery escape delivers the reported lowest MSC error and highest surface-code magic-state fidelity, outperforming grafting under matched conditions.
application_angle: The protocol supplies a practical path toward fault-tolerant T gates and other non-Clifford gadgets on superconducting quantum processors.

title: QCap: a physics-corrected graph neural network for the capacitance matrix of any planar superconducting device layout
abstract: Electromagnetic simulations of device layouts to extract capacitance are computationally intensive, a major obstacle to accurate design of circuit devices. Machine learning models can bypass these simulations, but previous approaches have been restricted to layouts using only particular components, and require thousands of simulations of those same components as training data. We present QCap, a model that accurately predicts the Maxwell capacitance matrix of an arbitrary superconducting device layout in seconds, compared to minutes to hours of Ansys Q3D simulations. We develop a novel design-embedding algorithm that converts the layout into a universal graph format, allowing the model to work with any layout created with any tool. To achieve high accuracy, we obtain a coarse physics prior from a fast method of moments simulation of capacitance, then train the model to correct this prior. On 4,009 test designs withheld from training data the model outputs agree with Q3D simulations to a median error of 0.177%, and on never-seen component families it stays below 1% error. We demonstrate the model's scaling by obtaining the capacitance matrix of a 9-superconducting-qubit device in 12 seconds on a laptop (compared to 19.9 h and 228 GB of memory in Ansys) with sub-percent error, and capacitance of a (too large to simulate) 100-qubit, 781-conductor device in 3.4 min on a laptop. We provide the open-source models and data on SQuADDS and Hugging Face. Our results provide a powerful tool for large-scale accurate circuit design and guide the development of models to bypass other physical simulations.
one_liner: QCap predicts arbitrary planar superconducting-layout capacitance matrices in seconds using a physics-corrected graph neural network.
why_it_matters: It replaces a major electromagnetic-simulation bottleneck with sub-percent predictions that scale from unfamiliar components to 100-qubit layouts.
detailed_summary: QCap embeds layouts from arbitrary design tools as universal graphs and corrects a coarse method-of-moments capacitance prior with a learned model. Across 4,009 held-out designs, its Maxwell capacitance matrices have 0.177% median error against Ansys Q3D, while unseen component families remain below 1% error. It solves a nine-qubit layout in 12 seconds rather than 19.9 hours and scales to a 100-qubit, 781-conductor design in 3.4 minutes on a laptop.
main_result: QCap achieves sub-percent capacitance accuracy with orders-of-magnitude lower runtime and memory demands than full Q3D simulation.
application_angle: Open models and data can accelerate large-scale qubit-layout optimization, parameter extraction, and automated superconducting-device design.

title: Demonstration of a Qubit Control Scheme Compatible with Superconducting Digital Signals
abstract: Superconducting quantum computing faces a critical scalability bottleneck arising from the escalating complexity of traditional analog control infrastructure. Single-Flux-Quantum(SFQ) systems operate at cryogenic temperatures and offer a potential route to addressing these challenges. Using microwave signals at qubit-dependent frequencies to trigger SFQ pulses requires many independent analog microwave sources, limiting the potential to reduce control wiring and increase integration density. A scalable SFQ control system therefore needs a scheme that can address qubits with different transition frequencies using a common clock. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a control scheme for implementing both single- and two-qubit gates. The scheme uses guiding waveforms to rapidly generate bipolar high-speed pulse sequences on a common clock, providing a basis for future implementation in SFQ control systems. Numerically, this scheme achieves a simulated fidelity of 99.99% for 40ns $R(\varphi, \fracπ{2})$ gates with arbitrary initial phases and 99.9% for 100ns controlled-Z(CZ) gates. Experimentally, by utilizing an arbitrary waveform generator(AWG) operated at a fixed sampling rate of 25GSa/s to deliver the bipolar high-speed pulse sequences, we successfully demonstrate 40ns single-qubit gates with an average gate fidelity of 99.94% estimated using cross-entropy benchmarking(XEB) and 120ns CZ gates with 99.63% fidelity. These results demonstrate the feasibility of common-clock encoded pulse control for both single- and two-qubit gates.
one_liner: Common-clock bipolar pulse control achieves 99.94% single-qubit and 99.63% CZ gate fidelity in a superconducting-qubit experiment.
why_it_matters: The approach reduces reliance on qubit-specific microwave sources and supports denser cryogenic SFQ-compatible control infrastructure.
detailed_summary: The proposed scheme uses guiding waveforms to encode high-speed bipolar pulse sequences on a common clock for qubits with different transition frequencies. Simulations predict 99.99% fidelity for 40 ns arbitrary-phase single-qubit rotations and 99.9% for 100 ns CZ gates. Using a fixed-rate 25 GSa/s AWG, the experiment realizes 40 ns single-qubit gates at 99.94% XEB fidelity and 120 ns CZ gates at 99.63%.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates high-fidelity single- and two-qubit gates using pulse encoding compatible with future SFQ signal generation.
application_angle: Common-clock addressing could reduce analog microwave hardware, cryogenic wiring, and control-system complexity in scaled superconducting processors.

title: Observation of temporal routing of topological edge states
abstract: The switching or routing of topological edge states is crucial for disorder-immune state transfer. Previous experimental observations have primarily relied on optical waveguide arrays that treat the spatial coordinate as an equivalent temporal dimension. However, direct experimental observation of the routing dynamics of topological edge states in physical time remains challenging. Here, we report the experimental observation of temporal routing of topological edge states. By constructing a lattice composed of two coupled nonlinear Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chains, the topological edge states exhibit temporal routing behavior controlled by nonlinearity. As the excitation voltage increases from the linear regime, we observe that the voltage intensity distribution transitions from periodic interchain exchange to slowed interchain exchange and ultimately to localization with strongly suppressed interchain exchange, thereby validating the phenomenon of temporal routing. These dynamics are experimentally observed within a finite time window limited by circuit dissipation. Our findings provide valuable insights into the temporal manipulation of topological edge states.
one_liner: Coupled nonlinear SSH chains directly reveal voltage-controlled routing and localization of topological edge states in physical time.
why_it_matters: The experiment moves topological-state routing from spatial analogies to real-time dynamics and exposes nonlinearity as a practical control knob.
detailed_summary: The experiment constructs two coupled nonlinear Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chains and tracks their edge-state voltage distributions over physical time. Increasing excitation drives the response from periodic interchain exchange to slower transfer and finally localization with strongly suppressed exchange. Although circuit dissipation limits the observation window, the measurements directly validate nonlinear temporal routing dynamics.
main_result: The authors directly observe excitation-controlled temporal exchange, slowdown, and localization of topological edge states.
application_angle: Nonlinear temporal routing could enable robust switching and state-transfer functions in topological photonic or wave-based networks.

title: MASQ: Measurement-Adaptive Sampling for Near-Clifford Quantum Error Correction Circuits
abstract: Classical sampling of quantum error correction (QEC) circuits supports fault-tolerant protocol evaluation, but estimating rare logical failures requires many independent shots. Frame-active-state simulators isolate non-stabilizer information in a dense active-state vector, yet dense-state processing remains exponential in the active width. This paper presents MASQ, an exact measurement-adaptive sampler for near-Clifford QEC circuits based on selective materialization of non-Clifford rotations. At each measurement boundary, MASQ materializes only rotations in a measurement-relevant closure capturing direct and indirect non-commuting dependencies, deferring the rest to limit active-state expansion. Stabilizer-assisted elimination further removes rotations certified to be invisible to all future measurements. A circuit-dependent schedule is computed once and shared across shots, while adaptive caching of conditional Born probabilities and batched execution reduce repeated sampling work while preserving the measurement-record distribution. Across 19 QEC benchmarks, MASQ reduces peak active width by up to 40 active virtual qubits and achieves up to 8,098-fold CPU throughput speedup over Clifft on multi-round circuits.
one_liner: MASQ accelerates exact sampling of near-Clifford QEC circuits by materializing only measurement-relevant non-Clifford rotations.
why_it_matters: Faster rare-event sampling can substantially reduce the classical cost of evaluating fault-tolerant protocols and logical failure rates.
detailed_summary: MASQ is an exact measurement-adaptive sampler that restricts active-state expansion to the closure of non-Clifford rotations relevant to each measurement. Stabilizer-assisted elimination removes rotations invisible to future measurements, while shared schedules, conditional-probability caching, and batching amortize repeated work. Across 19 QEC benchmarks, it reduced peak active width by up to 40 virtual qubits and delivered up to an 8,098-fold CPU-throughput improvement over Clifft.
main_result: MASQ preserves the measurement-record distribution while achieving up to an 8,098-fold CPU speedup and reducing peak active width by as many as 40 qubits.
application_angle: The method enables much larger exact Monte Carlo campaigns for estimating rare logical failures in fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

title: CHEQ: A Concurrent Hardware Evaluation Platform for QEC Decoders via Batch-Invariant Circuit-Level Noise Sampling
abstract: Hardware quantum error correction (QEC) decoders require validation of logical error suppression and timing compliance before deployment. Rare logical failures and deadline violations demand extensive sampling, while algorithm-level software evaluation does not directly measure hardware response times. Circuit-level noise models contain many error mechanisms but few firings per shot at low physical error rates, making exhaustive per-shot scanning inefficient. We present CHEQ, an FPGA platform integrating on-chip sampling, concurrent decoder evaluation, scoring, and RISC-V control. Its Sampling Units use geometric skipping to sample firing locations from detector error models and amortize mechanism traversal across shots within each batch. Under independent random draws and exact geometric sampling, the shot distribution is invariant to batch size, enabling a memory-throughput tradeoff. A throughput model guides joint selection of the Sampling Unit count, batch size, and decoder count under FPGA resource constraints. Across evaluated conditions, the pooled one-sided 95% upper bound on the weighted root-mean-square relative firing-rate difference from Stim is 0.16%. At a batch size of 4,096, a Sampling Unit uses only 4.8%-11.2% of a Helios decoder's LUTs for code distances 7, 9, 11, and 13. On an AMD VCU118 FPGA at code distance 7 and physical error rate 10^-3, two Sampling Units supply 20 Helios decoders at 49.2 million shots/s, completing 10^10 shots in 3.4 minutes without host-side shot generation.
one_liner: CHEQ integrates exact low-rate noise sampling and concurrent hardware-decoder evaluation on an FPGA at tens of millions of shots per second.
why_it_matters: It enables rapid, hardware-timed validation of QEC decoders under circuit-level noise without host-side shot-generation bottlenecks.
detailed_summary: CHEQ combines on-chip detector-error-model sampling, concurrent decoder execution, scoring, and RISC-V control on an FPGA. Geometric skipping avoids exhaustive scanning of rarely firing error mechanisms, while batch-invariant sampling permits memory-throughput tradeoffs without altering shot statistics. On an AMD VCU118, two sampling units supplied 20 Helios decoders at 49.2 million shots per second and processed 10^10 shots in 3.4 minutes.
platform_or_system: AMD VCU118 FPGA QEC evaluation platform
main_result: CHEQ generated circuit-level noise for 20 hardware decoders at 49.2 million shots per second with firing rates closely matching Stim.
application_angle: The platform supports deployment-oriented testing of both logical-error suppression and real hardware decoding deadlines.

title: Logical error prediction and geometry selection for rectangular surface codes under biased circuit-level noise
abstract: Realistic quantum hardware often exhibits biased noise, but at the circuit level this bias may affect only a subset of operations and need not be transferred uniformly to logical errors. The logical response to a given physical bias is therefore central to selecting resource-efficient surface code geometries. Here, we study unrotated rectangular surface codes under standard depolarizing and superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise models. We first construct geometry-dependent logical error rate models from unbiased circuit-level simulations. We then use logical sensitivities to compare the responses to localized idle-bias and global physical error perturbations, defining logical-error-type-dependent response coefficients from an unbiased reference circuit without fitting to finite-bias data. These coefficients are incorporated through effective error parameters, yielding a median fold error of 1.09 over the evaluated finite-bias conditions. Geometries selected by the model are validated through direct biased circuit-level simulations. At a physical error rate of 0.004 and a target logical error rate of 10^{-3}, the validated rectangular codes reduce physical qubit overhead by up to 42.4% and 26.2% under the two noise models, respectively, relative to unrotated square codes. These results provide a practical link between circuit-level bias response and resource-efficient surface code design.
one_liner: A sensitivity-based model selects rectangular surface-code geometries that exploit circuit-level noise bias while meeting logical-error targets.
why_it_matters: Bias-aware geometry selection can lower the physical-qubit cost of fault tolerance without requiring extensive finite-bias fitting.
detailed_summary: The study models unrotated rectangular surface codes under depolarizing and superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise. Logical sensitivities extracted from unbiased reference simulations are converted into response coefficients and effective error parameters, producing a median fold error of 1.09 across tested biased conditions. Direct simulations validate geometries that reduce physical-qubit overhead by up to 42.4% and 26.2% relative to square codes at a physical error rate of 0.004 and target logical error rate of 10^-3.
main_result: Validated bias-aware rectangular codes reduced physical-qubit overhead by up to 42.4% while satisfying the evaluated logical-error target.
application_angle: The approach provides hardware designers with a practical method for matching code geometry to measured circuit-level noise asymmetry.

title: Circuit compilation in the quspect quantum SDK: selecting routings after coupling-constrained resynthesis
abstract: quspect is an open-source quantum computing SDK that provides circuit construction, C++ state-vector simulation with adjoint gradients, support for variational and combinatorial-optimization algorithms, Hamiltonian simulation, control-pulse envelopes and backends for several cloud quantum processors. Here we describe and evaluate its circuit compiler. Routing and synthesis interact: inserting a SWAP can change the circuit structure that later optimization exploits. At its highest optimization level, the compiler evaluates a screened set of routing candidates by their cost after coupling-constrained resynthesis.
