The pipeline combines parity-state A* search for small CNOT-phase regions, heuristic synthesis for larger regions, and numerical three-qubit instantiation with a per-block 10^-9 check. For a fixed phase polynomial, A* certifies the minimum CX count when it reaches a goal within budget. On an evaluation set of 55 circuits from 41 arXiv papers on five topologies, the compiler uses 0.616 times as many two-qubit gates as Qiskit O3 (95% circuit-cluster bootstrap interval 0.555-0.679) at 0.592 times its depth. BQSKit level 2 reaches 0.853 and tket 0.930. On a 17-qubit superconducting processor, the compiled circuits had the fewest CZ gates in all six scenarios of the main run. Ablations assess the contributions within the integrated pipeline.
one_liner: The quspect compiler ranks routing choices after coupling-constrained resynthesis, sharply reducing entangling gates and circuit depth.
why_it_matters: Lower two-qubit-gate counts and depth can directly improve the fidelity and feasibility of workloads on connectivity-limited processors.
detailed_summary: The quspect compiler evaluates screened routing candidates only after coupling-constrained resynthesis, capturing interactions between SWAP insertion and subsequent optimization. It combines parity-state A* search, scalable heuristic synthesis, and numerically checked three-qubit instantiation. Across 55 circuits and five topologies, it used 0.616 times the two-qubit gates and 0.592 times the depth of Qiskit O3; on a 17-qubit superconducting processor, it produced the fewest CZ gates in all six reported scenarios.
main_result: Quspect reduced two-qubit gates to 61.6% and depth to 59.2% of Qiskit O3 on the evaluated circuit set.
application_angle: The compiler can increase executable circuit size and fidelity on near-term devices constrained by sparse coupling and noisy entangling gates.

title: Dual-Comb Spectrometry Enabled by Gain-Assisted Electro-Optic Fiber Ring Resonators
abstract: Broadband dual-comb spectroscopy (DCS) with widely tunable repetition rates and simplified frequency stabilization is desirable for diverse sensing applications. Here, we demonstrate DCS using two gain-assisted fiber ring resonators that share a continuous-wave (CW) laser and incorporate intracavity electro-optic (EO) phase modulation. Intracavity gain compensates for round-trip losses, sustaining repeated phase modulation and enabling flat-top comb spectra with a 20-dB bandwidth exceeding 1.8 THz. Harmonic-order selection provides widely tunable repetition rates from approximately 5 to 0.2 GHz without substantially compromising the spectral bandwidth. The comb phase noise closely follows that of the radio-frequency (RF) drive at low offset frequencies. Without active frequency stabilization, the two combs exhibit an instrument-limited beat-note linewidth of 2 Hz, indicating high mutual coherence. The generated dual combs enable high-speed DCS at the single-interferogram rate, providing a platform for dynamic spectroscopic measurements. This all-fiber architecture, together with its simplified operation, offers a promising route towards compact and readily integrable dual-comb instruments.
one_liner: Gain-assisted electro-optic fiber rings generate mutually coherent, broadband dual combs with widely tunable repetition rates.
why_it_matters: The all-fiber design combines broad bandwidth, flexible repetition rate, and stabilization-free coherence for compact dynamic spectroscopy.
detailed_summary: Two gain-assisted fiber ring resonators share one continuous-wave laser and use intracavity electro-optic phase modulation to form dual frequency combs. Optical gain compensates round-trip loss, enabling flat-top spectra with more than 1.8 THz of 20-dB bandwidth and repetition rates tunable from about 5 to 0.2 GHz. Without active frequency stabilization, the comb pair exhibits an instrument-limited 2 Hz beat-note linewidth and supports spectroscopy at the single-interferogram rate.
main_result: The system produced over 1.8 THz of comb bandwidth, 0.2–5 GHz repetition-rate tuning, and a 2 Hz mutual beat-note linewidth without active stabilization.
application_angle: Its compact all-fiber architecture is suited to high-speed measurements of dynamically changing chemical, biological, or physical spectra.

title: Topological Timing of Bound States by Spacetime Mass Windings
abstract: Topology usually determines where a wave is trapped. Here we show that it can also determine when a trapped state brightens or dims. We consider a dimerized photonic lattice in which a real Dirac mass, varying in space, binds a Jackiw-Rebbi state, while staggered gain and loss, switched in time, act as an imaginary Dirac mass on that same state. Together, the two masses form a mass field in space and time whose isolated zeros carry an integer winding. Combining a continuum Dirac description with finite-lattice simulations, we show that the sign of this winding fixes whether the bound state reaches a maximum or a minimum at the switch, while the gain and loss remain below the bulk gap. The windings obey a conservation law: they are created and annihilated in pairs, and their sum along a boundary determines which extrema are protected. Full-wave simulations of a passive waveguide array, in which the propagation distance plays the role of time, reproduce these predictions with loss alone. These results provide a topological handle on the timing of localized optical responses, relevant to switching, gating, and pulse shaping of confined modes in integrated photonic circuits and topological lasers.
one_liner: Spacetime winding of real and imaginary Dirac masses topologically determines when a localized photonic state brightens or dims.
why_it_matters: Topological protection is extended from spatial localization to the timing of optical extrema, offering a robust control mechanism for integrated photonics.
detailed_summary: A dimerized photonic lattice uses a spatially varying real Dirac mass to bind a Jackiw-Rebbi state and a time-switched imaginary mass to control its amplitude. The integer winding around isolated zeros of the combined spacetime mass field fixes whether the localized state reaches a maximum or minimum at the switching event. Continuum, finite-lattice, and passive full-wave waveguide simulations agree, with propagation distance serving as effective time and loss implementing the required dynamics.
main_result: The sign of a conserved spacetime mass winding determines and protects whether the bound-state intensity peaks or dips at the switching point.
application_angle: The effect offers topology-based timing control for optical switching, gating, pulse shaping, confined modes, and topological lasers.

title: Optimizing interference zeros for finite-pulse transmission in waveguide quantum electrodynamics
abstract: A photon pulse occupies a range of frequencies, so suppressing reflection at its carrier need not minimize the error of the transmitted pulse. We study two separated emitters coupled to a common waveguide at several contact points. Interference between the contact paths can make the coupling that drives each emitter quadratic in frequency detuning. With matched propagation and emitter resonances centered on the carrier, the reflected fields cancel once more. Their combined reflection probability is then sixth order at zero loss. Separating each local double zero into two simple zeros can nevertheless improve transmission of a finite pulse. We minimize the leading narrowband error within this common static adjustment, counting reflection, absorption, and distortion of the transmitted mode. For a Gaussian pulse without loss, the minimum is two-fifths of the error for coincident zeros. Independent emitter loss favors a smaller separation because photons entering separate reservoirs do not share the cancellation of the reflected fields. The optimum follows from the pulse spectrum and the relative weight of these two processes. Uniform and Su--Schrieffer--Heeger waveguides realize the mechanism. In the latter, coordinated contact and resonance adjustments also preserve the full ratio of complex transmission amplitudes for opposite incidence directions. Finite-band calculations determine how the benefit changes with bandwidth and contact errors.
one_liner: Splitting interference zeros reduces finite-pulse transmission error in multi-contact waveguide QED, reaching two-fifths of the coincident-zero error.
why_it_matters: The optimization offers a static route to higher-fidelity photon transmission while accounting for reflection, absorption, pulse distortion, loss, and fabrication errors.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes two spatially separated emitters coupled to a common waveguide through multiple contact points. Although coincident quadratic coupling zeros produce sixth-order reflection suppression at zero loss, separating each double zero into two simple zeros better matches a finite Gaussian spectrum and lowers the leading narrowband error to two-fifths. Loss shifts the optimal separation, and finite-band calculations quantify sensitivity to bandwidth and contact errors in uniform and Su–Schrieffer–Heeger waveguides.
main_result: A static splitting of interference zeros substantially improves finite-pulse transmission, with a lossless Gaussian minimum equal to 40% of the coincident-zero error.
application_angle: The method can improve routing and transmission fidelity for shaped single-photon pulses in integrated quantum photonic networks without dynamic control.

title: Generating Massive Mechanical Superpositions through Qubit-Mediated Interference
abstract: We propose a method towards demonstrating a quantum superposition of a massive mechanical resonator without the need for exact ground-state cooling, a requirement that becomes increasingly difficult to satisfy for low-frequency resonators. Our scheme relies on coupling the resonator to a spin-qubit. Using magnetic force coupling between the motion of the mechanical resonator and the spin-qubit, the resonator is forced into attracted and repelled states as the spin-qubit is coherently controlled. Interference between the resonator states can be observed when a series of $\tfracπ{2}$-pulses is applied to the spin-qubit within the coherence time of the resonator. The protocol describes a true which-path interference experiment suitable for use at ultra-low temperatures, since it requires only three $\tfracπ{2}$-pulses, separated in time by half a mechanical period, thus minimizing the heat-load and duration of the experiment. By analysing the experimental requirements necessary to successfully execute the protocol, we show that the protocol is suitable for resonators in a broad regime of resonance frequencies, ranging from 1kHz resonators, which have the advantage of a relatively high spin-coupling, to resonators of more than 100kHz, whose mechanical mode is easier to cool. We show that interference remains visible for resonator mode occupations exceeding 10 phonons. Lastly, we observe that an implementation of the protocol with low-frequency mechanical resonators provides a promising approach towards testing objective collapse models.
one_liner: Three spin-control pulses can reveal interference between massive mechanical states without exact ground-state cooling, even above 10 phonons.
why_it_matters: The low-pulse-count protocol relaxes cooling and heat-load constraints while enabling macroscopic-superposition tests across resonators from 1 kHz to above 100 kHz.
detailed_summary: A spin qubit magnetically coupled to a mechanical resonator creates spin-dependent attracted and repelled motional states. Three π/2 pulses, separated by half a mechanical period, recombine the paths and map their interference onto the qubit within the resonator coherence time. The analysis predicts visible interference for initial occupations above 10 phonons and covers mechanical frequencies from about 1 kHz to beyond 100 kHz.
main_result: The proposed three-pulse protocol retains observable mechanical interference above 10 phonons without requiring exact ground-state preparation.
application_angle: It provides an experimentally economical route to massive-superposition demonstrations and objective-collapse tests using low-frequency mechanical devices.

title: Anti-aging Squeezed Quantum Battery
abstract: Exhibiting the superiority of energy storage and conversion over its classical counterpart, quantum battery (QB) emerges as a promising platform to revolutionize traditional energy technologies. However, their practical performance is severely constrained by the ubiquitous decoherence in microscopic world, which causes rapid aging and reduced ergotropy. Here, we propose a decoherence-tolerant QB consisting of a continuous-variable bosonic mode. Acting as the quantum resource, the utilized squeezing endows the QB with unprecedented energy capacity and ergotropy. Through investigating the non-Markovian decoherence effect on the QB, we find that such squeezing enhanced performance can be persistently preserved under the influence of decoherence as long as a bound state is present in the energy spectrum of the total system formed by the QB and the environment. This decoherence-tolerance feature is even maintained under moderate finite-temperature condition. Providing a useful energy storage paradigm for designing long-lived QBs, our result sheds light on the realization of anti-aging QBs.
one_liner: A squeezed bosonic quantum battery can retain enhanced capacity and ergotropy under non-Markovian decoherence when a system–environment bound state forms.
why_it_matters: The work identifies a concrete spectral mechanism for preserving useful stored quantum energy, including under moderate finite-temperature conditions.
detailed_summary: The proposal uses squeezing in a continuous-variable bosonic mode to increase both stored energy and extractable work. A non-Markovian open-system analysis shows that a bound state in the combined battery–environment spectrum prevents the squeezing-enabled advantage from decaying away. The predicted protection persists at moderate finite temperature, providing a design condition for long-lived bosonic batteries.
main_result: Formation of a system–environment bound state preserves squeezing-enhanced energy capacity and ergotropy against decoherence.
application_angle: Spectral engineering of photonic or resonator environments could support longer-lived quantum energy-storage elements with improved usable capacity.

title: Quantum Codes for Distributed Quantum Fault Sensing
abstract: Targeted recovery in modular quantum processors requires identifying the component affected by a fault. Independent qubits can monitor faults through repeated preparation and measurement. Bell-pair probes improve the guaranteed correct-site probability for unknown local channels, but require partners kept away from the fault. Can entanglement among exposed probes supply this advantage without protected storage? We establish a quantum-code criterion for optimal distributed fault sensing of one unknown local qubit channel with strength in a prescribed positive range. For one interrogation with zero false alarms and no background noise, suitable code states attain the optimal worst-case correct-site probability, improving on independent probes by 50% with every qubit exposed. Exact attainment is equivalent to mutually orthogonal input and single-qubit Pauli error subspaces. Pairwise entanglement gives no improvement, and entanglement depth at most four cannot exceed 95.54% of the optimum without protected ancillas. Approaching the optimum without protected ancillas also requires a number of probes proportional to the array size to participate in larger entangled factors. For a persistent fault under memoryless depolarizing background of fixed strength 0 < eta < 1, independent probes already attain the optimal logarithmic interrogation scaling at fixed success between zero and one and a positive false-alarm budget. In three 1000-site comparisons with specified readouts, an encoded-probe protocol certifies fewer interrogations than independent probes and only one more than optimally decoded ideal Bell pairs, while storing no protected qubits.
one_liner: Quantum-code probes localize an unknown faulty qubit channel with a 50% worst-case advantage over independent probes while exposing every qubit.
why_it_matters: The results define when encoded probes improve fault localization in modular processors and quantify the multipartite entanglement needed without protected ancillas.
detailed_summary: The paper derives a code criterion for optimally identifying one unknown local qubit channel with zero false alarms and no background noise. Optimal code states require mutually orthogonal input and single-qubit Pauli-error subspaces and improve worst-case correct-site probability by 50% over independent probes. Pairwise entanglement gives no gain, entanglement depth four reaches at most 95.54% of optimum, and a 1000-site comparison shows encoded probes nearly match ideal Bell-pair performance without protected storage.
platform_or_system: Encoded probe array in a modular quantum processor
main_result: Suitable quantum-code states attain optimal single-fault localization and a 50% worst-case improvement over independent exposed probes.
application_angle: Encoded diagnostic states could reduce interrogation overhead when locating faulty modules in large quantum processors that lack reliable protected ancillas.

title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits
abstract: Symmetric circuits require every symmetry of the input to extend to an automorphism of the circuit. In the classical setting, their connection to descriptive complexity yields strong unconditional lower bounds. We extend this approach to the quantum model of symmetric computation defined by Castro-Silva, Gur, and Strelchuk (ITCS 2026), proving a tradeoff between circuit size and entanglement width (the smallest $b$ such that, on every computational-basis input, the state after each layer factors into states on at most $b$ qubits each). Our main result identifies a graph property decidable in classical polynomial time that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits on $n$-vertex graphs with entanglement width $o(n/\log n)$ can compute. The bound holds for circuits with arbitrary one-qubit and two-qubit gates and unrestricted depth, and remains valid under the weaker notion of symmetry with respect to even permutations of vertices. Our proof is based on a new quantum pebble game based on the partial trace. The resulting indistinguishability theorem transfers classical pebble-game lower bounds to quantum circuits with restricted entanglement. By contrast, without entanglement restrictions, we show that every graph property in BQP can be computed by a uniform family of polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits. Restricting to circuits with no entanglement at all, we show that polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width 1 can compute every graph property definable in fixed-point logic with counting. Finally, we give an efficient symmetric implementation of QAOA for MAX 3XOR, providing a starting point for studying entanglement lower bounds in quantum optimization algorithms.
one_liner: Polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits need entanglement width of order n/log n to compute some classically tractable graph properties.
why_it_matters: The unconditional tradeoff isolates multipartite entanglement as a necessary resource for certain symmetry-constrained quantum computations, independent of circuit depth.
detailed_summary: The authors prove that some polynomial-time graph property cannot be computed by polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits whose entanglement width is o(n/log n), even with unrestricted depth and arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates. A new partial-trace quantum pebble game transfers classical indistinguishability lower bounds into the quantum setting. They also show unrestricted-entanglement symmetric circuits capture graph properties in BQP and provide a symmetric QAOA implementation for MAX 3XOR.
main_result: The work establishes an unconditional size–entanglement tradeoff requiring near-linear entanglement width for a specific efficiently decidable graph property.
application_angle: The bound informs hardware and compiler designs for permutation-symmetric algorithms by showing when limited entanglement connectivity fundamentally blocks computation.

title: Measurement-Conditioned Bloch-Sphere State Steering with a Continuous-Variable Pointer
abstract: We investigate measurement-conditioned state steering of a qubit coupled to a continuous-variable pointer through a state-dependent displacement interaction. A position measurement on the pointer induces a nonunitary conditional transformation of the qubit, allowing its post-measurement state to move along a trajectory on the Bloch sphere. We derive the conditional state, the measurement-outcome distribution, and the corresponding Bloch-sphere coordinates. For a real Gaussian pointer, the conditional state follows a meridian, whereas a phase-engineered Gaussian pointer produces a trajectory with a measurement-dependent azimuthal angle. We further describe outcome-dependent unitary feedback for preparing a prescribed target state from a known initial qubit state. We distinguish this state-preparation task from implementing a universal deterministic single-qubit gate, which does not follow from the proposed interaction and measurement alone. Finally, we derive the quantum Fisher information of the joint qubit--pointer state for estimating the displacement-generating parameter and discuss the implications of pointer squeezing, phase engineering, and experimental implementation. The results provide a framework for analysing conditional Bloch-sphere steering using continuous-variable measurement resources.
one_liner: Continuous-variable pointer measurements steer a coupled qubit along controllable Bloch-sphere trajectories and support outcome-dependent target-state preparation.
why_it_matters: The framework connects pointer shaping, squeezing, measurement, feedback, and metrological sensitivity in an experimentally accessible hybrid quantum-control primitive.
detailed_summary: A state-dependent displacement entangles a qubit with a continuous-variable pointer, after which a pointer-position outcome induces a nonunitary conditional qubit transformation. Real Gaussian pointers produce meridional Bloch-sphere paths, while phase-engineered Gaussians generate outcome-dependent azimuthal motion. The authors derive target-state feedback and the joint-state quantum Fisher information, while clarifying that the primitive alone is not a universal deterministic one-qubit gate.
platform_or_system: Qubit coupled to a Gaussian continuous-variable pointer
main_result: Pointer phase engineering and measurement-conditioned feedback enable tunable Bloch-sphere steering and preparation of a prescribed qubit state.
application_angle: The scheme offers a hybrid photonic interface for conditional qubit preparation, feedback control, and displacement-parameter sensing.

title: Giant and sign-tunable spin Hall effect of light in a nonlocal nonlinear Rydberg medium
abstract: We demonstrate that long-range Rydberg atom interactions provide a tunable mechanism for generating the giant spin Hall effect of light (SHEL) in a cold atomic medium. For a coherently driven 87Rb medium with Rydberg S states, we derive the linear, local, and nonlocal Kerr susceptibilities for the two orthogonal probe polarization components and evaluate the resulting spatial and angular SHEL shifts. The nonlocal third-order susceptibility reshapes the complex birefringence of the medium, and drastically enhances the y-polarized SHEL shift by about one to two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, it can reverse the direction of both the spatial and angular shifts relative to the predictions of linear response. The effect is controllably tuned by the laser detuning, the quantization-axis orientation, the atomic density, and the principal quantum number of the Rydberg state. In the 87Rb medium, we find that the spatial and angular shifts reverse sign when the principal quantum number of the Rydberg state are around n=40 and 60, respectively. At high-lying excited Rydberg states, the spatial shift can be enhanced to several tens of micrometres-a magnitude that should be directly observable in experiment. These results demonstrate that Rydberg-mediated nonlocal optical nonlinearity is an efficient mechanism for spin-dependent light transport and for future photonic sensing applications.
one_liner: Rydberg-mediated nonlocal Kerr response enables giant, sign-tunable spin Hall shifts of light in a cold 87Rb medium.
why_it_matters: Tens-of-micrometre, optically tunable spin-dependent shifts could support directly measurable photonic sensing and beam-steering functions.
detailed_summary: The authors derive linear, local Kerr, and nonlocal Kerr susceptibilities for orthogonal probe polarizations in coherently driven cold 87Rb with Rydberg S states. Long-range Rydberg interactions reshape the complex birefringence, enhancing the y-polarized spatial and angular spin Hall shifts by one to two orders of magnitude. Calculations predict sign reversals near principal quantum numbers n=40 and n=60 and spatial shifts reaching several tens of micrometres at high-lying states.
main_result: Nonlocal Rydberg interactions produce giant, controllable spin Hall shifts and can reverse both their spatial and angular directions.
application_angle: The large observable shifts offer a tunable mechanism for polarization-sensitive optical sensing and spin-dependent photonic transport.

title: Quantum Random Number Generators: principles, practical challenges and mainstream implementations
abstract: Quantum random number generators have become a cornerstone technology for modern digital cryptography, including key generation, quantum key distribution, and post-quantum cryptographic systems. While existing reviews typically concentrate on specific entropy sources or implementation platforms, a comprehensive perspective encompassing the complete QRNG pipeline remains largely absent. This work addresses this gap by providing a unified review of the theoretical foundations, practical methodologies, and technological developments that underpin modern QRNGs. We examine randomness from both classical and quantum perspectives and survey the principal discrete-variable and continuous-variable entropy sources, together with entropy estimation, randomness certification, extraction techniques, randomness enhancement protocols, and statistical validation methods. Beyond the fundamental components, we review representative implementations reported in the literature, comparing performance metrics, architectural trade-offs, integration strategies, and attainable generation rates across different technological platforms. Practical deployment challenges, including scalability, trust assumptions, hardware integration, and cryptographic adoption, are also discussed. By complementing the discussion with a broad survey of state-of-the-art implementations and applications, this review provides researchers with a comprehensive reference on the current landscape, open challenges, and future directions of quantum random number generation.
one_liner: A unified review maps the full QRNG pipeline from quantum entropy sources through certification, extraction, validation, and deployment.
why_it_matters: It connects device physics to cryptographic readiness, helping practitioners compare trust models, integration trade-offs, and attainable rates.
detailed_summary: This review covers discrete-variable and continuous-variable quantum entropy sources alongside entropy estimation, certification, extraction, enhancement, and statistical testing. It compares representative implementations across platforms using performance, architecture, integration, and generation-rate metrics. The authors also examine scalability, trust assumptions, hardware integration, and adoption in key generation, QKD, and post-quantum cryptography.
main_result: The work provides an end-to-end taxonomy and comparative survey of modern QRNG principles, implementations, performance, and deployment challenges.
application_angle: The review supports selection and engineering of QRNG systems for cryptographic key generation, QKD, and post-quantum security infrastructure.

title: Tomographic reconstruction of non-Markovian Gaussian noise in continuous-variable photonic systems
abstract: Memory effects in continuous-variable (CV) photonic systems can make standard Markovian Gaussian noise models inaccurate, even when the average noise strength is correctly calibrated. We propose a theoretical and simulation-based tomography framework for reconstructing such memory effects directly from time-resolved homodyne data. The method estimates an effective time-local Gaussian generator, represented by drift and diffusion matrices, using a regularized maximumlikelihood procedure constrained by complete positivity (CP) of the finite-time Gaussian channel. This description covers any Gaussian-preserving noise dynamics for which a well-defined time-local generator exists, rather than being restricted to particular noise mechanisms. Non-Markovianity is then diagnosed at the generator level through temporary violations of local CP-divisibility, rather than from time dependence alone. This distinction is important because ordinary nonstationary noise can remain CP-divisible, whereas genuine memory can produce a non-CP-divisible reduced generator while the accumulated channel remains physical. Numerical benchmarks covering memorydependent loss, nonstationary thermal excitation, and pseudomode-mediated memory show that the reconstruction distinguishes CP-divisible time-dependent noise from genuine non-CP-divisible dynamics and captures the corresponding signatures in the Gaussian covariance evolution. The framework therefore provides a practical route for diagnosing non-Markovian Gaussian noise in CV photonic quantum systems.
one_liner: Time-resolved homodyne tomography reconstructs Gaussian drift and diffusion to distinguish memory effects from nonstationary noise.
why_it_matters: Diagnosing genuine non-Markovian noise can improve calibration, modeling, and mitigation in continuous-variable photonic processors and links.
detailed_summary: The proposed framework infers a time-local Gaussian generator, represented by drift and diffusion matrices, from time-resolved homodyne data. A regularized maximum-likelihood fit constrains the accumulated finite-time channel to remain completely positive. Simulations of memory-dependent loss, nonstationary thermal excitation, and pseudomode memory show that temporary failures of local CP-divisibility identify genuine memory rather than mere time variation.
main_result: Simulated tomography reconstructs Gaussian noise dynamics and separates CP-divisible nonstationarity from genuinely non-CP-divisible memory effects.
application_angle: The method provides a practical diagnostic for characterizing temporal noise correlations in CV quantum processors, sensors, and communication systems.

title: Optical rectification and Pockels effect in the organic nonlinear crystal MBI for quasi-discrete THz time-domain spectroscopy
abstract: Organic nonlinear optical (NLO) crystals offer efficient nonlinear frequency conversion for broadband THz spectroscopy. Unfortunately, only a subset of NLO crystals is compatible with the telecom (~1.5 $μ$m) pump wavelength region, where convenient MHz-rate femtosecond fiber lasers are available. Here, we present ultra-broadband (1-30 THz) THz generation and detection using a benzoindolium iodide (MBI, C$_{24}$H$_{24}$NOI) crystal illuminated by a 1.5 $μ$m MHz-rate fiber laser. At 200 mW of average pump power, the crystal delivers ~1 $μ$W of THz radiation as quasi-discrete peaks covering the whole emission region with a prominent peak at 11.8 THz. High-dynamic range (>40 dB) time-domain spectroscopy is demonstrated within minutes of integration.
one_liner: An MBI organic crystal driven at 1.5 µm generates and detects quasi-discrete 1–30 THz radiation with over 40 dB dynamic range.
why_it_matters: Compatibility with MHz-rate telecom fiber lasers enables compact, rapid, broadband THz spectroscopy using a single nonlinear-crystal platform.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses benzoindolium iodide for THz generation by optical rectification and detection through the Pockels effect under 1.5 µm pumping. With 200 mW average pump power, the crystal produces about 1 µW of quasi-discrete THz emission spanning 1–30 THz, including a strong peak at 11.8 THz. Time-domain measurements achieve more than 40 dB dynamic range within minutes of integration.
main_result: The MBI platform demonstrates 1–30 THz generation and detection with approximately 1 µW output and greater than 40 dB measurement dynamic range.
application_angle: The system could enable fast, broadband THz material spectroscopy with convenient MHz-rate fiber-laser sources.

title: Finite-key security of BB84 with passive receivers via reduction to active measurements
abstract: In BB84 with passive receiver basis choice (passive BB84) and threshold detectors, the distribution of detection bases can depend on the incoming photon number. Its relation to BB84 with active receiver basis choice (active BB84), in which the basis is chosen using independent randomness, is therefore nontrivial. We establish a reduction theorem that expresses the secret-key-length formula for passive BB84 in terms of an active BB84 formula. The theorem allows a passive key-length formula to be obtained by simple substitutions into an existing active formula, without constructing a passive-specific security proof from scratch. It applies to key-length formulas derived using the Shor--Preskill, Koashi, and Renner approaches, because the reduction uses only properties shared by these approaches. Our result illustrates a modular approach that separates receiver analysis from the security proof and allows the proof of a common reference protocol to be reused for different implementations.
one_liner: A reduction theorem converts finite-key formulas for active-receiver BB84 into security bounds for passive threshold-detector receivers.
why_it_matters: The modular reduction avoids rebuilding implementation-specific proofs and simplifies rigorous finite-key analysis of practical passive QKD receivers.
detailed_summary: Passive BB84 is complicated because the observed detection-basis distribution can depend on the incoming photon number. The authors derive a reduction that maps a passive-receiver secret-key-length calculation to an existing active-BB84 formula through substitutions. Because it relies on properties common to the Shor–Preskill, Koashi, and Renner approaches, the construction supports multiple standard proof frameworks.
platform_or_system: Passive-basis BB84 receiver with threshold detectors
main_result: The theorem reuses active-BB84 finite-key formulas to obtain passive-receiver key lengths without a new security proof from first principles.
application_angle: It can streamline security certification and implementation analysis for compact QKD receivers using passive optical basis selection.

title: Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor
abstract: We introduce sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), which combines the original formulation of QPD [Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, (2026)] with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity for molecular systems. We show that sparse sampling reduces the sample complexity of QPD from $\mathcal{O}(N_s)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N_s)$, where $N_s$ is the number of sampled points of the autocorrelation function (i.e.\ distinct circuits), without increasing circuit depth at chemical accuracy. With a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine--tryptophan residue pair in water as an example, we show that on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, sparse QPD resolves the Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates. For a suitably large quantum processor, we demonstrate numerically in the weakly correlated regime that the method extends to larger systems.
one_liner: Sparse quantum prolate diagonalization reaches chemical accuracy for an embedded molecular Hamiltonian on a trapped-ion processor.
why_it_matters: Logarithmic sampling in the spectral grid reduces distinct circuit requirements while retaining chemical accuracy at substantial circuit depth.
detailed_summary: Sparse QPD combines quantum prolate diagonalization with compressed sensing to exploit sparsity in molecular Hamiltonian spectra. It reduces the number of sampled autocorrelation points, and therefore distinct circuits, from O(N_s) to O(log N_s) without increasing the depth required for chemical accuracy. On Quantinuum Helios, the method resolves energies of a two-orbital active-space-embedded arginine–tryptophan Hamiltonian in water using circuits containing up to 448 two-qubit gates.
main_result: Hardware experiments achieve chemical-accuracy molecular energies while sparse sampling reduces the distinct-circuit complexity from O(N_s) to O(log N_s).
application_angle: The approach could lower measurement and circuit-execution overhead for quantum chemistry calculations on near-term and larger trapped-ion processors.

title: Axion electrodynamics and the advection-diffusion structure of TEM modes in hollow-conductor waveguides
abstract: We present a systematic investigation of transverse electromagnetic (TEM) modes in hollow-conductor waveguides filled with a dielectric medium described by axion electrodynamics. While such modes do not propagate in conventional single-conductor waveguides, the coupling of the axion field to an external magnetic field enables their propagation. We show that the resulting TEM modes are governed by an advection-diffusion-type equation for the transverse electrostatic potential, establishing a direct mathematical connection between axion electrodynamics and advection-diffusion phenomena. We illustrate this connection through explicit solutions and field profiles for cylindrical waveguides, considering uniform and rigid rotational drift fields, both individually and in combination, as well as different values of the parameter controlling the advection-to-diffusion ratio (Péclet number). These results establish a transport-based framework for understanding how spatial variations of the axion-electrodynamics background shape the transverse electromagnetic fields in hollow-conductor waveguides.
one_liner: Axion–magnetic-field coupling enables TEM propagation in hollow single-conductor waveguides through an advection–diffusion-like field equation.
why_it_matters: The transport analogy offers a new framework for designing and interpreting axion-modified electromagnetic modes and spatial field profiles.
detailed_summary: The authors derive an advection–diffusion-type equation for the transverse electrostatic potential of TEM modes in axion-filled hollow-conductor waveguides under an external magnetic field. Cylindrical-waveguide solutions are presented for uniform drift, rigid rotational drift, and their combination across different Péclet numbers. The calculations show how spatial variation in the axion-electrodynamics background reshapes transverse electromagnetic fields.
main_result: Axion coupling permits otherwise forbidden TEM modes and maps their transverse-field structure onto an advection–diffusion problem.
application_angle: The framework could guide waveguide-based electromagnetic probes or engineered analog systems sensitive to axion-like material responses.

title: Cancellation of cryocooler-induced vibration in trapped-ion systems
abstract: Mechanical cryocoolers offer numerous benefits for the operation of vacuum systems containing trapped atomic ions. However, the fidelity of laser-based gates can be degraded by phase noise induced by the cryocooler vibrations. We present a feed-forward vibration-cancellation system that directly measures inner shield displacement with an auxiliary interferometer and applies a compensating phase correction to the laser drive. The interferometer signal is demodulated, and a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) system unwraps the displacement measurement signal, computes the required correction phase, and updates the RF drive of an in-line acousto-optic modulator (AOM) to correct for the vibration-induced dephasing. With cancellation active, the qubit coherence time improves from $3.0\pm0.4$ ms to $35\pm5$ ms, consistent with a simulation based on the measured vibration spectrum. We further validate the cancellation by artificially increasing the mechanical coupling of the cryocooler to the vacuum chamber. The vibration-induced decoherence rate is suppressed by a factor of approximately 70 at an RMS (root mean square) displacement of 0.65 $\mathrmμ$m.
one_liner: Interferometric feed-forward phase correction suppresses cryocooler vibration noise and extends trapped-ion qubit coherence from 3.0 ms to 35 ms.
why_it_matters: It directly addresses a major integration penalty of compact cryogenic ion traps using real-time sensing and FPGA-based optical-phase stabilization.
detailed_summary: An auxiliary interferometer measures inner-shield displacement caused by a mechanical cryocooler. An FPGA unwraps the displacement signal, computes a compensating phase, and updates the RF drive of an in-line AOM. Cancellation increases qubit coherence from 3.0±0.4 ms to 35±5 ms and suppresses vibration-induced decoherence by about 70-fold at 0.65 μm RMS displacement.
main_result: Real-time feed-forward cancellation produced an approximately twelvefold coherence-time improvement and about 70-fold suppression of vibration-induced decoherence.
application_angle: The method enables mechanically cooled trapped-ion processors to retain laser-phase stability without requiring complete passive vibration isolation.

title: Tunable Microresonator Arrays Induced by Geometric Phase
abstract: Unlike periodic field-intensity patterns, which can be generated by interference of coherent beams, periodic material structures are usually created by periodic modification. In contrast, we show here that a millimeter-long bundle of four conventional side-coupled optical fibers with a slowly varying transverse arrangement can support a nearly periodic array of whispering-gallery-mode microresonators, whose period can be tuned mechanically down to about $100\,μ\mathrm{m}$.
one_liner: A slowly varying four-fiber geometry creates a mechanically tunable, millimeter-long array of whispering-gallery microresonators with periods near 100 μm.
why_it_matters: It offers a simple route to reconfigurable resonator arrays without periodically fabricating or modifying the constituent material.
detailed_summary: The work shows that four conventional side-coupled optical fibers with a slowly varying transverse arrangement can support a nearly periodic sequence of whispering-gallery-mode resonators. The array extends over millimeter scales despite the absence of periodic material modification. Mechanical adjustment tunes the resonator spacing down to roughly 100 μm.
main_result: Geometric-phase engineering generates a mechanically tunable, nearly periodic whispering-gallery microresonator array in conventional fibers.
application_angle: The structure may support reconfigurable filtering, distributed light–matter interaction, and compact coupled-resonator photonic devices.

title: Development of a Discrete Variable Representation of a Field-Adaptive Hermite Basis for Accurate Modeling of Magnetically Confined Systems
abstract: Accurate magnetic-field evolution of spectra requires a common wavefunction representation that consistently describes multiple states across different field regimes. Discrete Variable Representation (DVR) methods combine accurate basis-based kinetic-energy evaluation with flexible real-space potential representation, enabling arbitrary non-analytic potentials to be treated. Here, we develop a magnetic-field-dependent Hermite function-based (Hermite-B) DVR that adapts naturally to magnetic confinement, efficiently representing compressed wavefunctions across a wide range of field strengths while remaining centered in regions relevant to the scalar confinement potential. This ensures accurate treatment of the field-dependent kinetic energy while addressing two key challenges: maintaining accuracy from the Zeeman to Landau regimes and accommodating diverse confinement potentials. We also introduce a spatial restriction scheme that confines Hermite DVR grid points to a fixed-length domain, enabling compact representations for smooth potentials. The method is benchmarked for two-dimensional quantum dots in perpendicular magnetic fields against analytical models and compared with finite-grid, sine DVR, and field-free Hermite DVR calculations. The performance of field-independent DVR methods for magnetically confined systems is also investigated for the first time. Excellent agreement with exact analytical spectra and wavefunctions is obtained, with Hermite-B requiring the fewest basis functions and smaller Hamiltonian matrices, improving computational efficiency. Applications to arbitrary confinement potentials and tilted magnetic fields demonstrate its versatility beyond analytically solvable systems. The proposed method offers a robust, accurate, and efficient framework for large-scale calculations of realistic semiconductor nanostructures and molecular systems in external magnetic fields.
one_liner: A magnetic-field-adaptive Hermite DVR models confined quantum states accurately from Zeeman to Landau regimes using smaller Hamiltonian matrices.
why_it_matters: Efficient high-field simulation can accelerate realistic design and interpretation of semiconductor nanostructures and magnetically confined quantum devices.
detailed_summary: The proposed Hermite-B discrete variable representation adapts its basis to magnetic confinement while retaining flexible real-space treatment of non-analytic potentials. Benchmarks on two-dimensional quantum dots reproduce analytical spectra and wavefunctions while requiring fewer basis functions than finite-grid, sine-DVR, and field-free Hermite-DVR approaches. A fixed-domain restriction further reduces representation size, and tests with arbitrary potentials and tilted fields demonstrate broader applicability.
main_result: Hermite-B achieved analytical-level spectral and wavefunction accuracy with the smallest basis sets and Hamiltonian matrices among the compared methods.
application_angle: The method supports efficient simulation of realistic semiconductor nanostructures and molecular systems used in magnetic-field-dependent device and sensor design.

title: Dynamical Decoupling via Continuous Unitary Design
abstract: Dynamical decoupling is a cornerstone of quantum control for protecting and engineering quantum systems. However, conventional schemes rely on idealized instantaneous pulses, limiting their performance under realistic finite-duration and imperfect controls. To overcome this limitation, we establish a dynamical decoupling framework based on continuous unitary designs, which intrinsically suppresses arbitrary static noise during continuous control. We further derive closed-form phase conditions to suppress Rabi-amplitude errors, unifying universal decoupling, finite-pulse compatibility, and control-error robustness within a single analytical framework. We experimentally validate our approach on a superconducting quantum cloud platform, demonstrating significantly extended coherence times and the highest robustness against Rabi-amplitude errors and detuning among the tested sequences.
one_liner: Continuous unitary designs provide finite-duration dynamical decoupling that suppresses static noise and remains robust to amplitude and detuning errors.
why_it_matters: The approach replaces idealized instantaneous pulses with experimentally realistic controls suited to improving coherence in deployed quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate dynamical decoupling through continuous unitary designs that average arbitrary static noise during finite-duration control. Closed-form phase conditions additionally suppress Rabi-amplitude errors, combining universal decoupling and control-error robustness in one analytical construction. Experiments on a superconducting quantum cloud platform show longer coherence and the strongest amplitude-error and detuning robustness among the tested sequences.
main_result: Continuous unitary-design sequences extended coherence while outperforming tested alternatives in robustness to Rabi-amplitude errors and detuning.
application_angle: The protocol can improve memory, gate, and sensing performance on superconducting hardware with realistic bandwidth and calibration errors.

title: Variable-length MDI QKD under source imperfections and local randomization over horizontal links
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) provides security guarantees that hold despite device imperfections and finite-size effects. We address these challenges in measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD, combining its intrinsic untrusted detection with an imperfection model for Alice's and Bob's sources via fidelity bounds. We establish variable-length general security under the Marginal-constrained Entropy Accumulation Theorem (MEAT), estimating the relevant Rényi entropies through conic optimization. We evaluate our model under a horizontal channel link, reporting secret keys for blocks as small as n~3x10^4 rounds under atmosphere-free conditions, and show that compensating for unequal channel attenuation through appropriately chosen transmitted amplitudes improves performance in asymmetric configurations, enabling communication distances beyond 80 km for commercial satellite systems.
one_liner: Variable-length MDI-QKD remains secure with imperfect sources and finite blocks, while optimized amplitudes support asymmetric horizontal links beyond 80 km.
why_it_matters: It combines detector-side security, realistic source imperfections, and finite-size operation in a framework relevant to terrestrial and satellite QKD.
detailed_summary: The security proof combines measurement-device-independent QKD with fidelity-bounded source imperfections and variable-length general security under the Marginal-constrained Entropy Accumulation Theorem. Relevant Rényi entropies are estimated through conic optimization. Simulations yield secret keys for blocks near 3×10^4 rounds without atmospheric loss, while unequal transmitted amplitudes compensate asymmetric attenuation and extend modeled commercial-satellite links beyond 80 km.
main_result: The framework produces finite-size secret keys with imperfect sources and predicts more than 80 km reach through amplitude optimization in asymmetric links.
application_angle: It provides a security and parameter-optimization route for practical terrestrial or satellite-assisted QKD with unequal channels and limited data blocks.

title: PRISM: A Logical-Physical Boundary Compiler for Dual-Rail Qubits
abstract: Quantum computers can encode each logical qubit across multiple physical degrees of freedom so that errors on the physical qubits can be detected or corrected. A compiler must then translate each logical gate into native instructions, and one gate can have several equivalent realizations that interact through different wires. Routing moves those wires, so a realization chosen before routing can force SWAPs that another would avoid, making code expansion and physical routing a phase-ordering problem. PRISM therefore keeps each gate's realizations open across the logical--physical boundary and commits to one only when routing reaches a layout that can execute it. We formalize which physical circuits implement a gate, which respect the fault model, and which the compiler keeps, and define when a gate can execute under a layout. For dual-rail cavity qubits, logical $\mathrm{CR}_z$ has four loss-admissible realizations, one per rail pairing, and its logical availability graph is exactly the simple quotient of the occupied device graph by the rail pairs. Across 25 workloads with 7 to 25 logical qubits on three device graphs, PRISM reduces routing SWAPs by 20.4--30.8\% and physical depth by 8.8--10.1\% relative to a greedy search that fixes each realization before routing. On the grid and hexagonal lattice, the SWAP reductions hold through 32 logical qubits. By shortening routes, PRISM also reduces photon loss on device models and therefore needs 44.3\% fewer attempts per retained shot at 16 logical qubits, as a geometric mean over workloads and device graphs, and it lowers decoded logical error in a three-round Steane memory under skip-gate leakage.
one_liner: PRISM jointly selects dual-rail gate realizations and physical routes, avoiding premature choices that create unnecessary SWAPs.
why_it_matters: Lower routing overhead reduces circuit depth and photon loss, improving the practicality of loss-aware dual-rail quantum processors.
detailed_summary: PRISM delays selection among equivalent physical gate realizations until routing finds an executable layout. For dual-rail cavity qubits, it exploits four loss-admissible realizations of logical CRz gates. Across 25 workloads, it reduces SWAPs by 20.4–30.8% and physical depth by 8.8–10.1%, while requiring 44.3% fewer attempts per retained shot at 16 logical qubits.
main_result: The compiler cuts routing SWAPs by up to 30.8% and reduces modeled photon-loss overhead and decoded logical error.
application_angle: The method can improve throughput and fidelity in hardware where logical qubits span multiple physical modes or rails.

title: Frequency Multiplexing of Purcell-Enhanced Optically Coherent NV Centers
abstract: Integrating optically coherent quantum emitters into nanophotonic structures is key to scalable quantum networks. Realizing them with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond is hindered by the degradation of optical coherence accompanying nanofabrication. Here, we overcome this challenge by integrating multiple NV centers into a monolithic diamond photonic crystal nanocavity while preserving near-lifetime-limited optical coherence. We observe linewidths as narrow as 19 MHz, enabling the frequency multiplexing of spectrally distinct NV centers within a common cavity mode, while maintaining charge-state stability over several minutes under resonant excitation. Tuning the cavity into resonance with the NV zero-phonon line enhances the optical emission, consistent with Purcell enhancement predicted by finite-element simulations. Additionally, individual cavities can be independently brought into resonance with NV zero-phonon lines on the same chip. These results combine bulk-like optical coherence with frequency multiplexing and cavity-enhanced emission, establishing a scalable nanophotonic platform for NV-based quantum network nodes.
one_liner: Multiple near-lifetime-limited NV centers are frequency-multiplexed within a shared monolithic diamond photonic-crystal cavity.
why_it_matters: It combines coherent emitters, cavity enhancement, and spectral multiplexing on one chip—key ingredients for scalable quantum-network nodes.
detailed_summary: The authors integrate multiple NV centers into a monolithic diamond photonic-crystal nanocavity while retaining optical linewidths as narrow as 19 MHz. Spectrally distinct emitters are frequency-multiplexed through a common cavity mode and remain charge-stable for minutes under resonant excitation. Cavity tuning enhances zero-phonon-line emission consistently with finite-element predictions, and separate cavities can be independently aligned on the same chip.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates frequency-multiplexed, optically coherent NV centers with cavity-enhanced emission in an integrated diamond platform.
application_angle: Independent cavity tuning and multiplexed coherent emitters support denser, more scalable quantum-repeater and network-node architectures.

title: Performance of Fusion-Based Quantum Computing with Imperfect Photon Indistinguishability
abstract: Fusion-based quantum computation (FBQC) is a promising route to fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, connecting small entangled resource states through linear-optical fusion measurements. While logical encoding can substantially improve resilience to photon loss, whether these benefits extend to other noise remain an open question. In this work, we show that this is not generally the case when accounting for partial photon distinguishability during resource state generation and fusion measurement. We develop hardware-motivated noise models to capture these effects and investigate their impact on fault tolerance in the 6-ring fusion network. We compare unencoded and Shor(2,2)-encoded resource states prepared using all-photonic and emitter-assisted repeat-until-success (RUS) schemes. For the all-photonic construction, encoding reduces the distinguishability threshold from 0.136% to 0.08%. In contrast, the RUS construction tolerates more distinguishability, with comparable unencoded and encoded thresholds (0.256% and 0.271%, respectively). These results expose a fundamental limitation of evaluating logical encodings under idealized resource-state assumptions and demonstrate that resource-state generation can critically determine the fault tolerance of photonic architectures.
one_liner: Hardware-aware modeling shows that logical encoding does not universally improve FBQC tolerance to imperfect photon indistinguishability.
why_it_matters: The results reveal that resource-state generation—not encoding alone—can determine whether a photonic fault-tolerance strategy succeeds.
detailed_summary: The study models partial photon distinguishability during both resource-state generation and fusion measurements in the 6-ring fusion network. With all-photonic preparation, Shor(2,2) encoding lowers the distinguishability threshold from 0.136% to 0.08%. Emitter-assisted repeat-until-success preparation performs better, giving similar unencoded and encoded thresholds of 0.256% and 0.271%.
main_result: Emitter-assisted resource generation tolerates roughly 0.26% distinguishability, whereas encoding degrades the threshold for the all-photonic construction.
application_angle: The thresholds provide hardware specifications for photon sources, emitters, and fusion modules in fault-tolerant photonic computers.

title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
abstract: Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.
one_liner: A 41-qubit superconducting processor teleports logical states between two distance-three surface-code qubits using lattice surgery.
why_it_matters: This is an experimental step toward routing quantum information and executing fault-tolerant operations between encoded qubits.
detailed_summary: The experiment implements lattice-surgery teleportation between two distance-three logical qubits on a 41-physical-qubit superconducting circuit. Time-resolved logical observables track information transfer from the source patch to the target. Repeated stabilizer measurements after merging the patches restore fault tolerance, while gate-count and sequence-duration optimization further improve teleportation fidelity.
main_result: The processor teleports encoded quantum states between two distance-three logical qubits and improves fidelity through repeated stabilizer cycles and sequence optimization.
application_angle: Lattice-surgery teleportation enables modular movement and interaction of logical information in future fault-tolerant superconducting processors.

title: Quantum amplification with a linear quantum coupler
abstract: Josephson parametric amplifiers (JPAs) are essential components for quantum-limited microwave measurement, but their dynamic range is often constrained by Kerr and other pump-induced nonlinear effects. In this work, we systematically study the performance of a parametric amplifier based on the linear inductive coupler (LINC). Starting from the driven-circuit Hamiltonian, we derive the effective three-wave-mixing amplifier model, including leading flux-driven nonlinear corrections relevant to realistic operation. We analyze the resulting gain response, saturation behavior, and intermodulation distortion, comparing them with representative state-of-the-art JPA designs. Our results show that the symmetry-protected structure of the LINC suppresses static Kerr nonlinearity. Moreover, suitable circuit-parameter optimization can further reduce the dressed-squeezing and driven-Kerr effects, leading to considerable improvements in power-handling metrics. These results identify the LINC architecture as a promising platform for high-linearity Josephson parametric amplification.
one_liner: A linear inductive coupler is analyzed as a symmetry-protected, high-linearity Josephson parametric amplifier with suppressed Kerr effects.
why_it_matters: Greater dynamic range could improve quantum-limited microwave readout where conventional parametric amplifiers saturate or distort.
detailed_summary: Starting from the driven-circuit Hamiltonian, the authors derive an effective three-wave-mixing model for a linear inductive coupler amplifier, including leading flux-driven nonlinear corrections. They analyze gain, saturation, and intermodulation distortion against representative JPA designs. Symmetry suppresses static Kerr nonlinearity, while parameter optimization reduces dressed-squeezing and driven-Kerr effects.
main_result: The analysis predicts substantially improved power handling through symmetry-protected static-Kerr suppression and optimized driven nonlinearities.
application_angle: A higher-linearity amplifier could expand the usable readout power and multiplexing capacity of superconducting quantum systems and microwave sensors.

title: Performance analysis of a Rydberg atom THz radiometer concept
abstract: THz receiver technology lies between electronics and photonics; as such, its implementation is not as mature. This warrants investigation into alternative THz receivers such as Rydberg atom sensors, which are highly susceptible to electric fields. In particular, the conversion architecture has been demonstrated to coherently transduce thermal radiation. This system offers room-temperature operation and does not necessarily require a local oscillator at the frequency of the input signal. We provide an assessment of the feasibility of such sensors for THz radiometry within the context of Earth observation.
one_liner: A Rydberg-atom conversion receiver is assessed as a room-temperature THz radiometer for Earth-observation measurements.
why_it_matters: Atomic transduction may offer an alternative to immature THz receiver technologies without requiring a THz-frequency local oscillator.
detailed_summary: The paper evaluates the feasibility of a Rydberg-atom conversion architecture for detecting thermal radiation at THz frequencies. The concept exploits the strong electric-field sensitivity of highly excited atoms and previously demonstrated coherent transduction. Its prospective performance is considered specifically against the requirements of Earth-observation radiometry.
main_result: The work establishes a performance framework for assessing Rydberg conversion sensors as practical THz radiometers.
application_angle: The concept targets remote sensing and Earth observation with room-temperature operation and potentially no input-frequency local oscillator.

title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
abstract: Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.
one_liner: Reduced nonlinear flow models are combined with Koopman-von Neumann circuits and surface-code estimates for early fault-tolerant simulation.
why_it_matters: It provides an end-to-end hardware estimate linking model accuracy, circuit cost, runtime, and physical-qubit requirements for a practical nonlinear-flow problem.
detailed_summary: The study couples sparse polynomial reduced-order models to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann transport, obtaining polylogarithmic per-step rotation scaling with grid cells at fixed dimension and polynomial degree. For a saturating cylinder wake, it estimates 1% relative RMS field error in 1.62 hours using roughly 560,000 physical qubits. IBM experiments additionally implement noise-mitigated nonlinear radial transport circuits.
platform_or_system: Surface-code quantum computer and IBM superconducting hardware
main_result: A cylinder-wake simulation is projected to reach 1% relative RMS field error in 1.62 hours on about 560,000 physical qubits.
application_angle: The workflow helps determine when reduced nonlinear dynamics may become feasible on early fault-tolerant quantum computers and how model order should be selected.

title: Scrambling leads to entanglement cost in NLQC
abstract: In a non-local quantum computation (NLQC), shared entanglement along with a single simultaneous round of quantum communication is used to implement a joint channel. NLQC has many applications, most of which benefit from an understanding of lower bounds on the entanglement needed to implement a given channel as an NLQC. However, the properties of a channel that lead to it having an entanglement cost in NLQC have remained unclear, with most lower bounds only applying to specially constructed examples. Here, we give a new lower bound technique for unitaries based on scrambling: we find that a unitary has zero entanglement cost if and only if it does not scramble. Further, we find that the tripartite mutual information, an entropic object that quantifies the degree of scrambling, provides a quantitative lower bound on entanglement cost in NLQC. This is the first known lower bound on entanglement cost for unitaries in NLQC which is faithful. Our results also relate scrambling and NLQC for the first time. Leveraging the faithful scrambling based bound, we then show that the controllable correlation, an earlier studied quantity, is also a faithful lower bound, resolving an earlier conjecture of Cleve and May.
one_liner: Scrambling is shown to be exactly the property that forces nonzero entanglement cost in one-round non-local quantum computation.
why_it_matters: The work supplies the first faithful unitary lower bound for NLQC entanglement cost, clarifying resource demands in distributed quantum protocols.
detailed_summary: The authors prove that a unitary has zero entanglement cost in non-local quantum computation if and only if it does not scramble information. They derive a quantitative lower bound from tripartite mutual information, making the bound faithful for arbitrary unitaries rather than only specially constructed cases. The result also proves that controllable correlation is a faithful lower bound, resolving a prior conjecture.
main_result: Tripartite mutual information provides a faithful quantitative lower bound on the entanglement required to implement a unitary through NLQC.
application_angle: The bound can guide entanglement provisioning and feasibility analysis for low-latency distributed quantum computation and cryptographic protocols.

title: Collective Superconducting-Qubit Interfaces for Microwave-to-Optical Quantum Transduction
abstract: Microwave-to-optical quantum transduction is essential for connecting superconducting quantum processors through optical networks. Mechanically mediated transducers, however, remain limited by weak electromechanical coupling, dissipation, and added noise. In this work, we study a transducer in which an ensemble of superconducting qubits couples collectively to a shared optomechanical resonator. For weak signals, we show that ensemble size and optical pump strength together set the conversion efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth, with pump heating limiting efficiency to a finite optimal pump strength. Near half excitation, the collective coupling grows nearly linearly with ensemble size, accelerating transfer of an excitation into the mechanics. We show that this speedup is offset by relaxation of the additional excited qubits, so the single-qubit coupling and lifetime still set the coherence requirement. Transferring exactly one excitation also requires an anharmonic mechanical mode, which an auxiliary qubit coupled to the mechanics can provide. In a lossless prescribed-Kerr benchmark with four qubits and $g_{\rm sm}/(2π)=3.81\,\mathrm{kHz}$, a mechanical anharmonicity of $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ raises the final joint single-photon intracavity target probability from $19.6\%$ to $99.7\%$. Finally, we quantify the effects of decoherence, disorder, residual qubit--qubit interactions, and pump-induced qubit noise, finding that pair-dependent interactions reduce the optical retrieval efficiency from 58\% to 35\%. These results establish the coherence and selectivity requirements for collective quantum transduction.
one_liner: Collective superconducting-qubit coupling is analyzed as a route to faster, selective microwave-to-optical quantum transduction.
why_it_matters: It identifies concrete coherence, anharmonicity, disorder, and pump constraints for networking superconducting processors over optical links.
detailed_summary: An ensemble of superconducting qubits couples collectively to a shared optomechanical resonator, with ensemble size and optical pumping controlling efficiency, noise, and bandwidth. Collective excitation accelerates transfer, but relaxation of the additional excited qubits preserves stringent single-qubit coherence requirements. In a lossless four-qubit benchmark, 100 kHz mechanical anharmonicity raises the joint single-photon target probability from 19.6% to 99.7%, while pair-dependent interactions reduce modeled retrieval efficiency from 58% to 35%.
platform_or_system: Superconducting-qubit ensemble coupled to an optomechanical resonator
main_result: Collective coupling can strongly accelerate excitation transfer, but near-unity single-photon preparation requires mechanical anharmonicity and tight control of decoherence and interactions.
application_angle: The architecture targets coherent conversion of superconducting-processor microwave signals into photons suitable for long-distance optical quantum networks.

title: Qubit-qumode simulation of molecular torsion in photoisomerization
abstract: Photochemical reactions driven by large nuclear motion, such as the photoisomerization of retinal, depend strongly on both the global anharmonic forces of the potential and the periodic topology of molecular torsion. In this work, we develop a hybrid discrete (qubit) and continuous variable (qumode) quantum simulation framework for photochemical reactions that maps electronic states to qubits, vibrations to qumodes, and the periodic torsion to a compact qumode encoding. Applying this approach to the two-mode Hahn-Stock and three-mode PSB3 models of retinal photoisomerization, we compare i) local vibronic approximations, ii) the full trigonometric potential on the noncompact line, and iii) the same potential on the compact circle, which matches the molecular torsion topology. We numerically show that the topological description can significantly alter relevant observables. We realize the compact torsion via both a wrapped Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) encoding and a two-qumode circle encoding and introduce two methods that reduce the hardware resources of both encodings. Spreading an encoded coordinate over several qumodes lowers the average occupation number of each mode, and adding counterterms to the Hamiltonian reduces the required squeezing amount. We expect that these methods make percent-level simulations of the considered molecules promising targets for hybrid qubit-qumode hardware. For more complex molecules, each additional nuclear coordinate is represented directly as a single qumode or an encoded register using the same native operations, so the framework extends naturally to larger systems.
one_liner: A hybrid qubit-qumode framework captures the periodic topology and anharmonic dynamics of molecular torsion in photoisomerization.
why_it_matters: It shows that correct torsional topology can materially change observables and proposes resource reductions for percent-level molecular simulations on hybrid hardware.
detailed_summary: Electronic states are mapped to qubits, vibrations to qumodes, and periodic torsion to compact continuous-variable encodings. Simulations of Hahn-Stock and PSB3 retinal models show that representing torsion on a circle rather than a noncompact line can significantly alter observables. Wrapped GKP and two-qumode circle encodings are developed, with coordinate spreading and Hamiltonian counterterms reducing occupation and squeezing requirements.
main_result: Compact torsional encodings reproduce topology-dependent photoisomerization dynamics while resource-reduction methods lower per-mode occupation and required squeezing.
application_angle: The framework offers a hardware-oriented route to percent-level simulation of retinal models and other photochemical reactions involving large nuclear motion.

title: Experimental constraints on gauge hidden-variable models in Bell tests
abstract: Quantum mechanics assigns identical statistics to measurement procedures that realize the same final effect, irrespective of the transformations used to reach it. We test this operational equivalence with polarization-entangled photons by implementing one of Bob's analyzer settings either directly or through closed wave-plate trajectories $C_γ$ calibrated to produce the same measurement operator. Motivated by ontological descriptions in which a hidden frame is transported between contexts, we formulate a local path-memory model and derive the mixed-context bound $|S_γ^{\rm mix}|\leq 2+2p_γ$. The quantity $p_γ$ is a coupling-dependent counterfactual mismatch probability: it bounds a contextual Bell expression, but neither generates nor predicts the quantum Bell correlation. We therefore test path memory through the observable difference between direct and looped implementations, using a no-signaling phenomenological response in which a hidden holonomy $δ_γ$ modifies one correlation term in $S_γ^{\rm mix}$. The direct reference violates the Bell inequality, while the looped mixed-context curves remain indistinguishable from it within the experimental precision. Our results support the quantum equivalence of calibrated measurement implementations and constrain path-sensitive hidden-variable extensions that predict an observable memory of the optical history.
one_liner: Polarization-entangled photons test whether optically equivalent analyzer paths leave a measurable hidden-variable memory.
why_it_matters: The experiment validates operational equivalence within its precision and constrains path-sensitive hidden-variable extensions of Bell-test physics.
detailed_summary: Bob's analyzer setting is realized either directly or through calibrated closed wave-plate trajectories that produce the same measurement operator. The authors derive a mixed-context bound for a local path-memory model and parameterize a possible hidden holonomy through its effect on one correlation term. Although the direct reference violates the Bell inequality, the looped and direct mixed-context curves remain experimentally indistinguishable.
main_result: No observable difference is found between direct and closed-loop implementations of the same polarization measurement within experimental precision.
application_angle: The result strengthens confidence that calibrated photonic measurement modules are insensitive to their optical control history while bounding exotic path-memory effects.

title: High-rate low-distance color codes
abstract: Experimental implementations of two-dimensional color codes encoding a single logical qubit have surpassed the fidelity of physical qubits. A natural next step is to investigate higher-rate codes that encode multiple logical qubits. Here we propose small, high-rate 2D color codes for this purpose. We design distance-$3$ codes with encoding rates up to $1/3$ and distance-$4$ codes with encoding rates up to $1/4$. We prove that these rates are optimal for color codes with only color boundaries on surfaces with non-negative Euler characteristic. We benchmark the codes by simulating Steane-style error correction with real-time feedback and no post-selection in a linear trapped-ion chain model with all-to-all connectivity. The two best-performing codes have parameters $[[20,4,4]]$ and $[[16,4,4]]$ and achieve break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of $0.22\%$ and $0.26\%$, respectively.
