These results match the performance of Shor-style error correction with bivariate bicycle codes that use weight-$5$ measurements.
one_liner: Small high-rate 2D color codes encode four logical qubits and reach simulated break-even under trapped-ion error correction.
why_it_matters: The proposed codes increase logical-qubit density while retaining competitive fault-tolerance thresholds for near-term trapped-ion demonstrations.
detailed_summary: The work constructs distance-3 color codes with rates up to 1/3 and distance-4 codes with rates up to 1/4, proving these rates optimal under the stated surface and boundary restrictions. Steane-style error correction is simulated with real-time feedback and no post-selection in an all-to-all connected linear ion chain. The leading [[20,4,4]] and [[16,4,4]] codes reach break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of 0.22% and 0.26%, respectively.
main_result: The [[20,4,4]] and [[16,4,4]] color codes achieve simulated break-even at 0.22% and 0.26% two-qubit gate infidelity.
application_angle: These compact codes could enable higher-density logical memories and multi-logical-qubit error-correction experiments on trapped-ion processors.

title: Singlet flags: using native entanglement to restore the circuit distance of shuttled qLDPC codes in silicon
abstract: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes could greatly reduce the qubit count of silicon spin-qubit processors, but their checks are long-range and of high weight. Shuttling one ancilla electron through every data qubit of a check measures such checks, but a single fault on the ancilla spreads to several data qubits, so the circuit distance can fall far below the code distance. We make the mobile ancilla one half of a spin singlet whose partner stays at home; a Bell measurement at the end of the check provides a flag for isolated bit-flip faults acquired during the walk. Using new distance-6 codes with check weights 8, 10 and 12, and exact circuit distances from two independent solvers, we show that without the flag the circuit distance falls as check weight grows, to 1 at weight 12, while with it every weight-8 and weight-10 code recovers circuit distance 5 or 6 and corrects as many faults as the code. For codes of distance 8 to 12 the flag raises the circuit distance by one to four, and the Gross code [[144,12,12]] rises from 7 to 10. In circuit-level simulations of shuttled spin qubits, the flag lowers logical error rates by typically 2-10x across bivariate-bicycle, circulant-permutation and surface codes, and the gain survives percent-level flag-readout errors and bit flips on the singlet's electrons. BP+OSD does not reach the full circuit distance of the flagged circuits, so our flagged logical error rates are upper bounds: decoding the same shots exactly raises the flag's gain on the distance-6 codes from 3-7x to 5-17x for the weight-6 BB code, and from 1-12x to 5-90x at weights 8 and 10 for p >= 2.5x10^-4.
one_liner: A stationary singlet partner flags faults on a shuttled spin ancilla, restoring much of the circuit distance of silicon qLDPC codes.
why_it_matters: The scheme mitigates dangerous error propagation during long-range stabilizer checks without abandoning electron shuttling or high-rate qLDPC encoding.
detailed_summary: The protocol pairs a mobile ancilla electron with a stationary singlet partner and performs a final Bell measurement to flag isolated bit-flip faults accumulated during stabilizer measurement. Exact solvers show distance recovery to 5 or 6 for all studied weight-8 and weight-10 distance-6 codes, while an unflagged weight-12 circuit falls to distance 1. Circuit-level simulations find typical logical-error reductions of 2–10×, with exact decoding producing gains as high as 90× in tested regimes.
main_result: Singlet flags restore substantial circuit distance and reduce simulated logical error rates despite realistic flag-readout and singlet-spin errors.
application_angle: The method offers a hardware-native route to implementing high-weight qLDPC checks with mobile electrons in scalable silicon quantum processors.

title: Simultaneous spectral measurement and programmable filtering on a universal silicon photonic chip
abstract: Spectral measurement and spectral filtering are two fundamental operations in optics, yet they are conventionally implemented using separate optical systems, hindering their simultaneous and programmable operation on a common platform. Here, we demonstrate a universal silicon photonic chip that unifies spectral measurement and programmable filtering within a single integrated architecture. The chip comprises two 8 * 8 programmable unitary transformation circuits interconnected through optical intensity modulators, forming a universal linear optical circuit. In contrast to conventional universal circuits employing equal-length interconnections, we deliberately introduce different optical path lengths between the two unitary circuits. The resulting wavelength-dependent phase evolution provides spectral diversity while preserving the programmability of the universal circuit, enabling parallel spectral measurement and programmable filtering. The fabricated chip achieves a spectral resolution of 0.05 nm over a bandwidth exceeding 100 nm, simultaneously measures eight independent laser sources, and generates multiple programmable spectral filter functions. We further demonstrate simultaneous spectral measurement and filtering during dynamic reconfiguration of the filter functions. These results establish universal photonic circuits as a versatile platform for integrating spectral sensing and programmable optical processing on a single chip.
one_liner: A universal silicon photonic circuit simultaneously measures spectra and implements dynamically programmable optical filters.
why_it_matters: Combining sensing and filtering on one reconfigurable chip can shrink optical instruments while enabling adaptive, real-time spectral processing.
detailed_summary: The chip connects two programmable 8×8 unitary transformation circuits through intensity modulators, with deliberately unequal optical paths providing wavelength-dependent phase diversity. It reaches 0.05 nm spectral resolution across more than 100 nm of bandwidth and simultaneously measures eight independent lasers. Programmable filter functions can be reconfigured while spectral measurement continues.
main_result: The fabricated chip performs concurrent eight-channel spectral measurement and programmable filtering with 0.05 nm resolution over a bandwidth exceeding 100 nm.
application_angle: The architecture supports compact adaptive spectrometers, optical monitors, and signal processors that sense and condition spectra on the same chip.

title: Addressable transversal CCZ gates on almost good quantum LDPC codes and nearly optimal magic state protocols
abstract: Assuming uniform subfield product expansion, we construct quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes with distances $Ω_ε(N/\log^2N)$ and at least $N^{1-ε}$ individually addressable logical CCZ gates on pairwise disjoint triples of logical qubits, for every fixed $0<ε<1$. With all logical qubits outside these triples initialized to $|0\rangle$, any subset of the corresponding logical CCZ gates can be implemented with a transversal physical CCZ circuit. As applications, we obtain two nearly optimal magic state protocols: CCZ distillation with arbitrarily small overhead exponent $γ\rightarrow 0$ and error suppression of nearly linear order, and a magic state fountain that directly prepares $N^{1-ε}$ encoded CCZ magic states with nearly linear distance $Ω_ε(N/\log^2N)$. The construction uses balanced products of expanding graph covers. The assumption concerns Reed--Solomon codes on three subfields of characteristic two and pairwise coprime extension degrees, a local hypothesis studied in a companion manuscript. We design the expanding graph covers to admit many common classical codewords, which yield logical operators whose pairings select the logical CCZ gates independently. Without the product expansion assumption, the graph covers also yield classical LDPC codes over a fixed field with almost linear dimension and linear distance that satisfy a multiplication property: the coordinatewise product of any three codewords lies in a second LDPC code of linear distance.
one_liner: Almost-good qLDPC codes are constructed with many independently addressable transversal logical CCZ gates and near-optimal magic-state protocols.
why_it_matters: If its expansion assumption holds, the construction could sharply reduce the overhead of non-Clifford resources in fault-tolerant quantum computers.
detailed_summary: Assuming uniform subfield product expansion, the authors construct qLDPC codes with distance Ωε(N/log²N) and at least N^(1−ε) addressable CCZ gates on disjoint logical-qubit triples. Any chosen subset of these logical gates is implemented by a transversal physical CCZ circuit when other logical qubits are initialized to |0⟩. Applications include CCZ distillation with an arbitrarily small overhead exponent and a fountain producing N^(1−ε) encoded CCZ magic states.
main_result: The construction provides nearly linear-distance qLDPC codes supporting polynomially many independently selectable transversal logical CCZ gates under a stated expansion hypothesis.
application_angle: It targets lower-overhead magic-state production and non-Clifford execution for large fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Observation of Exact Mobility-Edge Phases in Two-Dimensional Photonic Quasicrystals
abstract: Mobility edges, separating localized and extended states in energy, are central to localization physics. While exact mobility edges have been established in several one-dimensional quasiperiodic models, their realization in two dimensions remains largely unexplored. Here, we uncover a general route to exact mobility edges in the two-dimensional Aubry-Andre quasicrystal by introducing auxiliary subsystems. Through isospectral reduction, we reveal a hidden self-dual structure that yields exact mobility-edge conditions, separating extended, localized, and partially localized states in the spectrum. Tailoring the auxiliary structures controls the effective couplings and resulting mobility edge configurations, while auxiliary resonances further support flat-band states. In a decorated Lieb-type quasicrystal, we experimentally realize these predicted phases in photonic waveguide lattices and probe their energy-dependent localization through site-selective quench dynamics. Our results provide a versatile platform for controlling localization and can be readily extended to other physical platforms and higher-dimensional systems.
one_liner: Photonic waveguide lattices realize exact mobility-edge phases in a two-dimensional decorated Aubry–André quasicrystal.
why_it_matters: Experimentally controllable 2D mobility edges provide a new tool for routing, trapping, and studying waves with energy-selective localization.
detailed_summary: Isospectral reduction exposes a hidden self-duality in a two-dimensional Aubry–André model augmented with auxiliary subsystems, yielding exact boundaries among extended, localized, and partially localized states. Auxiliary structures tune effective couplings and mobility-edge configurations, while their resonances can generate flat bands. The predicted phases are observed in decorated Lieb-type photonic waveguide lattices using site-selective quench dynamics.
main_result: The experiment observes theoretically exact, energy-dependent mobility-edge phases in a two-dimensional photonic quasicrystal.
application_angle: Tunable localization could enable wavelength- or mode-selective confinement, transport control, and robust photonic-state engineering.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control
abstract: Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with $n$ physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/ε)$ logical qubits, where $ε$ is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/ε)$; an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to ${\sf polylog}(n/ε)$.
one_liner: A fixed, clocked planar quantum processor achieves universal fault tolerance using only a constant number of external control wires.
why_it_matters: Moving repetitive control into a fabricated local circuit could relieve the wiring and syndrome-I/O bottlenecks facing large solid-state quantum chips.
detailed_summary: The proposed processor moves quantum information through a planar array whose qubits, except for a few instruction ports, repeatedly execute a fixed geometrically local depth-3 circuit. Classical instructions enter through a constant number of external wires connected to individual qubits. An accuracy-threshold theorem establishes universal computation below a noise threshold, although the fully local design has a large logical-gate time; noiseless on-chip classical broadcast reduces that time to polylogarithmic scaling.
main_result: The architecture supports universal fault-tolerant computation with constant external wiring and a fixed periodically applied local circuit.
application_angle: It offers a path toward quantum chips controlled more like classical processors, with dramatically reduced cryogenic wiring and off-chip data traffic.

title: General Noise Channels and Mid-Circuit Measurements for Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batched Execution
abstract: Many studies of quantum protocols require fast sampling of large amounts of measurement data from noisy quantum circuits, such as for training machine-learning decoders for quantum error correction. Exact simulation of realistic noise is expensive, while stabilizer-based simulators are fast but approximate, for example through Pauli twirling, which generally alters the output statistics. Pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) accelerates exact trajectory simulation by sampling noise before state evolution. This method requires the outcome probability of every stochastic event to be independent of the state, which excludes mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels. We present a generalization of PTSBE to measurement and Kraus operators without approximation. Each event is partially pre-sampled, while deferred outcomes are drawn during grouped execution via multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. We implement the method for GPUs as an extension of CUDA-Q. On distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, it is up to 24x faster than conventional trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q. On 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, it is up to 83x faster and outperforms the near-Clifford simulator Clifft when more than about 25% of the gates are non-Clifford. With repeated sampling of each final state, its sampling rate per trajectory exceeds that of CUDA-Q by nearly five orders of magnitude. Our method also allows us to compare exact amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled channel on a surface-code memory, revealing that twirling overestimates the detection rate by 21% and raises the logical error rate of a lookup decoder by 8%. This work makes exact, high-throughput simulation practical for general noisy circuits, from data generation for training decoders to studying measurement-based fault-tolerant protocols under realistic noise.
one_liner: Generalized batched pre-trajectory sampling accelerates exact GPU simulation of noisy circuits with Kraus channels and mid-circuit measurements.
why_it_matters: Fast exact sampling enables realistic decoder training and exposes biases that Pauli-twirled noise models can introduce into error-correction studies.
detailed_summary: The method partially pre-samples stochastic events, then resolves state-dependent outcomes during grouped execution through multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. Its CUDA-Q implementation is up to 24× faster for distance-3 topological memories under amplitude damping and up to 83× faster for 30-qubit circuits with mid-circuit measurements. In a surface-code example, Pauli twirling overestimates detection events by 21% and increases a lookup decoder's logical error rate by 8%.
main_result: The approach delivers exact high-throughput trajectories for general noise and measurements, reaching up to 83× acceleration and nearly five orders higher repeated-sampling throughput.
application_angle: It makes realistic large-dataset generation practical for decoder training, hardware-noise studies, and measurement-based fault-tolerance protocols.

title: Analysis of the Second-Harmonic Generation Process in Nonlinear Metasurfaces Based on Multiple Quantum Wells: The Approach of Nonlinear Current Density, and The Development of Boundary Conditions
abstract: Using plasmonic metasurfaces integrated with nonlinear materials, such as multiple quantum wells (MQWs), has been an excellent solution to enhance nonlinear light-matter interactions. In this approach, a plasmonic resonator enhances the intensity of the fundamental harmonic within the MQWs region, increasing the strength of the intersubband transitions inside the MQWs. As a result, the efficiency of second harmonic generation (SHG) increases significantly. In this paper, we present a new approach to analyze the SHG process in nonlinear metasurfaces based on MQWs. In this approach, first, we formulate the nonlinear current density within the MQW region, which serves as the radiation source of the second harmonic wave. Notably, the saturation effect in MQWs, that limits the nonlinear response, is accounted for. Second, we address the development of boundary conditions for the second harmonic (SH) field in periodic structures, which ultimately leads us to define periodic boundary conditions for the SH field. Third, we combine these elements into a semi-analytical framework and validate it against previously reported experimental data. Finally, an efficient MQWs structure and plasmonic metasurface are designed for the fundamental wavelength of 8 $μ$m. After implementing the proposed algorithm, we observe that the designed nonlinear metasurface achieves a significant conversion efficiency of 0.02% under the incident intensity of 23.5 kW/cm$^2$. KEYWORDS: Second harmonic generation, metasurface, multiple quantum wells, nonlinear current density, periodic boundary conditions
one_liner: A semi-analytical model predicts second-harmonic generation from plasmonic metasurfaces containing saturable multiple quantum wells.
why_it_matters: The framework links nonlinear current sources and periodic boundary conditions to experimentally validated design of efficient mid-infrared frequency converters.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate the nonlinear current density generated in multiple quantum wells, including saturation of the intersubband response, and use it as the source of the second-harmonic field. They derive periodic boundary conditions for that field and incorporate them into a semi-analytical solver validated against reported measurements. A metasurface designed for an 8 μm pump is predicted to reach 0.02% conversion efficiency at 23.5 kW/cm².
main_result: The designed 8 μm metasurface achieves a predicted SHG conversion efficiency of 0.02% at 23.5 kW/cm².
application_angle: The model supports faster engineering of compact mid-infrared frequency converters and nonlinear optical sensing elements.

title: Scattering features of a self-dual spectral singularity in coupled ring resonators with balanced gain and loss
abstract: We theoretically and numerically discuss the general scattering property of a coupled two-ring-resonators externally coupled to a straight bus waveguide. Specifically, we require one ring resonator to be light field amplifying and another to be that dissipative, where the associated attenuation and gain factors for a field amplitude after one-round trip are formed in a reciprocal pair as well as the effective wave propagation constants are same. Obtained from reciprocity and an effective PT-symmetric transfer matrix, we exploit parametrization to propose a general phase diagram, identifying overall scattering outcomes. Especially, we find that the formation of a self-dual spectral singularity, namely coherent perfect absorption-lasing (CPAL), is occurred at a certain relation of a coupling coefficient and an attenuation factor as well as resonant whispering gallery modes. Reducing light amplification and dissipation strengths in each rings narrows the spectral bandwidth associated with CPAL. We further discover that any system with the CPAL parameters would exhibit a same scattering feature: transmission extinction, CPAL, and uni-directional reflectionless at the loss ring side, with respect to an incident wavelength. Additionally, a transmission extinction can be away from the resonance. These analytical predictions are verified by electromagnetic simulations.
one_liner: Balanced-gain-and-loss ring resonators exhibit a self-dual singularity combining coherent perfect absorption and lasing.
why_it_matters: Its unified phase diagram provides design rules for switchable extinction, amplification, and directional reflection control in integrated photonics.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes two coupled ring resonators connected to a bus waveguide, with reciprocal round-trip gain and attenuation and matched propagation constants. A PT-symmetric transfer-matrix parametrization maps the scattering regimes and identifies the coupling, loss, gain, and resonance conditions for coherent perfect absorption-lasing. Electromagnetic simulations verify transmission extinction, CPAL, and loss-side unidirectional reflectionlessness.
main_result: The work derives and numerically verifies universal scattering signatures and parameter conditions for a self-dual CPAL singularity.
application_angle: The predicted regimes could enable compact photonic switches, absorbers, lasers, and direction-selective signal-control devices.

title: Analysis of a Homodyne-Like Measurement Scheme Using Photon Counters and Weak Local Oscillator
abstract: In standard homodyne detection, an unknown optical signal state is combined with a local oscillator (LO) at a beam splitter (BS), and the appropriately integrated intensities at the two outputs of the BS are subtracted to obtain an approximate quadrature measurement. Accurate quadrature measurements require a high-amplitude LO and high-efficiency detectors. By varying the LO phase, the optical state in the mode matching the LO can be reconstructed. In many practical settings, a high-intensity LO is not desirable, which has led to the exploration of homodyne-like measurement schemes that replace photodiodes with photon-counting detectors and use an LO with a low average photon number. In this paper, we investigate what features of the unknown state can be determined by counting the total-photon number in one or both outgoing paths after the BS, keeping the mode of the LO fixed but adjusting its phase and magnitude. We find that it is possible to determine the unknown optical state in the mode matching the LO conditional on the number of photons in the orthogonal modes on the same path. If both the phase and the intensity of the LO can be varied, the statistics of just one of the detectors is sufficient to infer these parameters, but both detectors are required when the LO has a fixed intensity. Our analysis is carried out in the infinite-data limit, assuming access to the full photon-number distribution from one or both detectors.
one_liner: Photon counters and a weak local oscillator can reconstruct mode-resolved optical-state information without conventional strong-LO homodyne detection.
why_it_matters: The scheme could extend optical-state characterization to settings where bright local oscillators or efficient analog photodiodes are impractical.
detailed_summary: The authors analyze photon-number statistics after mixing an unknown optical state with a weak local oscillator at a beam splitter. They show that the LO-matched state can be inferred conditional on photon occupation of orthogonal modes in the measured path. One detector suffices when both LO phase and intensity are varied, whereas fixed LO intensity requires both output detectors, assuming infinite data and full number distributions.
main_result: Mode-matched optical-state parameters are theoretically identifiable using weak-LO photon counting, with detector requirements set by LO tunability.
application_angle: This offers a route to quantum optical tomography with lower LO power and photon-counting-compatible instrumentation.

title: Quantum Mpemba effect in a driven-dissipative atom-waveguide coupled system
abstract: The quantum Mpemba effect (QME) describes the counterintuitive phenomenon in which a more strongly perturbed quantum system relaxes toward its steady state faster than a less perturbed one. Here, we investigate the QME in a weakly driven-dissipative atomic array coupled to a one-dimensional chiral waveguide. Starting from the steady state, we introduce a local quench by resetting a single atom to its ground state and examine the subsequent relaxation dynamics. We find that quenching atoms near the array boundaries induces faster initial relaxation through enhanced coupling to superradiant modes and direct photon emission into the waveguide, giving rise to an edge-enhanced QME. Strong directional decay further amplifies this effect by promoting the spatial accumulation of superradiant modes near the preferred boundary, leading to a skin-enhanced QME. At later times, relaxation is increasingly governed by long-lived subradiant modes localized predominantly in the bulk of the array. By coupling two atomic arrays with different interparticle spacings, we further demonstrate an interface-induced QME, where quenching an atom near the interface makes the system relax more slowly at early times but approach its steady state faster at later times, owing to weak participation in both superradiant and subradiant modes. Our findings reveal how the spatial structure of collective decay modes and directional dissipation jointly govern anomalous quantum relaxation, offering potential routes toward accelerated steady-state preparation in waveguide QED systems.
one_liner: Collective superradiant and subradiant modes produce edge-, skin-, and interface-controlled quantum Mpemba relaxation in chiral waveguide QED.
why_it_matters: Spatially selecting a local quench may accelerate steady-state preparation in dissipative atomic and photonic quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: A weakly driven atomic array coupled to a one-dimensional chiral waveguide is locally quenched by resetting one atom to its ground state. Boundary quenches couple strongly to superradiant modes and direct waveguide emission, while directional decay concentrates those modes near one edge and enhances the effect. Coupled arrays with different spacings additionally produce interface-dependent relaxation governed by changing participation in superradiant and subradiant modes.
main_result: The calculations demonstrate edge-, non-Hermitian-skin-, and interface-enhanced quantum Mpemba effects controlled by quench position.
application_angle: Engineered collective decay could shorten initialization and steady-state preparation times in waveguide-QED processors and quantum simulators.

title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
abstract: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.
one_liner: A Kitaev chain combines protected Majorana edge memory with fast bulk dynamics to implement topological quantum reservoir computing.
why_it_matters: The proposal turns topology into a computational resource that unifies long-lived storage and autonomous temporal processing in one quantum system.
detailed_summary: The proposed reservoir stores information in long-lived Majorana edge modes while using rapid bulk dynamics for processing. Matched interfaces enable programmable writes, and interactions consolidate information autonomously from the bulk into protected edge degrees of freedom. Simulations show improved performance on tasks requiring retention of long temporal histories and expose tradeoffs between memory protection and accessibility.
main_result: Topological edge modes and interacting bulk dynamics jointly improve reservoir-computing tasks that require long-term temporal memory.
application_angle: The architecture suggests a hardware-efficient route to quantum machine learning on emerging topological or fault-tolerant platforms.

title: Accelerating Quantum Error Correction Simulations under Coherent Noise with Compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product States
abstract: Reliable assessment of quantum error correction requires understanding how coherent errors affect logical performance. Although tensor networks naturally capture coherent interference, entanglement growth and large qubit counts make repeated sampling costly. Here we develop a compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product State (CAMPS) framework that reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles qubits released by measurements, evolves a compressed residual state, and accelerates sampling through rotation fusion and compilation tailored to the MPS layout. Surface-code benchmarks under fixed-sign coherent noise yield accurate logical error estimates at small bond dimensions, while random-sign simulations up to distance $d=9$ and on the $[[72,12,6]]$ bivariate bicycle code match the Pauli-twirling approximation results. Compared with uncompiled CAMPS, compiled CAMPS converges at smaller bond dimensions and achieves order-of-magnitude sampling speedups at equal bond dimension, opening a scalable route to studying coherent error propagation in larger fault-tolerant circuits.
one_liner: Compiled Clifford-augmented matrix product states accelerate coherent-noise simulation of surface and bivariate-bicycle quantum codes.
why_it_matters: Faster sampling enables more realistic evaluation of coherent error propagation in larger fault-tolerant circuits and code families.
detailed_summary: The compiled CAMPS method reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles measured qubits, compresses the residual state, and fuses rotations for the MPS layout. Surface-code tests under fixed-sign coherent noise give accurate logical-error estimates at modest bond dimension. Random-sign simulations reach distance nine and the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code, while matching Pauli-twirling results and delivering order-of-magnitude speedups over uncompiled CAMPS at equal bond dimension.
main_result: Compiled CAMPS reduces required bond dimensions and produces order-of-magnitude sampling speedups while preserving logical-error accuracy.
application_angle: The simulator can guide code selection, decoder studies, and coherent-error mitigation before costly deployment on fault-tolerant hardware.

title: Reliability of quantum communication over erasure channels
abstract: Quantum information can be reliably transmitted at rates below the quantum capacity with an error that vanishes as the number of channel uses grows. The reliability function characterizes the optimal exponential decay rate of this error. For quantum erasure channels with a prime input dimension, we determine the reliability function exactly at all positive communication rates below capacity that meet or exceed an explicit critical rate. Notably, stabilizer coding strategies attain this optimal reliability throughout this regime.
one_liner: The reliability function of prime-dimensional quantum erasure channels is solved exactly above an explicit critical communication rate.
why_it_matters: The result supplies rigorous error exponents for quantum links and proves that practical stabilizer codes are optimal throughout the identified rate regime.
detailed_summary: The paper determines the optimal exponential decay rate of transmission error for prime-dimensional quantum erasure channels. The exact result applies to all positive rates below capacity that meet or exceed an explicit critical rate. Stabilizer coding achieves the resulting reliability function across this regime.
main_result: An exact reliability function is obtained above the critical rate, with stabilizer codes attaining the optimal error exponent.
application_angle: The bounds enable quantitative code and link-budget design for reliable quantum communication over lossy channels.

title: CCZ gate beyond the strong Rydberg-blockade regime
abstract: We present a protocol for implementing a controlled-controlled-Z (CCZ) gate on a neutral-atom platform, employing three individually addressable atoms confined in a linear array of optical tweezers and operating under finite Rydberg-Rydberg interaction (RRI). The protocol combines successive excitation of the Rydberg atoms with analytically determined pulses and uses two Rydberg levels to access opposite-sign interaction shifts. We show two different paths to get the conditional phase in the target atom: a pair of target pulses with opposite phases and a single detuned target pulse followed by a local phase correction. We derive analytical expressions for the time-integrated Rydberg populations to calculate the associated decay errors and also evaluate gate performance through master-equation simulations. Numerical comparisons with a fast Rydberg-antiblockade (RAB)-based CCZ protocol show improved gate performance at larger interatomic separations within the parameter regime considered. Monte Carlo sampling further quantifies the sensitivity to thermally induced position fluctuations. These results identify the tradeoffs between gate duration, Rydberg-state exposure, and interaction sensitivity, providing an analytically specified route to native three-qubit phase gates beyond the strong-blockade regime.
one_liner: An analytically specified neutral-atom CCZ gate operates with finite Rydberg interactions rather than requiring strong blockade.
why_it_matters: Native three-qubit gates beyond strong blockade could relax atom-spacing constraints while exposing concrete tradeoffs among speed, decay, and motion sensitivity.
detailed_summary: The protocol addresses three individually controlled atoms in a linear optical-tweezer array and uses two Rydberg levels with opposite-sign interaction shifts. Two conditional-phase constructions are analyzed using integrated Rydberg populations and master-equation simulations. In the studied regime, the scheme outperforms a fast antiblockade CCZ protocol at larger atom separations, while Monte Carlo sampling quantifies errors from thermal position fluctuations.
platform_or_system: Three neutral atoms in optical tweezers
main_result: The proposed finite-interaction CCZ protocol provides improved simulated performance at larger separations within the evaluated parameter regime.
application_angle: It offers a route to native three-qubit operations when strong Rydberg blockade is unavailable or geometrically restrictive.

title: In-memory measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution
abstract: Quantum memories offer to significantly extend the performance of quantum networks, but their complexity and limited performance at telecommunication wavelengths have so far hindered practical deployment. We propose a new memory-assisted measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol based on in-memory interference. Our approach leverages progress in atomic ensemble memories that enable the interference of a stationary matter qubit and a travelling photonic qubit inside a single quantum memory. We quantitatively evaluate the performance of this scheme against memoryless MDI-QKD and existing two-memory architectures, showing that it not only achieves superior secret key rates and surpasses the memoryless bound at substantially shorter distances, but also reduces hardware requirements by halving the number of memories and detectors. Our results further indicate that off resonant cascaded absorption (ORCA) memories are a particularly promising platform for implementing this protocol, and we outline a concrete design compatible with their capabilities. These findings demonstrate that in-memory interference provides a higher performance, and resource efficient route toward near term memory enhanced quantum secure communications.
one_liner: In-memory interference enables memory-assisted MDI-QKD using one memory and fewer detectors than conventional two-memory designs.
why_it_matters: The protocol improves modeled secret-key performance while halving key hardware resources, strengthening the case for near-term memory-enhanced secure networks.
detailed_summary: The scheme interferes a stationary matter qubit with a traveling photonic qubit inside an atomic-ensemble quantum memory. Quantitative comparisons predict higher secret-key rates and an earlier crossover beyond the memoryless MDI-QKD bound than existing alternatives. A proposed ORCA-memory implementation uses half as many memories and detectors as standard two-memory architectures.
main_result: The modeled protocol surpasses memoryless and two-memory MDI-QKD benchmarks while requiring only one memory and a reduced detector count.
application_angle: Reduced hardware complexity and favorable distance scaling make memory-assisted MDI-QKD more accessible to near-term quantum-network experiments.

title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.
one_liner: Parameterized quantum-circuit agents learn distinct musical behaviors through reinforcement and demonstrate meaningful operation on IBM quantum hardware.
why_it_matters: It is an unusual hardware-tested application of hybrid quantum learning, though its relevance is quantum computing rather than experimental sensing.
detailed_summary: The agentic-orchestra framework trains parameterized quantum-circuit agents through musically defined rewards rather than corpus imitation. Atomistic agents treat pitch and rhythm separately, whereas holistic agents act on combined note events. Experiments on IBM quantum hardware reportedly produced musically meaningful learned behavior and generalization to unseen MIDI material.
platform_or_system: IBM quantum processor with hybrid classical control
main_result: Quantum-circuit agents learned reward-conditioned musical behaviors that transferred to previously unseen MIDI inputs on current IBM hardware.
application_angle: The work explores near-term quantum processors as interactive creative-learning engines, although it does not demonstrate a sensing capability.

title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires continuous quantum error correction (QEC) to suppress physical noise. While Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, universal computation breaks this paradigm: executing non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard, real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements. Consequently, the controller must extract syndromes, decode them, and update the Pauli frame in real time, closing the entire QEC loop within a strict $1\,μ\text{s}$ cycle. However, prior proposals on Pauli frame tracking remain largely theoretical, leaving the microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed control pipelines unaddressed. To this end, we present QuFrame, a control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking that closes the QEC loop within $1\,μ\text{s}$ while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. By introducing QuFrameISA, we cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. To strictly guarantee the $1\,μ\text{s}$ deadline, QuFrame pairs an asynchronous primary decoder with an on-chip fallback decoder that resolves in $144\,\text{ns}$, natively reconciling divergent updates in hardware without degrading logical error rates.
one_liner: QuFrame tracks and resolves distributed Pauli-frame updates fast enough to close a fault-tolerant QEC control loop within 1 μs.
why_it_matters: Real-time frame handling is a hardware bottleneck for non-Clifford fault-tolerant computing, and QuFrame supplies a concrete low-latency controller architecture.
detailed_summary: QuFrame separates instruction execution from continuous Pauli-frame management through a dedicated ISA and per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines. Instructions are reconciled with the current frame using a table lookup, while a management unit supports lock-free concurrent commits. An on-chip fallback decoder resolves updates in 144 ns and reconciles them with an asynchronous primary decoder to guarantee the 1 μs cycle target.
main_result: The architecture closes the modeled QEC feedback loop within 1 μs while sustaining QPU-rate instruction throughput.
application_angle: It addresses the classical real-time control needed to execute measurement-dependent non-Clifford gates in scalable fault-tolerant processors.

title: Doppler effect on dual-downlink time-bin quantum key distribution and a proposed ephemeris-assisted witness-field correction
abstract: Time-bin entanglement is promising for satellite Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) due to its compatibility with telecom fiber networks, but its phase-sensitive measurements are vulnerable to Doppler effects induced by satellite motion. We present a spectral-temporal framework for time-bin-entangled photon pairs generated onboard a satellite via Spontaneous Parametric Down Conversion (SPDC) and distributed to two Optical Ground Stations (OGSs) over independent downlinks with distinct Doppler shifts. Each OGS is equipped with an Unbalanced Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (UMZI) used to perform Bennett-Brassard-Mermin 1992 (BBM92) entangled-photon QKD. In a simulated Low Earth Orbit (LEO) pass with matched 400 ps analyzer delays, the received time-bin separation changes by at most 8.8 fs per link, while the combined carrier phase shifts by about 38 rad, which primarily degrades phase-basis correlations. After zero-Doppler calibration, this phase separates into independent signal-and idler-link contributions, allowing each station to correct its link Doppler phase shift locally, without real-time phase exchange between the stations. We propose an ephemeris-assisted feed-forward architecture, in which an auxiliary interferometer analyzes a co-propagating classical witness field to reconstruct the local Doppler-induced phase, which a phase modulator then compensates on the quantum channel. In a noise-free model, a 1 Hz sample-and-hold correction rate keeps the phase-basis Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) below 2% and retains 93% of the ideal asymptotic key yield. After 18 accumulated passes, the corrected finite secret key reaches 95% of its ideal length, whereas relabeling the parity from the ephemeris without optical correction reaches only about 8%.
one_liner: A witness-field feed-forward scheme compensates Doppler-induced phase errors in dual-downlink satellite time-bin QKD.
why_it_matters: The modeled correction preserves most of the ideal key yield using local 1 Hz updates, addressing a major phase-stability obstacle for satellite QKD.
detailed_summary: The study models SPDC time-bin pairs sent from a LEO satellite to two ground stations with independent Doppler shifts and matched 400 ps interferometers. Although timing changes remain below 8.8 fs per link, the combined carrier phase shifts by roughly 38 rad and degrades phase-basis correlations. Ephemeris-assisted witness interferometers estimate each local phase for feed-forward optical correction; at 1 Hz, the noise-free model keeps QBER below 2% and retains 93% of ideal asymptotic yield.
main_result: Simulated local Doppler correction recovers 93% of ideal asymptotic yield and 95% of finite-key length after 18 accumulated passes.
application_angle: The architecture provides a concrete stabilization strategy for phase-sensitive satellite QKD using ephemerides, classical witness fields, and ground-station modulators.

title: Long-distance continuous variable entanglement distribution over deployed fibre
abstract: Continuous-variable (CV) entanglement offers deterministic generation and room-temperature coherent detection for quantum networks, but distributing it over deployed fibre has been hindered by the need to stabilise optical phase, polarisation, and timing at remote receivers. Here we demonstrate, to our knowledge, the first distribution of CV entanglement over deployed metropolitan fibre using independent coherent receivers. The two modes of a two-mode squeezed vacuum state are delivered to remote nodes through 23 km ($\approx 7$ dB loss) and 450 m ($\approx 1$ dB loss) deployed fibre links. Each node uses its own free-running laser and polarisation-diverse coherent receiver. Co-propagating pilot tones enable digital recovery of timing, phase and polarisation, while inter-mode correlations fix the quadrature alignment. We certify entanglement with a Simon-Duan value of $1.915\pm 0.013$, below the separability bound of 2 and a logarithmic negativity of $0.067\pm0.011$. By replacing optical stabilisation with digital reconstruction, our approach offers a practical route towards scalable CV quantum networks.
one_liner: CV entanglement is distributed over deployed metropolitan fibre using independent free-running lasers and digitally reconstructed coherent receivers.
why_it_matters: Digital recovery of phase, timing, and polarization removes demanding optical stabilization, advancing scalable CV quantum-network links.
detailed_summary: The two modes of a two-mode squeezed-vacuum state are sent through deployed fibre links of 23 km with about 7 dB loss and 450 m with about 1 dB loss. Independent free-running lasers and polarization-diverse coherent receivers operate at the remote nodes, while pilot tones and inter-mode correlations enable digital timing, phase, polarization, and quadrature recovery. The experiment obtains a Simon-Duan value of 1.915 ± 0.013 and logarithmic negativity of 0.067 ± 0.011.
main_result: The system certifies CV entanglement across a 23 km deployed metropolitan-fibre link without shared receiver lasers or active optical stabilization.
application_angle: The architecture supports more deployable CV quantum networking using telecom-style coherent receivers and digital signal processing.

title: Efficient simulation of variational quantum circuits: representation, accuracy and CPU/GPU allocation
abstract: Classical circuit simulation supports quantum software development and verification and provides a baseline for assessing quantum advantage. We compare gate-based statevector simulation, direct Pauli evolution and matrix product states for molecular and spin Variational Hamiltonian Ansatze and hardware-efficient ansatze on CPU/GPU systems, varying width, depth, precision and resource allocation. In the tested implementations, direct Pauli evolution benefits complex molecular VHA, whereas GPUs accelerate wider spin and hardware efficient circuits. Matrix product state is useful when limited entanglement permits accurate compression; corrected CPU FP32 can meet the tested tolerance while costing more than FP64. Workload size, startup, worker memory and task-specific profiling can change the preferred allocation. Matched NumPy Pauli updates accelerate two-layer full LiH by 3.45-fold; the GPU gives approximately 30-fold acceleration over 18-thread Aer for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM, both in FP64. We provide a procedure for choosing representation, precision and worker allocation jointly, comparing the cost of complete energy evaluations under accuracy, memory and core constraints.
one_liner: Benchmarks identify when statevectors, direct Pauli evolution, or MPS methods best simulate variational circuits on CPU and GPU hardware.
why_it_matters: Jointly selecting representation, precision, and compute allocation can substantially reduce the cost of developing and verifying quantum algorithms.
detailed_summary: The study benchmarks statevector simulation, direct Pauli evolution, and matrix product states for molecular, spin, and hardware-efficient variational ansätze. It varies circuit width, depth, numerical precision, memory, and CPU/GPU allocation while evaluating full energy-estimation workloads. Matched NumPy Pauli updates yield a 3.45-fold speedup for two-layer LiH, while a GPU provides about 30-fold acceleration over 18-thread Aer for a 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM circuit in FP64.
main_result: The benchmarks show that the optimal simulator and processor depend strongly on ansatz structure, entanglement, precision requirements, and workload scale.
application_angle: The proposed selection procedure can accelerate quantum-software verification and improve resource planning before execution on quantum processors.

title: Linear-mode photon counting performance and intrinsic dark current in HgCdTe APDs for quantum optical applications
abstract: The performance of HgCdTe APDs for single photon detection at T=80 K has been characterized using a hybrized Resistive Trans-Impedance Amplifier (RTIA) and a deported Capacitance Trans-impedance amplifier (CTIA). The single-photon detection capacity was characterized with the HgCdTe APDs operated in linear mode with high APD gain, M>400, and hybridized with the RTIA. The measurements revealed an external photon detection efficiency (PDE) of 42 % to 55 %, and a dark count rate (DCR) of 2.6 MHz to 17 MHz, for an amplitude threshold ranging from 2.5 to 4.5 times the rms noise of the amplifier. Taking into account the unity gain quantum efficiency, QE=63%, this corresponds to an internal PDE ranging from 66 % to 86 %. Using the deported CTIA, it was demonstrated that the high level of DCR is not the intrinsic limit of the APD technology. The CTIA approach enables direct measurement of the APD dark current, Idark, with gain-normalized dark current levels as low as Idark/M=10.9 fA at M = 450. This corresponds to a DCR of 150 Hz which is compatible with the requirements for most of the quantum photonics applications.
one_liner: Linear-mode HgCdTe APDs achieve high internal photon-detection efficiency, while direct dark-current measurements indicate a 150 Hz intrinsic-equivalent DCR.
why_it_matters: The results suggest that readout electronics, rather than HgCdTe APD material limits, cause the previously observed megahertz dark-count rates.
detailed_summary: At 80 K and avalanche gain above 400, RTIA-hybridized HgCdTe APDs show 42–55% external photon-detection efficiency and 2.6–17 MHz measured dark-count rates, depending on threshold. Correcting for 63% unity-gain quantum efficiency gives 66–86% internal detection efficiency. A deported CTIA directly measures gain-normalized dark current down to 10.9 fA at gain 450, corresponding to an estimated 150 Hz dark-count rate.
main_result: Direct dark-current measurements indicate that HgCdTe APDs can combine high internal detection efficiency with an intrinsic-equivalent dark-count rate near 150 Hz.
application_angle: Improved low-noise readout could make these detectors useful for infrared quantum optics, photon-starved sensing, and quantum communication.

title: From BBM92 Measurements to Secure Keys: Challenges in a Practical Implementation
abstract: The protocol introduced by C. H. Bennett, G. Brassard and N. D. Mermin in 1992 (BBM92) is one of the most important and widely adopted quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols. As with any other QKD protocol, its practical security depends on satisfying the assumptions underlying its theoretical security proofs. Here, we examine two common implementations of BBM92: a conventional passive receiver and a time-multiplexed configuration that halves the number of detectors. We characterise the passive polarisation analysers common to both architectures and present experimental results obtained with the time-multiplexed receiver, employing a continuous-wave (CW) pumped spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) source of polarisation-entangled photon pairs and threshold detectors. We investigate the challenges encountered during post-processing when attempting to satisfy the requirements of existing security proofs and discuss the gap between theoretical security assumptions and the extraction of a provably secure cryptographic key.
one_liner: An experimental BBM92 study exposes practical obstacles to turning entangled-photon measurements into keys covered by existing security proofs.
why_it_matters: It identifies where realistic receivers and post-processing can violate proof assumptions, preventing measured correlations from becoming provably secure keys.
detailed_summary: The work compares a conventional passive BBM92 receiver with a time-multiplexed architecture that halves the detector count. It characterizes the shared passive polarization analyzers and experimentally tests the multiplexed receiver using a CW-pumped SPDC source of polarization-entangled pairs and threshold detectors. The analysis focuses on post-processing requirements that are difficult to reconcile with assumptions in available security proofs.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates BBM92 measurements with a detector-saving receiver but finds unresolved gaps between the implementation and conditions for provably secure key extraction.
application_angle: The findings guide receiver design, characterization, and security-proof selection for deployable entanglement-based QKD systems.

title: Mid-Infrared Integrated Acousto-Optic Phase Modulation on GaAs/AlGaAs
abstract: We demonstrate a mid-infrared (7.5-10 um) integrated acousto-optic phase modulator operating at 460MHz based on a GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure. The combination of broad mid-infrared transparency and piezoelectric properties of GaAs based structures allows monolithic integration of all the device functions (electro-acoustic transduction and acousto-optic interaction) on a single material platform. Addressing the challenge presented by comparable mid-infrared and acoustic wavelengths, simultaneous propagation and confinement of surface acoustic waves and guided light is achieved using a deep-etched sub-wavelength grating. We develop a comprehensive and quantitative simulation framework to design the modulator devices, characterize their acoustic properties in a heterodyne vibrometer and perform a full, quantitative analysis of the device performance by inserting them in an integrated Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Remarkable agreement with simulations validates the proposed design flow, and opens the way to improved integrated acousto-optic devices operating in the longer end of the mid-infrared.
one_liner: A monolithic GaAs/AlGaAs device provides 460 MHz integrated acousto-optic phase modulation across the 7.5–10 µm mid-infrared band.
why_it_matters: It extends integrated high-frequency phase control into the long-wave mid-infrared using a single material platform and a simulation-validated design flow.
detailed_summary: The device combines electro-acoustic transduction and acousto-optic interaction on a piezoelectric GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure. A deep-etched subwavelength grating simultaneously confines guided mid-infrared light and surface acoustic waves despite their comparable wavelengths. Acoustic vibrometry and quantitative measurements in an integrated Mach-Zehnder interferometer agree closely with the multiphysics simulations.
main_result: The integrated modulator demonstrates 460 MHz phase modulation from 7.5 to 10 µm with measured behavior closely matching quantitative simulations.
application_angle: The platform could enable compact spectral control, sensing, and signal processing for molecular-fingerprint-region mid-infrared systems.

title: On a local hidden-variable model for postselected EPR correlations
abstract: A theoretical and numerical analysis of a Bell-type experiment is presented, where linear polarization measurements on nonmaximally entangled two-qubit states are modeled through a sigmoid-based threshold mechanism that violates the fair-sampling assumption required by the CHSH inequality. Numerical simulations characterize how closely this local construction can reproduce quantum-like correlations in the postselected detected sample, for both the |Phi_r> and |Psi_r> states over a range of entanglement parameters. For the tested configurations, the model produces CHSH-type violations only in the postselected detected sample through a setting-dependent detection mechanism, operating outside the assumptions of both the CHSH inequality and Mermin's 82.8% efficiency bound. The model is not in conflict with loophole-free Bell experiments, which specifically close the detection loophole exploited here. The CH--Eberhard analysis in the one-detector-per-side configuration yields J < 0 throughout the full range of entanglement parameters, as required for a strictly local model. The model is further extended with a local adaptive-threshold mechanism implementing one-sided memory. A paired comparison shows that this specific memory rule produces a systematic and reproducible shift in the CH--Eberhard parameter J relative to the fixed-threshold model, while leaving the CH--Eberhard analysis qualitatively unchanged under the tested conditions. The results characterize how a local, setting-dependent postselection mechanism shapes Bell-test statistics across a range of entanglement parameters, within the specific configurations and threshold rules tested.
one_liner: A local threshold-detection model reproduces quantum-like EPR correlations only after setting-dependent postselection exploits the detection loophole.
why_it_matters: The analysis clarifies how biased detection and memory can mimic Bell violations, reinforcing the need for loophole-resistant photonic experiments and protocols.
detailed_summary: The theoretical and numerical model applies sigmoid-based detection thresholds to polarization measurements of nonmaximally entangled two-qubit states. CHSH-type violations appear only in the postselected detected subset because sampling depends on the measurement setting; the model therefore lies outside fair-sampling assumptions and does not challenge loophole-free Bell tests. CH-Eberhard calculations retain J < 0 across the tested entanglement range, including after adding a one-sided adaptive-threshold memory rule.
main_result: The local model generates apparent CHSH violations through detection-biased postselection while remaining nonviolating under the applicable CH-Eberhard analysis.
application_angle: The results help diagnose detector-selection artifacts in photonic Bell tests and strengthen validation practices for device-independent quantum communication.

title: Gutzwiller Quantum-Classical Embedding for Dynamics Simulations of Correlated Electron Systems
abstract: Simulating the real-time dynamics of correlated electron systems requires a nonperturbative treatment of local correlations over long times, a challenge for classical methods. We present the time-dependent Gutzwiller quantum-classical embedding framework, t-GQCE, for generic multi-orbital lattice models with time-dependent Hamiltonians. Within the time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation, the lattice dynamics is mapped onto a noninteracting quasiparticle lattice, propagated classically, coupled to finite interacting embedding models propagated on quantum processors. The two parts exchange only embedding Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices, and the framework is agnostic to the quantum dynamics solver. We demonstrate it with adaptive variational quantum dynamics simulations of interaction quenches in the Hubbard model on the Bethe lattice. Without ghost orbitals, the embedding problem reduces to a single qubit, simulated on IBM quantum hardware with two qubits, including an ancilla. With more ghost orbitals, t-GQCE suppresses the artificial undamped oscillations of the conventional Gutzwiller approximation and approaches nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory results for weak and strong quenches. Statevector simulations with 2, 4 and 6 ghost orbitals per spin, or 8, 12 and 16 qubits, give adaptive circuits that follow the embedding states with infidelities below $5\times10^{-4}$. Under trapped-ion noise models, circuit compression, measurements in rotated orbital bases with post-selection, and noise mitigation reduce the measurement errors severalfold. At one third of the error rates of a hardware-benchmarked noise model, they reach an accuracy of $0.01$ for the single-particle density matrix and the double occupancy with $10^5$ shots per time step, and the Quantinuum H2-Emulator gives similar accuracy.
one_liner: A hybrid Gutzwiller embedding scheme couples classical lattice propagation to quantum-processor simulations of finite interacting models.
why_it_matters: It offers a hardware-oriented route to long-time dynamics of correlated electrons while exchanging only compact Hamiltonian and density-matrix data.
detailed_summary: The t-GQCE framework maps a time-dependent multi-orbital lattice problem to a classically propagated quasiparticle lattice coupled to finite interacting embeddings handled by a quantum solver. Adaptive statevector circuits with 8–16 qubits achieved embedding-state infidelities below 5×10^-4 and approached nonequilibrium DMFT results as ghost orbitals were added. Under trapped-ion noise models and on the Quantinuum H2-Emulator, compression, rotated-basis measurements, post-selection, and mitigation yielded roughly 0.01 accuracy for density matrices and double occupancy under reduced error rates.
main_result: The method reproduced correlated quench dynamics with high-fidelity adaptive circuits and demonstrated mitigated embedding simulations on IBM and Quantinuum-related platforms.
application_angle: The architecture could enable useful quantum-assisted simulations of nonequilibrium materials before fully fault-tolerant processors become available.

title: No-Go Theorems for Ordered Universal Entanglement Purification
abstract: Entanglement purification is a fundamental tool for obtaining high-fidelity entangled states used in various quantum technologies. It aims to increase the fidelity of noisy shared entangled states with a fixed maximally entangled state through LOCC. In distributed quantum systems, such as networks employing quantum repeaters, limited memory, probabilistic entanglement generation, and unequal storage times can leave a finite collection of nonidentical pairs. Their states may remain incompletely characterized even when calibrated preparation and storage records establish their fidelity ordering. Recent work has investigated whether fidelity ordering permits nontrivial universal purification. A nontrivial universal $n$-to-1 protocol must, conditioned on success, never lower the highest input fidelity and strictly increase it for at least one allowed joint input. Although no-go results have been established for a restricted class of LOCC protocols, the corresponding question for general LOCC has remained unresolved. Here, we study ordered universal purification under separable operations. Specifically, for every fixed finite $n\ge2$, we prove that when independently prepared two-qubit pairs range over the full family of states above a fixed fidelity threshold $0\le F_*<1$, any separable success map that never lowers the highest input fidelity on the allowed ordered inputs must preserve that fidelity exactly whenever it succeeds. This excludes nontrivial universal LOCC purification even for arbitrarily high input fidelities, without imposing a positive lower bound on success probability. ...
one_liner: A no-go theorem rules out nontrivial universal purification of fidelity-ordered, nonidentical two-qubit entangled pairs by LOCC.
why_it_matters: It identifies a fundamental limitation for repeater protocols when stored entangled pairs are ordered by fidelity but otherwise incompletely characterized.
detailed_summary: For every finite n≥2, the authors consider independently prepared two-qubit pairs drawn from the full state family above any fixed fidelity threshold below one. They prove that any separable success map that never reduces the best ordered input fidelity must preserve that fidelity exactly whenever it succeeds. Because LOCC is contained within separable operations, no nontrivial universal ordered n-to-1 LOCC purification protocol exists under these assumptions.
main_result: Universal fidelity-improving purification is impossible even for arbitrarily high-fidelity ordered inputs and without a lower bound on success probability.
application_angle: Quantum-network designers must use additional state knowledge, restricted noise models, or nonuniversal strategies to improve heterogeneous stored links.

title: Number-correlated photon entanglement with a quantum memory interferometer
abstract: Strong photon-photon interactions are central to quantum optical technologies yet remain challenging to realise at the single-photon level. Here, we show how embedding a quantum memory within a Mach-Zehnder interferometer enables a coherent transformation that converts single-mode photon states into number-correlated entangled states. Using an off-resonant ladder-type atomic interaction, storage and retrieval within a quantum memory maps a single-photon excitation onto a pair of photons across distinct optical modes via a driving control field. Embedding this within an interferometer deterministically produces an effective transformation in the photon number basis: $\sum_n a_n |n\rangle \to \sum_n a_n |n\rangle |n\rangle$ without relying on conventional optical nonlinearities. Measurement of one mode enables photonic non-demolition detection, state preparation, and frequency conversion as applications of the same underlying transformation. These results establish quantum memories embedded within an interferometric architecture as a platform for measurement-induced photon-photon interactions and the generation of Gaussian and non-Gaussian entangled states.
one_liner: A quantum memory inside a Mach–Zehnder interferometer converts a single-mode photon state into number-correlated optical entanglement.
why_it_matters: The scheme supplies an effective photon–photon interaction without conventional single-photon optical nonlinearities.
detailed_summary: An off-resonant ladder-type atomic memory uses storage, control-field interaction, and retrieval to map one photonic excitation onto paired photons in distinct optical modes. Interferometric embedding realizes the coherent number-basis transformation Σ_n a_n|n⟩→Σ_n a_n|n⟩|n⟩ deterministically at the model level. Measuring one output mode supports nondemolition detection, conditional state preparation, and frequency conversion, while the full transformation generates Gaussian or non-Gaussian entanglement.
main_result: The proposed architecture deterministically generates number-correlated two-mode states from arbitrary single-mode photon-number superpositions.
application_angle: A common memory-interferometer module could serve entanglement generation, heralded photonic processing, nondemolition detection, and wavelength conversion.

title: Instanton tunnelling as a verifiable benchmark for digital quantum simulation: circuit structure, classical simulability and hardware reproducibility
abstract: We use instanton-mediated tunnelling in the quartic double well as a benchmark for digital quantum simulation that is checkable against an exact answer at every step. The instanton enters through the classical analysis; the hardware tests the dynamics of the lattice model. A unary (single-excitation) encoding maps N lattice sites to N qubits, with the single-excitation dynamics as a reference that remains classically cheap at any N. For a second-order Trotter circuit with adjacent, equal-angle XX/YY pairs on each bond, we prove that the Schmidt rank across any cut is at most four at every gate boundary and at most two after each pair, independently of N. Matrix-product-state simulations of this gate list reproduce the exact splitting up to N = 48. For this bond-wise formula the admissible Trotter step shrinks roughly as N^-2, so one tunnelling period costs about N^3.3 two-qubit gates; a kinetic/potential splitting keeps the step near 0.065 up to N=128, so this scaling belongs to splitting the kinetic term bond by bond. At a coarser, separately bounded step we measure the full transfer at N=8 on two superconducting processors, recovering the lattice splitting to a few percent and its dependence on the barrier height, which at this resolution is set by the lattice rather than by the instanton. Over 9 repetitions, runs taken minutes apart agree to shot noise, while runs hours to weeks apart differ by up to 6.1%, also on a fixed set of qubits; with sessions as the sampling unit, the processors differ in the damping, while a difference in the splitting is not established. Normalising by the measured single-excitation population extends the usable depth about 4-fold but does not improve the splitting. A Gaussian start state, which needs no diagonalisation, reproduces the splitting of the eigenvector-based start to within 1.6 percentage points.
one_liner: Instanton tunnelling in a discretized double well provides an exactly checkable benchmark for digital quantum simulators.
why_it_matters: The benchmark separates algorithmic errors, classical simulability, short-term reproducibility, and long-term hardware drift using a controlled physical model.
detailed_summary: A unary encoding maps N lattice sites to N qubits, while the chosen XX/YY Trotter circuit maintains Schmidt rank at most four across every cut and is therefore classically tractable. Matrix-product-state calculations reproduce the exact splitting through N=48 and expose unfavorable gate scaling for bond-wise kinetic splitting. Experiments at N=8 on two superconducting processors recovered the lattice tunnelling splitting within a few percent, with minute-scale agreement at shot noise but session-to-session deviations reaching 6.1%.
main_result: Two processors reproduced barrier-dependent tunnelling splittings while the benchmark quantified circuit scaling and hardware drift over minutes to weeks.
application_angle: The model provides a reproducible, analytically anchored test for validating digital-simulation accuracy and tracking calibration stability.

title: On Reaction Depth and Fast Fault-Tolerant Boolean Logic
abstract: Reducing runtimes of quantum applications is critical for practical viability. On quantum computers, the runtime can depend both on the speed of quantum operations and on how often the program must wait for the classical coprocessor to determine adaptive operations. Some recent approaches to reducing this overhead have focused on minimizing the "reaction depth" of a computation, informally defined as the number of times the classical coprocessor must be consulted while running a quantum program. In this work, we formalize the notion of reaction depth. We find several subtleties in this theory. For example, we distinguish the reaction depth of a circuit from that of a circuit run, and show that the magic depth of a unitary can be higher than the reaction depth once compiled into Clifford computation and magic state injection. We then focus on the specific case of coherent Boolean logic, a common and expensive component in quantum algorithms. We use a natural gateset for fast operations with Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes, which consists of homogeneous $Z$- and $X$-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs), alongside a supply of Toffoli states. We prove that, using this gateset, any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented on a quantum computer with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth, at the cost of exponential space and leaving some qubits "dirty". Using the same gateset we find two efficient AutoAND circuits that require only a Toffoli state and homogeneous PPMs. We then give efficient implementations of the quantum ripple-carry adder and quantum schoolbook multiplier, which require a low number of heterogeneous PPMs for uncomputation. We find implementations competitive with the state-of-the-art despite the restricted gateset.
one_liner: Fault-tolerant Boolean circuits can attain constant quantum and reaction depth using homogeneous Pauli-product measurements and Toffoli states.
why_it_matters: Reducing classical feedback rounds can shorten logical runtimes on architectures where adaptive control is a major bottleneck.
detailed_summary: The work formalizes reaction depth and distinguishes the depth of a circuit from that of an individual run. With homogeneous X- and Z-type Pauli-product measurements plus Toffoli resource states, any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented at constant quantum and reaction depth, although the general construction uses exponential space and leaves dirty qubits. Efficient AutoAND, ripple-carry-adder, and schoolbook-multiplier constructions are also developed for the restricted gate set.
main_result: The authors prove constant-depth Boolean computation under the selected primitives and give resource-efficient arithmetic circuits competitive with prior designs.
application_angle: The constructions target faster logical arithmetic on machines constrained by measurement latency and classical feed-forward.

title: Coherent-Response and Thermal-Fluctuation Information in Cavity-Magnon Magnetometry
abstract: Magnetic sensing with cavity--magnon systems typically relies on the coherent response, while field-dependent fluctuations are treated as measurement noise. Here, we show that the variance of a measured microwave quadrature provides a distinct source of magnetic-field information. For repeated phase-sensitive measurements of a calibrated quadrature, we derive the Gaussian likelihood and show that its Fisher information separates exactly into two terms. The coherent-displacement term depends on the field derivative of the quadrature mean, and the thermal-fluctuation term depends on the field derivative of its variance. Both terms are accessible from the same measurement record, but their optimal operating conditions differ. For the amplitude quadrature, the dimensionless coherent response factor reaches its global maximum at cooperativity $C=2$, corresponding to a coupling strength $g=\sqrt{2κ_aκ_m}$, and at linewidth-normalized detunings $δ_a=δ_m=\pm 1$. In the near-resonance approximation, the reduced variance-information term is globally maximized at cavity--magnon frequency matching, $Δ_a=Δ_m$, and approaches a finite limit at large cooperativity. We map the relative contributions of the two terms across drive frequencies, drive strengths, and temperatures. Strong coherent driving favors displacement-based sensing, whereas at finite temperature the variance contribution can dominate under weak driving and remain finite even when the coherent-displacement contribution vanishes.
