These results establish a measurement-specific framework for cavity--magnon magnetometry and identify operating regimes for exploiting the quadrature mean, its variance, or both.
one_liner: Cavity–magnon magnetometry can extract magnetic-field information from both coherent quadrature shifts and thermal variance changes.
why_it_matters: Using fluctuation information can preserve or improve sensitivity in weak-drive regimes where the conventional coherent response becomes negligible.
detailed_summary: For repeated phase-sensitive microwave measurements, the Gaussian Fisher information separates exactly into contributions from the field dependence of the quadrature mean and variance. The amplitude-quadrature coherent response is globally optimized at cooperativity C=2 and normalized detunings δ_a=δ_m=±1. Near resonance, variance information is maximized by cavity–magnon frequency matching and can dominate at finite temperature under weak driving, even when the displacement contribution vanishes.
main_result: The analysis identifies distinct optimal regimes for mean- and variance-based field estimation and shows that thermal fluctuations can carry dominant sensing information.
application_angle: Jointly processing quadrature mean and variance could broaden operating regimes and improve low-drive microwave magnetic sensing.

title: The magical memory cost of entanglement spectrum compression
abstract: How much quantum memory is needed to faithfully retain the entanglement spectrum of a bipartite pure state after separating out Bell pairs through local unitaries? We derive the exact tradeoff between Bell-pair yield, residual memory, and reconstruction fidelity under local unitaries, defining an operational measure of entanglement-spectrum complexity. Smoothed entanglement spread bounds this memory cost from below, while diverging nonlocal magic forces unbounded memory at any fixed positive fidelity. Chaotic circuit dynamics exhibit a transient memory peak whose height increases with system size, followed by declining cost despite continued entropy growth. A large typical Haar-random state requires only an accuracy-dependent memory, whereas stationary fermionic Gaussian states retain a growing cost with size. In the circuits studied, the multiscale spectral structure associated with entanglement catalysis also has a practical consequence for matrix product state compression, yielding a multiplicative overhead not captured by the conventional entropy-based bond dimension estimate.
one_liner: Exact bounds connect Bell-pair extraction, residual quantum memory, and faithful reconstruction of a state's entanglement spectrum.
why_it_matters: The results quantify memory overheads that entropy-only estimates miss when compressing entangled states for quantum networks and tensor-network simulation.
detailed_summary: The authors derive an exact tradeoff among Bell-pair yield, residual memory, and reconstruction fidelity under local unitaries. Smoothed entanglement spread lower-bounds the cost, while diverging nonlocal magic requires unbounded memory at fixed positive fidelity. Circuit and state-family studies reveal transient memory peaks and a multiplicative matrix-product-state compression overhead beyond entropy-based estimates.
platform_or_system: Bipartite quantum states and chaotic circuits
main_result: Entanglement-spectrum complexity exactly determines the residual memory needed after locally extracting Bell pairs.
application_angle: The framework can guide memory allocation and compression strategies for distributed entanglement and classical tensor-network representations.

title: Squeezed Cooling and Lasing with Cold Atoms in Cavity-QED
abstract: A squeezed laser undergoes a lasing transition into a squeezed cavity mode, where stimulated emission generates a bright coherent field with a laser-like coherence time while maintaining one field quadrature below the vacuum noise level. Here we propose an optical implementation that needs neither a nonlinear crystal nor injected squeezed light, based on engineered interactions between ensembles of rubidium atoms and a squeezed cavity mode via cavity-assisted Raman transitions. A first ensemble cools the cavity into a squeezed vacuum, a mechanism we term squeezed cooling, yielding up to 9 dB in the intracavity field, surpassing the 3 dB limit of optical parametric oscillators. Tuned for output instead, it reaches up to 18 dB of output squeezing. Incoherently pumping a second ensemble drives a lasing transition into the squeezed mode, emitting a bright beam with long coherence time and noise below vacuum spanning a megahertz-wide band, away from the sharp phase-diffusion peak of excess noise at the carrier frequency, and robust to relaxation oscillations. We characterize lasing thresholds, superradiant emission, and linewidth narrowing, and identify the experimentally accessible regime where the system exhibits the defining features of a squeezed laser.
one_liner: Laser-dressed rubidium ensembles could cool and lase into a squeezed cavity mode without nonlinear crystals or injected squeezed light.
why_it_matters: The scheme promises bright, long-coherence squeezed output with up to 18 dB squeezing across a megahertz-scale band using cavity-QED hardware.
detailed_summary: Cavity-assisted Raman interactions engineer a squeezed cavity mode using cold rubidium ensembles. One ensemble produces squeezed cooling with up to 9 dB intracavity squeezing or 18 dB output squeezing, while a pumped second ensemble drives lasing into that mode. The predicted beam combines long coherence time with sub-vacuum noise over a megahertz-wide band away from the carrier's phase-diffusion peak.
platform_or_system: Cold rubidium ensembles in cavity QED
main_result: The proposed system reaches 9 dB intracavity or 18 dB output squeezing and supports bright squeezed lasing with megahertz-band sub-vacuum noise.
application_angle: A crystal-free squeezed-light source could support precision interferometry, continuous-variable processing, and low-noise optical sensing.

title: The limits of magic-state cultivation
abstract: Fault tolerance is understood through Pauli algebra, which fails at non-Clifford gates. Circuits such as magic-state cultivation, which checks an encoded T state with physical T gates, have therefore lacked an exact theory of which faults are harmful. We develop such a theory and show that, for any circuit that prepares a magic state with non-Clifford gates and postselection, one stabilizer code on the non-Clifford gates decides which faults are harmful. This ties cultivation to distillation, bounds its T-count from below and gives an exact test. For a single check on an ideally encoded state, the fault distance reduces to Pauli algebra on the code. As a use case, we analyze the S gates that have stood in for T gates in the design of cultivation. We show that this proxy can only overstate the fault distance of such a check, and that the checks in use, on color and surface codes, tolerate at most half as many faults as their code allows. The theory also yields nearest-neighbor checks that keep the full distance, certified up to code distance nine.
one_liner: A stabilizer-code theory exactly identifies harmful faults in postselected, non-Clifford magic-state preparation circuits.
why_it_matters: It exposes overestimated fault distances in existing cultivation checks and provides nearest-neighbor designs that retain full code distance.
detailed_summary: The paper shows that a stabilizer code defined on the non-Clifford gates determines which faults harm a postselected magic-state preparation circuit. This yields an exact fault test and a lower bound on T-count, connecting cultivation to distillation. Applying the theory shows that common S-gate proxy checks on surface and color codes tolerate at most half the faults allowed by the underlying code, while new nearest-neighbor checks preserve full distance through distance nine.
main_result: The authors derive an exact harmful-fault criterion and certify local cultivation checks that retain full code distance up to distance nine.
application_angle: The method enables more reliable design and resource estimation for non-Clifford state factories in fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Time-Varying Medium from an Ensemble of Laser-Dressed Quantum Emitters
abstract: We propose a minimal quantum-mechanical model of a frequency dispersive, time-modulated medium that explicitly incorporates the pumping mechanism. It consists of a homogeneous ensemble of quantum emitters dressed by a pump laser. We analyze their dispersive, time-varying response to a perturbative probe field by deriving the macroscopic polarizability of the ensemble, and then solving Maxwell's equations via the Floquet formalism. This yields a rich band structure that departs from conventional analyses in which the modulation source is neglected, arising from the interplay between the dispersive polaritonic and time-varying responses. These results shed light on the role of the modulation source in time-varying media and pave the way toward realizing dispersive time-varying media from driven quantum-mechanical systems.
one_liner: Laser-dressed quantum emitters provide a microscopic route to dispersive time-varying media with pump-dependent Floquet band structures.
why_it_matters: Including the physical modulation source reveals polaritonic bands absent from conventional prescribed-modulation models and suggests realizable dynamic photonic media.
detailed_summary: The work models a homogeneous ensemble of quantum emitters dressed by a pump laser and probed perturbatively. A macroscopic polarizability is derived from the emitter dynamics and inserted into Maxwell's equations, which are solved using Floquet theory. The resulting band structure reflects coupled dispersive-polaritonic and temporal-modulation effects that are missed when the pump source is omitted.
main_result: A pump-explicit microscopic model predicts a rich Floquet-polaritonic band structure for dispersive time-modulated optical media.
application_angle: The approach offers a design path toward experimentally realizable frequency converters, nonreciprocal photonics, and dynamically controlled wave propagation.

title: Quantum Simulation of First-Quantised Chemistry with a Sum-of-Squares Representation
abstract: Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. In the low-qubit and low-filling regime, our algorithm is therefore the method of choice for chemistry in orbital basis sets.
one_liner: A first-quantized chemistry algorithm cuts Toffoli counts by up to 16× for low-filling molecular problems with limited logical qubits.
why_it_matters: It targets chemically realistic orbital spaces while reducing both gate and qubit requirements in the hardware-constrained fault-tolerant regime.
detailed_summary: The algorithm combines a non-convex sum-of-squares Hamiltonian representation with spectral-gap amplification for first-quantized phase estimation in generic orbital bases. Logical-level compilations for six molecules containing 4–24 electrons and 5–14 times as many orbitals show up to a 16-fold Toffoli reduction over a leading second-quantized method. It remains cheaper up to several hundred to roughly 1,400 logical qubits and lowers the minimum qubit count by factors of 1.4–2.
main_result: In low-filling benchmarks, the method uses up to 16× fewer Toffoli gates and 1.4–2× fewer minimum logical qubits than second quantization.
application_angle: The reduced resource requirements bring dynamical-correlation calculations closer to processors with only a few hundred logical qubits.

title: Dressed-State Quantum Information Processing Using a Multilayer Ion Trap Chip with an Integrated Radio Frequency Resonator
abstract: We present the experimental preparation of a radio frequency (RF)-dressed-state qubit, the coherent operation of a single RF-dressed qubit, and the selective readout of RF-dressed hyperfine states of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions trapped using a novel microstructured ion trap chip. We demonstrate the individual addressing of RF-dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal. To this end, we developed, manufactured, and characterized a trap chip specifcally designed for quantum information processing with RF-dressed-state qubits. The chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated resonator that creates a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude along the axis of a linear ion crystal. This RF gradient enables the individual addressing of dressed qubit states as well as their coupling. We characterize the ion trap chip experimentally using the hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of laser cooled $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions and by applying a single, global, modulated RF field oscillating near 12.6 GHz that drives dressed-state resonances. We present a microfabricated multilayer ion trap chip specifically designed for quantum information processing based on dressed-state qubits. This ion trap chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated radio frequency (RF) resonator, creating a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude that allows for individual qubit addressing and qubit-qubit coupling. We experimentally characterize this ion trap chip demonstrating dressed-qubit state preparation, coherent single dressed-qubit operation, and dressed-state-selective read-out using hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$. For this purpose, a global modulated RF driving field oscillating near 12.6 GHz is applied to the ions. In addition, we demonstrate individual addressing of dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal.
one_liner: A multilayer ion-trap chip with an integrated RF resonator enables preparation, control, readout, and individual addressing of dressed qubits.
why_it_matters: The experiment integrates the magnetic-field gradient needed for scalable dressed-state control directly into microfabricated trapped-ion hardware.
detailed_summary: The microfabricated multilayer trap incorporates an RF resonator that generates a magnetic-field-amplitude gradient along a linear ion crystal. Using laser-cooled ytterbium-171 hyperfine states and a global modulated drive near 12.6 GHz, the authors demonstrate dressed-state preparation, coherent single-qubit operations, and state-selective readout. The gradient also permits individual addressing of two dressed qubits in a Coulomb crystal and is intended to mediate coupling.
main_result: The chip demonstrates coherent dressed-qubit control and selective individual addressing in a two-ion crystal using an integrated RF-field gradient.
application_angle: Integrated RF control can reduce wiring and optical-addressing complexity in scalable trapped-ion quantum processors.

title: Residual Allan Stability under Periodic Auxiliary Ramsey Sampling
abstract: The timing of auxiliary Ramsey measurements can change the frequency stability associated with a drifting pulse shift at a fixed nominal Fisher-information rate for a constant shift. For periodic instantaneous observations of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck shift with causal prediction between updates, we derive the exact residual covariance averaged over the update cycle and the corresponding Allan variance at arbitrary averaging times. Relative to a continuous Kalman reference at the same information rate, periodic estimation increases the cycle-averaged estimation-error variance, reduces the short-time residual Allan variance, and increases its long-time value. Its covariance decays more slowly at the origin and has a larger integral. We extend the result to instantaneous sensing of the sum of finitely many independent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck modes. Integrated observations preserve the short-time ordering for the scalar shift, and numerical calculations resolve the dependence of the crossover on window duration. A zero-order-hold comparison shows that the short-time ordering can change when the same estimator drives a different correction command. A three-level Ramsey model of coherent population trapping (CPT) maps the discriminator response to an effective information budget and illustrates how the dark times affect the choice of schedule.
one_liner: Exact analysis shows how periodic auxiliary Ramsey sampling reshapes residual frequency stability for drifting pulse shifts.
why_it_matters: The results provide concrete scheduling rules for Ramsey-based references and sensors whose systematic shifts drift across multiple timescales.
detailed_summary: The authors derive exact cycle-averaged residual covariance and Allan variance for periodic instantaneous observations of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck frequency shift with causal prediction. At fixed information rate, periodic estimation lowers short-time residual Allan variance but raises its long-time value relative to continuous Kalman estimation. The framework extends to multiple drift modes and is mapped onto a three-level coherent-population-trapping Ramsey discriminator.
main_result: Periodic sampling produces an analytically quantified short-time stability benefit and long-time penalty whose crossover depends on the observation and correction protocol.
application_angle: The model can guide Ramsey timing, dark-time selection, and feedback design in atomic clocks, frequency references, and drift-limited quantum sensors.

title: Theory of Particle Scattering on Superconducting Qubits: From Single Devices to Quantum Arrays
abstract: Superconducting qubits provide microwave-scale transitions and thus offer quantum targets for direct particle scattering with extremely small energy transfer. We develop a general framework for inelastic scattering in which an incident particle exchanges an off-shell photon with a superconducting quantum circuit, inducing a transition from a lower-energy internal state of the circuit to a higher-energy one. The target dependence is encoded in a finite-momentum electromagnetic transition current and, for charge-dominated response, in a qubit transition form factor. A key feature of particle scattering is that a microwave-scale excitation does not necessarily correspond to a long-wavelength interaction, since nonrelativistic particles can transfer spatial momenta much larger than the deposited energy. The full finite-momentum device response is therefore essential. We specialize the formalism to transmon qubits, construct a realistic electrostatic response for a planar Xmon-style transmon, and apply it to photon-mediated scattering of eV-scale bosonic dark matter, including final-state Bose stimulation. We find that the resulting enhancement substantially improves the projected sensitivity at the lowest masses. Owing to the exceptionally low transition threshold of superconducting qubits, this approach opens sensitivity to dark matter in the eV-to-keV mass range, which remains largely unexplored by existing direct-detection experiments. We further show that $N$ independently operated qubits give the expected rate proportional to $N$, while suitably prepared Dicke states can in principle achieve a collective enhancement approaching $N^2$ when spatial coherence is maintained across the array. These results establish superconducting qubits as quantum targets for direct particle scattering and provide a framework for optimizing low-threshold dark-matter searches.
one_liner: A finite-momentum scattering framework turns superconducting qubits and coherent qubit arrays into low-threshold particle detectors.
why_it_matters: Microwave transition thresholds could open direct-detection sensitivity to eV–keV dark matter, with possible collective enhancement from coherent arrays.
detailed_summary: The work formulates inelastic particle scattering from superconducting circuits through finite-momentum electromagnetic transition currents and qubit form factors. A realistic planar Xmon transmon model is applied to photon-mediated scattering of eV-scale bosonic dark matter, including final-state Bose stimulation. Independent qubits give rate scaling proportional to N, while spatially coherent Dicke states can in principle approach an N² enhancement.
platform_or_system: Planar Xmon transmons and qubit arrays
main_result: The framework projects sensitivity to eV–keV dark matter and identifies Bose-stimulated and coherent-array mechanisms that enhance scattering rates.
application_angle: It provides device-level design tools for using superconducting quantum processors as direct detectors of extremely small particle energy deposits.

title: The Clifford Hierarchy from Clifford Stabilizers in 2D
abstract: The Bravyi-König theorem limits the constant-depth logical gates of 2D topological Pauli stabilizer codes to be in the Clifford group. Known qubit codes with Clifford stabilizers exceed it by only one level of the Clifford hierarchy, and this was conjectured to hold generally. We show that this bound can be completely bypassed, and that topological codes with Clifford stabilizers in 2D can realize transversal logical gates at any level of the Clifford hierarchy. We present two explicit constructions of codes based on copies of the quantum doubles of $D_4$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2$, with $k$ logical qubits and a logical $C^{k-1}Z$ gate, which is at level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy. The physical circuits realizing the gates consist only of physical $Z$ or $CZ$ gates. The main new ingredient comes from the logical encoding, which depends crucially on non-Abelian group multiplication.
one_liner: Two-dimensional topological codes with Clifford stabilizers are constructed with transversal gates at arbitrary Clifford-hierarchy levels.
why_it_matters: The result removes a presumed gate-set ceiling for 2D topological architectures and expands routes to low-overhead fault-tolerant logical operations.
detailed_summary: The authors construct 2D topological codes based on copies of the quantum doubles of D4 and Z2. For k logical qubits, the encoding supports a logical controlled-(k−1)-Z gate at level k of the Clifford hierarchy. The corresponding physical circuits require only Z or CZ gates, with the higher-level logical action arising from an encoding that exploits non-Abelian group multiplication.
main_result: Clifford-stabilizer codes in two dimensions can realize transversal logical gates at every level of the Clifford hierarchy.
application_angle: The constructions suggest new fault-tolerant code architectures that obtain complex logical gates from simple physical Z and CZ operations.

title: Modeling couplings and quench dynamics of hundred-qubit quantum processors
abstract: Quantum processors now operate beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, yet their design and verification rest on precise models of the device. Understanding which properties of quantum processors can still be predicted on classical computers is central both to building these machines and to delimiting claims of quantum advantage. Here we address this question at the device level, using continuous unitary transformations to derive effective Hamiltonians non-perturbatively for two-dimensional superconducting processors at a cost polynomial in qubit number. For a 96-transmon array with tunable couplers, we extract the effective qubit couplings, state-dependent interactions (e.g., ZZ couplings), and eigenstate locality that guide processor design. This computation parallelizes over tensor contractions and thus takes an hour at most per design point on a single GPU, enabling rapid design iterations of the full array. Combining these effective models with semiclassical sampling, we then predict the quench dynamics of 100 qubits and 180 couplers at half filling, a sector of dimension $10^{29}$, and validate the approach against exact dynamics of smaller arrays. We show that our approach captures relaxation, thermalization, and transport, but not the bitstring statistics underlying cross-entropy benchmarks. The predicted transport carries a fingerprint of the device: under a staggered detuning, excitations cross over from ballistic to diffusive spreading, slow down at a doublon resonance, and diffuse at different rates on each sublattice. Our results chart which observables lie within classical reach and offer a practical tool for designing future devices.
one_liner: Polynomial-cost models predict couplings and selected quench observables across superconducting processors containing about 100 qubits.
why_it_matters: Hour-scale full-array modeling on one GPU could accelerate processor design while clarifying which large-device behaviors remain classically predictable.
detailed_summary: Continuous unitary transformations are used to derive non-perturbative effective Hamiltonians for a 96-transmon array with tunable couplers, including effective exchange, ZZ interactions, and eigenstate locality. Each design point takes at most about an hour on one GPU. Coupled with semiclassical sampling, the model predicts relaxation, thermalization, and transport for 100 qubits and 180 couplers, but not cross-entropy bitstring statistics.
main_result: The method efficiently reproduces device couplings and macroscopic quench transport, including a ballistic-to-diffusive crossover and doublon-resonance slowdown.
application_angle: It enables rapid full-chip design iteration, calibration-oriented modeling, and realistic assessment of classically verifiable processor observables.

title: Self-testing in Fermionic Networks
abstract: Self-testing certifies quantum states and measurements from observed correlations alone, without assumptions on the inner workings of the devices. Its standard formulation, however, models the devices as manipulating qudits, of arbitrary or even infinite dimension. Yet febits, information encoded in the presence or absence of a fermion in a mode, can produce correlations in quantum networks that no qudit model reproduces under the same locality constraints. We first show that the modeling choice in terms of qudits or febits matters for self-testing: some correlations that self-test a unique qudit strategy admit two fermionic realizations inequivalent under local parity-preserving isometries. We then develop a fermionic self-testing framework and show that the correlations of a three-party rewiring network single out febit states and measurements up to such isometries, providing the first genuine fermionic self-test.
one_liner: A three-party network protocol provides the first self-test that genuinely certifies fermionic states and measurements.
why_it_matters: Fermionic encodings can evade conclusions drawn from ordinary qudit models, making parity-aware certification essential for fermionic quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The paper shows that correlations uniquely self-testing a qudit strategy may still permit two inequivalent fermionic realizations under local parity-preserving isometries. It then develops a fermionic self-testing formalism appropriate to occupation-encoded febits. Correlations from a three-party rewiring network certify the intended fermionic states and measurements up to the physically relevant isometries.
main_result: The proposed correlations constitute the first genuine fermionic self-test under local parity-preserving equivalence.
application_angle: The framework supports assumption-light certification of fermionic nodes, encodings, and operations in future quantum communication networks.

title: A measurement-free quantum error correction protocol for superconducting cavities
abstract: The realization of large-scale quantum computation will require quantum error correction (QEC). One way to reduce the demands placed on QEC is to correct dominant physical errors at a lower level before passing the remaining errors to an outer code. Recently, Krastanov et al. [Nat. Commun. 12, 191 (2021)] proposed a measurement-free error-correction protocol based on coherent control of photonic modes that corrects for photon loss. Here, we adapt this approach to a circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) architecture using three superconducting microwave cavities coupled by Josephson-junction-based nonlinear elements. We encode the logical qubit in the lowest-order binomial code of one cavity, while the two other cavities serve as ancillas. Using numerical simulations with experimentally realistic parameters, we demonstrate that our protocol can correct single-photon loss with 99% fidelity. Furthermore, we optimize the waiting time between successive rounds of error-correction, and show that the logical lifetime can be extended by a factor of 1.2-1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$ encoding, surpassing break-even performance. Our work highlights the potential of gate-based, measurement-free QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
one_liner: A three-cavity cQED protocol coherently corrects single-photon loss with 99% simulated fidelity and exceeds break-even lifetime.
why_it_matters: Avoiding measurements and real-time feedback could simplify lower-level protection of bosonic memories before errors reach an outer code.
detailed_summary: The protocol encodes a logical qubit in the lowest-order binomial code of one superconducting microwave cavity and uses two additional cavities as ancillas. Josephson-junction nonlinear elements implement coherent, measurement-free correction of photon loss. Simulations with experimentally realistic parameters report 99% single-loss correction fidelity and a 1.2–1.8× lifetime increase over an unprotected Fock encoding.
main_result: Optimized correction cycles surpass break-even performance, extending simulated logical lifetime by 1.2–1.8× while correcting one photon loss with 99% fidelity.
application_angle: The approach offers a hardware-compatible route to autonomous-style bosonic protection without measurement latency or classical feedback electronics.

title: Characterizing a neutral atom quantum simulator accessible in cloud
abstract: Quantum simulators have become a reality in recent years, with several platforms now remotely accessible through the cloud. These systems give researchers the opportunity to run quantum programs without requiring either a dedicated laboratory or extensive experimental expertise, and, in several cases, they have already enabled the execution of relevant protocols with remarkable results. However, despite the impressive progress in the performance of these machines, they still suffer from various noise sources, some of which are not always completely clear to the end user, which limits their applicability to tasks that are sufficiently robust against noise of various kinds. In this work, we investigate the behavior of Fresnel, a remotely accessible neutral-atom analog quantum simulator provided by Pasqal. We design and perform a series of experiments probing the machine's response to various pulse sequences and experimental settings, and identify the main noise sources affecting its dynamics. Based on these data, we construct an effective model of the system's noisy evolution and use numerical optimization to infer the noise strengths. The resulting model accurately reproduces the simulator's dynamics, showing how effective noise models can be built for cloud-based quantum resources.
one_liner: Experiments on Pasqal’s cloud-accessible Fresnel neutral-atom simulator identify dominant noise sources and calibrate an effective noisy-dynamics model.
why_it_matters: The work gives remote users a practical way to characterize hidden hardware noise and assess whether analog quantum protocols will remain reliable on a cloud platform.
detailed_summary: The authors probe the Fresnel neutral-atom analog simulator with multiple pulse sequences and experimental settings. They infer noise strengths through numerical optimization and construct an effective noisy-evolution model. The calibrated model accurately reproduces the measured simulator dynamics.
main_result: A data-driven effective noise model reproduces the dynamics of a remotely operated neutral-atom quantum simulator.
application_angle: The characterization workflow can help cloud users benchmark hardware, design noise-robust protocols, and interpret remote experimental results more reliably.

title: Colloquium: Isotopes for medicine and fundamental physics
abstract: Isotopes, variants of elements distinguished by their neutron number, have important applications for medicine and fundamental science. This review explores the historical challenges and new technologies for enriching and detecting isotopes. We motivate the work by challenges posed by three of history's greatest scientists: James Clerk Maxwell's thought experiment on thermodynamics, Ernest Rutherford's practical dilemma in radiochemistry, and Albert Einstein's questions about the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics. The journey to meet these challenges has catalyzed the development of innovative techniques for isotope separation. These advancements can mitigate the worldwide crisis in the supply of enriched isotopes. We then explore the expected impact of these new technologies on medicine, which include radioisotopes for cancer therapy and stable isotopes as tracers for metabolism. We explain the importance of developing scalable techniques for isotope detection and how it can help with early detection of certain diseases. Finally, we turn to basic science, outlining proposed new tests of quantum mechanics that utilize radioactive atomic clocks to probe the fundamental nature of determinism and distinguishability of atoms.
one_liner: This colloquium surveys emerging isotope-enrichment and detection technologies for medicine, scalable sensing, and fundamental tests with radioactive clocks.
why_it_matters: Improved isotope production and detection could ease supply constraints, expand diagnostic and therapeutic access, and enable new precision tests of quantum physics.
detailed_summary: The review traces historical and modern methods for isotope separation and detection, emphasizing technologies that could address shortages of enriched isotopes. It discusses radioisotopes for cancer therapy, stable-isotope metabolic tracers, and scalable detection for earlier disease diagnosis. It also outlines proposed tests of quantum mechanics using radioactive atomic clocks.
main_result: The review connects advances in isotope separation and sensing with medical applications and proposed radioactive-clock tests of quantum mechanics.
application_angle: Scalable isotope technologies could strengthen medical-isotope supply chains, improve diagnostics and therapy, and support precision fundamental-physics experiments.

title: Tunable source of entangled microwaves by nonlinear scattering of magnons
abstract: We propose a route to prepare entangled states of microwaves propagating in spatially separated transmission lines using the intrinsic nonlinear dynamics of ferromagnetic spin waves (magnons). We first show that a driven magnon mode can produce entangled magnon pairs at low temperatures by spontaneous parametric down-conversion enabled by three-magnon processes. The anisotropic magnon properties in thin films result in strict phase-matching conditions which allow only a well-defined pair of magnon modes to be amplified. This mode selectivity allows to out-couple each amplified mode to an independent microwave transmission line, producing non-degenerate propagating microwave entanglement with current experimental parameters. In addition, we prove that the frequency difference between the two entangled microwaves can be dynamically tuned across a few-GHz range by changing the orientation of a bias magnetic field. Our figures of merit - .g., the amount of microwave entanglement - can be largely improved by optimizing material and geometry. Our work establishes that quantum states of propagating magnons can be created by their nonlinear dynamics alone, and opens a pathway toward integrating magnons in hybrid quantum platforms.
one_liner: Three-magnon down-conversion in a thin ferromagnetic film is proposed as a tunable source of entangled microwaves in separate transmission lines.
why_it_matters: The scheme offers a materials-based route to frequency-tunable propagating microwave entanglement for hybrid quantum networks and distributed microwave systems.
detailed_summary: A driven magnon mode generates entangled magnon pairs through spontaneous parametric down-conversion enabled by intrinsic three-magnon interactions. Thin-film anisotropy imposes phase matching that selects a well-defined mode pair, with each mode coupled to a separate microwave line. Modeling with current experimental parameters predicts non-degenerate propagating entanglement whose frequency separation can be tuned over several gigahertz by rotating a bias field.
platform_or_system: Ferromagnetic thin film with microwave transmission lines
main_result: The proposed device produces spatially separated entangled microwaves with a dynamically tunable few-gigahertz frequency difference.
application_angle: The source could connect magnonic devices to superconducting, spin, and microwave quantum platforms while supplying tunable entanglement for quantum links.

title: Gravitational Wave Detection via Massive-Particle Interferometry
abstract: Gravitational-wave (GW) observations provide a powerful means of testing general relativity and exploring the physics of black holes and the early universe, motivating the development of complementary detection techniques. Here, we propose and theoretically investigate a GW detector based on massive-particle interferometry, in which the signal is encoded in the relative phase accumulated by a quantum particle traversing a closed-loop trajectory and a reference path. We derive the frequency-dependent GW-induced phase response and examine the parameters on which it depends. These parameters provide a means of tuning the detector response over a broad frequency range, motivating the exploration of tabletop detectors for GW signals at frequencies comparable to and below the LIGO band, in the idealized limit. By exploiting the trajectory-dependent gravitationally induced phase, the proposed scheme offers a distinct and potentially complementary approach to GW detection and motivates further investigation of its experimental feasibility and practical sensitivity.
one_liner: A massive-particle closed-loop interferometer is theoretically proposed to sense gravitational waves through trajectory-dependent quantum phase shifts.
why_it_matters: The concept could complement optical observatories by enabling tunable tabletop searches in frequency ranges near and potentially below the LIGO band.
detailed_summary: The proposed detector compares the phase accumulated by a massive quantum particle on a closed-loop trajectory with that of a reference path. The authors derive the frequency-dependent gravitational-wave phase response and identify trajectory and system parameters that tune it. Sensitivity is studied in an idealized regime, while experimental feasibility and realistic noise remain open questions.
main_result: The analysis derives a tunable gravitational-wave-induced phase response for massive-particle interferometry across a broad idealized frequency range.
application_angle: If experimentally feasible at sufficient sensitivity, the architecture could provide a compact and complementary gravitational-wave detection modality.

title: Compiling Constraints into Neuromorphic Ising Machines
abstract: Most practical combinatorial optimization problems involve constraints, and an Ising machine that flips one spin at a time can respect them only through energy penalties that raise barriers between feasible solutions. Here we show that a higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine can enforce constraints through programmable transitions rather than penalties. In an autoencoder-like architecture, each inner-layer neuron represents a move, a family of multi-spin transitions that maps every feasible state to another feasible state, receives the energy change of its move through connections that outer-layer neurons multiplicatively switch on or off, and updates the state through the same connections. A compiler turns constraints into this wiring with a number of auxiliary clauses that grows only polynomially for parity, cardinality, one-hot, partition and permutation constraints. Restricting the search to feasible states reduces constraint handling to move design, and we show that the fastest-annealing moves are not those that mix fastest but those that lower the deepest energy barriers, and that moves chosen from the objective lower them further than random ones. On third-order graph matching, the machine needs orders of magnitude fewer iterations than penalty-based neuromorphic machines. Configured as a sampler on a field-programmable gate array, it decodes the surface code with maximum-likelihood accuracy up to code distance 15 within 52 $μ$s per shot and, under noisy syndrome measurements, decodes in real time for millisecond measurement rounds up to distance 9 with fewer logical errors than belief-propagation decoders.
one_liner: A constraint-compiled neuromorphic Ising machine performs feasible-state optimization and FPGA surface-code decoding without conventional penalty barriers.
why_it_matters: Its 52-microsecond decoding latency and improved logical-error performance point to practical real-time classical control for quantum error correction.
detailed_summary: The architecture encodes allowed multi-spin moves as inner-layer neurons, keeping transitions within the feasible subspace rather than imposing large constraint penalties. A compiler generates polynomial-size wiring for several common constraint families, and graph-matching tests require orders of magnitude fewer iterations than penalty-based machines. On an FPGA, the sampler reaches maximum-likelihood surface-code accuracy through distance 15 in 52 microseconds per shot and supports real-time noisy-syndrome decoding through distance 9 for millisecond measurement rounds.
main_result: The FPGA implementation decodes surface codes with maximum-likelihood accuracy up to distance 15 at 52 microseconds per shot.
application_angle: The approach could serve as a low-latency decoder and constraint solver in the classical control stack of fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Ising-Encoded Computational Homogenization: Stress as a Quantum Observable
abstract: Computational homogenization requires repeated solutions of representative volume element (RVE) problems to determine the effective response transferred to the macroscale, including the homogenized stress. Here, we develop a basis-encoded, energy-based variational quantum formulation for linear-elastic computational homogenization. The reduced finite-element energy of the RVE is expressed as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem and mapped to an Ising Hamiltonian, whose ground state represents the equilibrium fluctuation field on the encoding grid. Using the Hellmann--Feynman theorem, differentiation of the strain-dependent Hamiltonian with respect to the prescribed macroscopic strain yields stress observables whose expectation values recover the conventional volume-averaged homogenized stress. A key structural result is that, although the equilibrium Hamiltonian is two-local, the stress observables are one-local. In linear elasticity, the two-qubit coupling coefficients are independent of macroscopic strain, hence, differentiation eliminates all two-qubit coupling terms, leaving only identity and single-qubit Pauli-$Z$ operators. These observables are diagonal in the same computational basis as the Ising Hamiltonian and can therefore be evaluated from the same computational-basis measurements used for the energy. Consequently, the homogenized stress can be obtained directly from the optimized quantum state using the same computational basis measurements as the Ising Hamiltonian, without requiring reconstruction of the microscopic displacement field or an additional measurement basis. Ground states are approximated using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), and the formulation is demonstrated on a two-dimensional periodic RVE.
one_liner: An Ising-encoded VQE formulation extracts homogenized stress from the same computational-basis measurements used to estimate an elastic RVE’s energy.
why_it_matters: Reducing stress evaluation to one-local observables avoids displacement reconstruction and extra measurement bases, lowering quantum measurement overhead.
detailed_summary: The reduced finite-element energy of a periodic representative volume element is encoded as a QUBO and mapped to a two-local Ising Hamiltonian. Applying the Hellmann–Feynman theorem yields homogenized-stress observables containing only identity and single-qubit Pauli-Z terms because strain differentiation removes the two-qubit couplings. A two-dimensional periodic RVE demonstration uses VQE ground-state approximations and reuses computational-basis samples for both energy and stress.
platform_or_system: VQE-based Ising model of an elastic RVE
main_result: Homogenized stress is recovered as a one-local observable from the optimized state without reconstructing microscopic displacement or changing measurement basis.
application_angle: The measurement-efficient formulation could support quantum-assisted multiscale materials simulation if useful VQE implementations become available at relevant problem sizes.

title: Counterfactual attribution of surface-code failures under non-Pauli noise: dependence on trajectory pairing
abstract: Under Pauli noise in a stabilizer memory, attributing a quantum error-correction failure to the noise that caused it has a canonical answer; under non-Pauli noise the attribution depends on how trajectories are paired with their counterfactuals. We define a failing shot's cause set, the sites whose removal alone removes the failure, and separate it from pairing-independent net effects. The pairing enters wherever a fixed random draw meets a Born probability; making it maximal at every random step selects shared random numbers, while continuity does not. In a distance-three surface code, exact non-Pauli noise and its Pauli twirl fail at rates equivalent within a registered margin, yet under shared draws 20.2% of exact-noise failures need three or more sites, against 2.3% under the twirl. Other admissible pairings move the mean coherent cause count from 1.61 to 80 times the minimum the marginals allow, yet pairing-independent quantities barely separate the two models. Shot-level attributions should therefore state their pairing and report pairing-independent effects alongside.
one_liner: Surface-code failure attribution under non-Pauli noise can vary dramatically with the chosen counterfactual trajectory pairing.
why_it_matters: The work exposes a major interpretability caveat for diagnosing coherent errors, even when exact and Pauli-twirled models predict similar logical failure rates.
detailed_summary: The authors define a failing shot’s cause set as noise sites whose individual removal prevents the logical failure, while separating these attributions from pairing-independent net effects. In a distance-three surface code, exact non-Pauli noise and its Pauli twirl have similar failure rates, yet shared-random-number pairing assigns three or more causal sites to 20.2% versus 2.3% of failures. Other valid pairings change the mean coherent cause count by up to 80-fold relative to its marginally allowed minimum.
main_result: Shot-level causal explanations of coherent-noise failures are highly pairing-dependent despite nearly unchanged logical failure rates and net effects.
application_angle: Reliable quantum-error-correction diagnostics should report the counterfactual pairing and include pairing-independent metrics before guiding hardware calibration.

title: Interfacing Silicon Nitride Nanophotonics with Cuprous Oxide Rydberg Excitons
abstract: Rydberg excitons in cuprous oxide (Cu$_2$O), the solid-state counterpart of Rydberg atoms, are hydrogen-like electron--hole quasi-particles with micron-sized wavefunctions and strong long-range interactions that promise optical nonlinearities at the few-photon level. Exploiting them in a waveguide quantum electrodynamics (WQED) setting can enable what atomic Rydberg platforms achieve only with ultrahigh vacuum and laser cooling/trapping---a guided optical mode interfaced with the Rydberg medium---while adding the scalability and advanced fabrication of integrated photonics. Here we demonstrate a monolithic, CMOS-compatible interface of Cu$_2$O Rydberg excitons with a SiN$_x$ nanophotonic waveguide. Under non-resonant excitation, excitonic emission from the Cu$_2$O microcrystal is coupled to the guided mode, routed along the waveguide, and collected from an output grating. The spectrum shows the phonon-assisted 1$s$ orthoexciton emission together with the low-lying 2$p$ and 3$p$ lines of the yellow Rydberg series. Spatially selective excitation excludes substrate background and direct scatter, and the enhanced linear polarization of the grating-collected signal identifies the TE-like guided mode as the collection channel. These results establish the complete material--device--measurement stack for a novel platform of nonlinear quantum nanophotonics based on Rydberg excitons.
one_liner: A CMOS-compatible SiN waveguide monolithically interfaces guided light with Cu2O Rydberg-exciton emission.
why_it_matters: The device combines scalable integrated photonics with solid-state Rydberg excitons, laying groundwork for strong few-photon nonlinearities without atomic trapping.
detailed_summary: A Cu2O microcrystal is integrated with a SiNx nanophotonic waveguide and excited non-resonantly. Excitonic emission couples into the guided mode, propagates along the device, and exits through a grating while retaining the phonon-assisted 1s orthoexciton and yellow-series 2p and 3p features. Spatial selectivity and enhanced linear polarization identify a TE-like guided collection channel and suppress substrate or scattering backgrounds.
main_result: The study demonstrates a complete monolithic material-device-measurement interface between Cu2O Rydberg excitons and a guided SiNx optical mode.
application_angle: The platform could support chip-scale few-photon nonlinear optics, quantum light processing, and scalable waveguide-QED devices.

title: A fast and accurate model for gradient-based inverse design of multimode waveguides
abstract: Multimode photonic inverse design requires fast, accurate computational models that provide geometry gradients. Based on coupled-mode theory (CMT), we propose a differentiable surrogate model. Its parameter-extraction method uses a change of modal basis to obtain coupled-mode parameters from cross-sectional mode data. We also provide a complete, easy-to-implement propagation and optimization workflow. Using finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulation data as a common reference, we compare the prediction accuracy of our model and forward dataset-based eigenmode expansion (EME) for randomly generated thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) waveguide profiles that traverse modal coupling regions. Using identical modal libraries, the model reduces the maximum per-mode mean absolute transmission error by 17-37% compared with forward EME. We demonstrate a spot-size converter design that preserves the fundamental TM$_0$ mode in its hybridization region with the first-order TE$_1$ mode and obtain nine structures, each with FDTD-verified transmission above 98%. These tests demonstrate the model's utility for large-scale photonic inverse design, enabling rapid exploration of the design parameter space by combining gradient information with improved prediction accuracy.
one_liner: A differentiable coupled-mode surrogate accelerates gradient-based inverse design of strongly coupled multimode waveguides.
why_it_matters: It improves predictive accuracy while supplying geometry gradients, enabling rapid optimization of practical multimode integrated-photonic components.
detailed_summary: The model extracts coupled-mode parameters from cross-sectional mode data through a modal-basis transformation and supports differentiable propagation and optimization. Against FDTD references for random thin-film lithium-niobate profiles, it reduces the maximum per-mode mean absolute transmission error by 17–37% relative to forward EME using the same modal libraries. Optimization yields nine spot-size-converter structures with FDTD-verified transmission above 98% through a TM0–TE1 hybridization region.
main_result: The surrogate outperforms forward EME in transmission prediction and produces nine inverse-designed converters exceeding 98% FDTD-verified transmission.
application_angle: The workflow can shorten design cycles for high-efficiency mode converters and other large-scale integrated-photonic components.

title: The computational complexity of bosonic Lindbladian fixed points
abstract: We study the computational complexity of estimating observables and sampling from stationary states, or fixed points, of bosonic Lindbladian dynamics with bounded-degree polynomial interactions. While the complexity of transient bosonic dynamics has been investigated, understanding the computational power of bosonic fixed points requires addressing subtleties of infinite-dimensional systems, including the existence, uniqueness, and convergence of stationary states. We establish a broad complexity landscape spanning universal quantum computation, efficient classical simulation, sampling hardness, and undecidability. First, we show that universal quantum computation can be embedded into observable estimation at the unique fixed point of a bosonic Lindbladian with a Hamiltonian of degree at most twelve and only linear photon loss. Moreover, this fixed point can be prepared from vacuum in polynomial time. On the classical side, we identify Gaussian regimes with incoherent pumping that admit efficient photon-number sampling and establish stability of classical approximability under sufficiently weak non-Gaussian Kerr perturbations. Conversely, for Gaussian fixed points without incoherent pumping, we establish hardness of exact sampling under constant-rate linear loss and hardness of approximate sampling at inverse-polynomial loss rates under standard boson-sampling conjectures. We also relate sampling from non-Gaussian fixed points to variants of boson sampling. Finally, we prove that deciding the existence of a stationary density operator is $\mathsf{RE}$-hard, even for purely dissipative Lindbladians with degree-five jump operators acting on at most four modes.
one_liner: Bosonic Lindbladian fixed points span universal quantum computation, classically tractable regimes, sampling hardness, and undecidability.
why_it_matters: The results map which driven-dissipative bosonic hardware can be efficiently simulated and which stationary states encode powerful or intractable computation.
detailed_summary: Universal quantum computation is embedded in observable estimation at a unique fixed point generated by degree-12 Hamiltonian interactions and linear photon loss, with polynomial-time preparation from vacuum. Gaussian fixed points with incoherent pumping permit efficient photon-number sampling and remain classically approximable under sufficiently weak Kerr perturbations. Other Gaussian and non-Gaussian regimes inherit exact or approximate sampling hardness, while stationary-state existence is RE-hard even for degree-five dissipative jump operators on at most four modes.
main_result: The paper establishes a broad fixed-point complexity landscape ranging from efficient classical sampling to universal computation, sampling hardness, and RE-hard existence problems.
application_angle: It provides theoretical criteria for selecting bosonic dissipative architectures as quantum processors, samplers, or classically simulable devices.

title: High-fidelity six-dimensional optical data storage
abstract: Multi-dimensional optical data storage, wherein each voxel encodes multiple bits of information within a three-dimensional isotropic medium, presents a revolutionary approach to dense data storage. This approach exploits multiple degrees of freedom of light, such as intensity, polarization and wavelength, to selectively control distinct optical responses in the medium. However, increasing dimensionality exacerbates crosstalk between different encoding dimensions, thereby compromising recording fidelity. In this study, we introduce a novel six-dimensional (6D) multiplexing approach that exploits ultrafast interactions of polarized light with a three-dimensional medium. By manipulating three light parameters within a Poincaré-like semi-sphere, we systematically induce three distinct material responses in laser-induced nanostructures, each corresponding to a unique physical quantity: fluorescence, phase retardance, and slow axis orientation. Thanks to such multiple one-to-one correspondence between light parameters and material responses, we achieve unprecedented high fidelity, attaining a raw accuracy of 99.45%. Furthermore, this independently controlled 6D multiplexing technique maximizes the effective user capacity to 0.38 petabits per disc. The versatility of laser-induced nanostructures across multiple physical dimensions enables diverse applications, ranging from high-capacity data storage to microfluidics, optical elements, integrated photonics, micromechanics, and quantum technologies.
one_liner: Polarized ultrafast laser writing achieves six-dimensional optical storage with 99.45% raw accuracy and 0.38-petabit effective disc capacity.
why_it_matters: Independent mapping of light controls to fluorescence, retardance, and axis orientation suppresses the crosstalk that normally limits multidimensional storage.
detailed_summary: The scheme varies three optical parameters over a Poincaré-like hemisphere to create laser-induced nanostructures with independently readable fluorescence, phase retardance, and slow-axis orientation. This near one-to-one mapping reduces cross-dimensional crosstalk and yields 99.45% raw decoding accuracy. The reported multiplexing density corresponds to an effective user capacity of 0.38 petabits per disc.
main_result: The authors demonstrate independently controlled 6D multiplexing with 99.45% raw accuracy and an effective capacity of 0.38 petabits per disc.
application_angle: The method targets durable high-density archival storage and may also enable encoded optical elements, integrated photonics, and microfabricated devices.

title: Algorithmic Quantum Sensing
abstract: We introduce a unified framework for sensing time-dependent fields through the lens of classical and quantum algorithms. First, we develop three pulse sequence protocols, namely randomized, matched, and pooled spectroscopy, which outperform established approaches such as dynamical decoupling across a wide range of tasks. These protocols attain the optimal sensitivity for linear and nonlinear AC sensing on conventional spin or qubit platforms, improving existing devices by changing only their pulse sequences. We then introduce quantum computational spectroscopy (QCS), which couples quantum sensors to a quantum processor. QCS combines two new primitives: a quantum computational frequency comb that coherently converts any classical signal into a quantum oracle, and a family of quantum algorithms that use the oracle to extract signal information in superposition. Variations can be implemented on current platforms with only one memory ancilla. We show that the ultimate limit imposed by quantum mechanics lies polynomially beyond the Heisenberg limit, and that QCS achieves it. Attaining this new limit requires quantum computation, establishing a fundamental separation between conventional and quantum computational sensing. Moreover, QCS retains beyond-Heisenberg scaling for broadband signals under constant-strength sensor depolarization, while we prove that the same noise limits any protocol lacking quantum computation to standard-quantum-limit scaling. Our result provides the first asymptotic, beyond-quadratic quantum advantage in AC metrology when noise is aligned with the signal, proving that Lindblad span conditions do not apply to broadband quantum sensing. Our work builds an algorithmic theory for designing sensing protocols and establishes quantum sensing as a new frontier for quantum algorithms, with quantum advantages that surpass the Heisenberg limit and that persist under noise.
one_liner: Quantum computational spectroscopy uses sensor-processor algorithms to surpass the Heisenberg limit for time-dependent-field sensing, even under noise.
why_it_matters: It predicts a beyond-quadratic metrological advantage and offers pulse-only improvements for existing sensors plus ancilla-light routes toward quantum-enhanced devices.
detailed_summary: Randomized, matched, and pooled spectroscopy protocols attain optimal sensitivity for linear and nonlinear AC sensing on conventional spin or qubit sensors using modified pulse sequences. Quantum computational spectroscopy then coherently maps a classical signal into an oracle and processes frequency information in superposition, with variants requiring only one memory ancilla. The framework reaches a polynomially beyond-Heisenberg limit and retains beyond-Heisenberg scaling for broadband signals under constant-strength sensor depolarization, where non-computational protocols fall to standard-quantum-limit scaling.
platform_or_system: Pulsed spin or qubit sensor coupled to a quantum processor
main_result: Quantum computational spectroscopy achieves the proposed ultimate sensing limit beyond Heisenberg scaling and preserves an asymptotic advantage under aligned broadband noise.
application_angle: The framework offers immediate pulse-sequence upgrades for current sensors and a path to processor-assisted broadband spectroscopy and weak-field detection.

title: Syndrome-based Calibration Using Gate-Error Amplification
abstract: We present Gate-Error Amplification for Recalibration with Syndromes (GEARS), a runtime calibration framework that uses gate-error amplification to efficiently tune control parameters during quantum error correction. Maintaining reliable control of large qubit arrays throughout hours-long computations requires repeated calibration to compensate for hardware drift. In conventional calibration, targeted qubits are temporarily removed from the code, introducing non-negligible space-time overhead. An elegant alternative uses syndrome information already collected during error correction as feedback for in situ recalibration, but acquiring signal requires sufficient (1) measurement budget or (2) probe strength, i.e., the size of deliberate control perturbations. More measurements improve statistical precision but result in slower control updates, while stronger perturbations produce larger calibration signals at the cost of additional errors. GEARS augments syndrome-based calibration with an established gate characterization technique called gate-error amplification. Our approach repeats selected CZ gates and probes their controls in spatially separated groups, strengthening local calibration signals while limiting the logical cost of probing. Surface code simulations show that GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces measurement requirements by approximately a factor of eight at matched gradient SNR and fixed probe strength. In closed-loop calibration, GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces excess expected logical failures by approximately 31-40% relative to calibration without amplification across the evaluated execution windows. Under time-dependent drift, GEARS increases the estimated critical drift frequency by approximately 1.9x. These results indicate that deliberately amplifying gate errors during operation can improve the long-time performance of quantum computations.
one_liner: GEARS amplifies selected CZ-gate errors to accelerate in-code calibration using surface-code syndrome data.
why_it_matters: It offers faster tracking of hardware drift without removing qubits from the code, reducing the logical cost and latency of runtime calibration.
detailed_summary: GEARS repeats selected CZ gates in spatially separated groups to strengthen calibration gradients extracted from surface-code syndromes while limiting correlated logical damage. Simulations with depth-three amplification reduce the measurements needed for matched gradient SNR by about 8×. Closed-loop tests predict 31–40% fewer excess logical failures and an approximately 1.9× higher critical drift frequency than calibration without amplification.
main_result: Depth-three gate-error amplification reduced calibration measurement demand by about 8× and excess expected logical failures by 31–40% in simulation.
application_angle: The method could support continuous, low-overhead recalibration of large qubit arrays during hours-long fault-tolerant computations.

title: Parallel transversal entangling gates for fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computing
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity entangling gates that can be implemented efficiently across multiple qubit pairs. We present a scheme for simultaneous pairwise entangling operations, i.e., a transversal controlled-$Z$ gate, across neighboring wells in a double-well trapped-ion architecture. A tailored dynamical decoupling scheme suppresses unwanted couplings with a pulse count that scales quadratically with the number of ions. We show that incorporating a genuine geometric cancellation reduces the pulse count and, for selected register sizes, allows the parallel operation to be completed faster than an equivalent sequence of two-qubit gates while requiring a significantly smaller two-photon Rabi frequency. We assess the experimental feasibility of the protocol by analyzing the impact of decoherence and crosstalk arising from laser wave-vector misalignment. To gain insight into the robustness of fault-tolerant protocols against realistic imperfections of the proposed transversal gate scheme, we investigate how crosstalk-induced gate errors affect the fault-tolerant preparation of a logical Bell state between two $[[4,1,2]]$ quantum-error-detection code blocks. These results highlight the potential of transversal entangling gates as a building block for trapped-ion-based scalable fault-tolerant quantum error correction.
one_liner: A trapped-ion protocol executes parallel pairwise CZ gates across neighboring wells with tailored dynamical decoupling.
why_it_matters: Parallel transversal gates could shorten fault-tolerant circuits and lower laser-power demands while suppressing unwanted ion-ion couplings.
detailed_summary: The scheme implements simultaneous pairwise controlled-Z operations across neighboring wells in a double-well trapped-ion register. Tailored dynamical decoupling suppresses unwanted couplings, while geometric cancellation lowers the pulse count for selected register sizes. The study also models decoherence and wave-vector-misalignment crosstalk and evaluates their effects on logical Bell-state preparation between two [[4,1,2]] code blocks.
main_result: For selected register sizes, the transversal CZ operation can be faster than sequential two-qubit gates while requiring substantially lower two-photon Rabi frequency.
application_angle: The protocol provides a potentially efficient entangling primitive for scalable trapped-ion quantum error correction.

title: Probing thin films and their interfaces via angle-resolved second-harmonic generation
abstract: Increasing demands on the performance and reliability of optical thin films stimulate the development of more sensitive characterisation methods capable of investigating thin-film interfaces or local mechanical stress. Second-harmonic generation (SHG) is a phenomenon that can serve as a non-destructive probe, tracing local symmetry changes in the film surface, bulk, and buried interfaces. Here, we investigate the decomposition of the SHG response from these three regions by combining angle- and polarisation-resolved measurements. We utilised a theoretical model of SHG accounting for multiple reflections and optical interference in a thin layer. The theory was first experimentally evaluated using Ta2O5 films deposited on different glass substrates. The fitting procedure accurately reproduced the measured SHG responses, revealing pronounced substrate-dependent variations in the buried-interface contribution, while the surface and effective-bulk responses remained similar. As the next step, we studied the reliability of the SHG signal decomposition into the surface, bulk and buried-interface components. The decomposition was evaluated by generating synthetic datasets and testing whether their retrieval was unique and accurate. The influence of film thickness, measurement noise, uncertainties in linear-optical parameters, and the polarisation channels used on the retrieval of nonlinear susceptibilities was also examined. Our results demonstrate that reliable separation of SHG contributions requires accurate linear optical parameters, global fitting of multiple polarisation channels, and sufficiently pronounced interference features, outlining the capabilities and practical limitations of SHG-based region-specific characterisation of optical thin films.
one_liner: Angle- and polarization-resolved SHG separates surface, bulk, and buried-interface responses in optical thin films.
why_it_matters: The method enables nondestructive, region-specific thin-film characterization while identifying the conditions required for reliable parameter retrieval.
detailed_summary: The authors combine angle- and polarization-resolved SHG measurements with a multilayer model incorporating multiple reflections and thin-film interference. Fits to Ta2O5 films reveal strong substrate-dependent changes in the buried-interface contribution while surface and effective-bulk responses remain similar. Synthetic-data retrieval tests show that reliable decomposition requires accurate linear-optical inputs, global multi-channel fitting, and sufficiently strong interference features.
platform_or_system: Ta2O5 optical thin films on glass
main_result: The model reproduced measured SHG responses and resolved substrate-sensitive buried-interface contributions under well-conditioned measurement settings.
application_angle: This approach could nondestructively diagnose interfaces, symmetry changes, and local stress in precision optical coatings.

title: Evolving Decoding Algorithms for Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Quantum computation entails robustness engineering: a noisy quantum state is measured continuously, and a classical algorithm (the decoder) must infer corrections that reliably remove the noise, fast enough to keep up. We write several published belief-propagation (BP) decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes in a Domain-Specific Language (DSL), and search over it with grammatical evolution. Written in the language, the published decoders show their parameters in plain view, allowing us to re-parameterise BP+OSD (ordered statistics decoding) and BP+LSD (localized statistics decoding) decoders with damping, before any search, making each 17.1--41.0$\times$ faster at a higher error rate, and BP+OSD-0 about 103 faster than the ldpc package's version tuned on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code. Evolution over the language finds decoders that improve the time-error front. One makes 23% fewer logical errors than BP+OSD-0 with damping at 0.64$\times$ its time, and decoders evolved from random code are more accurate than ldpc's tuned BP+OSD-0 at 1/31 of its time or less. Frozen at one operating point, the two fastest evolved decoders generalize well across noise levels, code sizes and round counts, staying at the time-error front. Ultimately, we demonstrate that capturing expert knowledge within a DSL creates a powerful intermediate layer---one that effectively bridges human intuition and machine-driven optimization to unlock highly efficient quantum error correction.
one_liner: A decoder DSL and grammatical evolution jointly optimize the speed and logical-error performance of qLDPC decoding.
why_it_matters: Faster decoders that retain accuracy across operating conditions help classical control keep pace with real-time quantum error correction.
detailed_summary: Published BP+OSD and BP+LSD decoders are expressed in a domain-specific language that exposes algorithm structure and tunable parameters. Simple damping-based reparameterization yields 17.1–41.0× speedups at lower error rates, while one BP+OSD-0 implementation is reported as about 103× faster than the tuned ldpc-package version on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code. Evolution then finds decoders on improved time-error fronts, including one with 23% fewer logical errors at 0.64× the runtime of damped BP+OSD-0.
main_result: Evolved decoders achieved improved runtime-error tradeoffs and generalized across noise levels, code sizes, and syndrome-round counts.
application_angle: The approach could generate low-latency decoders tailored to practical fault-tolerant processors and their classical compute constraints.

title: High-fidelity control of long-lived data qubits via a noisy mediator
abstract: Long-lived qubits are attractive for storing quantum information, but they are often difficult to control or couple directly. A common strategy is to use mediator qubits to generate effective interactions for gate implementation. However, the mediator typically has a shorter coherence time than the data qubits, so mediator relaxation and dephasing are expected to limit the achievable gate fidelity. Here, we show that this limitation can be overcome. We present a reset-assisted control method that suppresses mediator-induced errors and enables high-fidelity single- and two-qubit gates on a quantum register of long-lived data qubits. Although mediator quantum jumps render the data-qubit evolution stochastic, repeated mediator reinitialization drives the resulting evolution paths toward the desired target operation. An analytical quantum-trajectory analysis reveals the physical mechanism of error suppression and provides compact fidelity formulas for adapting the method to different platforms. Our results relax the requirement for long mediator coherence, broadening the range of mediators that can support high-fidelity control.
one_liner: Repeatedly resetting a noisy mediator suppresses its quantum-jump errors during control of long-lived data qubits.
why_it_matters: High-fidelity gates may no longer require mediator coherence comparable to that of the data qubits, widening viable hardware choices.
detailed_summary: The proposed protocol uses a short-lived mediator to implement single- and two-qubit gates on long-lived data qubits while repeatedly reinitializing the mediator. Although relaxation and dephasing make individual data-qubit trajectories stochastic, the resets steer those trajectories toward the target operation. An analytical quantum-trajectory treatment explains the suppression mechanism and supplies compact fidelity formulas for adapting the method to different platforms.
platform_or_system: Long-lived qubit register with resettable mediator
main_result: Reset-assisted control suppresses mediator-induced errors and enables high-fidelity single- and two-data-qubit operations despite noisy mediator dynamics.
application_angle: The technique could simplify coupling and control architectures for memories or processors built from difficult-to-address, long-coherence qubits.

title: Finite-Key Analysis for Multiple-Antenna Quantum Key Distribution with Continuous Variables
abstract: Multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) techniques, known for their use in wireless communications, can also find applications in quantum communications systems. This is, for instance, relevant to satellite-based quantum communications when atmospheric turbulence and the time-varying nature of the channel can make their implementation difficult. Here, we study the application of MIMO techniques to continuous-variable (CV) quantum key distribution (QKD) in the realistic setting where a finite number of signals are exchanged. We show how data collected during the brief overpass time of low-earth-orbit satellites over ground stations can be processed to estimate MIMO channel parameters, extract a secret key, and quantify the key generation rate. For $2\times 2$ MIMO settings with Gaussian encoding and heterodyne detection, our finite-key analysis indicates that MIMO CV-QKD could outperform both multiplexed (with a nominal 3~dB improvement) and single-mode (with a nominal 6~dB nominal improvement) scenarios. Furthermore, we conjecture that the ultimate enhancement of a multiple-antenna CV-QKD system can be characterized by the product of the number of its inputs and outputs.
one_liner: A finite-key framework evaluates 2×2 MIMO continuous-variable QKD for short, turbulent satellite communication windows.
why_it_matters: It connects multi-aperture optical links to composable finite-data key estimates relevant to brief low-Earth-orbit satellite passes.
detailed_summary: The work develops finite-key processing for estimating MIMO channel parameters and extracting secret keys from the limited signals available during a low-Earth-orbit overpass. For a 2×2 configuration with Gaussian modulation and heterodyne detection, the analysis predicts higher key-generation performance than multiplexed and single-mode baselines. The authors further conjecture that the ultimate multi-antenna enhancement scales with the product of the numbers of inputs and outputs.
main_result: Finite-key calculations indicate that 2×2 MIMO CV-QKD can outperform both multiplexed and single-mode transmission during finite satellite passes.
