application_angle: Multiple optical apertures could improve secret-key yield and robustness for turbulence-limited satellite quantum networks.

title: The classical complexity of quantum state transmission
abstract: Quantum communication provides a natural means to transmit quantum information, but how difficult is it to make such a transmission using only classical communication resources? We address this question by introducing classical communication models for quantum preparations and defining their minimum cost as the classical complexity. We prove that this complexity equals the amount of classical communication required to simulate quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments, thus establishing a resource equivalence between quantum state transmission and quantum correlations. This calls for a general characterisation of the classical complexity of the noisy quantum state space, which we show grows exponentially with the quantum dimension and as a power-law in the inverse noise. It reveals the rapidly scaling fundamental cost of classical simulation. Moreover, we develop a toolbox of methods to certify classical complexity in quantum preparation devices, including an exact semidefinite-programming characterisation, analytical witnesses for symmetric preparations and convex programming scalable up to hundreds and sometimes thousands of qubit states. Our results establish classical complexity as a fundamental measure of quantum communication advantage, revealing the intrinsic cost of classically simulating quantum theory and providing practical tools for its certification.
one_liner: Classical simulation of quantum-state transmission incurs costs that grow exponentially with Hilbert-space dimension and polynomially with inverse noise.
why_it_matters: The work turns quantum communication advantage into a certifiable resource measure and supplies optimization tools applicable to realistic preparation devices.
detailed_summary: The authors define classical complexity as the minimum classical communication needed to reproduce quantum preparations. They prove its equivalence to the cost of simulating prepare-and-broadcast correlations and derive exponential scaling with quantum dimension plus power-law scaling with inverse noise. Certification methods include an exact semidefinite program, analytical witnesses for symmetric ensembles, and scalable convex programs handling hundreds to thousands of qubit states.
main_result: The study establishes a resource equivalence and practical certificates showing rapidly growing classical costs for noisy quantum-state transmission.
application_angle: The framework can benchmark communication advantage and certify preparation hardware without requiring full classical simulation at scale.

title: A receiver-side approach to confirm phase randomization in BB84 time-bin QKD with weak coherent pulses
abstract: In quantum cryptography using time-bin BB84 protocols, the relative phase of symbol pulses has to be random to avoid vulnerability to coherent attacks. Typically this phase randomization is checked on the sender side. Here, we propose a protocol for monitoring and confirming phase randomization independently on the receiver side during operation. The proposed method can be implemented on the single-photon level without the need for any physical adaptation of the receiver. This can provide an additional tool for monitoring against possible eavesdropping attempts that affect the phase randomization.
one_liner: A receiver-side monitor verifies phase randomization in weak-coherent-pulse, time-bin BB84 QKD at the single-photon level.
why_it_matters: It adds an operational security check independent of the transmitter and requires neither receiver hardware modification nor bright optical probing.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes verifying the random relative phase of time-bin symbol pulses from measurements made at the receiver. The protocol operates at the single-photon level and is designed to run during QKD operation without physical changes to the receiver. It provides an independent check against attacks or faults that compromise transmitter-side phase randomization.
main_result: The proposed receiver-side protocol can confirm source phase randomization during operation using existing single-photon detection hardware.
application_angle: The method offers a deployable defense-in-depth monitor for practical fiber QKD links and potentially compromised transmitters.

title: DUV (257 nm) LIDT of Anti-Reflective Coatings
abstract: Laser-induced damage threshold in the deep ultraviolet (DUV) was used to perform tests on AR coated windows intended for industrial processes. The 257 nm wavelength was generated from Yb:YAG fundamental (1030 nm) and the long-term LIDT stability (up to 100000 shots) was selected as representative for minimal industrial qualification. Selected setup for the fourth harmonics generation consists of two stages, generation of second harmonic and subsequently the fourth harmonic with 13,4% conversation efficiency. In both 1-on-1 and S-on-1 experiments, the optics coated with Al2O3/SiO2 by ion beam sputtering technique demonstrated the highest LIDT value of 0.73 and 0.5 J/cm2 respectively. Various damage morphologies, color centers, ballistic damage, delamination, and blistering were observed across the samples with respect to the 1-on-1 and S-on-1.
one_liner: Ion-beam-sputtered Al2O3/SiO2 antireflection coatings achieved the highest measured 257 nm laser-damage thresholds in long-run tests.
why_it_matters: The measurements identify a durable coating stack and document failure modes relevant to qualifying DUV optics for high-duty industrial laser systems.
detailed_summary: A two-stage harmonic-conversion setup generated 257 nm light from a 1030 nm Yb:YAG source with 13.4% fourth-harmonic conversion efficiency. Under 1-on-1 and S-on-1 protocols extending to 100,000 shots, ion-beam-sputtered Al2O3/SiO2 coatings reached 0.73 and 0.5 J/cm², respectively. Observed failures included color centers, ballistic damage, delamination, and blistering.
main_result: Al2O3/SiO2 coatings delivered the best reported thresholds, reaching 0.73 J/cm² in 1-on-1 and 0.5 J/cm² in S-on-1 testing.
application_angle: The results support coating selection and lifetime qualification for industrial DUV beam-delivery and processing optics.

title: Improving the signal-to-noise ratio through postselection of coincident detections in anticounterfeiting and quantum key distribution
abstract: In quantum communications and other photon-counting applications, reliably detecting weak optical signals against a strong noise background remains a fundamental challenge. In this paper, we develop a simple idea: when a signal is carried by pairs (or more generally multiplets) of photons emitted simultaneously, postselection of coincident detections recorded on two detectors makes it possible to improve-sometimes drastically-the Signal to Noise Ratio. Essentially, this is made possible by the fact that genuine and accidental coincidences scale differently with the width of the postselection window. As long as the window remains wide enough to retain detections from the same pair, the genuine coincidence rate is approximately unchanged. In contrast, coincidences formed from independent clicks decrease linearly as the window is narrowed. The resulting signal-to-noise ratio, therefore, increases inversely with the window width. Our approach makes it possible to reveal photon-pair signals that are otherwise hidden beneath a much stronger uncorrelated background. We analyze here applications of this idea to quantum key distribution, metrology, and anti-counterfeiting.
one_liner: Narrow coincidence-window postselection recovers correlated photon-pair signals buried beneath much stronger uncorrelated detection noise.
why_it_matters: The technique improves photon-counting SNR with timing postprocessing and can benefit noisy QKD, metrology, and optical authentication systems.
detailed_summary: The method postselects coincident clicks from simultaneously emitted photon pairs or multiplets using two detectors. While genuine coincidences remain nearly constant if the timing window still contains both photons, accidental coincidences decrease linearly as that window narrows. Consequently, the signal-to-noise ratio scales inversely with coincidence-window width over the useful regime.
main_result: Coincidence-window narrowing can reveal correlated optical signals that are otherwise obscured by a substantially stronger uncorrelated background.
application_angle: Software-level timing selection could extend the operating margin of photon-counting QKD, metrology, and anticounterfeiting receivers.

title: Cooperativity-enhanced single-photon emission in a topological quantum emitter chain
abstract: Single-photon emitters are one of the key elements in state-of-the art quantum technologies, yet optimizing and manipulating their emission requires precise fabrication of the emitter systems themselves. Here, we propose a route to tailored single-photon emission by exploiting cooperative effects in a topological single-photon emitter chain. Although the involvement of multiple emitters normally suppresses single-photon emission, we show that localized topological edge modes restore single-photon emission and protect against local perturbations. At the same time, cooperative effects occur due to the collective nature of the edge modes, leading to directional emission and linewidth narrowing. Our findings open new possibilities for tailoring single-photon emission by combining cooperativity and topological effects.
one_liner: Topological edge modes in a cooperative emitter chain restore antibunched emission while producing directionality and linewidth narrowing.
why_it_matters: The proposal combines topological robustness with collective optical effects, offering a new design route for tailored on-chip single-photon sources.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes a chain of coupled quantum emitters whose localized topological edge modes support single-photon emission despite collective participation by multiple emitters. The edge localization protects the emission response against local perturbations. At the same time, the collective mode enables directional radiation and a narrowed optical linewidth.
platform_or_system: Topological chain of coupled quantum emitters
main_result: Localized edge modes preserve single-photon character while cooperative interactions yield robust, directional, spectrally narrowed emission.
application_angle: The architecture could enable fabrication-tolerant quantum-light sources with engineered directionality and linewidth for photonic circuits.

title: CAVQS: Context-Aware Variational Quantum Circuit Synthesis via Unitary Redistribution and Dynamic Reconstruction
abstract: Variational quantum circuit synthesis jointly searches circuit structure and continuous parameters to reduce costly two-qubit gates, but block-based workflows typically instantiate blocks independently, limiting simplification across block boundaries. Moreover, fully unitary synthesis does not exploit opportunities created by permitted output measurements and classical feedforward. We present CAVQS, a context-aware variational synthesis framework that combines unitary redistribution and dynamic reconstruction. First, CAVQS uses QR decomposition to transfer unitary factors between overlapping blocks, preserving the overall transformation while reshaping local synthesis targets to enable cross-block reductions. Second, for blocks that precede permitted terminal measurements, CAVQS constructs ancilla-free dynamic implementations with a CNOT-budgeted pre-measurement search and analytic branch-unitary construction, thereby minimizing expected CNOT cost. Across random-circuit targets, CAVQS reduces mean two-qubit gate counts by 28.79%-42.52%, 2.05%-52.62%, and 30.51%-74.64% relative to QFAST, SQUANDER, and Fast-USYN, respectively, on common successful instances. On 4--6-qubit quantum algorithm benchmarks, the corresponding reductions are 27.27%-36.77%, 20.65%-69.10%, and 36.31%-71.88%, respectively.
one_liner: CAVQS reduces two-qubit gate counts through cross-block unitary redistribution and measurement-aware dynamic circuit reconstruction.
why_it_matters: Lower CNOT counts directly address fidelity and runtime limits on near-term processors while exploiting measurement and feedforward capabilities.
detailed_summary: CAVQS applies QR decomposition across overlapping blocks to redistribute unitary factors and expose reductions unavailable to independently synthesized blocks. Before permitted terminal measurements, it builds ancilla-free dynamic implementations using a CNOT-budgeted search and analytical branch unitaries. Across random and 4–6-qubit algorithmic targets, it reports substantial mean two-qubit-gate reductions against QFAST, SQUANDER, and Fast-USYN.
main_result: CAVQS cuts mean two-qubit gate counts by up to 74.64% on common successful random instances and up to 71.88% on algorithm benchmarks.
application_angle: The compiler can translate small algorithms into shallower, less error-prone circuits for hardware supporting mid-circuit measurement and feedforward.

title: Efficient calculation of the full Laguerre-Gaussian spectrum of entangled biphotons
abstract: The spatial biphoton state generated by spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) enables applications in high-dimensional quantum information processing and is often described in Laguerre-Gaussian (LG) modes. However, calculating the full LG spectrum for arbitrary radial and orbital angular momentum (OAM) indices requires computationally demanding multidimensional integrations. We present a generating-function approach that analytically performs the four-dimensional transverse spatial integral without approximating the phase-matching function. The source geometry can be completely described by a few dimensionless parameters, which reduce to two parameters for wave-vector-degenerate photons with equal waists. Our derived expressions for the full LG spectrum allow for computationally efficient and numerically stable evaluation at high mode orders, addressing a crucial obstacle in previous works. To illustrate our approach, we compare OAM spectra obtained by projection onto the lowest radial order and by radially insensitive detection, and investigate how high-dimensional maximal entanglement can be approached by tuning source parameters. Our results provide a new analytical tool for efficiently characterizing and engineering high-dimensional spatial entanglement in SPDC.
one_liner: A generating-function method efficiently computes the full high-order Laguerre-Gaussian spectrum of SPDC biphotons without approximating phase matching.
why_it_matters: Fast, stable access to radial and OAM mode weights enables practical design and characterization of high-dimensional spatial entanglement sources.
detailed_summary: The authors analytically evaluate the four-dimensional transverse integral governing SPDC projection onto arbitrary radial and OAM Laguerre-Gaussian modes. The resulting generating-function expressions retain the full phase-matching function and reduce the source geometry to a small set of dimensionless parameters. Numerical examples compare lowest-radial-order and radially insensitive detection and identify parameter regimes approaching high-dimensional maximal entanglement.
main_result: The method delivers numerically stable and computationally efficient full LG spectra at high radial and OAM orders.
application_angle: It supports optimization of high-dimensional photonic entanglement sources for quantum communication and information processing.

title: Stitching Quantum Codes into Quilts: Universal Logic with no Ancillary Qubits
abstract: Proposals abound for performing fault-tolerant logical Pauli-product measurements between quantum codes beyond the surface code. We introduce a new construction, the code quilt, whereby a target joint logical operator of two or more codeblocks is directly measured without the use of an ancillary system. We construct explicit circuits to perform a logical measurement using the quilt construction, which also require no physical qubits beyond the ancillas already in place to perform idle syndrome extraction on the codeblocks in question. We give a detailed structural analysis of the construction, which is based on a subsystem code, and provide several sets of sufficient conditions under which the relevant code-capacity distance is preserved. We give two variants of the protocol. The first, where the gauge generators of the subsystem code are measured directly, is provably not fault tolerant in the large-distance limit but admits a particularly practical circuit implementation in which the physical qubit degree increases by at most two. The second has more favourable asymptotic properties, although we do not prove its fault tolerance in the general case. We then perform an extensive empirical analysis of the technique, in particular of the first variant, as applied to bivariate bicycle and surface codes, finding code-capacity-distance preserving quilts for measuring 25,000 randomly selected logical operators. We optimise to find sparse and decongested detector bases for each and, for a randomly selected subset, find circuits that we estimate to be distance preserving. Finally, we perform decoding experiments on a subset of these circuits and find that their logical error probability is comparable to that of idle memory for operations involving the 144-qubit bivariate bicycle code and distance-12 rotated surface code at physical error rates between $1.5\times 10^{-3}$ and $3\times 10^{-3}$.
one_liner: Code quilts directly measure joint logical operators across code blocks using no ancillary qubits beyond existing syndrome-extraction hardware.
why_it_matters: Ancilla-free logical Pauli-product measurements could reduce qubit overhead for universal fault-tolerant operations across several promising code families.
detailed_summary: The construction temporarily joins multiple code blocks through a subsystem-code structure to measure a target joint logical operator. Explicit protocols reuse syndrome-extraction ancillas, with one practical variant increasing physical-qubit degree by at most two. Tests over 25,000 random logical operators found distance-preserving quilts, while selected circuits for 144-qubit bivariate bicycle and distance-12 surface codes achieved logical error rates comparable to idle memory.
main_result: The study demonstrates low-connectivity, ancilla-free logical measurements with empirically distance-preserving circuits and memory-like logical error rates.
application_angle: The approach may lower the hardware and routing overhead of universal logic in modular fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Imaginary-Time Density Correlations Encode Quantum Entropy and Free Energy
abstract: In the classical limit, maximum-entropy inference yields an estimate of the excess entropy from the static structure factor through a single momentum sum. Quantum mechanically this estimate fails, because interactions also change the kinetic energy, while delocalization and exchange add information that equal-time correlations do not contain. We show that imaginary-time density correlations contain this information, and that with them the classical relation carries over to quantum systems. Such correlations are available from path-integral simulations and X-ray Thomson scattering. Relative-entropy inference over imaginary-time paths, with an ideal Bose or Fermi gas as reference, gives closed forms for the excess entropy and free energies, within the same Gaussian approximation as the classical relation. They recover the classical result and estimate entropy that the classical relation misses. We test them on weakly interacting bosons, interacting fermions on a ring, and the warm dense electron gas. The closed forms need only imaginary-time density correlations and their ideal-gas reference at a single state point, without using the interaction potential. Our approach can extend other classical entropy estimators to quantum systems.
one_liner: Imaginary-time density correlations yield closed-form estimates of quantum excess entropy and free energy within a Gaussian inference framework.
why_it_matters: The method extracts thermodynamic information missed by equal-time structure factors using observables available from simulations and X-ray Thomson scattering.
detailed_summary: The authors extend classical structure-factor entropy inference to quantum systems by applying relative-entropy inference to imaginary-time density paths. Within a Gaussian approximation, they derive excess-entropy and free-energy formulas requiring only measured correlations and an ideal Bose or Fermi reference at one state point. Tests cover weakly interacting bosons, ring-confined fermions, and the warm dense electron gas.
platform_or_system: X-ray Thomson scattering and path-integral correlation data
main_result: Imaginary-time correlations recover quantum entropy contributions absent from equal-time estimators without requiring the interaction potential.
application_angle: The formulas could improve thermodynamic inference for warm dense matter and other quantum materials probed by X-ray scattering.

title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
abstract: A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to $9.4\times$ faster in a CPU.
one_liner: Non-binary detector error models preserve full Pauli-channel structure while producing sparser graphs and faster, more accurate belief-propagation decoding.
why_it_matters: Exact, compact noise models can reduce classical decoding cost and improve QEC performance on hardware-relevant surface, color, and bicycle codes.
detailed_summary: Each circuit fault location is represented by one random variable over its original error alphabet rather than decomposed into independent binary mechanisms. A split-merge-regroup transformation constructs compact models from Clifford circuits while exactly representing arbitrary Pauli channels. Across surface, color, and bivariate bicycle codes, the resulting Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, and BP with OSD runs up to 9.4 times faster on a CPU while improving decoding performance.
main_result: Non-binary models reduce Tanner-graph edges by 4–5 times and accelerate BP-OSD decoding by up to 9.4 times with better logical performance.
application_angle: Their smaller graphs and scalar BP messages are attractive for low-latency FPGA, ASIC, and CPU decoders in fault-tolerant processors.

title: When lies look like noise: certifying untrusted entanglement swapping
abstract: Entanglement swapping lets quantum repeaters distribute entanglement over long distances, a prerequisite for the quantum internet. We study its security in a noisy network whose intermediate nodes perform the quantum operations faithfully but may misreport the classical outcome that end users rely on. We show that the ideal functionality of entanglement swapping cannot be realised, because it gives the adversary no influence over the delivered state, whereas a node that relabels its report does have such influence. Including honest noise in the ideal setting does not help unless it also concedes a bounded fraction of misreported pairs. We therefore propose a cut-and-choose protocol that tests a random subset of pairs to certify the rest. Since no test can distinguish a misreport from readout noise, the protocol certifies the error above a pre-agreed minimum noise level, which is the misreport rate under our threat model. This yields a quality-of-service guarantee, in which a failure witnesses that the node did not deliver as agreed. Unlike verification schemes that consume the state they certify, the untested pairs remain available for use, with a finite-size guarantee. Certifying a 1% misreport rate on 10^6 pairs costs 10^4 to 1.7x10^5 test pairs, for minimum noise levels ranging from 0 to 5%. The main cost is memory, since 1% requires holding 10^5 to 10^6 pairs at once, far beyond the capacity of today's quantum memories. Verifying and releasing in blocks ties the memory to the block size at the cost of a weaker rate: a (10^4)-qubit memory certifies 14% on 4.7x10^5 delivered pairs.
one_liner: A cut-and-choose protocol certifies entanglement swapping when intermediate nodes operate correctly but may falsify their reported outcomes.
why_it_matters: It supplies a finite-size quality-of-service guarantee for untrusted quantum repeaters while leaving untested entangled pairs available for applications.
detailed_summary: The analysis shows that ideal entanglement-swapping functionality cannot capture adversarial relabeling because a false classical report changes the delivered state. The proposed protocol randomly tests some pairs and certifies the remainder relative to an agreed minimum noise floor, since misreports are indistinguishable from readout noise. Certifying a 1% misreport rate among one million pairs requires roughly 10,000–170,000 tests, but also exposes a major quantum-memory bottleneck.
main_result: The protocol provides finite-size certification of retained swapped pairs, with explicit test and memory costs under outcome-misreporting attacks.
application_angle: It enables service-level verification for future repeater networks and quantifies the memory capacity needed for deployable certification.

title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.
one_liner: Rapids co-designs a streaming neural QEC decoder with FPGA arithmetic to decode distance-19 surface-code rounds in under one microsecond.
why_it_matters: Sub-microsecond decoding with substantially lower logical error rates addresses a central classical-control bottleneck in superconducting fault-tolerant computers.
detailed_summary: Rapids uses neural-network operations selected for efficient FPGA mapping and trains directly with the device's integer arithmetic. A single FPGA processes each distance-19 surface-code syndrome round in under one microsecond, with a logical error rate 240 times below existing real-time hardware decoders. The architecture also supports color and [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle codes and can scale across multiple FPGAs or custom silicon.
main_result: Rapids achieves sub-microsecond distance-19 surface-code decoding and a 240-fold logical-error reduction over prior real-time hardware decoders.
application_angle: The scalable implementation can keep pace with fast superconducting syndrome cycles while reducing the qubit overhead needed to offset decoder errors.

title: Fast electrons and high energy photons produced in strong-field ionization of atoms as diagnostics of multi-petawatt laser beams
abstract: We calculate numerically energy spectra and angular distributions of photoelectrons and X-ray photons emitted in the process of tunnel photoionization of argon by a focused laser beam of multi-petawatt power. By scanning the beam power and varying the degree of focusing and the field polarization, we show these distributions to be sensitive both to the peak laser intensity and to the field configuration in the focal spot. Investigated parameters of the laser beam correspond to those of several recently commissioned lasers of multi-petawatt power. These findings, in line with the earlier reported proposals, provide a basis for the development of a reliable ionization diagnostics of extremely intense laser fields.
one_liner: Argon ionization spectra provide a noninvasive diagnostic of peak intensity and focal-field structure in multi-petawatt laser beams.
why_it_matters: Reliable focal diagnostics are essential for commissioning extreme-intensity lasers whose peak fields are difficult to measure directly.
detailed_summary: Numerical calculations predict the energy spectra and angular distributions of photoelectrons and X-ray photons generated by tunnel ionization of argon in focused multi-petawatt fields. Scans over beam power, focusing, and polarization show that these observables respond to both peak intensity and focal-field configuration. The modeled parameters correspond to several recently commissioned laser facilities.
main_result: Electron and X-ray emission distributions encode measurable signatures of laser peak intensity, focusing, and polarization.
application_angle: The approach could support reliable in situ characterization and commissioning of extreme-intensity laser focal spots.

title: Optimal Error corrected Hamiltonian estimation with nuisance parameters
abstract: Realistic quantum sensing is often affected by both noise and unknown nuisance parameters. Under Markovian dynamics, existing error correction approaches have often sought to suppress nuisance responses alongside environmental noise. Here we show that this local suppression of nuisance parameters is unnecessary and can be overly restrictive: nuisance parameters and Markovian noise impose fundamentally different constraints and require distinct treatments. We establish a general framework for quantum sensing with parameters encoded in a general time dependent Hamiltonian, in the presence of both nuisance parameters and Markovian noise. We derive a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling, determine the exact optimal precision, and construct protocols that attain it. Our results show that to achieve Heisenberg scaling Markovian noise must be suppressed locally by quantum error correction, whereas nuisance parameters need not, and in general should not, be eliminated locally. Instead, optimally designed coherent control can separate their accumulated effects from the target signal over the full sensing evolution. Consequently, Heisenberg scaling can remain attainable even when the target signal is instantaneously aligned with nuisance parameter directions, in sharp contrast to alignment with Markovian noise. This distinction substantially enlarges the regime in which Heisenberg scaling is attainable and provides a general principle for designing robust quantum sensors.
one_liner: A general error-corrected sensing framework attains optimal precision despite Markovian noise and unknown nuisance parameters.
why_it_matters: It expands the conditions for Heisenberg-limited sensing by separating local noise correction from global coherent discrimination of unwanted signals.
detailed_summary: The work treats parameters encoded by a general time-dependent Hamiltonian while allowing both unknown nuisance terms and Markovian noise. It derives a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling, obtains the exact optimal precision, and constructs attaining protocols. Markovian noise must be locally suppressed by quantum error correction, whereas coherent control can separate accumulated nuisance responses over the full evolution.
platform_or_system: Error-corrected quantum sensor with coherent control
main_result: Heisenberg scaling remains achievable even when the target Hamiltonian is instantaneously aligned with nuisance directions, provided Markovian noise is locally corrected.
application_angle: The framework guides robust sensor-control and error-correction designs for realistic devices with environmental noise and imperfectly known backgrounds.

title: When the Noise Gets Noisy: Quantum Error Correction with Disordered Noise and Misinformed Decoding
abstract: Experimental demonstrations of quantum error correction often exhibit noise that varies across space and time, and attempting to characterize this disorder has been shown to substantially improve decoding performance. However, theoretical studies of quantum error correction typically assume fixed, perfectly known, homogeneous noise. Here we model decoding with incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of disordered noise channels by treating physical error rates as random variables. We show that the decoding performance is set by a small number of information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution: the entropy determines the threshold while Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold decay rate of logical failures. Furthermore, our results give a quantitative measure of the benefits of characterizing this noise. We numerically investigate both maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight-error decoding of surface codes, showing good agreement with theory across the code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise settings, including with noise distributions seen in open-access superconducting devices. When it comes to error correction in realistic settings, reporting the average entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficient of noise distributions could therefore be more informative than the mean or median error rates of a device's components.
one_liner: Surface-code performance under disordered, mischaracterized noise is predicted by entropy and Bhattacharyya metrics rather than mean error rates.
why_it_matters: The results identify practical noise summaries that can improve decoder assessment and guide characterization of heterogeneous quantum processors.
detailed_summary: Physical error rates are modeled as random variables to study decoding with incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of spatially and temporally disordered noise. The noise-distribution entropy sets the threshold, while Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold decay of logical failures. Maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight-error simulations agree with the theory across code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level settings, including distributions from open-access superconducting devices.
main_result: A small set of information-theoretic functionals predicts thresholds, logical-error decay, and the value of improved noise characterization.
application_angle: Reporting entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficients could enable more informative hardware benchmarking and better-informed decoder calibration.

title: On the design of sequential quantum repeaters with error detection
abstract: Long-distance, trust-free quantum communications rely on the development of scalable quantum repeater schemes. Sequential entanglement generation with error detection is a promising approach that combines manageable implementation requirements with a hop-by-hop architecture compatible with existing classical infrastructure. In this paper, we investigate key design choices for such schemes over a repeater chain using quantum key distribution as a benchmark. We find that simple quantum error-detecting codes, such as repetition codes or quantum parity codes, perform well under near-term hardware assumptions and outperform strategies without any encoding. In particular, we show that two-qubit repetition codes may well be all that we need to implement in many practical scenarios. We also examine different architectures for the generation of initial entanglement and assess their merits. Additionally, we show that moderate improvements in some hardware components can partially mitigate the slow technological progress of others.
one_liner: Simple error-detecting codes, often just a two-qubit repetition code, improve sequential quantum-repeater performance under near-term assumptions.
why_it_matters: The study points to low-overhead repeater designs that may deliver useful QKD gains without demanding fully fault-tolerant hardware.
detailed_summary: The paper benchmarks sequential, hop-by-hop repeater chains using quantum key distribution and compares encoding and initial-entanglement architectures. Repetition and quantum parity codes outperform unencoded strategies under near-term hardware assumptions. Across many practical scenarios, a two-qubit repetition code is sufficient, while selective component improvements can offset slower progress elsewhere.
main_result: Low-complexity error-detecting encodings improve repeater-chain QKD performance, with two-qubit repetition codes often providing adequate protection.
application_angle: The findings support implementable near-term repeater nodes compatible with hop-by-hop deployment and existing classical infrastructure.

title: Authenticating quantum key distribution through random position checks
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) requires some form of authentication in order for the parties to be sure they are not unknowingly generating a key with an adversary pretending to be one of the honest parties. In this work, we propose a protocol in which the position of one of the parties is used as the authentication credential for key distribution. Our protocol essentially consists of a BB84 QKD protocol with quantum position verification (QPV) rounds randomly interleaved in. The approach is efficient compared with previous approaches, which required running an entire QPV protocol for every bit requiring authentication. We undertake an initial security analysis of the protocol for a restricted set of attacks.
one_liner: Randomly interleaving quantum position-verification checks with BB84 uses a party's location as the QKD authentication credential.
why_it_matters: Position-based checks could reduce the authentication overhead of combining QKD with quantum position verification.
detailed_summary: The proposed protocol inserts randomly selected quantum position-verification rounds into an otherwise BB84-style key-distribution exchange. A participant's physical position serves as the authentication credential. This is more efficient than earlier approaches requiring a complete position-verification protocol for every authenticated bit, although the presented security analysis covers only a restricted attack class.
platform_or_system: BB84 QKD with interleaved position checks
main_result: Random position-verification rounds provide a more efficient route to location-based authentication for QKD under the analyzed restricted attacks.
application_angle: The protocol may enable geographically bound QKD access where location can supplement or replace conventional authentication credentials.

title: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA
abstract: Remark: This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026. Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$. Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle ${O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{O} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof. Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In particular, relative to a classical oracle ${O}$ with $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O}$, there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).
one_liner: A classical-oracle construction separates QMA from the entire QCMA hierarchy and preserves quantum cryptographic primitives even when P equals QCMA.
why_it_matters: It shows theoretically that quantum-state advantages and quantum cryptography need not depend on standard quantum computational advantage or classical-proof hardness.
detailed_summary: The authors introduce Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise, a query problem in QMA that is hard for the full QCMA hierarchy. They construct a classical oracle relative to which P, BQP, QCMA, and the QCMA hierarchy coincide but remain strictly below QMA. In the same oracle setting, pseudorandom quantum states and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys still exist.
main_result: Quantum-proof advantage and several quantum cryptographic primitives persist relative to an oracle even when P, BQP, and the QCMA hierarchy collapse together.
application_angle: The separation clarifies which security capabilities can derive specifically from quantum states rather than generic quantum computation.

title: Topological phases protected by half-chiral symmetry
abstract: Chiral (or sublattice) symmetry describes bipartite systems such as the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain where same-sublattice A-A and B-B hoppings are forbidden, enabling the protection of topological phases. Here we identify new topological phases protected by half-chiral symmetry wherein chiral symmetry is preserved on only one sublattice, as may occur with sublattice imbalance (e.g. graphene-hBN) or localized orbitals (e.g. zincblende). Unlike conventional symmetry operators described by group theory, half-chiral symmetry is an algebraic constraint on the sublattice-projected Hamiltonian such as $PHP=0$, requiring a new framework for topological protection. We develop such a framework, identifying real-space bulk topological invariants and corresponding topological boundary modes that stick to zero energy. In two dimensions we construct a half-chiral Kekule honeycomb model and show that its unusual higher-order topology protects a single zero-energy mode at a single corner.
one_liner: Half-chiral symmetry protects zero-energy boundary modes even when chiral symmetry survives on only one sublattice.
why_it_matters: The framework expands the design space for topological photonic and electronic lattices with sublattice imbalance or localized orbitals.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate half-chiral symmetry as a projected-Hamiltonian constraint, such as PHP=0, rather than a conventional group-theoretic symmetry. They derive real-space bulk invariants and associated boundary modes pinned to zero energy. A two-dimensional Kekule honeycomb model exhibits higher-order topology with one protected zero mode localized at a single corner.
main_result: A new algebraic symmetry class is shown to protect zero-energy boundary states, including a single-corner mode in two dimensions.
application_angle: The results provide design principles for robust localized modes in photonic lattices and sublattice-asymmetric materials.

title: Free-Space Excitation of Frozen Waves and Topological Edge States in Graphene at a Time Interface
abstract: Time-varying two-dimensional materials, such as graphene under ultrafast photoexcitation, offer a promising platform for engineering temporal interfaces for electromagnetic waves. Rapidly promoting valence electrons to the conduction band generates a high-energy, non-thermal hot-electron population that subsequently thermalizes with the pre-existing thermal electron population. We study the excitation of plasmonic modes in graphene by the time interface created by ultra-fast photoexcitation using a graphene electron-transport model that is self-consistently coupled to electromagnetic simulations. We find that in addition to dynamic, propagating plasmonic modes, the time interfaces result in the excitation of static, spatially varying electromagnetic modes in the interaction region sustained by streaming transverse electrons. We also demonstrate a novel technique for coupling free-space light directly to highly localized topological edge states at the magnetic-inversion boundary on graphene, eliminating the need for near-field excitation techniques.
one_liner: Ultrafast graphene time interfaces excite frozen electromagnetic waves and enable free-space access to localized topological edge states.
why_it_matters: Direct far-field excitation could simplify ultrafast, deeply subwavelength plasmonic and topological-photonic devices.
detailed_summary: A self-consistent electron-transport and electromagnetic model describes graphene following ultrafast photoexcitation. Besides propagating plasmons, the temporal interface generates static, spatially varying fields sustained by streaming transverse electrons. The study also proposes direct free-space coupling to localized edge states at a magnetic-inversion boundary, avoiding near-field launchers.
main_result: Graphene time interfaces support both dynamic plasmons and frozen field patterns while permitting direct free-space excitation of topological edge modes.
application_angle: The coupling scheme may enable compact ultrafast plasmonic routing, field localization, and topological electromagnetic components.

title: Frequency-bin-encoded quantum secret sharing with fast basis switching
abstract: Frequency-bin encoding offers unique opportunities for fiber-native quantum information processing, yet its full potential has been hampered by challenges in rapid state control and protocol scaling. Leveraging high-speed microwave processing, we overcome several extant hurdles and unlock new fundamental capabilities in frequency-based quantum communications. First, we demonstrate three-party quantum secret sharing, representing, to our knowledge, the first multiparty ($N\geq 3$ users) quantum communication protocol implemented entirely with frequency encoding. Second, we demonstrate active, pseudorandom switching of frequency-bin quantum states and measurement bases at 20 MHz symbol rates, enabling real-time protocol operation without relying on hardware-intensive passive basis-selection schemes. Even under fast switching, we preserve high-contrast three-party correlations ($\geq 0.91$) and low quantum bit error rates ($\leq 4.5\%$). Our work extends frequency-bin quantum communication beyond static, two-party protocols, opening a pathway toward scalable, reconfigurable, and real-time spectrally encoded quantum networking.
one_liner: A frequency-bin platform demonstrates three-party quantum secret sharing with active basis switching at 20 MHz.
why_it_matters: It advances frequency-bin networking from static two-user links toward fast, reconfigurable multiparty quantum communication.
detailed_summary: The experiment implements a three-user quantum secret-sharing protocol entirely in frequency-bin encoding. High-speed microwave control provides pseudorandom switching of prepared states and measurement bases at a 20 MHz symbol rate. The system retains three-party correlation contrast of at least 0.91 and quantum bit error rates no greater than 4.5% during fast operation.
main_result: The platform realizes real-time three-party secret sharing with 20 MHz active basis switching, high correlation contrast, and low QBER.
application_angle: The approach supports scalable, fiber-compatible quantum networks with software-reconfigurable users, states, and measurement bases.

title: Spatially multiplexed opto-electronic Ising machine with single-shot parallel readout of 100,000 spins
abstract: Ising machines offer a promising route to solving NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems by mapping them onto the ground state of the Ising model. Free-space optical implementations are attractive for their inherent parallelism, scalability, and energy efficiency, yet nearly all rely on individual, sequential spin updates, leaving most of this parallelism unexploited. Here, we reclaim it with a free-space optical analog Ising machine built from off-the-shelf components in which every spin is addressed in parallel and read out in a single camera shot, while letting the system evolve under analog dynamics rather than being written and read one spin at a time. We demonstrate this architecture with over 100,000 spins, the largest spatially multiplexed analog Ising machine reported to date, with a realistic path beyond one million spins limited only by spatial-light-modulator and camera resolution. Across sparse and dense MaxCut and fully connected number-partitioning instances, our machine matches state-of-the-art solution quality. Because every spin updates in parallel, throughput increases with system size, unlike time-multiplexed machines, which slow as problems grow. The same free-space geometry also lets us solve more than 50 problem instances simultaneously, further boosting throughput. Together, these results mark an important step towards a scalable, and energy-efficient Ising machine.
one_liner: A free-space opto-electronic Ising machine updates and reads more than 100,000 spatially multiplexed spins in parallel.
why_it_matters: Single-shot parallel readout and simultaneous problem solving offer a practical route to higher-throughput optical optimization hardware.
detailed_summary: The machine uses off-the-shelf free-space optical components to address all spins concurrently and recover their states in one camera exposure. It operates with over 100,000 spins and matches state-of-the-art solution quality on MaxCut and number-partitioning benchmarks. The same optical geometry solves more than 50 instances simultaneously and could scale beyond one million spins with improved modulator and camera resolution.
main_result: The system demonstrates parallel analog evolution and single-shot readout of over 100,000 spins while maintaining competitive optimization quality.
application_angle: Its size-dependent throughput and commodity components make it promising for scalable, energy-efficient combinatorial optimization accelerators.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Key Distribution Hardware Across Operating Conditions
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is entering national fibre networks, but published secret key rates (SKRs) are measured over different distances, wavelengths, classical traffic loads and clock rates, so systems are hard to compare. We write the SKR as the product of the transmitter clock rate, the channel transmittance and the secret key per received pulse. This third factor, the noise-normalised key rate (NNKR), needs four commonly reported parameters and depends mainly on the equipment wherever the SKR is proportional to transmittance. A companion metric, the implementation efficiency (IE), compares the SKR with the ideal key rate of its channel, including classical-traffic noise. For fixed loss-limited equipment, NNKR is independent of channel loss, whereas the fraction of the repeaterless bound varies 1.6-fold over 2-25 dB. An analytic model relates the flat loss range of NNKR to the detector noise count rate and dead time. We apply both metrics to ten published coexistence experiments, and NNKR to 42,115 measurements from four systems of two vendors and four high-rate laboratory systems. For one production system, NNKR has a 6.9% coefficient of variation over 17 dB of attenuation and agrees within 0.7 dB with three of four published deployments of that platform. Under coexistence, that platform's NNKR and IE stay within 0.5 dB of their standalone values. In decibels, NNKR is a sum of component penalties, as in an optical link budget, and for one laboratory system the budget from its published parameters and measured secure fraction closes within 0.3 dB.
one_liner: Noise-normalized metrics enable fair QKD hardware comparisons across loss, clock rate, wavelength, and classical coexistence conditions.
why_it_matters: A link-budget-style benchmark can expose equipment penalties and compare deployed QKD systems without conflating hardware with channel conditions.
detailed_summary: The paper factors secret key rate into transmitter clock rate, channel transmittance, and noise-normalized key rate, or NNKR, and introduces implementation efficiency relative to an ideal channel. The metrics are evaluated on ten coexistence studies, 42,115 measurements from commercial systems, and four high-rate laboratory platforms. For one production system, NNKR varies by only 6.9% across 17 dB attenuation, remains within 0.5 dB under coexistence, and yields a component budget closing within 0.3 dB for one laboratory system.
platform_or_system: Fiber-optic QKD hardware and coexistence links
main_result: NNKR and implementation efficiency provide loss-aware, hardware-centered comparisons that remain stable across broad attenuation and traffic conditions.
application_angle: The metrics can improve procurement, field acceptance, vendor comparison, and diagnosis of QKD equipment in operational fiber networks.

title: Augmenting Quantum Neural Networks with Contractive Layers
abstract: Classical neural networks combine diverse layers with complementary roles to achieve rich expressive capabilities across complex learning tasks. Rapid advances in quantum science and technology have motivated growing interest in their quantum counterparts, quantum neural networks, raising the question of how their expressivity can be enhanced through the design of new quantum layers. Of particular interest are layers that enrich the accessible function space while introducing only a small number of additional trainable parameters. In this Letter, we introduce the contractive layer as a promising building block for quantum neural networks. This layer comprises all-to-all couplings governed by a single trainable parameter, enabling efficient control of quantum information flow while maintaining experimental relevance to Rydberg atom arrays. Using observable learning as a benchmark, we show that contractive layers enhance expressivity more efficiently than simply increasing the depth of conventional brick-wall circuits. This advantage stems from a systematic increase in the accessible target-space dimension per trainable parameter. We further demonstrate similar improvements in image recognition tasks. These results highlight contractive layers as a practical route to expressive quantum neural networks on near-term quantum devices.
one_liner: Single-parameter all-to-all contractive layers improve quantum neural-network expressivity more efficiently than added circuit depth.
why_it_matters: The layer maps naturally to Rydberg interactions and could increase useful model capacity without a large parameter or control overhead.
detailed_summary: The proposed contractive layer uses all-to-all couplings governed by one trainable parameter to reshape quantum-information flow. Observable-learning simulations show a larger accessible target-space dimension per parameter than deeper conventional brick-wall circuits. Improvements also appear in image-recognition tasks, and the interaction structure is designed to remain relevant to Rydberg-atom hardware.
main_result: Contractive layers increase quantum-model expressivity per trainable parameter and outperform simple circuit deepening on learning benchmarks.
application_angle: The design offers a hardware-aligned way to build more capable near-term quantum learning circuits with modest calibration and optimization cost.

title: Physical Learning for Autonomous Tuning of Spin Qubits in Electrostatically Defined Quantum Dots
abstract: Tuning electrostatically defined quantum dots remains a primary bottleneck in the scalability of semiconductor spin qubits. While existing solutions rely on machine learning algorithms, these approaches require global information, introduce latency bottlenecks, and tax the limited cooling power available at cryogenic stages. Here, we demonstrate an FPGA-in-the-loop learning paradigm that bypasses digital computing overhead by utilizing multiplexed gradient descent (MGD) for tuning. Implemented on an FPGA and an emulated quantum dot device, our system autonomously tracks environmental drift, dynamically recovers from discrete charge jumps, and maintains steady-state stabilization in low signal-to-noise ratio regimes, without prior knowledge of the device's cross-capacitance matrix. The system also navigates the charge-stability landscape to stabilize the quantum dot around optimal operating points. These results demonstrate a ``compute-in-place'' platform, with a logic and power footprint suited to future cryo-CMOS integration, that provides autonomous stabilization of quantum dots at desired operating points, creating an auto-tuning system for spin qubits that is resilient to electrostatic drifts, changing noise profiles, and two-level fluctuations.
one_liner: FPGA-based multiplexed gradient descent autonomously stabilizes an emulated quantum dot without knowing its cross-capacitance matrix.
why_it_matters: Compute-in-place tuning could reduce latency, digital overhead, and cryogenic power demands in scalable semiconductor spin-qubit systems.
detailed_summary: The authors implement multiplexed gradient descent on an FPGA connected in the loop to an emulated electrostatically defined quantum dot. The controller tracks drift, recovers from discrete charge jumps, and remains stable at low signal-to-noise ratio without prior cross-capacitance calibration. It also navigates the charge-stability landscape toward selected operating points.
main_result: The system autonomously finds and maintains quantum-dot operating points despite drift, charge jumps, noise changes, and two-level fluctuations.
application_angle: The compact logic and power footprint supports future cryo-CMOS controllers for scalable spin-qubit calibration and stabilization.

title: Unconventional Photon Blockade in Second-Order Nonlinearity Coupled Cavities with Asymmetric Dissipation
abstract: We investigate the unconventional photon blockade in a second-order nonlinearity coupled double-cavity system with asymmetric dissipation. By treating the cavity decay rates as independent parameters, we analytically derive two exact families of optimal blockade conditions. While the first family recovers and generalizes the symmetric-dissipation results of previous studies, the second family, arising uniquely from an asymmetric dissipation ratio of $κ_B = 2κ_A$, completely locks the relative phase of the interference pathways. Importantly, we find that this asymmetric dissipation not only renders the optimal blockade condition strictly immune to frequency detuning, but also enhances the blockade depth by an order of magnitude compared to the resonant case. Furthermore, the mean photon number remains almost unaffected, proving that this enhanced robustness is achieved without sacrificing the brightness of the single-photon source. These findings offer a promising route toward robust single-photon generation in passive cavities with second-order nonlinearity.
one_liner: Asymmetric cavity loss produces detuning-immune unconventional photon blockade in coupled second-order nonlinear resonators.
why_it_matters: The scheme promises substantially deeper antibunching without reducing brightness, easing practical fabrication and frequency-control requirements.
detailed_summary: The work analytically derives two exact families of optimal blockade conditions for coupled cavities with second-order nonlinearity and independently controlled decay rates. A family unique to κB = 2κA locks the relative phase of interfering excitation pathways and makes the optimum insensitive to frequency detuning. The predicted blockade is an order of magnitude deeper than in the resonant case while preserving mean photon number.
main_result: A 2:1 dissipation asymmetry yields detuning-immune photon blockade with roughly tenfold greater depth and nearly unchanged brightness.
application_angle: Passive nonlinear cavities using this condition could provide more fabrication-tolerant and frequency-robust single-photon sources.

title: Pulse-tube-vibration induced Larmor frequency jitter in anisotropic Kramers spins
abstract: We investigate the role of pulse-tube mechanical vibrations towards spin frequency noise in a cryogen-free dilution refrigerator. Our system comprises of a low mode-volume superconducting resonator coupled to 50 ppm $\text{Er}^{3+}:\text{CaWO}_4$ spins with highly anisotropic g-factors. By measuring single-shot spin echoes using narrow-bandwidth three-pulse sequences, we directly observe a vibration induced stochastic signal resulting from the spin's Larmor frequency moving into and out of the detection bandwidth. The sensitivity to these vibrations is substantially suppressed when a) the external magnetic field is aligned along the symmetry c-axis and b) spin temperature is modestly increased to 60~mK. We also benchmark the system as a quantum sensor for angular fluctuations, extracting a noise floor of 350 nanodegrees.
one_liner: Single-shot spin echoes reveal pulse-tube vibration as Larmor-frequency jitter in anisotropic erbium spins at millikelvin temperatures.
why_it_matters: The measurements identify practical routes to suppress vibration-induced decoherence and demonstrate nanoscale angular sensing in cryogenic spin hardware.
detailed_summary: A low-mode-volume superconducting resonator probes 50 ppm Er3+:CaWO4 spins with strongly anisotropic g-factors inside a cryogen-free dilution refrigerator. Narrow-bandwidth three-pulse sequences resolve stochastic echo signals as vibration shifts the Larmor frequency through the detection band. Aligning the field with the crystal c-axis or raising the spin temperature to 60 mK substantially suppresses the coupling.
platform_or_system: Er3+:CaWO4 spins coupled to a superconducting resonator
main_result: The experiment directly resolves pulse-tube-induced spin-frequency jitter and achieves an angular-noise floor of 350 nanodegrees.
application_angle: The findings guide vibration mitigation in cryogenic spin devices and enable anisotropic spins to serve as sensitive angular-fluctuation probes.

title: Symplectic Matroids, Stabilizer Codes, and Quantum Secret-Sharing
abstract: An $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear $[[n,k]]_q$ stabilizer code is represented by a totally isotropic subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^{2n}$ of dimension $n-k$, whose full-rank generator matrix has nonzero maximal minors on admissible column sets forming the bases of a representable symplectic matroid. Sarvepalli asked whether graphical symplectic matroids introduced by Chow give stabilizer codes with good parameters, when a Lagrangian matroid induces a quantum access structure, which code realizes it, and which polynomial carries the weight enumerator. We answer these questions. For a $3$-connected simple graph, every representation of a graphical symplectic matroid, over any field, gives a stabilizer code of distance exactly $2$, so the girth is not a lower bound. For a represented Lagrangian matroid and a dealer, we construct the dealer-shortened stabilizer code, its logical operators, an encoding isometry and explicit recovery maps, and we show that this is the code implemented by the stabilizer state through teleportation. A set of players recovers the secret, learns nothing, or learns part of it according to a rank formula on pairs of columns, which equals its mutual information with the dealer; for graph states it becomes a cut-rank condition. Over $\F_2$ a symplectic matroid of any rank has only one representation, so the code, its access structure and its weight enumerators depend on the matroid alone; for $q\ge3$ even the enumerator does not. Circuit-induced authorized sets always reconstruct when the matroid is self-dual, but not in general, and a six-qubit graph state shows that the two access structures can differ even then. Finally, a polynomial in the ranks of column pairs determines both weight enumerators.
one_liner: Symplectic-matroid structure is connected explicitly to stabilizer codes, recovery maps, and quantum secret-sharing access rules.
why_it_matters: The results clarify which participants can reconstruct or learn a quantum secret and expose limitations of graph-derived code constructions.
detailed_summary: The authors construct dealer-shortened stabilizer codes, logical operators, encoding isometries, and explicit recovery maps from represented Lagrangian matroids. A rank formula on column pairs classifies participant sets by full, zero, or partial information and reduces to cut rank for graph states. They also prove that codes from 3-connected simple graphical symplectic matroids have distance exactly two and characterize when representations determine access structures and weight enumerators.
main_result: The paper gives explicit secret-recovery constructions and rank-based access criteria while proving distance-two limitations for graphical symplectic-matroid codes.
application_angle: These tools support systematic design and verification of stabilizer-based quantum secret-sharing protocols and their authorized participant sets.

title: Monolithic ultraviolet-to- near infrared photodetection enabled by an aluminium oxide photonic platform
abstract: Broadband photonic integrated circuits require waveguide platforms that combine low optical loss across a wide spectral range with integrated photodetection. Here we demonstrate a monolithically integrated atomic-layer-deposited (ALD) aluminium oxide (Al$_2$O$_3$)-on-silicon platform enabling waveguide-coupled photodetection from the ultraviolet to the near-infrared. The architecture employs evanescent coupling between low-loss Al$_2$O$_3$ waveguides and silicon p-i-n photodiodes. The platform supports photodetection at 375, 658 and 780 nm, extending integrated silicon photodetection into the ultraviolet. The devices exhibit linear photocurrent scaling with optical power, dark currents of approximately 2 pA at 50 V reverse bias and nanosecond-scale temporal response. We further demonstrate centimetre-scale ultraviolet Mach-Zehnder interferometer circuits with integrated photodiodes. The same detector architecture is implemented with Si$_3$N$_4$ waveguides, whereas the lower ultraviolet propagation loss of Al$_2$O$_3$ enables an approximately 15-fold higher photodetection response at 375 nm. These results establish ALD Al$_2$O$_3$ as a broadband integrated photonics platform for sensing, spectroscopy and quantum technologies.
one_liner: An ALD aluminium-oxide photonic platform integrates waveguides and silicon detectors from 375 to 780 nm.
why_it_matters: Monolithic ultraviolet detection with low dark current and fast response expands integrated sensing, spectroscopy, and quantum-photonic capabilities.
detailed_summary: The platform evanescently couples low-loss ALD Al2O3 waveguides to silicon p-i-n photodiodes and detects light at 375, 658, and 780 nm. Devices show linear photocurrent, approximately 2 pA dark current at 50 V reverse bias, and nanosecond-scale response. Centimetre-scale ultraviolet Mach-Zehnder interferometers are integrated with detectors, and Al2O3 provides about 15 times the 375 nm response of a comparable Si3N4 implementation.
main_result: The monolithic platform demonstrates waveguide-coupled UV-to-near-IR detection and integrated UV interferometers with low dark current and nanosecond response.
application_angle: Its broad spectral reach and ultraviolet performance suit chip-scale spectroscopy, chemical or biological sensing, and quantum photonics.

title: Explicit construction of the normal cone at every nonlocal extreme behaviour of $\mathcal{Q}_{2222}$ and device-independent applications
abstract: The set of quantum correlations $\mathcal{Q}_{2222}$, in the simplest Bell scenario with two parties performing two binary measurements each, is an object of fundamental interest both in quantum foundations and for device-independent applications. A nonlocal extremal quantum behaviour in this set can maximize many different Bell expressions, yet these expressions are not all equally useful in a practical experiment. Here, firstly, we give an explicit characterization of every Bell expression maximized by any given nonlocal extremal quantum behaviour in this Bell scenario. This determines the full normal cone at every such behaviour and makes it possible to optimize over all Bell tests with the same ideal behavior. We then derive an exact variational formula for the quantum bound of an arbitrary Bell expression in this scenario. As an example illustrating the construction, we derive the normal cone for a family of extremal quantum behaviours of importance in device-independent randomness certification, from Phys. Rev. Lett. 129, 150403, 2022. Finally, we explore the consequences of this characterization for device-independent randomness generation in practical experiments. Specifically, for any given detection efficiency $η\in [0.75,0.98]$, we construct Bell tests and two-qubit experiments that certify more single-round min-entropy from one Bell score than any CHSH score can certify with the same detector efficiency, even when the quantum devices used for the CHSH test are optimized. The results provide a systematic way to choose Bell tests for a desired quantum behaviour and to improve their performance for device-independent applications under experimental imperfections.
one_liner: A complete normal-cone construction enables Bell tests optimized for device-independent randomness under finite detector efficiency.
why_it_matters: Tailored Bell expressions certify more randomness than optimized CHSH tests across realistic detection efficiencies from 75% to 98%.
detailed_summary: The paper explicitly characterizes every Bell expression maximized by any nonlocal extremal behavior in the two-party, two-input, two-output quantum-correlation set. It also derives an exact variational formula for the quantum bound of an arbitrary Bell expression in this scenario. Using the construction, the authors design two-qubit tests that outperform optimized CHSH randomness certification for detector efficiencies between 0.75 and 0.98.
main_result: Optimized Bell tests certify greater single-round min-entropy than any CHSH score at matched detector efficiency over the studied range.
application_angle: The method lets experiments select Bell inequalities that maximize certified randomness despite detector loss and other practical imperfections.

title: Actively stabilized Fabry-Pérot notch filters for correlated photons from cold two-level atoms
abstract: We report two actively stabilized Fabry-Pérot cavities operated as reflection-mode notch filters for biphotons generated by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a cold two-level atomic ensemble. In this source, elastic scattering at the excitation frequency increases the single-detector count rates and the accidental-coincidence background, thereby limiting the observed nonclassical correlations. One cavity is placed in each photon-collection mode. An acousto-optic modulator frequency-dithers an auxiliary field, and synchronous demodulation of the transmitted power provides the locking discriminator. Light resonant with the auxiliary field is transmitted, whereas the detuned components are reflected toward the photon detectors. By tuning the auxiliary field to the same frequency as the excitation field, we filter these components and direct a larger portion of the quantum-correlated sidebands to the detection. The cavities have linewidths of approximately 2 MHz and remain locked for longer than a typical correlation acquisition. The measured Cauchy-Schwarz parameter exceeds unity in both configurations, with a higher central value with filtering ($\overline{R} = 4.15 \pm 0.93$) than without ($\overline{R} = 2.33 \pm 0.20$). This architecture provides actively stabilized rejection of a narrow spectral interval, simultaneously, for two fields detected in different directions. Filter performance could be further improved by adjusting the cavity linewidth to better match the spectral width of the central component and by reducing losses in the filters.
one_liner: Dual stabilized Fabry–Pérot notch filters improve observed nonclassical correlations from a cold-atom biphoton source.
why_it_matters: The approach suppresses narrowband excitation leakage in two collection paths while preserving correlated sidebands, improving practical photon-pair measurements.
detailed_summary: Two reflection-mode Fabry–Pérot cavities filter elastic scattering from biphotons produced by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a cold two-level atomic ensemble. An AOM-dithered auxiliary field and synchronous detection stabilize approximately 2 MHz-wide cavity resonances throughout correlation acquisitions. Filtering raises the measured mean Cauchy–Schwarz parameter from 2.33 ± 0.20 to 4.15 ± 0.93, although cavity losses and linewidth mismatch leave room for improvement.
platform_or_system: Cold-atom biphoton source with dual Fabry–Pérot cavities
main_result: Actively locked notch filtering increased the central measured Cauchy–Schwarz parameter while retaining nonclassical correlations.
application_angle: The architecture can improve background rejection and correlation visibility in narrowband atomic quantum-photon sources and interfaces.

title: Adaptive-Optics-Aware Uplink and Downlink Analysis of Ground-to-HAPS FSO Links
abstract: In this paper, we present an adaptive optics (AO)-aware analytical framework for ground-to- high-altitude platform station (HAPS) free-space optical (FSO) links considering both uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) transmission. The proposed model combines atmospheric attenuation, Exponentiated Weibull (EW) turbulence, Beckmann-type pointing error (PE), and field-of-view (FoV)-limited angle-of-arrival (AOA) loss. Adaptive optics correction (AOC) is incorporated through the number of corrected modes, allowing the impact of partial and stronger wavefront compensation to be directly reflected in the channel statistics. Analytical and numerically tractable expressions are derived for the outage probability (OP), average bit-error rate (BER), and an ergodic achievable-rate lower bound (EALB) optical channel. High signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) approximations are also developed, showing that AOA/FoV blocking introduces irreducible OP and BER floors, while the decaying nonblocked component is governed by the small-channel-gain behavior of the turbulence and PE distributions. Numerical results demonstrate that the DL generally outperforms the UL because of the direction-dependent interaction with near-ground turbulence. The results also show that increasing the number of AOC modes improves OP, BER, and the EALB, although the improvement gradually saturates. The effects of average SNR, HAPS altitude, zenith angle, beam waist, boresight error, and receiver FoV are further investigated to provide practical design insight for AO-assisted ground-to-HAPS FSO systems.
one_liner: An AO-aware channel model quantifies uplink and downlink performance for ground-to-HAPS free-space optical links.
why_it_matters: It exposes hard outage and BER floors from field-of-view blocking and identifies where stronger adaptive-optics correction yields diminishing returns.
detailed_summary: The framework combines atmospheric attenuation, Exponentiated Weibull turbulence, Beckmann pointing error, and field-of-view-limited angle-of-arrival loss. Adaptive-optics correction enters through the number of corrected modes, enabling tractable outage, BER, and achievable-rate calculations. Numerical analysis predicts generally better downlink performance, saturating gains with additional corrected modes, and irreducible error floors when angle-of-arrival blocking occurs.
main_result: The model derives tractable performance metrics and shows that AO improves link quality but cannot eliminate field-of-view-induced outage and BER floors.
application_angle: The results guide AO order, receiver field of view, beam size, geometry, and pointing tolerances for aerial optical communication links.

title: Communication advantages of a quantum switch of two pure-loss channels
abstract: The quantum switch can enable communication through otherwise unusable channels, a phenomenon known as causal activation. We show that a switch of two identical pure-loss channels can achieve strictly greater energy-constrained classical and quantum capacities than their sequential use, even when two-way classical communication is available.
