abstract: The Bohmian interpretation of quantum mechanics is controversial because it attributes deterministic trajectories to microscopic particles. We propose a reformulation that sidesteps this controversy: rather than applying Bohmian mechanics at the microscopic level, we recast it as an effective deterministic description of the macroscopic pointer of a measuring apparatus, with no claims about the fundamental nature of the microscopic world. In this form, the Bohmian trajectory becomes a practical tool for visualizing the emergence of a definite measurement outcome, broadly acceptable to physicists who would otherwise reject the Bohmian program.
one_liner: Bohmian trajectories are reframed as an effective deterministic description of a measuring apparatus’s macroscopic pointer.
why_it_matters: The reformulation offers a visualization of definite outcomes without asserting microscopic Bohmian ontology.

title: Depth-Dependent Collapse and Warm-Start Limits of a Symmetry-Preserving VQE for the J$_1$--J$_2$ Heisenberg Ring
abstract: Increasing circuit depth is expected to improve a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). We show that this expectation can fail, and that curing the failure does not guarantee the exact ground state. We study a symmetry-preserving ansatz of SingleExcitationMinus gates, started from the Néel state, on the frustrated spin-$1/2$ $J_1$--$J_2$ Heisenberg ring with $N=10$ and $12$ sites. With random initialization the fidelity, energy error, half-chain entropy and total spin change abruptly at intermediate depth ($L\approx 9$ for $N=10$, $L=10$--$12$ for $N=12$), giving improvement, degradation and recovery, a double-descent-like shape. The circuit family is nested and the gradient stays finite, so this is an optimization failure, not a loss of expressibility or a barren plateau. A chained warm start, which extends an optimized shallow circuit with identity layers, removes the collapse and improves energy error and fidelity almost monotonically for most frustration values. However, near $J_2/J_1=0.60$ ($N=10$) and over $J_2/J_1=0.60$--$1.00$ ($N=12$) the warm start stalls at a fidelity of $\approx 0.50$--$0.58$, although the energy error is small and the total spin stays in the $S=0$ sector. Removing the non-monotonic depth dependence is therefore not the same as reaching the ground state, and low energy and a singlet-like state are not sufficient: the fidelity, entropy and total spin must be satisfied together. The conclusions are limited to the system sizes and frustration values studied.
one_liner: A symmetry-preserving VQE shows depth-dependent optimization collapse, while warm starts improve convergence but can miss the exact ground state.
why_it_matters: It cautions that low energy and correct symmetry alone cannot validate VQE states; fidelity and entanglement checks remain necessary.

title: Oblique incidence and non-commuting limits: a remark on the convergence of Fresnel integrals
abstract: The Gaussian integrals of quantum mechanics and of paraxial optics are oscillatory and only conditionally convergent. Textbooks usually make them converge by adding a small imaginary part to the time or by analytic continuation. We point out that the one-dimensional Fresnel integral converges by itself, while in two dimensions the result depends on the shape of the expanding domain: over squares it converges, over discs it oscillates for ever. The second case is the field of a uniformly excited plane of dipoles, which Feynman uses to explain the refractive index. Lai, Lau and Wong showed that at oblique incidence the integral converges and that normal incidence is recovered in the limit; we note that the two limits do not commute, and that this provides a transparent introduction to the regularization of the time-sliced path integral, where the ordering of the integrations in time plays the role of the physical prescription.
one_liner: Fresnel integrals can depend on domain shape, and oblique-incidence and infinite-domain limits need not commute.
why_it_matters: It clarifies why physical prescriptions and integration order matter in oscillatory path integrals.

title: Exact classical bounds of bipartite correlation Bell inequalities using improved branch-and-bound
abstract: We present an improved branch-and-bound (IBB) algorithm for the exact computation of classical (local) bounds of bipartite correlation Bell inequalities. We strengthen pruning in the standard BB algorithm in two ways: a heuristic search based on see-saw iteration supplies a strong initial lower bound, and greedy row reordering of the Bell matrix reduces the tail bounds used during the exact search. An OpenMP implementation combines these improvements with shared-memory parallelism and dynamic work redistribution. Random-matrix benchmarks show substantial runtime reductions in matrix sizes, while explicit constructions demonstrate exact local-bound computations for square matrices up to $130 \times 130$ and rectangular matrices of sizes up to $81 \times 321$. Applications provide improved lower bounds on finite-order Grothendieck constants for $d=3,4,5,7$ and uniform-input XOR games with quantum-to-classical ratios exceeding $\sqrt2$. The method retains an exponential worst-case search for this NP-hard optimization problem, and its practical performance depends on matrix structure and tail-bound preprocessing depth.
one_liner: An improved branch-and-bound algorithm exactly computes classical bounds for substantially larger bipartite Bell inequalities.
why_it_matters: It expands exact analysis of Bell tests, Grothendieck constants, and XOR-game quantum advantages.

title: Entanglement cost and classical capacity of multimode Gaussian states and channels
abstract: Gaussian states and operations are central to continuous-variable quantum information and communication. For systems with any finite number of modes, we prove that entanglement of formation, Gaussian entanglement of formation, and entanglement cost coincide for every finite-energy bipartite Gaussian state. Their common value is strongly superadditive and lower-bounds entanglement of formation and entanglement cost for arbitrary non-Gaussian states with the same covariance matrix. We then determine the entanglement cost of every multimode Gaussian channel as well as its classical capacity under a mean energy constraint. These quantities reduce to Gaussian covariance optimizations, and the capacity is attained by pure Gaussian signals with Gaussian displacement modulation, independently across channel uses. The proof combines geodesic convexity of entanglement for pure Gaussian states with a relative-entropy inequality for arbitrary states. We also obtain a closed formula for the entanglement cost of a family of four-mode bound entangled states.
one_liner: The work determines entanglement cost and energy-constrained classical capacity for general finite-mode Gaussian states and channels.
why_it_matters: It reduces key continuous-variable communication resources to tractable Gaussian covariance optimizations.

title: Problem-adjusted $X$-mixer eigenstates for improved QAOA
abstract: We show that the use of problem-adjusted excited eigenstates of the $X$-mixer Hamiltonian can be beneficial for the performance of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) when applied to problems with degenerate ground states. We show that this advantage persists in the presence of quantum gate and readout noise, with the problem-adjusted excited initial states achieving better optimal performance than the standard ground state initialization. The realized advantage depends on the number of QAOA layers and whether or not the initial state has a reasonable time evolution path into the ground space of the problem Hamiltonian. We also explain how to prepare these problem-adjusted $X$-mixer eigenstates exactly, as well as how to approximate them using a linear combination of ladder operators. Finally, we discuss how the power of these initial states can be applied to any problem Hamiltonian regardless of the degeneracy of its ground state by making use of a Grover-style mixer Hamiltonian.
one_liner: Problem-adjusted excited eigenstates of the X-mixer can improve QAOA performance, including under gate and readout noise.
why_it_matters: Better initial states may raise QAOA solution quality for optimization problems with degenerate ground spaces.

title: Non-Invertible Quantum Cellular Automata I: Microscopic Definition of Non-Invertible Symmetries
abstract: We introduce non-invertible quantum cellular automata (QCAs), defined as locality-preserving quantum channels that are dualizable and pure. This provides an operator-algebraic definition of non-invertible symmetries of quantum lattice systems, formulated in terms of their action on local operators. Focusing on quantum spin chains, we motivate these defining conditions and conjecture that every such quantum channel admits a realization by dualizable topological defects or, equivalently, by dualizable sequential quantum circuits. We construct a broad class of examples, including on-site non-invertible symmetries that are anomalous, as well as higher-dimensional examples. In Part II of this work, we reconstruct topological defects whose boundary algebras yield an index theory that classifies non-invertible QCAs up to blend equivalence.
one_liner: Non-invertible QCAs are defined as pure, dualizable, locality-preserving quantum channels acting on lattice observables.
why_it_matters: The framework gives a microscopic operator-algebraic description of non-invertible lattice symmetries.

title: Comment on "The eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the toroidal dipole operator'
abstract: We show here that the spectrum of the operator $\hat{T}_3^{(θ)}$ studied by Anghel and Dolineanu (Phys. Scr. {\bf 98} (2023) 015223) is continuous, not discrete, contrary to what is claimed by the authors of the paper to which this comment refers. Consequently, there is no splitting of the energy levels corresponding to this operator that could be observed experimentally.
one_liner: The toroidal dipole operator studied in earlier work has a continuous spectrum rather than the claimed discrete spectrum.
why_it_matters: This removes the predicted energy-level splitting and its proposed experimental signature.

title: Unique continuation for the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian
abstract: We prove a unique continuation property for eigenstates of the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian, viewed as functions of the electron configuration with values in the spin-photon space. The vector potential may lie in $L^6_\mathrm{loc}$, with its divergence, curl, and the scalar potential in $L^p_\mathrm{loc}$ for some $p>2$. As an application, we prove a Hohenberg-Kohn theorem at positive coupling strength: the spin-summed ground-state density and combined current density determine the external potentials up to a gauge transformation and an additive constant.
one_liner: A unique-continuation theorem for Pauli-Fierz eigenstates yields a positive-coupling Hohenberg-Kohn result.
why_it_matters: It establishes when density and current determine external potentials in matter coupled to quantized light.

title: Optimal Min-Entropy Estimation with High Probability
abstract: Min-entropy plays a fundamental role in assessing the unpredictability of randomness sources. In particular, NIST SP 800-90B specifies min-entropy estimation as a key procedure for entropy sources used in cryptographic random bit generators, illustrating the practical importance of reliable min-entropy estimation. In this paper, we settle the sample complexity of min-entropy estimation with high probability in both the classical and quantum cases. Specifically, for min-entropy estimation with additive error $\varepsilon$ and probability at least $1-δ$, the sample complexity is $Θ(d\log(d/δ)/\varepsilon^2)$ for classical distributions on $d$ symbols and $Θ((d^2+d\log(1/δ))/\varepsilon^2)$ for quantum states on a $d$-dimensional Hilbert space. Our results admit short and simple proofs.
one_liner: The paper establishes optimal high-probability sample complexities for classical and quantum min-entropy estimation.
why_it_matters: It sharpens the data requirements for certifying randomness sources used in cryptographic generators.

title: Causality, determinism and predictability: Probing nature through classical and quantum eyes
abstract: In this article, mainly focussed on students and interested readers, we discuss how the understanding of causality, determinism and predictability is transformed as we move from the classical world view to the quantum description. We first explain how determinism and predictability operate in classical dynamics and outline the notion of causality. A paradigm shift occurs within the framework of quantum mechanics where we have to revisit, and even give up, the notions of determinism, predictability and maybe even strict causality. An engrossing and fascinating debate ensues, after the formulation of quantum mechanics among the giants of physics like Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Pauli, and many others. While some questions have been settled in the last century in favour of quantum world view, there are still many open questions, most important of which is the role of gravity in shaping events within the quantum framework.
one_liner: A student-oriented review traces how quantum mechanics reshapes classical ideas of causality, determinism, and predictability.
why_it_matters: It offers an accessible conceptual bridge between classical physics, quantum debates, and open questions about gravity.

title: Non-equilibrium topological order from Floquet anyon proliferation in the toric code
abstract: We analyze the dynamics of Kitaev's toric code in Floquet quenches where the drive coherently creates and propagates fermionic $f$ anyons. We show that the long-time state departs from pure-state topological order but retains long-range entanglement, thereby realizing a Floquet analog of intrinsic mixed-state topological order. As a key result enabling this analysis, we derive decompositions of the entanglement entropy and logarithmic negativity that separate the ground-state value, including topological terms, from a contribution given by the driven quasiparticles. For a drive inducing non-interacting $f$ dynamics, these decompositions allow us to leverage numerical methods for free fermions and to link the emergence of the proposed long-time ordered state to the equilibration of $f$ anyons to a periodic Gibbs ensemble. For drives inducing Floquet eigenstate thermalization of $f$, our results suggest a scenario where Floquet heating of the $f$ sector stabilizes a genuine non-equilibrium topological phase, in contrast with the usual view of heating as an obstacle to order in periodically driven systems.
one_liner: Floquet-driven anyon proliferation in the toric code can retain long-range entanglement and mixed-state topological order.
why_it_matters: It suggests periodic heating can stabilize, rather than merely destroy, nonequilibrium topological phases.

title: Quantum simulation of neutral-meson mixing and decay on a reprogrammable photonic processor
abstract: Neutral mesons oscillate into their antiparticles while decaying, so their dynamics is generated by a non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonian which a quantum simulator restricted to unitary operations cannot implement directly. We propose a reprogrammable photonic processor that simulates this open-system evolution through dilation and analyze it at the circuit level. The effective Hamiltonian is reconstructed exactly from measured lifetimes, mass and width differences, and the CP-violation parameter $|q/p|$. Through a singular-value decomposition and a single ancilla that encodes the total decay probability, its propagator is embedded in a four-mode unitary, which is compiled at each time step into a rectangular interferometer on a hexagonal mesh of tunable Mach-Zehnder units. Circuit simulations including coupler, propagation, and bend losses show that one fixed device, reprogrammed only through its control voltages, reproduces the flavor oscillation and decay of neutral kaons and of $B_d$ and $B_s$ mesons, with $x=Δm/Γ$ from 0.77 to 26.9. Over 500 time steps per system, the mean fidelity lies between 0.99979 and 0.99982, and no step falls below 0.9996. Because every optical path crosses nine tunable units, uniform insertion loss reduces only the transmitted power, whereas unit-to-unit loss variations lower the fidelity quadratically, $1-\langle F\rangle \simeq 0.08σ^2$ for a loss standard deviation $σ$ in dB. A leading-order analysis traces this coefficient to the routing of light through the mesh, reproduces the fitted value to within 2%, and explains why it is the same for all three mesons; a mean fidelity of 0.999 tolerates $σ\approx 0.11$ dB. The ancillary outputs encode the total decay probability without postselection, and the reported probabilities are normalized to the collected optical power.
one_liner: A reprogrammable four-mode photonic circuit simulates neutral-meson oscillation and decay with mean fidelity above 0.9997.
why_it_matters: It provides a compact optical route to emulating non-Hermitian particle dynamics and CP-sensitive decay.

title: Integral Tensor Isomorphism via Cubic Rings and Lattice Methods
abstract: We prove that isomorphism of integral $2\times3\times3$ tensors under $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ is decidable in bounded-error quantum polynomial time. For a tensor $T=(A,B)$ with nonzero determinant form $\det(xA-yB)$, we use the parametrization of Wood by balanced modules to reduce the isomorphism problem to principality tests for compatible lattices, and use the algorithms of Bley, Hofmann, and Johnston to solve this in BQP. When the determinant form vanishes identically, we get either an integral $2\times2\times2$ core, or a polynomial kernel vector of degree one or two. The linear-kernel case yields another compatible lattice problem, while the quadratic-kernel case reduces to a fixed system of polynomial congruences and unimodular lifting. A quantifier-elimination argument decides these congruences in deterministic polynomial time given the prime factorization of the modulus, which quantum integer factorization supplies. Finally, we show that zero padding preserves integral $2\times2\times2$ tensor isomorphism, yielding a polynomial-time reduction from real-quadratic principality to the identically singular $2\times3\times3$ problem.
one_liner: Integral 2×3×3 tensor isomorphism is shown decidable in bounded-error quantum polynomial time.
why_it_matters: It connects tensor equivalence to cubic rings, lattice principality, congruence solving, and quantum factoring.

title: Local interference algorithms for observables in large random circuits
abstract: In quantum dynamics, it is generally believed that interference effects lead to a sign problem for classical Monte Carlo sampling methods, rendering sampling ineffective. In this paper we show that this is generically not the case for the task of simulating the evolution of observables in random instances of circuit dynamics. Specifically, we consider two examples of observables which give large signals despite the randomness of the dynamics: first order out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in unstructured random circuits without conservation laws and time-ordered charge-charge correlators (TOCs) in particle number-preserving random circuits. We show that these observables can be approximated by classical stochastic processes and that these approximations can be systematically improved with a series expansion that incorporates coherent corrections associated with clusters of gates. We design and implement algorithms that combine Monte Carlo sampling and tensor network methods to approximate the series. We observe numerically that the computational complexity of approximating TOCs and OTOCs scales polynomially in the circuit size and in the target precision. We study the accuracy of these algorithms by directly mapping their ensemble-averaged errors to partition functions of replica statistical models, allowing for perturbative analysis and numerics in $1$d brickwork geometries. Our theoretical analysis explains the empirical observation of polynomial complexity of these algorithms and is consistent with polynomial complexity extending to arbitrarily small precision and to the thermodynamic limit.
one_liner: Hybrid Monte Carlo–tensor-network algorithms efficiently approximate OTOCs and charge correlators in large random circuits.
why_it_matters: The results challenge the view that interference generically makes observable dynamics classically intractable.

title: Modeling quantum information scrambling in realistic protein NMR experiments
abstract: Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are important probes of operator spreading and information scrambling, and have recently been proposed as a means of extracting molecular structural information through nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). Realizing this potential requires accurate modeling of OTOCs in complex molecular environments within experimentally relevant settings. Here, we develop an end-to-end computational pipeline connecting molecular structures to OTOC dynamics in protein systems. Our framework incorporates molecular motion through molecular dynamics simulations, orientational averaging appropriate for powder samples, and spin-network truncation, using an experimentally realizable double-quantum effective Hamiltonian. We apply this framework to a dataset of over 350 carbon-carbon spin pairs across 10 protein systems, spanning interspin distances of 5-17 A. We find that OTOC arrival times scale approximately linearly with interspin distance, revealing system-dependent operator-spreading velocities that enable correlations to propagate over extended distances within milliseconds. Our sensitivity analysis further shows that individual OTOCs predominantly constrain a single structural parameter, primarily associated with interspin distance. Together, these findings highlight the potential of OTOCs to probe spatially extended spin correlations on timescales compatible with solid-state NMR experiments.
one_liner: An end-to-end protein NMR pipeline links molecular structure and motion to experimentally realizable OTOC dynamics.
why_it_matters: OTOC arrival times may reveal long-range molecular distances and spin-propagation velocities within millisecond experiments.

title: From nonlocal correlations to local symmetry breaking: Asymmetry dynamics of crosscap states
abstract: Under unitary dynamics preserving a global symmetry, bipartite entanglement typically grows while an initially broken symmetry is locally restored. Here, we show that this conventional scenario can be reversed when symmetry-breaking coherence is initially encoded in long-range entanglement. We investigate this phenomenon in a family of charge deformed crosscap states, characterized by antipodal entangled pairs with tunable entanglement and symmetry breaking. We first characterize their static properties, finding a Page-like entanglement profile and an entanglement asymmetry that vanishes for subsystems smaller than half the system size, but grows logarithmically for larger subsystems. For symmetric subsystems, we also analyze the symmetry-resolved entanglement and investigate how it evolves as the subsystem is continuously deformed away from a symmetric partition. Following a quench to a free-fermion tight-binding chain, we uncover an unconventional dynamics in which the entanglement entropy decreases whereas the entanglement asymmetry increases, so that initially symmetric subsystems dynamically develop local symmetry breaking. This behavior is quantitatively captured by a quasiparticle picture describing the propagation of antipodal correlations. Our results reveal how symmetry-preserving dynamics can redistribute globally encoded symmetry-breaking coherence, making it locally accessible, and establish the initial entanglement structure as a key ingredient in determining the fate of local symmetries out of equilibrium.
one_liner: Crosscap-state quenches can decrease entanglement entropy while generating local symmetry breaking from nonlocal coherence.
why_it_matters: It shows that initial entanglement structure can reverse conventional symmetry-restoration dynamics.

title: Expressivity of two-dimensional Gaussian fermion tensor network states
abstract: Tensor network states (TNS) provide a family of efficiently compressed approximations to physically relevant many-body quantum states. An important quantity that characterizes the computational resources required by a TNS is its bond dimension. While in one dimension an area law for the Renyi-0 entropy guarantees an exact matrix product state representation with a bond dimension independent of the system size, an analogous statement does not hold for general states in two dimensions (2D). This leaves open the question of how the expressivity of 2D TNS is related to the entanglement properties of the states they represent. In this work, we focus on two families of 2D translation-invariant Gaussian fermionic states: single-band BCS superconductors and half-filled two-band insulators (including semimetals). For each family, we prove that an area law for the Renyi-0 entropy is equivalent to having an exact Gaussian fermionic TNS representation with a finite bond dimension determined by the Renyi-0 entropy. We also establish equivalent characterizations in terms of compactly supported Wannier-type orbitals and the momentum-space wavefunction, relating the spatial extent of these orbitals and the structure of the wavefunction to the required bond dimension.
one_liner: For two classes of 2D Gaussian fermion states, a Rényi-0 area law exactly characterizes finite-bond-dimension tensor networks.
why_it_matters: It connects tensor-network expressivity to entanglement, compact Wannier orbitals, and momentum-space structure.

title: Steerability in top quark decays at the LHC
abstract: Quantum information observables in top quark pair production have opened a new experimental window on non-classical correlations of particle interactions at colliders. Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) steering occupies a distinguished place in the quantum hierarchy, lying between entanglement and Bell nonlocality. We present a detailed collider analysis of steerability for top quark pairs at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). In particular, we utilize both the decay and kinematic methods to estimate the expected sensitivity of the LHC and High Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) to detect steerable states. We find that with the current LHC dataset of $139~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ the steerability of the $t\bar t$ state in the boosted region can be established at $7.7σ$ ($1.8σ$) in the semileptonic (dileptonic) channel with the decay method, corresponding to a measurement of the steerability integral at a precision of $1.5\%$ ($5.2\%$), while the kinematic method reaches a precision of $0.05\%$ in both channels. At the HL-LHC the decay-method precision improves to $0.3\%$ ($1.1\%$). Near threshold, where the inclusive selections used for entanglement and discord yield a state at the steerability boundary, an optimized selection $M_{t\bar{t}}\lesssim360$--$400$~GeV isolates a steerable singlet-dominated state, where the sensitivity is projected to reach $7σ$ ($3.4σ$). We also provide a detailed discussion on the interpretation of these results with respect to fictitious quantum states, and argue for the robust nature of the steerability measurement at colliders.
one_liner: Collider analyses project statistically significant EPR steering measurements in boosted and threshold top-quark pairs at the LHC.
why_it_matters: It extends experimental tests of quantum correlations at colliders beyond entanglement toward the stronger notion of steering.

title: Look Mum, No Hands! Quantum State Preparation without Time-Dependent Control
abstract: How much can be prepared with a quantum system whose Hamiltonian cannot be modulated in time? Common intuition suggests that the answer is not much. Without a knob to turn during the evolution, a system seems confined to a fixed trajectory through its state space, while time-dependent control can steer it almost anywhere. We put this intuition to the test by studying autonomous control, i.e., state preparation with a time-invariant Hamiltonian, where the only freedom lies in the static coupling strengths and the evolution time. We characterize basic mathematical properties of the autonomously reachable set and introduce two criteria of unreachability: a certificate that is cheap to evaluate and rigorously excludes that a target state can be reached for any choice of control parameters, and a stronger criterion based on exhaustive numerical optimization. With these tools we estimate the probability that a typical state in Hilbert space is unreachable under randomly drawn control terms. The dimensionality of the reachable set turns out to be independent of the system, yet the fraction of Hilbert space lying close to it depends strongly on the choice of control Hamiltonians. Strikingly, for sufficiently random controls and long enough evolution times, almost every state can become approximately reachable, even with the fewest generators that permit full controllability with time-dependent couplings. Autonomous control can approach the expressivity of time-dependent control, at the cost of longer evolution times.
one_liner: Static Hamiltonians with sufficiently random controls can approximately prepare almost any state given long enough evolution.
why_it_matters: Autonomous control may approach time-dependent control expressivity while reducing active modulation requirements.

title: Optimal Joint Bounds for Sparse Ground-State Energy Estimation and Ground-State Preparation
abstract: Ground-state energy estimation (GSEE) and ground-state preparation (GSP) are fundamental problems in quantum computing. Given a Hamiltonian $H$ with $\|H\|\le1$ and a guiding state $|ψ\rangle$ with overlap at least $γ>0$ with the ground space of $H$, the goal in GSEE is to estimate the ground-state energy of $H$ to additive error $δ$ with failure probability at most $\varepsilon$, while in GSP it is to prepare a state with ground-space weight at least $1-\varepsilon$, given a gap lower bound $Δ$. Their costs are measured by quantum query complexity, i.e., the number of oracle calls needed to access $H$. Recent work proved optimal bounds $Θ(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γδ))$ for GSEE and $Θ(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γΔ))$ for GSP in the time-evolution and block-encoding models. However, these models do not directly account for the sparsity of $H$, measured by the maximum number $s$ of nonzero entries in any row or column. In the sparse-access model, oracles instead return the locations and values of these entries. This introduces the additional parameter $s$, and it remained open how query complexity depends jointly on $s$, $γ$, $δ$ or $Δ$, and $\varepsilon$. We resolve this by proving sparse-query lower bounds $Ω(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γδ))$ for GSEE and $Ω(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γΔ))$ for GSP, even for stoquastic Hamiltonians. We also show that these constructions recover the earlier time-evolution and block-encoding lower-bound scalings. We then give matching upper-bound algorithms in the reversible in-place sparse-location model. Thus, we obtain $Θ(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γδ))$ for GSEE and $Θ(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γΔ))$ for GSP, showing that $\sqrt{s}$ is necessary and sufficient and completing the joint dependence on all problem parameters.
one_liner: Matching bounds establish a necessary and sufficient square-root dependence on sparsity for ground-state energy and preparation queries.
why_it_matters: The work completes the optimal joint complexity scaling across sparsity, overlap, precision, gap, and failure probability.

title: Symmetry classification of hyperfine rovibrational molecular phase space
abstract: Symmetry-based structures have advanced molecular spectroscopy and quantum information science, yet connections between these fields remain largely unexplored. We construct a phase space theory of a molecule by jointly treating rotational, vibrational, and nuclear-spin degrees of freedom as the quotient of orientations and normal coordinates by the molecule's point group. The various combinations of how these three degrees of freedom transform under symmetries organize a molecule's states into molecular species, and we show that each species is defined by a particular absolutely maximally entangled (AME) carrier state, or, for 45 species, by a two-dimensional space of them. Up to local unitaries and the order of the sectors, molecular species realize 21 AME states across 75 point groups: a product state, four maximally entangled pairs, and 16 genuinely tripartite states. A Fourier transform on the quotient relates orientation and angular-momentum descriptions while preserving these carrier states. We propose an example experimental protocol for preparing and driving symmetry-adapted bend states of $\mathrm{CaOCH_3}$.
one_liner: A symmetry-based molecular phase space classifies rovibrational and nuclear-spin species through entangled carrier states.
why_it_matters: It connects molecular spectroscopy with multipartite entanglement and suggests symmetry-adapted control protocols.

title: Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing for Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout
abstract: We introduce DIRAC, an ADC-less in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that uses analog computing to redraw the analog-digital boundary. Directly operating on the front-end's analog output, passive complex mixers perform the equivalent of digital demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators average their outputs into down-sampled per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes them, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives the mixers' local oscillators from the readout transmitter's baseband rather than per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration flow trains the matched filter jointly with the neural network, improving fidelity and enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, DIRAC matches the fidelity of a floating-point (FP32) digital pipeline for readout windows down to 750 ns, at 31.6$\times$ and 238$\times$ lower energy than the fixed-point (FxP) and FP32 pipelines. It cuts the total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% relative to FxP and room-temperature flex cables, respectively. At a fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, this yields, against FxP, a code distance larger by 2 to 6 and a 1.6-7.3$\times$ (Willow) and 4.9-204$\times$ (SI1000, $p = 10^{-3}$) lower logical error rate.
one_liner: DIRAC performs cryogenic analog demodulation and integration before low-rate digitization, eliminating Nyquist-rate readout ADCs.
why_it_matters: It preserves qubit-readout fidelity while sharply reducing 4 K energy and power, improving fault-tolerant scaling.

title: Quantum Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport in spacetime through spatiotemporal Kirkwood-Dirac distributions and spatiotemporal states
abstract: Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport is a mathematical framework that determines the most efficient way to transform one probability distribution into another while minimizing a given cost function. Its central constructions include the Wasserstein distances, which quantify the space of probability distributions, and dual formulations that link to convex analysis. Its standard quantum generalization replaces probability distributions with density operators and cost function with positive semidefinite cost operator, which should be regarded as spatial quantum optimal transport. In this work, we propose the quantum optimal transport problem in spacetime through the spatiotemporal phase-space Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distribution and spatiotemporal states and through spatiotemporal state. We show that the two formalisms are equivalent and related via spatiotemporal operator frames. In the Kirkwood-Dirac phase-space formalism, the spatiotemporal distribution and the cost function are complex-valued, and the spatiotemporal couplings are Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distributions that yield the correct marginals for the local states. In the spatiotemporal state formalism, the cost operators are generally non-Hermitian, and the spatiotemporal couplings are generally non-Hermitian and yield the correct reduced local states. The Margenau-Hill phase-space distribution gives rise to a real-valued optimal transport in spatiotemporal phase space; in the spatiotemporal state formalism, this corresponds to a Hermitian spatiotemporal coupling state. We give a rigorous definitions and a careful discussion of its duality. We also introduce a spatiotemporal quantum Wasserstein metric based on a metric in spatiotemporal phase spaces and show that it satisfies the metric axioms.
one_liner: Quantum optimal transport is extended across spacetime using equivalent quasiprobability and spatiotemporal-state formulations.
why_it_matters: The framework supplies duality and a spatiotemporal quantum Wasserstein metric satisfying the metric axioms.

title: Sub-Doppler Cooling of Potassium-41 in a Hybrid Quadrupole-Octupole Symmetry Magneto-Optical Trap
abstract: Sub-Doppler cooling processes rely on the near-degeneracy of the Zeeman sub-levels of the atom. Effective sub-Doppler cooling is only achieved when the ac-Stark shift of the molasses light is significantly larger than the Zeeman shift. This condition is typically achieved by switching off all magnetic gradients, and using Helmholtz coils to cancel Earth's magnetic field. Another way to achieve a nearly zero magnetic field gradient is to superimpose a second pair of oppositely oriented quadrupole coils with a different spatial geometry. At the ideal current ratio, this creates an octupole-symmetry magnetic field for the atoms. The resulting octupole magnetic field has a gradient increasing quadratically from zero at the center. In this work, the effectiveness of sub-Doppler cooling and trapping using D2 and D1 light is evaluated in such a hybrid trap for $^{41}$K. The temperature, lifetime, and phase-space density of the atoms are measured. For both D2 and D1 light, the octupole MOT is found to have a longer lifetime, while maintaining a similar temperature to the zero-field case. D1 gray-molasses temperatures down to $3.8(1)~μ$K and phase-space density up to $5.3(4)\times10^{-5}$ are measured for $14.3(1)\times10^6$ $^{41}$ atoms. The effectiveness of the hybrid quadrupole-octupole trap suggests the possibility of increasing the loading time for atoms into an optical dipole trap with active sub-Doppler cooling.
one_liner: A hybrid quadrupole–octupole trap enables long-lived potassium-41 samples with D1 gray-molasses cooling to 3.8 μK.
why_it_matters: The geometry may extend optical-dipole-trap loading while maintaining active sub-Doppler cooling.

title: QCCDCert: Formally Verified Compilation for QCCD Co-Design
abstract: Quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architectures enable scalable trapped-ion quantum computing by dynamically shuttling ions between specialized processing and storage zones. A QCCD can be built with many trap sizes and layouts. Comparing them requires compiling every program under each design's transport, capacity and control constraints, and trusting the target code of each compilation. We present a co-design framework built on one Lean-verified compiler. The hardware description and its operating rules are compiler inputs, so a single theorem covers every candidate design: the target code of every compilation preserves its program's behavior and obeys the hardware rules. Across 75 benchmark programs of 11 to 130 qubits, the best design found takes 66% less modeled execution time on average than the worst design of equal capacity. An AI agent that proposes devices based on our compiler's checked results beats the fastest of these designs on 71 of 75 programs. Our verified compiler provably avoids the 11 defects that we report in three previous compilers. It scales to hundreds of qubits, compiling 512-qubit programs for a 38-trap device in 1 to 29 minutes.
one_liner: QCCDCert uses one Lean-verified compiler to evaluate QCCD trap designs while proving program correctness and hardware compliance.
why_it_matters: Verified compilation enables trustworthy trapped-ion co-design and exposes defects in prior compilers.

title: Degree and normalization frontiers for bounded QSVT inversion
abstract: Quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) implements matrix inversion using bounded polynomials. Increasing polynomial degree can improve normalization and reduce amplified query cost, with savings that depend on the error criterion. However, existing bounded methods either fix the normalization or work far below the condition numbers of fault-tolerant resource estimates. We therefore analyze this trade-off for absolute reciprocal error, which controls inverse-operator accuracy, and for residual error, which suffices for normalized linear solves. For absolute reciprocal error, we establish a scaling limit to a constrained least-norm problem for entire functions and characterize its high-accuracy frontier using elliptic integrals. Constructions built from near-optimal limiting functions achieve certified query-cost savings over the rescaled minimax baseline of at least 11.8 percent at condition number ten thousand with error one millionth, and at least 22.8 percent at one million with error one ten-billionth. A simpler two-term rule also has certified savings, and its phase factors at condition number ten thousand pass numerical checks at selected points. For residual error, a sparse Chebyshev construction achieves certified savings over the residual-minimax baseline of at least 8.7 percent at condition number ten thousand with normalized-state error at most one hundred-millionth, and at least 13.1 percent at one million with error at most one ten-billionth. These results quantify the saving that a joint choice of degree and normalization gives beyond the minimax baselines.
one_liner: QSVT matrix inversion gains lower query cost by jointly optimizing polynomial degree and normalization under two error criteria.
why_it_matters: It quantifies certified savings over minimax baselines at condition numbers relevant to fault-tolerant resource estimates.

title: Quantum resources and the onset of the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem
abstract: The Monte Carlo sign problem poses a fundamental obstacle to classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, yet its connection to quantum resources remains poorly understood. We probe this connection by systematically tuning the degree of nonstoquasticity in random k-local Hamiltonians. In numerical tensor-network studies, we find the sign complexity and the quantum resources of entanglement and nonstabilizerness of the ground state to be strongly suppressed in a broad regime up to substantial nonstoquasticity. As nonstoquasticity is further increased, the considered quantum resources experience sharp crossovers into a regime where they are strongly enhanced. Surprisingly, numerical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations drastically deteriorate in the same region, even though the Hamiltonian is already considerably nonstoquastic well before it, indicating that the failure of ground-state QMC is correlated more with the resource content of the state than the sign structure of the Hamiltonian. We corroborate these findings analytically by constructing an approximate ground state of k-local Hamiltonians in the stoquastic limit. Moreover, we identify a distinct behaviour in graph states. Their nonstabilizerness always vanishes, but, as we demonstrate analytically, on bipartite graphs the sign can be easily cured while in multipartite graph states it cannot. Our results thus shed light on the highly subtle interplay between quantum resources and the computational difficulty encountered by QMC methods.
one_liner: QMC failure in random nonstoquastic Hamiltonians tracks sharp growth in ground-state quantum resources more than sign structure alone.
why_it_matters: It links simulation difficulty to entanglement and nonstabilizerness, refining how the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem is understood.

title: Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite Qubit System
abstract: Quantum Computing uses quantum mechanical phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement of quantum bits (qubits), to represent and manipulate information in multidimensional state spaces. This approach allows complex mathematical functions to be executed simultaneously rather than sequentially, making them much more efficient than classical computers. However, current quantum computers suffer from quantum decoherence, where small changes to their environment, such as thermal fluctuations and vibrations, affect the systems' fragile states. The goal of this study is to discuss the functionality of a proposed Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite qubit system by solving the unitary time-evolution of a quantum state vector for the system's Hamiltonian, using known axial and traverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K. The system can effectively transfer population between its two lowest states at rates predicted by the Rabi half-period, with 99.9% fidelity. Additionally, it can hold the population at a desired state without docohering. The results remained consistent for temperatures up to 10 K, meaning, unlike many common qubit systems, the proposed qubit system could function without a dilution fridge and is not fragile to thermal noise.
one_liner: Simulations propose Fe2+-doped forsterite as a qubit supporting 99.9% population-transfer fidelity and stable operation up to 10 K.
why_it_matters: The proposed system could reduce cryogenic requirements if its simulated thermal robustness is confirmed experimentally.

title: Spectral Disks for Quantum Markov Generators
abstract: Spectral bounds for Markov generators require a choice of time scale. In quantum dynamics, a rate read off from a jump representation, the escape rate from a pure state and the smallest spectral disk need not agree. We prove that the spectrum of every GKLS generator written without a Hamiltonian lies in a disk tangent to the imaginary axis, with radius given by the norm of the operator $Φ^\dagger(I)$ built from the jump map $Φ$. This settles the first two scaling conjectures of "Corralling spectra of generators of time-continuous Markov evolution (both classical and quantum)", J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. {59}, 175202 (2026). The third, escape-rate conjecture fails for a qutrit with a single normal jump. Nevertheless, twice the escape rate bounds every decay rate of any positive trace-preserving semigroup For GKLS generators with vanishing canonical Hamiltonian, four times the escape rate always supplies a spectral disk, and the factor four is optimal uniformly in dimension. We compare these bounds with classical Cassini ovals and thermodynamic ellipses, explain the obstacles to their quantum extensions, and formulate optimization over completely positive jump-map representations as a semidefinite program.
one_liner: New spectral-disk bounds relate decay rates of quantum Markov generators to jump-map norms and state escape rates.
why_it_matters: The work resolves two scaling conjectures, disproves a third, and gives an optimal dimension-uniform escape-rate factor.

title: Instrument indeterminacy: separating uncertainty in POVM effects and its neutrosophic reading
abstract: Neutrosophic annotation frameworks for quantum measurement attach an external triple $(t,i,f)$ to each Born probability, and explicitly leave open how indeterminacy could be defined operationally. We show that indeterminacy cannot be recovered from outcome probabilities, but can be computed from the pair (state, effect). For a binary POVM $\{A, I-A\}$ we define the instrument indeterminacy $\mathcal{I}_ρ(A) = 4 \mathrm{Tr}(ρ(A-A^2))$, which vanishes exactly when the state only sees the sharp part of the effect. The normalized Gini index of the outcome splits as $4TF = \mathcal{I}_ρ(A) + 4 \mathrm{Var}_ρ(A)$, a law of total variance that separates the instrument contribution from the state contribution; the identity is a special case of Massar's POVM uncertainty operator, and our contribution is its neutrosophic reading. Moving the system-apparatus cut to a Naimark dilation transfers exactly $\mathcal{I}_ρ(A)$ from indeterminacy to variance, which yields the missing operational definition. We extend the decomposition to $m$-outcome POVMs, relate the minimum indeterminacy of two incompatible unbiased qubit observables to their commutator through Busch's joint-measurability criterion, and show that $\mathcal{I}_ρ(A)$ equals twice the disagreement probability of a repeated Lüders measurement. The resulting estimator needs neither the state nor the effect and, in simulation, requires 2.5 to 6 times fewer shots than detector tomography for the same error.
one_liner: A state-effect measure separates intrinsic POVM unsharpness from state variance and admits an efficient repeated-measurement estimator.
why_it_matters: It gives operational meaning to measurement indeterminacy while reducing shot requirements relative to detector tomography.

title: Perspectives on the hidden subgroup problem over unitriangular groups
abstract: We investigate the quantum Hidden Subgroup Problem (HSP) over the upper unitriangular group $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$. While efficient quantum algorithms were discovered for some families of non abelian groups and nil-2 $p$-groups, no efficient algorithms are known for groups of nilpotency class higher than 2. The only techniques known for such groups scale exponentially in the size of the input. We first study the group $U_4(\mathbb{F}_p)$, the smallest upper unitriangular group exhibiting nilpotency class three. We analyze the application of the Pretty Good Measurement approach used for Heisenberg groups and show its limits. We then focus on the more general case $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$ to adapt existing techniques to this particular structure. In particular, we derive an algorithm for cyclic subgroups as a subroutine for a general algorithm, although it is not efficient in the size of the group. Our results highlight the difficulties introduced by the increasing nilpotency class and suggests some directions for an efficient quantum algorithm for the HSP over $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$.
one_liner: The study maps obstacles to solving the hidden subgroup problem over unitriangular groups and derives an inefficient cyclic-subgroup routine.
why_it_matters: It clarifies why methods successful for class-two groups struggle when nilpotency class increases beyond two.

title: Retinal arterial velocity-proxy waveforms from differential spectral broadening in laser Doppler holography
abstract: Laser Doppler holography (LDH) records pulsatile spectral broadening in retinal arteries. We compare vessel and local-background measurements to extract a signed differential-broadening waveform, $Δσ$. A minimal Gaussian convolution model motivates quadratic subtraction, and Doppler scaling relates the added width to a characteristic blood velocity. Real arteries show pulsatile waveforms, whereas identically processed imaginary arteries show only low-amplitude fluctuations around zero. We interpret the empirically scaled signal as a velocity proxy for waveform shape and within-vessel changes during a single acquisition under stable conditions.
one_liner: Differential spectral broadening in laser Doppler holography yields signed retinal arterial waveforms that serve as velocity proxies.
why_it_matters: The method isolates pulsatile vessel dynamics from local background without claiming absolute blood-flow velocity.

title: Uniformly Convergent Perturbation Theory for Open Quantum Systems at, near, and away from Exceptional Points
abstract: Near a Liouvillian exceptional point, spectral perturbation theory becomes ill-conditioned, yet the observable dynamics of a finite-dimensional open system remains regular in the perturbation. Using a Dyson expansion, which requires no diagonalization of the perturbed generator, we analyze the scaling, stability, and convergence of the perturbative corrections at, near and away from exceptional points. We derive scaling laws showing that nonperipheral Jordan blocks raise the degree of the polynomial-in-time factors multiplying decaying exponentials, which are present for any generator as resonances, and we quantify this excess. We further establish a uniform-in-time error estimate for the perturbative series, valid for any relaxing finite-dimensional Lindbladian and controlled by a parameter $q = |\varepsilon|R$, where $\varepsilon$ is the perturbation strength and $R$ is a constant built from unperturbed data. All constants of the bound remain continuous through an exceptional point when the coalescing eigenvalues are kept in one spectral cluster. The estimate extends to the frequency domain via the Laplace transform, and to time-dependent perturbations. We test it in a driven two-level system with a Liouvillian exceptional point, including perturbations that break its symmetry.
one_liner: A Dyson-based perturbation theory gives uniform-in-time error bounds for relaxing Lindbladians across exceptional points.
why_it_matters: It preserves stable dynamical predictions where eigenvalue-based perturbation methods become ill-conditioned.

title: Optical Neural Networks Should Be Evaluated by Function, Not Only Physics
abstract: Optical neural networks (ONNs) are attracting significant attention as alternative platforms for machine learning (ML). In an ONN, an optical module often takes over part of the computation inside a digital ML pipeline. How much of the task does the optical module itself perform, and how much does it contribute to any claimed system-level advantages, such as throughput or energy? This paper offers a simple, function-oriented evaluation methodology. Whatever its internal physics, the optical module appears to the surrounding digital pipeline as a mapping between real-valued tensors. We therefore evaluate it in three steps: (i) define its boundary in the pipeline, as real-valued tensors in and out; (ii) replace it with standard digital modules to identify those that match the optical system's performance on the same task and metric; and (iii) state system-level claims, such as speed or energy, per inference against the performance-matched digital module. We summarize steps (i) and (ii) in an Expressivity Card and demonstrate its use on published ONN systems. This helps isolate the optical module's contribution and provides a concrete digital reference for assessing its claimed system-level advantages, without the need to understand the physics. While we focus on optical systems as the most prominent example, the same approach applies to any physical analog computing platform used in ML, wherever a physical module takes over part of a digital pipeline.
one_liner: A function-oriented framework benchmarks optical neural modules against performance-matched digital replacements at identical pipeline boundaries.
why_it_matters: It provides a fairer basis for attributing task performance, speed, and energy advantages to physical analog computing modules.

title: Extreme value statistics for majorisation partial orders
abstract: We study extreme-value phenomena for random samples in partially ordered sets through their meets and joins, the order-theoretic analogues of minima and maxima. In this paper we consider the probability simplex equipped with either UT-majorisation or majorisation, with samples drawn uniformly from the corresponding simplex. We analyse these extrema both at fixed dimension and as the dimension grows, identifying almost-sure collapse to the bottom or top elements and critical scalings with nondegenerate limiting laws.
one_liner: Extreme-value laws are derived for random samples under UT-majorisation and majorisation using order-theoretic meets and joins.
why_it_matters: The results identify collapse regimes and critical scalings with nondegenerate limits on high-dimensional probability simplices.

title: Parisi Energy before Parisi Geometry in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
abstract: The fractured low-energy landscape of spin glasses presents a notorious barrier to optimization. While high-depth calculations indicate that the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can approach the Parisi ground-state energy of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, how it does so remains elusive. Here, we treat the QAOA distribution as a statistical-physics object and probe its geometry directly in the thermodynamic limit. We draw two independent bitstrings from the same problem instance and couple them through their macroscopic similarity. We find that typical QAOA samples remain macroscopically uncorrelated, even as their sensitivity to this coupling grows with circuit depth $p$. By contrast, the low-energy tail shows a much stronger tendency to overlap and reveals a Parisi-like phase with the same critical behavior as the thermal spin-glass transition. The onset of this organization moves toward the typical output as the circuit deepens, consistent with the separation vanishing only as $p\to\infty$. Together, these findings suggest a route distinct from structure-exploiting classical algorithms and thermal sampling, one in which the QAOA approaches the Parisi energy before Parisi geometry becomes typical.
one_liner: QAOA reaches low spin-glass energies before Parisi-like overlap geometry becomes typical across its output distribution.
why_it_matters: It suggests QAOA approaches the Parisi energy through a mechanism distinct from thermal sampling and structure-aware classical methods.

title: Renormalization and exact Bloch bands: the trigonometric Rosen-Morse model
abstract: We study the trigonometric Rosen-Morse potential as an isolated singular well and as an exactly solvable periodic lattice. The potential combines inverse-square singularities with Coulomb terms of opposite signs. In the strongly attractive regime, independent renormalization at the two endpoints gives a two-parameter family of spectra. Deep negative-energy levels form two asymptotic sequences with the same Efimov-like scaling and opposite first-order Coulomb corrections. In the weak-medium regime, self-adjoint matching conditions allow transmission between neighboring cells. We obtain the exact Bloch dispersion relation and determine the band widths, gaps, and electron and hole effective masses. At fixed band index, the bandwidth becomes exponentially small in the limit of large Coulomb coupling.
one_liner: The trigonometric Rosen-Morse model yields renormalized singular-well spectra and an exact Bloch dispersion for its periodic lattice.
why_it_matters: Its analytic bands, gaps, effective masses, and Efimov-like scaling offer a solvable testbed for singular quantum lattices.

title: Separating QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy via a Switching Lemma for Polynomials
abstract: We construct a classical oracle relative to which QMA is not contained in the QCMA hierarchy. Our main technical contribution is a switching lemma for bounded polynomials, which provides a new conceptual viewpoint on earlier sampler-based arguments separating QMA and QCMA. Crucially, the parameters of this switching lemma are independent of the number of input variables. The separation builds on the code intersection subset size problem of Bostanci, Huang, and Vaikuntanathan (FOCS 2026). We also construct a classical oracle relative to which QCMA collapses to P but QMA does not, and another relative to which QMA collapses to P but PP does not.
one_liner: A variable-count-independent switching lemma for bounded polynomials yields classical-oracle separations between QMA and the QCMA hierarchy.
why_it_matters: It introduces a new complexity-theoretic tool and clarifies the power gap between quantum and classical witnesses.

title: Chirp-stabilized charging of a two-level quantum battery
abstract: Resonantly driven two-level quantum batteries (QBs) suffer from strong pulse-area dependence and energy backflow inherent to Rabi oscillations. To address this limitation, we propose charging of a two-level QB with chirped pulses. We investigate four charging protocols formed by pairing hyperbolic secant (sech) or Gaussian pulse envelopes with linear or hyperbolic-tangent (tanh) frequency sweeps. We show that sufficiently strong chirp modulation converts the charging mechanism from pulse-area-governed Rabi rotation to adiabatic rapid passage. We analyze the underlying adiabatic dynamics and derive the criteria for robust chirped charging, which incorporate the sweep bandwidth, nonadiabatic transitions, and dissipative effects. Under strong chirp modulation, the final stored energy and ergotropy converge to stable plateaus that are nearly insensitive to the pulse area across an extended parameter window. Of the four schemes, the sech pulse with tanh chirp delivers the widest ergotropy plateau and the weakest pulse area sensitivity. Compared with counterdiabatic driving, the sech tanh protocol attains stable charging performance without demanding an extra drive quadrature. Furthermore, this chirp-enabled charging is resilient to static detuning and weak-to-moderate dissipation. This work establishes a practical route toward robust charging of quantum batteries using chirped pulse control.
one_liner: Chirped pulses drive a two-level quantum battery into robust adiabatic charging with weak pulse-area sensitivity.
why_it_matters: The sech–tanh protocol offers stable energy and ergotropy without the extra control quadrature required by counterdiabatic driving.

title: Hierarchical coupling in tripartite van der Waals cavity magnonics for a low-loss and tunable coupled-mode Hamiltonian
abstract: One of the greatest merits of cavity magnonics (CM) is the ability to explore rich coupled-mode physics, driven by the large \textit{in situ} flux tunability of magnonic resonances and magnon--photon coupling. Meanwhile, van der Waals (vdW) magnets offer an ultra-compact and highly integrated implementation of CM without complex fabrication processes. Nonetheless, the substantial magnon losses significantly hinder the combination of all these advantages. Here, we realize a hierarchical anti-crossing structure in a tripartite vdW CM with CrCl3 and realize an effective coupled-dual-mode Hamiltonian. We achieve an order-of-magnitude reduction in loss while maintaining a strong coupling condition. Additionally, we theoretically confirm the feasibility of simultaneous and \textit{in situ} tuning of both loss and coupling by varying the magnetic field direction and strength. Featuring a micrometer-scale thickness and a width of a few millimeters, our device is significantly smaller than those based on bulk crystals or crystal arrays. Our results establish vdW cavity magnonics as versatile platform for investigating intriguing phenomena predicted in coupled-mode systems.
one_liner: A tripartite CrCl3 cavity-magnonic device realizes hierarchical anticrossings and a tunable dual-mode Hamiltonian with much lower loss.
why_it_matters: It combines strong coupling, reduced loss, in situ tunability, and compact dimensions in a van der Waals platform.

title: Parity Push Post-Selection with Soft Parity Constraints for Quantum LDPC Codes
abstract: Post-selection lowers the logical error rate of a quantum error-correcting code by rejecting unreliable shots. For a code with $K$ logical observables, the logical gap, a standard post-selection criterion, involves $2^K$ logical classes, and existing approximations to it suffer from a non-convergence error floor or a shielding effect. We introduce a decoder-agnostic post-selection strategy for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, called parity push post-selection (PPPS), which re-decodes a shot once per logical observable with a push toward the opposite parity. Each push adds one check node and one variable node to the Tanner graph of the detector error model, and we accept a shot only when every re-decoding returns a solution in the original logical class. We show that, with degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding, PPPS accepts a shot exactly when the logical gap exceeds the push strength $λ$. Applied with the Relay-BP decoder to the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code at $p=10^{-3}$ and the [[144,12,12]] code at $p=3\times10^{-3}$ under circuit-level depolarizing noise, PPPS lowers the logical error rate by factors of about 50 and 75, respectively, at rejection rates near 1%. We observe that PPPS rejects failures that prior post-selection strategies cannot reject, and thus shows improved performance.
one_liner: Parity push post-selection re-decodes each logical observable to reject unreliable qLDPC shots without depending on a specific decoder.
why_it_matters: It cuts logical error rates by about 50–75 times at roughly 1% rejection in tested bivariate bicycle codes.

title: Subsystem evolution in the history state formalism
abstract: We present a relational framework for characterizing the evolution of quantum composite systems, based on the correlations within a history state describing the whole evolution relative to a quantum reference clock. While total system-clock entanglement entropy consistently measures the unitary evolution of the closed global system, a different picture emerges for the reduced state of an open subsystem, whose evolution is generally non-unitary due to environmental coupling. We introduce a general formalism that quantifies open-subsystem dynamics using a subsystem-clock mutual information derived from the history state. We demonstrate that this quantity serves as a consistent quantifier of subsystem evolution with respect to a given clock basis, can be applied to arbitrary dynamics, and reduces to system-time entanglement entropy in the global limit. Furthermore, maximizing this measure over all clock bases yields a basis-independent bound on the maximum evolution achievable relative to the clock, directly linked to the difference between the subsystem's entanglement with the rest of the history state and its entanglement with the environment. Finally, we derive analytical expressions for qubit clocks, illustrate our results using spin 1/2 and spin 1 quantum walks, and present a full matrix formalism of Kraus operators for describing the most general subsystem evolution.
one_liner: Subsystem-clock mutual information is proposed as a history-state measure of open-subsystem evolution relative to a quantum clock.
why_it_matters: It extends relational time methods beyond closed unitary systems and provides both clock-dependent and optimized bounds.

title: QWeaver: Quantum Circuit Cut Workflow with MLIR-based Compiler, Runtime, and Weaver Hybrid Tasks
abstract: Quantum computers available today are constrained by limited qubit counts and high noise levels, making the direct execution of large quantum circuits infeasible on a single device, and while quantum circuit cutting addresses this by partitioning a large circuit into smaller subcircuits for independent execution, orchestrating the full end-to-end workflow remains a significant programming challenge. In this paper, we present QWeaver, a task-graph-based programming and orchestration workflow framework for quantum circuit cutting that accepts OpenQASM quantum circuits as input and constructs a directed acyclic task graph. In this graph, the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR)-based circuit cut is the first task, responsible for analyzing and partitioning the input circuit into executable fragment representations; the generated fragments are then handed to a set of quantum circuit execution tasks that depend on the cut task and can be dispatched concurrently across available quantum backends via the Quantum Intelligent Runtime System (Q-IRIS). Finally, a weaving task, dependent on all execution tasks, performs classical post-processing that applies quasi-probability reconstruction techniques to combine the sampled measurement outcomes of all fragments and recover an accurate approximation of the original circuit's output distribution. We describe the architecture of QWeaver, its integration with Q-IRIS and the execution engine for the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR-EE), validate end-to-end reconstruction on GHZ and Harris-Ross instances, and evaluate systems and width trade-offs on structured GHZ simulator workloads.
one_liner: QWeaver compiles, executes, and reconstructs circuit-cut workloads through an MLIR-based task graph spanning multiple quantum backends.
why_it_matters: It turns circuit cutting into an automated end-to-end workflow and exposes practical reconstruction and scaling trade-offs.

title: Spectral Engineering of Charge Localization and Work Reliability in Collective Quantum Batteries
abstract: The performance of a quantum battery depends not only on how much energy it stores, but also on how rapidly useful charge can be restored after work extraction. We show how engineering the reservoir spectrum connects these properties in an interacting collective-spin battery. Interactions separate the Dicke transition frequencies, allowing frequency-selective pumping and loss to control where excitation accumulates and how populations move along the ladder. Analytical results relate the pump-to-loss ratio to charge localization, fluctuations, and extractable work. Two reservoirs producing the same mean charge can nevertheless exhibit markedly different localization and charging times. Under repeated extraction, finite-time recharging also generates correlations between successive work outputs. At matched mean work, these correlations can reverse the ordering of single-cycle and long-time fluctuations: a protocol with larger fluctuations in individual strokes can deliver more reliable accumulated work. An exact counting relation connects these statistics to net charging-energy transfer, while relaxation modes distinguish recovery of the stationary state from recovery of useful work. Finally, local dephasing redistributes population among collective-spin sectors, leading to an exact stationary symmetry-dilution law and a finite operating window for work extraction under a collective transverse controller.
one_liner: Reservoir spectral engineering controls charge localization, recharge speed, and multi-cycle work reliability in a collective-spin battery.
why_it_matters: It shows that equal mean charge or work can conceal major differences in fluctuations, correlations, and recovery dynamics.

title: Critical--localized reentry under periodic spacer control
abstract: Tracking a fixed fraction of a quasiperiodic spectrum tests whether repeated critical--localized alternation extends over a nonzero spectral weight. We find such alternation in a matched-dimer chain by varying only the spacer on-site energies and following a fixed interval of integrated-density-of-states (IDS) labels. An exact Bloch-determinant identity links the physical transfer discriminant to the bands of a periodic reference operator. For the golden cell frequency, we prove that, on a common full-measure set of phases and for every finite value of the spacer control, the physical spectrum in the open reference bands is critical, with purely singular-continuous spectrum and zero Lyapunov exponent, while the spectrum strictly outside the bands is pure point, with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions. Validated IDS bounds certify repeated critical--localized alternation of the same fixed spectral fraction at successive spacer controls. Spacer shifts move the physical levels and reference-band edges at different rates, allowing us to reshape finite-chain return windows and place their endpoints at prescribed controls. An affine recalibration relocates the control family exactly.
one_liner: Periodic spacer control produces rigorously certified reentry between critical and localized spectral regimes in a matched-dimer chain.
why_it_matters: It proves repeated phase alternation for a fixed nonzero spectral fraction and enables controlled placement of return windows.

title: Stationary Quantum Time Series: Spectral Theory of Process Memory and Measurement Records
abstract: Classical time series analysis converts temporal dependence into structure that can be learned from a single observed trajectory, through stationarity, ergodicity, spectral representation, and finite-memory models. Quantum experiments are naturally time series: every run is a sequence of interventions and outcomes, and the memory of an open system is written in its temporal statistics. However, the classical foundation cannot be translated directly: measuring a process and forgetting the outcome differs from not measuring at all, so no single family of joint probability distributions describes a quantum process. We develop a process-tensor framework for stationary quantum time series and establish its first structural theorems. For stationary combs of finite quantum Markov order l relative to a fixed informationally complete causal break, we construct a finite-dimensional causal transfer map of dimension at most d^{4l}, where d bounds the system Hilbert-space dimension at each step. ... These results supply the stationary foundation on which quantum spectral analysis, model identification, and single-trajectory inference can be built.
one_liner: A process-tensor framework establishes spectral and finite-memory foundations for stationary quantum time series and measurement records.
why_it_matters: It supports quantum spectral analysis, process identification, and inference from temporally correlated experimental trajectories.

title: Covering the Pauli Observables: Sampling Thresholds and the Design Effect of a Measurement Setting
abstract: Quantum state tomography and shadow-based estimation rely on measuring Pauli observables. An experiment does not measure them one at a time: it chooses a measurement setting that assigns one of the bases X, Y or Z to each qubit, and a single run in that setting yields estimates of every Pauli observable compatible with it. We say that the setting covers those observables. We determine how many random settings cover a prescribed fraction of all Pauli observables. As the number of settings grows exponentially with the number of qubits, the covered fraction has a sharp threshold at a growth rate of $3^{3/4}$ per qubit, set by the rate-distortion function of covering at zero distortion. We give an explicit expression for the number of settings needed to reach a target fraction, accurate up to a remainder that reduces to a small oscillation for many qubits, and show that random sampling is asymptotically optimal up to a factor of less than 1.69. Coverage does not determine what a setting contributes to an estimator. Observables covered by one setting are estimated from the same outcomes, so their estimates are correlated. We quantify this correlation through the design effect of a setting, which equals the squared Pauli expectation that the setting captures and depends on the target state. We derive its mean over settings in closed form for every state and show that it can be estimated without bias from the measurement data. In simulations on six qubits, measuring settings needs 7.6 to 38 times fewer circuit runs than measuring the same number of observables independently. At high coverage, fitting the outcome histograms instead of averaged estimates roughly halves the reconstruction error, mainly because the fit counts how many settings cover each observable. The correlation itself costs such a fit about a factor of two, and a larger design effect signals more to gain from modeling it.
one_liner: The work derives Pauli-setting coverage thresholds and a state-dependent design effect quantifying correlations among shared-outcome estimates.
why_it_matters: It guides efficient tomography and shows large circuit-run savings from measuring compatible observables together.

title: Aharonov-Bohm blockade of complete reversal in coupled Rabi cavities
abstract: When a common bias reverses two bistable fields, the system can pass through either of two single-reversal configurations on its way to the favored state. We show that interference between these two orders of reversal can block the final step. In a dimer of coupled quantum Rabi cavities, the four field configurations form a loop, and a complex photon-hopping amplitude threads it with an Aharonov-Bohm flux. Near half a flux quantum, the two paths to complete reversal interfere destructively: in microscopic simulations, a slow uniform sweep reverses one field with probability 0.998, although the final bias favors reversing both. A four-state model calibrated at zero bias predicts how the window of this Aharonov-Bohm blockade narrows with sweep time. The blocked state remains coherent. A differential pulse followed by a return sweep converts the relative phase of the two single-reversal configurations into a fringe in the joint field signs, with contrast 0.95. In a trimer, a phase gradient imprinted between sweeps determines whether the next sweep adds or removes a reversed field: reversing the second of two gradients changes the most probable outcome from three reversed fields to one.
one_liner: Synthetic Aharonov–Bohm flux makes two reversal paths interfere destructively, blocking complete field reversal in coupled Rabi cavities.
why_it_matters: It enables coherent control of bistable-field reversal through hopping phases, sweep timing, and phase gradients.

title: In Situ Training of Optical Neural Networks by Coding Agents
abstract: Optical neural networks promise fast, energy-efficient computing, but every device departs from its design and must be trained with the hardware. In situ training relies on an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or on gradient-free trial and error. Coding agents, large language models that write and run programs, have shown an emergent ability to understand and edit the weights of digital neural networks. Here we introduce optics as code, a method in which a coding agent trains an optical neural network from measurements alone, through a harness that returns camera images of its probes and requires a hypothesis per request. We discovered that the agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network with interpretable optical elements tuned on the hardware. It outperforms gradient-free methods in classification and image encoding, approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost. Needing neither per-device calibration nor gradients through the hardware, and improving with more capable models, optics as code offers a practical route to large, scalable optical neural networks and a general tool for calibrating and optimizing optical experiments.
one_liner: A coding agent trains optical neural networks directly from camera measurements by discovering interpretable hardware-level parametrizations.
why_it_matters: It reduces reliance on calibrated device models and costly gradient-free searches for scalable optical computing hardware.

title: Imaging chiral snake states in a qubit array with programmable gauge fields
