The gap-detecting measurement is gentle, so when the ground state is unique a single reusable copy of each reference ground state supports the full exploration (for degenerate ground states, polynomially many copies suffice). The quantum algorithm runs in polynomial time at inverse-polynomial gap resolution. We also give a classical algorithm that runs in quasipolynomial time at constant gap resolution. Numerical experiments demonstrate how our algorithm accurately determines the phase structure of several model quantum systems.
one_liner: An efficient quantum algorithm maps local-Hamiltonian phase diagrams and certifies detected transitions without prior order parameters or training data.
why_it_matters: It makes automated discovery of quantum phases verifiable under physically motivated assumptions.

title: Agentic MLIR-to-QIR Translation with Dual-Backend Testing: A Hybrid Deterministic and LLM Approach
abstract: Quantum frameworks each define their own Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect, so porting a circuit to a Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR) runtime needs a hand-written pass per dialect. Our translator selects among three paths: a deterministic compiler path for known grammars (Catalyst and Quake), a large language model (LLM) agentic path for unseen dialects, and a repair path invoked when deterministic output fails testing. A dual-backend pipeline executes the source MLIR and generated QIR on independent simulators, comparing output distributions by total variation distance (TVD). For smaller open-weight models we replace retrieval-augmented generation with inline context engineering and add a guardrail-assembler that rebuilds valid QIR from incomplete output. Across 41 circuits spanning three dialects and 1-100 qubits, the deterministic path is gate-exact on all 70 circuit-dialect pairs, averaging above 95% TVD similarity (1-TVD). On an unseen fault-tolerant (FTQC) dialect, four of six models produce valid logical-level QIR on the first iteration.
one_liner: A hybrid translator converts known and unseen quantum MLIR dialects to QIR using deterministic passes, LLM agents, repair, and dual-backend tests.
why_it_matters: It could reduce the manual compiler work needed to move quantum programs across frameworks and runtimes.

title: Generalizing and Combining Check Constructions: Design-Space Exploration for Fault-Tolerant Quantum State Preparation
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs logical states prepared such that single faults cannot spread into uncorrectable errors. Post-selection achieves this with added checks that detect dangerous faults and discard the run. How the checks are measured sets the depth and operation count of the circuit, and the best trade-off depends on the hardware. Existing automated methods, however, each use one check construction and yield fixed trade-offs. We first introduce Block Checks, in which several checks share one fault-tolerantly prepared auxiliary block, which places them and existing constructions in a single design space. Second, to explore that space, we propose a Pareto tree search that adds checks and auxiliary blocks, merges auxiliaries, and edits the circuit. On quantum codes of distance up to seven, the search finds best-known circuits for many new operation--depth trade-offs and surpasses existing methods. The code is open source as part of the Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT) at https://github.com/munich-quantum-toolkit/qecc, and all circuits are available in the QECirc library at https://qecirc.com.
one_liner: Block Checks and Pareto tree search broaden the circuit design space for fault-tolerant logical-state preparation.
why_it_matters: The method finds improved operation-depth trade-offs that can be matched to different hardware constraints.

title: A Computational and Experimental Framework for Fourier Optics in Python
abstract: Simulation of the propagation of light is useful for the design and dimensioning of optical systems. In this paper, we present the basics of propagation simulation using Fourier optics and practical implementation in Python, with a particular emphasis on dimensions. We first verify that our numerical wave-optics simulations maintain correct physical spatial scaling. Next, we benchmark numerical propagation against closed-form analytical formulas for Gaussian beams, lens focusing effects, and grating diffraction. We then show how those simulations can be used to generate diffractive optical elements such as Fresnel zone plates, and we bridge the gap between numerical simulations and experiments by collecting data and recovering phase information using a phase retrieval algorithm.
one_liner: A Python framework implements dimensionally correct Fourier-optics simulations validated against analytic models and experiments.
why_it_matters: It connects physically scaled optical simulation, diffractive-element design, measurements, and phase retrieval.

title: A Quantum Continuous Wavelet Transform
abstract: We construct a quantum continuous wavelet transform (QCWT) on a finite scale--translation grid whose scales may be non-dyadic. A quantum Fourier transform places the amplitude-encoded signal in the frequency basis, the scale-dependent multiplier is block-encoded with one flag qubit, and an inverse Fourier transform returns the complex, quadrature-weighted CWT coefficients in the success branch. For heralded circuits that act once on one copy of the input with an input-independent output factor, we bound the success probability and attain the bound by a frequency-conditioned scale preparation. When the scale prior is prepared independently of frequency, normalizing the multiplier separately at each scale is optimal and raises the success probability by factors of 4.9 and 14.6 in our examples; on logarithmic grids this architecture loses, relative to the bound, a factor of about the admissibility constant over the squared spectral peak times the logarithmic scale range. We give a fixed-point resource estimate for a reversible Mexican-hat multiplier, the multinomial law of scale--translation measurements, and Hadamard tests for complex coefficients. We show that a Fourier-basis measurement of the input, followed by classical randomization, reproduces the flag and scale outcomes of every such heralded circuit exactly, so it is at least as informative for global scale energies; a simulation study of Hurst exponent estimation agrees. What the QCWT adds is the joint scale--translation law: two chirps with identical Fourier-basis and time-basis measurement laws have QCWT laws at total-variation distance 0.27.
one_liner: A quantum continuous wavelet transform supports non-dyadic scales and exposes joint scale-translation information unavailable from simpler measurements.
why_it_matters: It clarifies both the achievable information and the resource and success-probability limits of quantum wavelet analysis.

title: Learning Integer Winding Evolution Times in Quantum Phase Estimation
abstract: Learning a Hamiltonian evolution time in Quantum Phase Estimation that produces phase distributions with low Shannon entropy circumvents the fundamental limit of digitization error of phase, independent of the number of phase qubits of accuracy. By introducing an optimization loop to minimize the Shannon entropy of measured eigenvalues produced by a QPE quantum circuit, minimum eigenvalue computation accuracy is greatly improved, which we show numerically on quantum magnet models. This technique works because standard QPE has a natural correspondence between entropy of the phase distribution and the analog accuracy of the minimum eigenvalue phase. This introduces for the first time a type of parameter learning to QPE, which makes near term practicality of QPE for fundamental sciences more feasible by using shorter depth QPE circuits.
one_liner: Learning integer winding evolution times by minimizing QPE output entropy improves eigenvalue accuracy with shorter circuits.
why_it_matters: The approach may make quantum phase estimation more practical for near-term studies of physical models.

title: Accelerating Diffusion Maps on a Quantum Computer: Spectral Filtering and Galerkin PDE Solvers
abstract: Diffusion maps generalize principal component analysis (PCA) to nonlinear manifolds, enabling spectral dimensionality reduction, geometric data analysis, and elliptic PDE approximation on point clouds. For large datasets of size $N$, however, classical matrix operations incur prohibitive $\operatorname{poly}(N)$ scaling, even when extracting low-dimensional spectral features or targeted scalar observables. We introduce a quantum algorithmic framework that bypasses explicit graph-Laplacian assembly by exploiting the symmetric factorization $G = A^T A$ directly at the block-encoding level. Combining Gaussian moment dilation, Laplace-weighted linear combinations of unitaries (LCU), and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), we implement spectral filters of $A$ to estimate heat-semigroup overlaps, regularized inverse queries, and energy responses, as well as to prepare spectral Galerkin solution states. A common-state construction further allows the block-encoding queries to be used across multiple scalar observables. Under polylogarithmic-cost block-encoding access to $A$ and state-preparation oracles, our heat-overlap algorithm achieves $O(\operatorname{polylog} N)$ gate complexity at fixed normalized precision, confidence, and spectral scale. Ideal statevector simulations validate our discrete circuit constructions, while a matched approximate-counting benchmark demonstrates the quadratic precision advantage of coherent amplitude estimation for energy readout.
one_liner: A block-encoded quantum framework accelerates diffusion-map spectral filtering, scalar queries, and Galerkin PDE solution-state preparation.
why_it_matters: Given efficient oracle access, selected manifold-learning tasks can scale polylogarithmically with dataset size.

title: Nodal Knotted Finite-Energy Spatiotemporally Localized Scalar Wave Solutions
abstract: Significant amount of information is available in wave optics about monochromatic paraxial beams characterized by nodal knots, the latter being threads of complete darkness (lines of zero intensity) tied into knots. Also, well -known are finite-energy spatiotemporally localized vector-valued wave solutions characterized by knotted to-pologies. Unfortunately, except for solutions to the Schrödinger-like equation describing anomalous dispersion, no scalar-valued spatiotemporally localized waves with analogous knotted topological structures are known to date. It is the goal in this article to fill in this gap by deriving finite-energy spatiotemporally localized scalar-valued wave solutions characterized specifically by Hopf and trefoil nodal knot topologies. This will extend to spatiotemporally localized pulsed fields the diverse important applications of mono-chromatic light beams, having nontrivial topological structures, in trapping and guiding particles, image processing and optical communications; also, in applications to biology and medicine.
one_liner: Finite-energy scalar wave solutions are derived with spatiotemporal localization and Hopf or trefoil nodal-knot structures.
why_it_matters: The solutions extend knotted optical fields from monochromatic beams to localized scalar pulses.

title: A universal modal-noise limit for multimode photonic systems
abstract: Modal noise limits the photometric and spectroscopic stability of every multimode-to-single-mode photonic system, yet it is quantified device by device. For isotropic modal excitation at fixed input power, the fractional power fluctuation of any linear multimode system is shown to be fixed by one number: the participation ratio M_eff of the eigenvalues of K = T†WT. Monte Carlo for spatially filtered fibres, lossy lanterns, and integrated mode converters confirms the law, which recovers the classical speckle limits. Extending K to K(λ) gives the spectral correlation of modal noise and a closed-form velocity error, maximal when the correlation width equals the line width.
one_liner: A universal participation-ratio law predicts power fluctuations and spectral correlations from modal noise in linear multimode photonic systems.
why_it_matters: It replaces device-specific noise estimates with a common metric applicable to fibers, lanterns, and mode converters.

title: The Complete Set of Solutions for the Equations of Temporal Coupled Mode Theory
abstract: Temporal coupled mode theory (TCMT) provides a compact description of resonant transport in optical systems in terms of a small set of physically transparent parameters, including the resonant coupling coefficients and direct background scattering matrix. In the formalism of TCMT, the background scattering matrix and the coupling vectors are constrained by time reversal symmetry, reciprocity, and energy conservation. While these constraints are well established, the general so- lution under these is only known for a few cases, in which spatial symmetry simplifies the problem. In this paper, we derive the complete set of solutions for the equations of temporal coupled mode theory that describes lossless single-mode or multi-mode resonators coupled to an arbitrary num- ber of ports. Our derivation utilizes an explicit Takagi decomposition of the symmetric unitary background scattering matrix. We provide a comparison with numerical simulations for both the single and multimode cases.
one_liner: The complete lossless TCMT solution is derived for single- and multimode resonators coupled to any number of ports.
why_it_matters: It removes reliance on special spatial symmetries when modeling resonant optical transport.

title: Analytic and Numerical Investigation of a Proposed Non-linear Extension of Quantum Mechanics
abstract: In this paper, additional properties of a previously introduced non-linear extension of quantum mechanics are investigated. Analytically, we uncover a limit in which the model reduces to ordinary linear quantum mechanics. We also perform a perturbation analysis about an exact solution studied in earlier work. The equations represent a system that is subject to a periodic driver, and we use Floquet theory to help determine its properties. Numerically, we compare the exact solution to the analytic approximation, and we exhibit several examples of how the non-linear effects influence particle trajectories, with particular emphasis on trajectories near the linear limit.
one_liner: Analytic perturbation, Floquet analysis, and simulations characterize a nonlinear quantum model near its ordinary linear limit.
why_it_matters: The work identifies how nonlinear corrections alter driven dynamics and particle trajectories near standard quantum mechanics.

title: Certified Separation Between Coherent and Adaptive Temporal Processing of Quantum-Error-Correction Readout
abstract: Repeated quantum-error-correction readout is normally converted into a classical time series: each syndrome pulse is measured on arrival and only the resulting classical record is retained. Nonorthogonal readout signals raise the question of whether preserving quantum information between rounds can improve the final recovery decision. We formulate this comparison as a loss-weighted state-discrimination problem. For an idealized two-round benchmark with quadrature phase-shift-keying (QPSK) signals, a receiver with a seven-dimensional persistent register has certified recovery-decision error below $24.2100\%$, whereas every separate adaptive receiver has error above $25.1431\%$. The certified separation is at least $0.933$ percentage points. The loss counts incorrect final error-mask decisions in the benchmark. In the strict architecture, where the counted register is the entire persistent state, four dimensions are necessary and sufficient to outperform the adaptive class. Certified separations also occur at three and four rounds with register dimensions $8$ and $36$, compared with $16$ and $64$ for full-prefix storage. We relate memory dimension to the structure of the temporal measurement, give a sufficient memory bound for collective measurements, and quantify robustness to register dephasing and accumulated channel error.
one_liner: Certified benchmarks show coherent temporal processing of nonorthogonal QEC readout can outperform all separate adaptive receivers.
why_it_matters: The result quantifies when retaining quantum memory across syndrome rounds improves recovery decisions.

title: Resilience of emergent Hamiltonian quantum memories in the presence of noise
abstract: Emergent Hamiltonians can freeze an entangled state prepared through coherent evolution, since that state is an eigenstate of the Hamiltonian under which it is then stored. We show that the freedom left in this construction allows the storage spectrum to be adapted to a noisy environment without changing the stored state. For a product of Bell pairs prepared from a density wave in an engineered chain, a selection rule prevents local density noise from connecting the target to any of its degenerate partners, so that rescaling the storage Hamiltonian by a factor $α$ moves every transition this noise drives. Under $1/f$ noise, the storage time then grows in proportion to $α$, a result we confirm by evolving the memory under explicit classical $1/f$ fields, whereas for an Ohmic bath the most favorable scale depends on its cutoff. Fermionic loss, treated as a solvable model, includes a transition that rescaling leaves at zero frequency, and an energy shift $μ$ per particle moves it away from zero, with an exact orbital solution giving the resulting lifetimes. Finally, among number-conserving quadratic reference Hamiltonians, $α$ and $μ$ are the only controls that keep the storage Hamiltonian nearest neighbor at every time along the preparation, so that the protocol combines local freezing with control over the storage spectrum.
one_liner: Storage-spectrum tuning improves emergent Hamiltonian quantum-memory lifetimes under several noise and loss mechanisms.
why_it_matters: It shows how local controls can protect a frozen entangled state without altering the state itself.

title: Quantum dynamical transitions when the corresponding classical phase space has a separatrix: extension of the QKNH theorem beyond double wells
abstract: In classical Hamiltonian systems with a slowly time-dependent parameter, adiabaticity breaks down at a separatrix, leading to probabilistic post-adiabatic transitions between different phase-space regions described by the Kruskal-Neishtadt-Henrard (KNH) theorem. Quantum mechanically, dynamical tunneling allows adiabaticity to persist where it breaks down classically, making the quantum-classical correspondence for separatrix crossing non-trivial. We recently established a quantum version of the KNH theorem (QKNH) by introducing the concept of a sweep-rate-dependent quantum separatrix in the instantaneous energy spectrum of the time-dependent system. The QKNH theorem relates the splitting of a quantum ensemble between the outgoing dynamical sectors at the quantum separatrix to their relative growth rates, and thus provides a quantum analog of the classical KNH rule. Here, we demonstrate that these findings are not restricted to double-well systems with tunneling through a potential barrier. We investigate a slowly driven quantum pendulum, in which the avoided crossings arise from above-barrier reflection. The resulting Landau-Zener probabilities have the same local lattice form as in the double-well problem, allowing the application of the QKNH theorem.
one_liner: The quantum KNH theorem is extended from double wells to a driven pendulum with above-barrier reflection.
why_it_matters: It broadens quantum-classical correspondence for slow separatrix crossings beyond tunneling systems.

title: Generation of coherent-state Schrödinger cat states in a two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model implemented with Josephson junctions
abstract: We investigate the generation of coherent-state Schrödinger cat states using a two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model (JCM) implemented in a Josephson-junction quantum circuit. We consider a specific superconducting flux-qubit implementation and estimate the resulting two-photon coupling constant. We numerically examine three types of noise: magnetic flux noise with $1/f$ fluctuations, energy relaxation associated with the flux-qubit $T_{1}$ decay, and photon loss in the bosonic mode obtained by quantizing the phase variable of the dc SQUID used for qubit readout. We find that photon loss has a particularly significant effect on cat-state fidelity. We also investigate the time evolution of the probability-amplitude distribution in the Pegg-Barnett phase-state basis for the $l$-photon JCM ($l=1,2,3,4$), starting from a coherent bosonic state. Finally, we assume that the bosonic mode is initially prepared in a displaced thermal state and then decoupled from the heat bath. We study the subsequent unitary evolution to determine how the initial temperature affects the fidelity and Wigner function of the generated cat states.
one_liner: A Josephson two-photon Jaynes-Cummings circuit generates cat states, with photon loss emerging as the leading fidelity limit.
why_it_matters: It identifies practical noise and temperature constraints for superconducting-circuit cat-state generation.

title: Curvature-Calibrated Friction and an Exact Gauge Symmetry for Quantum Hamiltonian Descent
abstract: A design problem constrained by a partial differential equation can be solved coherently on a quantum computer. The objective is block-encoded rather than measured, and Quantum Hamiltonian Descent consumes it directly. We identify two obstacles in this pipeline and repair both. First, the oracle construction assumes affine generators with positive semidefinite Hermitian parts, which covariance entries violate for every off-diagonal generator. Encoding the covariance as an affine combination of positive semidefinite atoms restores both conditions at every register point, at the price of a representational floor, median 45% of the fitted family's own objective range for a fixed rank-three dictionary and 22% with a variable diagonal. Second, adding a constant to the objective leaves the measurement distribution exactly invariant, yet the mean-objective friction heuristic in current use assigns such objectives different schedules. Calibrating the friction to the landscape curvature restores the symmetry, though not the constant in $ν= c\sqrtμ$, and a bracketed sweep at matched objective-phase exposure, not end-to-end cost, places the best tested friction between 0.032 and 0.25 of critical damping on a diffusion-design benchmark, a broad plateau an order of magnitude below the classical default.
one_liner: Quantum Hamiltonian Descent gains a valid covariance encoding and curvature-based friction with exact objective-shift symmetry.
why_it_matters: The changes repair key consistency problems in coherent quantum optimization for PDE-constrained design.

title: Distributed Fiber Monitoring on a Coherent DSP ASIC: Implementation of Longitudinal Power Monitoring
abstract: Coherent DSP ASICs and transceivers to date report a rich set of optical link metrics, yet these remain cumulative over the link and provide no spatial localization. This paper presents the implementation design of fiber-longitudinal power monitoring (LPM), which recovers spatially resolved power profiles from received traffic, on a coherent DSP ASIC chip. We first identify the challenges specific to DSP implementation, and describe the enabling algorithm and architecture. We then present the key design considerations for retaining the estimation fidelity of the on-chip LPM during in-service operation. On this basis, we implement LPM on a coherent DSP, a 3-nm 800G low-power DSP ASIC housed in an OSFP pluggable module, which constitutes, to our knowledge, the first coherent DSP ASIC and transceiver to perform distributed fiber monitoring and data communication simultaneously. The on-chip LPM is experimentally validated over links of up to 1005 km using 400ZR+ and 800ZR+ traffic, with no measurable impact on Q factor or module power consumption. Multi-vendor interoperability is also demonstrated, where the on-chip LPM operates on signals transmitted by third-party transceivers. These results extend coherent DSPs from cumulative to spatially resolved monitoring, allowing pluggable transceivers, deployable from DCI to long-haul, to act not only as cost-efficient transmission elements but also as distributed monitoring points across diverse optical network infrastructure.
one_liner: A 3-nm 800G coherent DSP ASIC performs in-service longitudinal fiber-power monitoring over links up to 1005 km.
why_it_matters: It adds spatial fault localization to pluggable transceivers without measurable transmission or power penalties.

title: High-Dimensional Structured Light Tomography with a Tilted Lens
abstract: In this work, we investigate high-dimensional spatial mode tomography using intensity measurements and the astigmatic transformation implemented with a tilted lens. We improve the method previously published in Ref. [1] to perform the spatial tomography not restricted to a fixed order, which allowed us to achieve good fidelity for a mode space dimension as high as $D=66\,$. Since the literature is not unanimous, we also present a comprehensive revision of light propagation through a tilted lens for an accurate description of the transformation used for tomography. We derive its effective focal lengths, and analyze its role as an astigmatic mode converter. Moreover, we establish its explicit domain of validity within the Hermite-Gaussian basis.
one_liner: Tilted-lens intensity tomography reconstructs structured-light states across mixed mode orders with dimension up to 66.
why_it_matters: It offers a simple route to higher-dimensional spatial-mode characterization with clarified operating limits.

title: Convex splitting by binary quantum hypothesis testing
abstract: How many independent quantum systems does it take to hide one system that is correlated with a reference? An observer can measure all the systems together with the reference to detect the correlation. We turn any such measurement into binary tests on a single system and the reference. For each test we bound the probability of declaring a signal when an independent pair was prepared. Averaging the largest signal acceptance probabilities allowed by these bounds controls the normalized trace distance in the convex-split lemma. A second bound gives a sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the state of the reference. Both bounds hold for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces. Comparing two distributions for the location of the hidden system gives one-shot bounds for private communication and one-way secret key distillation, including the public information available to an eavesdropper. For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, we recover the known Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private or key bits from $n$ independent repetitions and bound the remaining loss by $\log_2 n+O(1)$ at fixed errors. The position-based key distillation protocol attains this bound with $O(n)$ public bits.
one_liner: Binary quantum hypothesis tests yield convex-split bounds for hiding correlations and one-shot private communication.
why_it_matters: The framework extends to separable Hilbert spaces and recovers precise finite-blocklength privacy corrections.

title: Remote Use of Quantum Machines in the Adversarial Scenario
abstract: Networked quantum technologies allow users to operate quantum machines hosted by remote servers, but classical commands alone cannot ensure that only the intended user can prepare the useful inputs that activate them. We formulate the problem of adversarial remote use of quantum machines in the framework of quantum resource theories. A device controlled by Bob is correlated to a remote user, Alice, through a bipartite state, and also to an adversary Eve holding its purification. Alice and Eve compete to programme Bob's machine by remotely preparing its inputs: the conditional state carries the quantum resource, while the measurement outcome selects the machine operation. Remote use is truly advantageous when Alice is guaranteed to unlock a larger average task value than the adversary Eve, given the same marginal state of Bob. We show that for tasks with a convex figure of merit, the competition is governed by complementary upper roofs and, for spectral tasks, where the figure of merit is invariant under unitary operations, by a corresponding entanglement imbalance. Purification, work extraction, quantum batteries, and coherence distillation show that the same noisy state may secure exclusivity one machine but not another. Finally, we order Alice's and Eve's complete programming powers through a task-independent simulation preorder, based on the ensembles each party can prepare on Bob's side. Shared quantum correlations thereby become a key resource for controlling access to remote quantum machines.
one_liner: A resource-theoretic framework compares a user and adversary competing to remotely program the same quantum machine.
why_it_matters: It reveals when shared quantum correlations can guarantee exclusive access to useful remote operations.

title: Multi-Illumination Spectral Reflectance Reconstruction: A method for hyperspectral imaging using digital photography
abstract: Quantitative measurement of complex coloration patterns is essential for many biological studies and practical applications. Although color perception depends on the observer's visual system, an objective characterization is possible by measuring the spectral reflectance across the sample surface. Traditional methods for measuring spectral reflectance are either limited in spatial resolution, as with spectrometer probes, or limited in spectral detail, as with digital cameras. We present a method for reconstructing spatially resolved spectral reflectance of samples from multiple images taken under different illuminants with known spectral irradiance. Using an optimization scheme that minimizes pixel-value error while regularizing for the smoothness of the reflectance spectrum, our method generates high-resolution hyperspectral images. We tested our method using both existing spectral reflectance datasets and original multi-illumination images taken in a custom photo-box, demonstrating high accuracy and simple implementation of the method, as well as the ability to infer how samples are perceived by different visual systems. Our method can be a useful tool for objective quantification of complex visual patterns in color-related biological research and imaging applications.
one_liner: Multiple photographs under known illuminants reconstruct spatially resolved spectral reflectance through regularized optimization.
why_it_matters: It enables accessible high-resolution hyperspectral imaging for biological coloration and visual-pattern studies.

title: Momentum-space quantum Monte Carlo for twisted bilayer graphene: Interaction effects in the presence of remote bands
abstract: Twisted bilayer graphene hosts strong correlation effects within topological flat bands separated from remote dispersive bands. This separation motivates projection onto the central bands, which greatly reduces the computational complexity of many-body calculations, including momentum-space quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations. However, the interaction-induced Mott gap obtained in the projected model can be comparable to the noninteracting flat--remote band separation, raising the question of whether the projection remains valid. Here, we extend momentum-space QMC to explicitly include remote BM bands within a broad energy window at charge neutrality. We find that the projected description remains reliable over a broad parameter regime, up to $u_0/u_1\lesssim0.9$: the projected and remote-band calculations yield similar low-energy electron and trion spectra, and the Kramers intervalley-coherent ground state remains stable. In particular, the Dirac trion remains robust in the finite-temperature normal state when remote bands are included. Near the band-touching limit $u_0=u_1$, remote-band electrons acquire substantial low-energy spectral weight, accompanied by suppression of the trion weight and loss of the Kramers intervalley-coherent state. Our findings establish the broad validity of flat-band projection while reconciling the projected and THF viewpoints by identifying the near-band-touching regime in which explicit remote-band degrees of freedom become essential.
one_liner: Momentum-space QMC shows flat-band projection remains reliable in twisted bilayer graphene except near band touching.
why_it_matters: It identifies when remote bands must be included to describe correlated states and Dirac trions accurately.

title: Direct measurement of the on-shot focal-spot size of a kilojoule-class petawatt laser
abstract: We report a direct, on-shot determination of the focal-spot size of a kilojoule-class, four-beam petawatt laser. Encircled-energy curves were inferred from the energy transmitted around aluminum-coated spheres of varying diameters placed at the focal plane. The 50% encircled-energy diameter D50 of each beam was obtained by fitting a two-component Gaussian mixture with Bayesian inference. With all deformable mirrors optimized in closed loop, the best-corrected alignment beam reached D50 = 34 (+4/-5) um, three times the diffraction limit of 10 um. Under full-power conditions, the thermal distortion of the main amplifier broadened this beam to D50 = 102 (+9/-8) um and reduced its peak intensity ninefold, to 2.2 (+0.6/-0.9) x 10^18 W/cm^2 at 250 J and 1.3 ps. The energy fraction of the narrow component decreased from 68% to 38%. These reference values serve facility users, and a deformable mirror upstream of the pulse compressor, now on one beam only, doubles the on-shot peak intensity.
one_liner: Sphere-based encircled-energy measurements directly determine the on-shot focal spot of a kilojoule petawatt laser.
why_it_matters: The results quantify full-power thermal broadening and guide adaptive-optics improvements at high-energy facilities.

title: QFT-Based Hybrid PointNet-Quantum Neural Networks for LiDAR Point-Cloud Classification
abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical learning architectures provide a promising framework for integrating quantum feature transformations into complex data-processing tasks. Among these transformations, the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) offers a structured approach to feature processing, motivating an investigation of how its circuit configuration influences predictive performance, quantum resource requirements, and noise robustness. We present a hybrid PointNet-quantum neural network architecture for LiDAR point-cloud classification, combining classical feature extraction, amplitude encoding, and a variational quantum circuit. Five Fourier-processing configurations are systematically evaluated: No-QFT, Full-QFT-After, QFT-no-swap, IQFT-After, and Trainable-QFT. Experiments on KITTI, nuScenes, and PandaSet across three random seeds assess classification performance, class-level behavior, circuit complexity, and sensitivity to the IBM FakeManilaV2 noise model. Under ideal simulation, IQFT-After achieves the highest weighted F1-score on KITTI (0.857 $\pm$ 0.033), compared with 0.838 $\pm$ 0.023 for No-QFT. Removing the final SWAP gates in the QFT circuit reduces circuit complexity while preserving the Pauli-Z measurement features up to a fixed permutation that can be absorbed by the classification head. Under quantum noise, the circuit ranking changes, with IQFT-After exhibiting greater performance degradation and No-QFT and Trainable-QFT showing stronger robustness. Per-class analysis further identifies dataset-dependent differences in minority-class performance. These results demonstrate that Fourier-processing configuration influences both classification behavior and noise sensitivity, highlighting the role of circuit structure and hardware-aware evaluation in hybrid quantum learning for three-dimensional point-cloud data.
one_liner: Hybrid PointNet quantum networks reveal QFT configurations trade ideal LiDAR accuracy against circuit cost and noise robustness.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates why hardware-aware circuit selection is essential for quantum point-cloud classifiers.

title: Seamless Gradient Pixels for Multidimensional Optical Information Interrogation
abstract: Information from light interaction with its environment can be extracted from its numerous properties. Yet capturing and interpreting this information within a single and compact platform remains challenging because conventional systems rely on discrete components and detection channels. Here we introduce the concept of "gradient pixels" that provides a universal metasurface platform to interrogate optical field information in the infrared (IR) spectrum. By continuously varying a design parameter across two dimensions, we encode multidimensional optical information into measurable spatial patterns, e.g., both spectral and polarization information are acquired from a single snapshot image. A free-form gradient pixel further enables prescribed wavelength-selective spatial patterns within a single metasurface through tailored gradient profiles. Unlike isolated filter arrays, seamless gradient-pixels multiplex neighbouring meta-atoms, increasing channel spatial density and relaxing Q-factor constraints. A 250-$μ$m footprint of these meta-atoms achieves spectral resolution better than 100-pm over a 100-nm spectral span based on a serpentine configuration. Snapshot wavelength-polarization reconstruction yields polarization angular accuracy at 0.3$^\circ$. We extend this concept to perform near-field refractive index sensing at video rates using the same explicit parameter-space mapping. By linking far-field detection and near-field sensing, it enables spatially resolved analysis of optical fields and local dielectric environments through a common image-based readout. It offers prospects for multidimensional optical sensing, computational imaging and intelligent information processing.
one_liner: Gradient metasurface pixels encode spectral, polarization, and refractive-index information into compact image-based readouts.
why_it_matters: The approach could replace multiple optical channels with a dense, single-snapshot sensing platform.

title: Two Faces of Spacetime Density Matrices: Entanglement and Complexity
abstract: We establish a direct connection between entanglement and complexity through spacetime density matrices. For stationary pure states and complementary regions at different times, spacetime replica moments encode the return amplitude of a replica-defect quench. This representation defines an associated state spread complexity, which we call Krylov-Rényi complexity. It can equivalently be obtained by using a replica-defect excitation of the replicated background state as the seed and evolving it under the original replicated Hamiltonian. We further construct Krylov-von Neumann complexity as a probe limit from first-order replica data. Timelike entanglement and complexity provide complementary information at a fixed time, while the full time dependence of the timelike entropy determines the Krylov dynamics and hence the complexity. The replica construction fixes the seed and its evolution through the background state, subsystem geometry, and regulator, without an independently chosen probe operator. Like entanglement entropy, the resulting complexity is defined nonperturbatively and probes universal properties and dynamical information about the underlying theory.
one_liner: Spacetime density matrices connect timelike entanglement with Krylov-Rényi and Krylov-von Neumann complexity.
why_it_matters: The construction defines nonperturbative complexity directly from replica dynamics without choosing a separate probe operator.

title: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Transition
abstract: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH. As the first such machine may stay secret, a migration cannot wait for visible thefts, and once keys are extractable, legacy signatures no longer tell owners from attackers. We design a migration in which owners enroll post-quantum keys cheaply with their existing signatures before ECDSA is retired at a scheduled time, while a zero-knowledge proof of the wallet's BIP-39 seed can correct any such enrollment until a common deadline afterward; an account nobody enrolled stays frozen and recoverable by seed proof without a deadline. Each proof binds the new key, a nonce and a fee cap, so neither a paying sponsor nor a reordering block builder can redirect or replay it. Validators switch to hash-based keys first, at a finalized checkpoint and under a stated bound on the attacker's voting power. We prove the account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client. A three-layer recursive hash-based STARK yields a seed proof of about 190 KB that fits one transaction, verifies in 38 ms and takes a median of 111 s to generate on a laptop; four proofs aggregate into one. In a ten-node simulation with mainnet-derived accounts and fee demand, block space rather than proving sets the duration: the 4.45 million accounts with at least 0.1 ETH would migrate in 29.4 days if all enroll before ECDSA is retired and in 235 days if all recover after it in batches of four. In a mass enrollment, an enrollment waits a median of 19.1 minutes in the public mempool, longer than published estimates for a fast quantum computer to extract its key, so owners with a seed and an unexposed key should migrate by seed proof.
one_liner: A post-quantum Ethereum migration scheme combines correctable key enrollment with one-transaction zero-knowledge seed proofs.
why_it_matters: It offers a concrete path to protect exposed accounts while preventing sponsors, block builders, and attackers from redirecting recovery.

title: Real-Time Single-Pixel Imaging via Exploiting Temporal Mixing: A Unified Calibration and Composite Readout Framework
abstract: In high-speed optical measurements and computational imaging such as in single-pixel imaging temporal mixing arising from the mismatch between modulation and the electro-optical acquisition chain is conventionally treated as an unmitigated distortion that corrupts measurement orthogonality, breaks compressive sensing priors, fundamentally limits imaging speed, and induces catastrophic reconstruction failure. Here, we establish a transferable, unified calibration and composite-readout framework for single-pixel imaging that systematically repurposes temporal memory from a readout limitation into a powerful measurement resource. Beyond achieving robust high-fidelity recovery, this engineered approach enables cost effective, lower bandwidth configurations to consistently deliver superior image quality compared to higher bandwidth reference setups across diverse operating conditions turning a historical hardware bottleneck into an active imaging advantage. Specifically, target scenes are reconstructed directly from mixed observations without the need to recover individual pattern projections, thereby significantly advancing high-speed and video-rate single-pixel imaging capabilities. Crucially, the transferability of our framework allows calibration routines established on one hardware platform (such as digital micromirror device-based setups) to be readily transferred across different optical systems (such as rotating coding disks), paving the way for calibrated temporal memory as a versatile and generalized measurement paradigm for broader computational imaging.
one_liner: A calibration and composite-readout framework turns temporal mixing into a useful resource for real-time single-pixel imaging.
why_it_matters: It enables lower-bandwidth hardware to recover high-quality images directly from mixed measurements at high speed.

title: Insurance portfolio simulation with a quantum circuit
abstract: A central challenge in actuarial science is characterising the distribution of losses generated by an insurance portfolio. Copulas provide a natural framework for modelling joint distributions, but flexible high-dimensional copula fitting and sampling remains challenging in practice. We propose a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) approach adapted to insurance portfolios, combining (i) a tail-focused discretisation of heavy-tailed marginals, (ii) a Monte Carlo-style objective function that enables the numerical precision of the algorithm to scale when trained on a relatively small number of samples, and (iii) a two-stage hierarchical training scheme enabling efficient training on a simulator and fine-tuning on quantum hardware. On a mixed portfolio of equity returns and insurance losses, the trained circuit recovers the qualitative dependence structure, with near-independence between equity and losses and positive dependence among loss lines. Exponential quantile encoding substantially improves the fit to the tail of the aggregate loss distribution relative to a uniform encoding, and the hierarchical scheme substantially outperforms single-stage training of a circuit of the same size from random initialisation.
one_liner: A quantum circuit Born machine models dependent insurance losses using tail-focused encoding and hierarchical training.
why_it_matters: The method improves aggregate-loss tail modeling and supports simulator pretraining followed by quantum-hardware fine-tuning.

title: Beyond Error Mitigation: Using Boosting for Noisy Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) can recover information about ideal quantum computations from noisy circuit executions, but may require a large sampling overhead. Fundamental lower bounds show that recovering noiseless observables without problem-specific information can require superpolynomially many samples, with exponential overhead for broad classes of noisy circuits. However, problem-specific information can reduce the number of samples needed to obtain the required answer. We investigate this possibility in supervised quantum machine learning, where labeled examples provide information about the function to be learned. Binary classification provides such a setting, since correct prediction depends on the sign and margin of the classifier output rather than on accurate reconstruction of every noiseless expectation value. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework for comparing boosting of noisy parameterized quantum circuits with probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), requiring both methods to reach the same learning target. For the specified circuit architectures under Pauli noise, we establish a common hypothesis-class complexity bound: matching empirical margin loss gives the same upper bound on expected classification risk. We derive resource criteria and evaluate AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost in finite-shot teacher-student simulations across circuit depth and physical noise strength. Under the same classification-accuracy target, boosting requires fewer circuit executions as depth and noise increase. Boosting also achieves higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference. For the supervised-learning problems studied, these results demonstrate a task-dependent resource advantage: exploiting information retained in noisy outputs can avoid the cost of ideal-output reconstruction without sacrificing observed classification performance.
one_liner: Boosting noisy parameterized quantum circuits can outperform probabilistic error cancellation for supervised classification.
why_it_matters: Task-specific labels and margins can reduce circuit executions by avoiding unnecessary reconstruction of ideal observables.

title: Critical droplets and metastability in long-range chains
abstract: Metastable decay in first-order phase transitions proceeds through the nucleation of critical droplets. In the one-dimensional nearest-neighbor Ising chain, the cost of the two walls bounding a droplet is independent of its size. For interactions decaying as $1/r^{1+σ}$, this surface cost instead depends on the droplet size and competes with the bulk free-energy gain. The critical radius scales as $R_c\propto h^{-1/σ}$ at small $h$, where $h>0$ is the bias field. The value $σ=1$ separates two regimes: for $σ<1$, the activation barrier diverges as $h\to0^+$; at $σ=1$, it grows logarithmically; and for $σ>1$, it remains finite, as in the nearest-neighbor chain. A nonlocal $φ^4$ field theory yields critical droplets with algebraic tails and confirms the predicted radius and barrier scalings, while stochastic long-range dynamics independently reproduces the critical-radius scaling.
one_liner: Long-range Ising chains exhibit critical-droplet radii and metastable barriers governed by the interaction exponent and bias field.
why_it_matters: The results identify distinct nucleation regimes and connect microscopic dynamics with a nonlocal field theory.

title: Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Differential Privacy
abstract: Differential privacy has been successfully extended to quantum computing and information processing, where sensitive data are encoded in quantum states and protected by quantum noise mechanisms that keep the outcomes of any measurement on neighboring states nearly indistinguishable. In the quantum setting, however, the state submitted to a quantum computer may be entangled with a hidden reference system secretly held by an adversary. Such entanglement cannot be detected from the submitted state alone, and it poses a challenge with no counterpart in the classical setting. Existing frameworks of quantum differential privacy consider only measurements on the released state, leaving this scenario largely unexplored. In this paper, we identify the entanglement attack: an adversary submits one half of an entangled state to a quantum computer that runs a privacy mechanism, keeps the other half, and finally measures both halves jointly. We show that this attack may completely break a mechanism that satisfies quantum differential privacy with a finite parameter, driving its privacy parameter to infinity. To counter it, we propose entanglement-assisted quantum differential privacy (EA-QDP), a privacy framework that is native to quantum entanglement and remains valid against such attacks. We characterize exactly when a mechanism has a finite EA-QDP parameter, and show that the optimal parameter $\varepsilon^*_{\mathrm{EA}}$ of any quantum mechanism can be computed by a semidefinite programming problem (SDP). Building on this, we quantify the extra privacy leakage caused by entanglement and show that it can be bounded by choosing appropriate mechanisms, with the depolarizing channel being our recommended choice. Finally, we demonstrate both the attack and its countermeasure on simulated and physical quantum hardware, and the experimental results agree with our theoretical predictions.
one_liner: Entanglement-assisted quantum differential privacy protects mechanisms against adversaries holding a hidden entangled reference system.
why_it_matters: It closes a privacy loophole that can make conventionally private quantum mechanisms leak without bound.

title: Sign-Controlled BIC Merging and Flatband Formation in C2-symmetric Photonic Lattices
abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) on flatbands promise long-lived, weakly dispersive photons, yet their interplay remains elusive. Here, we develop a four-mode non-Hermitian Hamiltonian for $C_2$-symmetric photonic-crystal slabs. We show that the sign of the interpair coupling determines whether two Friedrich-Wintgen (FW) BICs and a symmetry-protected (SP) BIC occupy the same photonic band, a necessary condition for merging. In rectangular lattices, merging eliminates the quadratic radiative-loss term in a perfect-square form and strongly suppresses the quartic contribution, giving an effective $Q \sim k^{-6}$ scaling. Deviations from rectangular geometry induce noncollinear radiation polarizations, converting FW-BICs into quasi-BICs with $Q_{\mathrm{qBIC}} \sim (90^\circ-θ)^{-2}$ and restoring the asymptotic $Q \sim k^{-2}$ scaling. Unlike BIC band selection, quadratic band flattening is insensitive to the coupling sign and can occur without BIC merging, even in oblique lattices. Our results reveal distinct conditions governing BIC merging, higher-order radiation suppression, and band flattening.
one_liner: A four-mode model separates the conditions for BIC merging, higher-order loss suppression, and flatband formation in photonic lattices.
why_it_matters: The findings provide design rules for long-lived, weakly dispersive photonic modes in symmetric and distorted lattices.

title: Structure-Guided Synthesis of Low-Error Syndrome Extraction Circuits
abstract: Gate orders can change fault propagation and logical error rates even when syndrome-extraction circuits implement the same ideal stabilizer measurements. Optimizing these orderings independently for every check, however, becomes computationally demanding as code size increases. We present a synthesis method for structured Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes that groups checks by recurring connectivity and shares one relative gate order per group, reducing independent ordering choices. A CP-SAT solver jointly determines the shared orders and the execution time of each physical gate, enforcing resource and measurement constraints across the circuit. Noisy circuit simulations with decoding then guide the selection of the final circuit. We compare with state-of-the-art approaches, including Auto-Stabilizer-Check (ASC), PropHunt, and AlphaSyndrome. Across 15 quantum low-density parity-check codes from ten code families, our method achieves the lowest logical error rate estimates. Relative to ASC, the strongest baseline in our evaluation, the median reduction is 11.4% and the largest is 38.6%. Our circuits improve circuit-level distance over ASC on ten instances and preserve the code distance in seven. Across five timed codes, our method reduces the mean time to the first feasible circuit by factors of 21.4-136.6 relative to ASC, at equal or lower depth.
one_liner: A structure-guided CP-SAT method shares gate-order choices across related checks to synthesize lower-error syndrome-extraction circuits.
why_it_matters: It improves logical error rates and sharply reduces synthesis time across diverse quantum LDPC codes.

title: Moiré-Enabled Recursive Phase Unwrapping for Differential Atom Interferometry
abstract: Weak equivalence principle tests comparing different elements may be more sensitive to violations than those comparing isotopes. However, differences in effective wave vector complicate common-mode rejection of vibration noise. We propose a Moiré-enabled recursive phase unwrapping (MRPU) method for differential measurements with dual-species atom interferometers. The method exploits the moiré structure of the joint phase likelihood and temporal acceleration correlations to unwrap both phases and determine the relative acceleration. We implemented an $^{85}$Rb $\mathrm{D_1/D_2}$ line dual-scale-factor interferometer with an identical normalized transfer function and a large effective wave-vector difference to emulate different atomic species. Under $40\,\mathrm{rad}$ equivalent vibrational noise, this method achieved phase unwrapping over 5000 consecutive measurements, with a relative-acceleration Allan deviation of $1.47\times10^{-8}g$ at 997 shots. Numerical simulations under random vibrations and slow drifts show a $9.76 - 26.03\,\mathrm{dB}$ increase in the tolerable narrowband vibration amplitude. This method is promising for weak equivalence principle tests based on different atomic species, dark matter and dark energy detection, and high-dynamic-range atomic gravimetry.
one_liner: Moiré-enabled recursive phase unwrapping sustains dual-scale atom-interferometer measurements under strong vibration noise.
why_it_matters: It could improve different-species equivalence-principle tests and high-dynamic-range atomic gravimetry.

title: Precise experimental investigation of the reflection properties caused by s-polarized evanescent waves and the Casimir puzzle
abstract: We report a high-precision experiment on measuring the low-frequency magnetic field reflected from a metallic plate. This experiment is designed to give insight into why theoretical predictions of the fundamental Lifshitz theory using the standard response function to the electromagnetic waves are in contradiction with the data of numerous precision measurements of the Casimir force (the Casimir puzzle). To attain these ends, we measured the magnitude and phase of the lateral component of the magnetic field produced by an oscillating magnetic dipole and reflected from a metallic plate. These quantities are completely determined by the evanescent waves with the transverse electric (s) polarization. The obtained measurement data are compared with theoretical predictions using the standard Drude response function of the metal to the low-frequency electromagnetic waves. It is shown that there are both quantitative and qualitative disagreements with these predictions, so that in the region of low-frequency s-polarized evanescent waves the Drude response function is excluded by the data. Keeping in mind that just the s-polarized evanescent waves are responsible for the Casimir puzzle, our results highlight the causes for its emergence. It is emphasized that, in addition to the Casimir effect, searching for the adequate nonlocal response functions of metals to the evanescent waves is of utmost significance for many areas of physics as near-field optical microscopy, nanophotonics, surface plasmon polaritons, radiative heat transfer, and others.
one_liner: Precision magnetic-reflection measurements disagree with the Drude model for low-frequency s-polarized evanescent waves near metals.
why_it_matters: The result bears directly on the Casimir puzzle and the search for accurate nonlocal electromagnetic response models.

title: Nonmagnetic Impurity Effects on Majorana Braiding Quantum Gates in Vortex Cores
abstract: Using time-dependent many-body simulations, we investigate nonmagnetic impurity effects on vortex-core Majorana braiding. In the two-MZM $\sqrt{Z}$ gate, sufficiently strong attractive impurities suppress the topological gap $Δ_t$, reduce adiabaticity, and degrade the quantization of the geometric-phase difference; the repulsive impurities considered here cause no comparable damage despite stronger zero-energy nonequilibrium local density of states (LDOS) distortions. Slowing the braid or using a $2a_0$ detour restores near-quantization in the cases examined. In the four-MZM configuration, attractive impurities leave the low-energy spectrum nearly unchanged, whereas repulsive impurities mainly suppress the first excited state. Slower braiding substantially improves the $X$ gate success probability. A specific attractive-impurity pair yields near-unit success ($\approx 0.9985$), unlike two weak repulsive impurities. These findings clarify how nonmagnetic impurities affect the low-energy spectrum and adiabatic dynamics of vortex-core Majorana braiding and provide theoretical guidance for designing robust braiding protocols in realistic topological superconducting platforms.
one_liner: Simulations show that impurity type, braid speed, and path design strongly affect vortex-core Majorana gate fidelity.
why_it_matters: The results suggest practical ways to make Majorana braiding gates more robust to material disorder.

title: Material optimization of optical properties of particulate products by transition matrix method and sequential global programming
abstract: Material optimization of nanoparticle assemblies, such as structurally coloured photonic crystals, attracts increasing interest. We combine the transition matrix method (TMM), which avoids spatial discretization of particles and surrounding medium, with sequential global programming (SGP) to optimize optical properties of particulate products by iteratively assigning predefined catalogue materials to individual particles. We derive exact separable models, reproducing the fully coupled objective under single-particle material changes, and computationally accessible first-order correct approximations for general continuously differentiable objectives. These approximations aim to capture the nonlinear, potentially nonconvex dependence on individual material variables beyond their local first-order behaviour. Within SGP, globally minimizing the particle-wise subproblems can yield substantial improvements in few outer iterations, including steps away from unfavourable stationary points, as previously demonstrated for discrete dipole approximation-based SGP. The construction exploits the decomposition of the TMM system matrix into a material-dependent block-diagonal and a material-independent coupling matrix, while the state and adjoint problems remain fully coupled. Applications include extinction, scattering quantities, and colour objectives. In a 35-particle extinction minimization problem, the objective decreases by 31.0% in 13 iterations. A fine-grid evaluation of the fully coupled objective shows that no tested single-particle material change improves the final design. For a 627-particle photonic crystal, chroma increases by 58.4-122.1% for different particle diameters in 17-42 iterations. The optimized designs favour absorbing material in layers away from the incident light, consistent with experimental findings.
one_liner: A transition-matrix and global-programming method optimizes particle materials for extinction and structural color.
why_it_matters: It enables efficient material assignment in large photonic particle assemblies without spatial discretization.

title: A Quantum Genetic Algorithm for Optimization of Benchmark Test Functions using Entangled Qutrits
abstract: Typically, quantum genetic algorithms are based on qubits, a two-level quantum system. This work investigates the optimization of Rastrigin, Rosen-Brock and Table Holder Function in comparison with Classical Genetic Algorithm (CGA), using two quantum approaches: Quantum Genetic Algorithm (QGA), and Higher-Order Quantum Genetic Algorithm (HO-QGA) based on qutrits, a three-level system. HO-QGA uses higher-dimensional quantum representations, such as entangled qutrits, to test its capability of enhanced optimization. We show that the QGA convergence rate is higher than the CGA, and the solution quality is considerably improved. Based on this study, a three-state quantum object novelly provides more capabilities than qubits in terms of computational and information resources.
one_liner: A genetic algorithm using entangled qutrits is tested against qubit and classical methods on benchmark functions.
why_it_matters: The study explores whether higher-dimensional quantum representations can improve heuristic optimization.

title: A New Quantum Algorithm Framework for Integer Order Entropy Estimation
abstract: Entropy estimation for unknown distributions is a basic problem in statistical property estimation. In this paper, we propose a quantum algorithm framework for estimating Rényi entropy with fixed integer order $k\geq 2$. Given purified quantum query-access to a distribution on $n$ symbols, our algorithm estimates its order-$k$ Rényi entropy to within additive error $ε$ using $$\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{n^{u_k}}{ε^{1-u_k}} + \frac{n^{(k-1)/(2k)}}ε\right)$$ queries, where $u_k=\max_{2\leq j\leq k} \frac{(3k-j)2^{j-2}-k}{k(2^j-1)}$. The main ingredient is a recursive construction of collision states in which intermediate states are retained and reused. We bound both the preparation and reflection costs, and choose the number of retained states at each order so that all recursive steps fit within a common query budget. We combine this construction with a sequence of decreasing probability thresholds, estimating the contribution of the labels found along the way separately from the remaining power sum. A batch estimator gives the required bound in the high-precision regime, and an initial search removes the need for prior knowledge of the power sum.
one_liner: A recursive quantum framework estimates fixed integer-order Rényi entropy using retained and reused collision states.
why_it_matters: It advances quantum query efficiency for estimating statistical properties of unknown distributions.

title: Flat bands and bound states in the continuum in non-Hermitian pseudospin lattices
abstract: Flat bands support compact localized states (CLSs), whereas bound states in the continuum (BICs) remain spatially localized despite having energies embedded in the continuum of extended states. Here, we investigate the connection between these phenomena in a class of one-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices whose Bloch Hamiltonians take the pseudospin form H(k)=d(k)S. For integer pseudospin, the Hamiltonian intrinsically supports a zero-energy flat band and its associated compact localized states. When the effective pseudospin field has real transverse components and a purely imaginary longitudinal component, increasing non-Hermiticity compresses the dispersive bands toward the intrinsic zero-energy flat band, enabling their spectral overlap within a finite parameter range. The CLSs thus become embedded in the dispersive continuum and emerge as BICs. Adding a momentum-dependent Hermitian component along the gain-loss direction generally removes this spectral overlap without destroying the CLSs. We further extend this spectral mechanism to integer-pseudospin-n systems. These findings establish a connection between intrinsic flat-band localization and BIC formation through non-Hermitian spectral reconstruction.
one_liner: Non-Hermitian spectral compression embeds compact flat-band states within dispersive continua, producing BICs.
why_it_matters: It links two localization mechanisms and offers a route to engineer bound states through gain-loss control.

title: The influence of quantum scarring on the onset of Bohmian chaos
abstract: In the present work we investigate how the stable and unstable periodic orbits of a perturbed two-dimensional oscillator influence the Bohmian trajectories of the corresponding quantum system. In particular, we find that in our systems all Bohmian trajectories become chaotic in the long run and examine the times needed for them to approach their ergodic pattern. We show that these times are systematically shorter for orbits close to unstable periodic orbits than for orbits close to stable periodic orbits of the same period. We demonstrate that this behaviour is connected to scarring effects associated with both unstable and stable periodic orbits. We also investigate how the Bohmian dynamics changes when a stable periodic orbit undergoes a bifurcation and becomes unstable.
one_liner: Quantum scarring near stable and unstable periodic orbits controls how rapidly Bohmian trajectories become chaotic.
why_it_matters: It clarifies how classical orbit stability leaves measurable signatures in long-term quantum trajectory dynamics.

title: Dephasing-free plasma acceleration with millijoule picosecond lasers
abstract: Laser-plasma accelerators reach gradients a thousand times above radio-frequency cavities, but need joule-class femtosecond lasers firing about once per second, and electrons outrun the wave. A comb of laser lines spaced by the plasma frequency, each in its own mode of a matched channel, drives a wake moving at the speed of light. In particle-in-cell simulations a 175\,mJ, 0.5\,ps drive holds 21\,GV/m over 10\,mm with a 0.15\,rad phase drift; a test electron gains 208\,MeV, 2.6 times more than in one mode. Because the wave builds up resonantly, the required energy falls steeply with density: a 29\,mJ drive sustains 20\,GV/m, and a 10\,mJ drive, within reach of kilohertz industrial lasers, gives a test electron 170\,MeV over 30\,mm. A simulated stage transfers 5\,\% of the laser energy to the wake; the Manley--Rowe limit is about 18\,\% for five lines.
one_liner: Multimode laser combs drive near-light-speed plasma wakes with millijoule, picosecond pulses and minimal dephasing.
why_it_matters: The approach could bring compact plasma accelerators within reach of high-repetition-rate industrial lasers.

title: Rigid triaxial roto-vibrator in a finite system
abstract: We investigate the emergence of rigid triaxiality in a finite system, within the framework of the interacting boson model of nuclei. Appropriate Hamiltonians for a maximally-triaxial rigid shape are constructed. Closed expressions for wave functions, energies and E2 rates for states of the ground band are derived. Classical and quantum analyses reveal that for a fixed Hamiltonian, the system evolves from a $γ$-soft SO(6) structure for small $N$, to a $γ$-rigid structure for large $N$. Attention is paid to symmetry and spectral properties of both rotational and vibrational states.
one_liner: Interacting-boson Hamiltonians reveal a finite-size evolution from gamma-soft to rigid triaxial nuclear structure.
why_it_matters: Closed-form states and transition rates help explain how collective nuclear rigidity emerges with system size.

title: Photonic processors that carry their own unclonable fingerprint
abstract: Physically unclonable functions (PUFs) derive cryptographic keys from uncontrollable fabrication disorder, removing the need to store secrets in vulnerable non-volatile memory. Programmable photonic processors are natural candidates for PUFs, because each of their many tunable interferometers carries its own fabrication imperfections. However, we show that the mesh topology itself funnels light along short paths, so that most of this disorder contributes little to the response. Here we introduce an isotropic ring routing scheme that steers light to the core of a hexagonal mesh and redistributes it uniformly towards the perimeter, suppressing a distance-dependent power decay of 14.7 dB and raising the mean Shannon entropy of the response from 1.95 to 3.48 bits by reprogramming alone. Experiments on two independently fabricated 72-unit silicon processors show that a nominally identical device cannot reproduce the target's responses even after its passive phase profile is fully compensated. Combining isotropic routing with spectral readout yields 1107 bits per challenge, exceeding previous results by two orders of magnitude, with 49.8% inter-challenge and 50.0% inter-chip Hamming distances and a 4.9% intra-chip distance. These results establish general-purpose programmable photonic processors as reconfigurable, high-capacity hardware roots of trust.
one_liner: Isotropic optical routing turns fabrication disorder in programmable photonic meshes into high-capacity PUF responses.
why_it_matters: Programmable photonic chips could serve as reconfigurable hardware roots of trust without stored secret keys.

title: High-Speed Widefield Hyperspectral Imaging
abstract: Fourier-transform hyperspectral imaging is an emerging technology that combines widefield acquisition with flexible spectral resolution. Yet, it typically requires the acquisition of dense sequences of full-field interferograms during optical-path scanning, which ultimately reduces the final throughput. To circumvent this limitation, this manuscript introduces an event-based Fourier-transform hyperspectral microscopy technique that exploits the coupling of a neuromorphic event camera with a common-path birefringent interferometer operated under continuous scanning. Specifically, two complementary acquisition strategies are investigated, one with steady broadband illumination where the event stream corresponds to a derivative-like interferogram, and another with a temporal modulation of a broadband LED, which produces an intensity-like event response. Both approaches are able to retrieve the principal spectral profiles of photographic filters, showing a good qualitative match with both frame-based and spectrometer references. Compared against the typical 15-minute acquisition time for step-scan reference configuration, both methods represent a speedup larger than 3 orders of magnitude, entering real-time acquisition speeds: the derivative-based method acquires the useful interferometric range in approximately 200 ms, corresponding to an effective rate of approximately 5 hyperspectral cubes per second, whereas the modulation-assisted method achieves an experimentally measured spectral resolution of 17.9 nm at an effective acquisition rate of 2.5 datacubes per second. Finally, reflection-mode imaging and motion-compensated reconstruction of moving particles further demonstrate spatially resolved spectral recovery beyond static transmission measurements, establishing the solution as a promising technology for continuous, wide-field hyperspectral imaging.
one_liner: An event camera and scanning interferometer acquire widefield hyperspectral cubes at real-time rates.
why_it_matters: The method cuts acquisition from minutes to milliseconds and supports moving-sample spectral imaging.

title: Genuinely Out-of-Equilibrium Bose-Einstein Condensation
abstract: Bose-Einstein (BE) condensation typically occurs in the ground state. Prominent exceptions include excitons, whose ground state is the vacuum; consequently, they undergo BE condensation only in out-of-equilibrium regimes to counteract rapid decay. Here, we develop a driven-dissipative framework to address this challenge, demonstrating that BE condensates emerge under sufficiently strong excitation in one and two dimensions. In three dimensions, by incorporating effective loss rates and a specified injection energy, we find a percent-level condensate fraction, consistent in order of magnitude with the exciton experiment of Morita et al. (Nat. Commun. 13, 5388 (2022)).
one_liner: A driven-dissipative theory predicts nonequilibrium Bose-Einstein condensates under strong excitation across dimensions.
why_it_matters: It provides a framework for condensates, such as excitons, whose particles decay before reaching equilibrium.

title: Local-channel inequivalence within analytic symmetry-broken phases
abstract: Gibbs states at different temperatures can be inequivalent under two-way quasi-local channels even within a single phase with spontaneously broken continuous symmetry and analytic free energy. We prove this for the symmetry-invariant Gibbs states of a canonical ideal Bose gas at fixed density and a classical vortex-free Villain model on hypercubic lattices in $d\ge3$ dimensions. At lower temperatures, two distant observers can estimate the shared direction of order more accurately. The maximum mutual information they can obtain by separate measurements grows logarithmically with the radius of their regions. The leading term is the same throughout each ordered phase, while the constant term $\mathcal{C}(T)=\tfrac12\ln[Υ(T)/T]+c_{\mathrm{geom}}$ is strictly larger at lower temperatures. Here $Υ(T)$ is the phase stiffness and $c_{\mathrm{geom}}$ depends only on the region geometry. A quasi-local channel cannot increase this constant, so it is invariant under two-way conversion. Cooling would increase it and is therefore impossible between any two distinct temperatures in the ordered phase. On finite lattices, cooling with vanishing error requires a circuit whose causal radius grows at least linearly with the lattice side length. We also obtain the invariant for quantum and multicomponent Villain models and conjecture a stiffness formula for more general patterns of continuous symmetry breaking.
one_liner: Distinct temperatures within ordered phases remain inequivalent under reversible quasi-local quantum channels.
why_it_matters: A stiffness-dependent information invariant constrains cooling and the circuit depth required for thermal conversion.

title: Ellis: Extremely Fast Quantum Circuit Simulation under Qubit Loss and Leakage
abstract: Qubit loss and leakage are persistent errors: while a qubit remains lost or leaked, every operation acting on it is dropped. Consequently, the Clifford circuit executed differs from shot to shot. This variation breaks Pauli-frame simulation, which constructs each shot by XORing sampled Pauli flips onto a single \emph{common reference} measurement record. By rethinking the roles of tableau simulation and Pauli-frame simulation, we show that many key fault-tolerant primitives nevertheless retain a common reference under loss. These include CSS code memory, lattice surgery, and transversal CNOT. Such circuits can therefore be simulated exactly under Pauli noise and loss by a Pauli frame with per-shot masks for the dropped operations. We define \emph{frame-CSS} circuits as those that are CSS up to local single-qubit basis changes, given a loss model that specifies where qubits can be lost and reloaded. We prove that every frame-CSS circuit has a common reference, and we give a practically near-linear-time procedure that certifies whether a circuit is frame-CSS. We implement the certifier and a high-performance simulator in the open-source package \href{https://github.com/isaachyw/ELLIS}{\textsc{Ellis}} (Efficient Loss and Leakage Invariant-reference Simulation). On the gross code under qubit loss and Pauli errors, \ellis{} samples 952{,}000 shots per second on a single CPU core, at least $1000\times$ faster than Clifft~\cite{chase2026} and PPVM~\cite{luo2026ppvm}.
one_liner: Ellis exactly simulates frame-CSS fault-tolerant circuits under Pauli noise, qubit loss, and leakage using masked Pauli frames.
why_it_matters: It enables near-linear certification and CPU sampling up to 952,000 shots per second, over 1,000 times faster than cited alternatives.

title: The role of complementarity and quantum correlation in the uncertainty relations and the optimum states
abstract: Uncertainty relations are used in quantum mechanics to illustrate the complementarity of two observables, assuming there is a lower bound for the product of their dispersions that depends on the first-order quantum correlation and the commutation relation of those observables in an optimum state. In this work, we demonstrate that the complex parameter of the optimum state equation has real and imaginary parts that depend on the first-order quantum correlation and the commutation relation between the observables in the optimum state, respectively. We apply our results to a two-level system, finding that the first-order quantum correlation and the commutation relation of two spin-1/2 projections in the optimum state complement each other and, finally, when the term correlation is used, a lower bound for the uncertainty principle does not depend on any parameter of the optimum state, in contrast to the usual form of the Heisenberg principle.
one_liner: The optimum-state parameter in uncertainty relations is linked to quantum correlation and observable commutation through its real and imaginary parts.
